paragraphs.text: I. The Literal Meaning of Genesis, in Twelve Books.
Book One.

All divine Scripture is twofold. The Lord points to this when he says that a scribe instructed in the kingdom of God is like a householder who brings out of his treasure things new and old, and these two are also called testaments. In all the holy books, however, we must look at what eternal truths are conveyed there, what deeds are narrated, what future events are foretold, and what actions are commanded or urged. So when the narrative concerns things that were done, the question is whether everything is to be taken only in a figurative sense, or whether it must also be affirmed and defended as a faithful account of what actually happened. For no Christian will dare to say that these things are not to be taken figuratively, when he heeds the apostle saying, "Now all these things happened to them as figures," and recalls what is written in Genesis, "and the two shall be in one flesh," which the apostle commends as a great mystery in Christ and in the church.

If, then, that Scripture is to be examined in both ways, how is it meant, apart from its allegorical significance, that "In the beginning God made heaven and earth"? Does it mean in the beginning of time, or that these were made first of all, or in the Beginning who is the Word of God, the only-begotten Son? And how can it be shown that God makes changeable and temporal things without any change in himself? And what is meant by the words "heaven and earth"? Did spiritual and bodily creation together receive the name "heaven and earth", or bodily creation only, so that in this book the writer should be understood to have said nothing about the spiritual creation, and to have said "heaven and earth" meaning the whole of bodily creation, higher and lower? Or is the unformed matter of both called heaven and earth? That is, on the one hand spiritual life as it can exist in itself, not turned toward the Creator (for by such turning it is formed and perfected, and if it does not turn, it is formless); and on the other, bodily matter, if it can be conceived by taking away every bodily quality that appears in formed matter, once there are forms of bodies that can be perceived by sight or by any other bodily sense?

Or is "heaven" to be understood as spiritual creation, perfect and always blessed from the very outset in which it was made, and "earth" as bodily matter that is still imperfect? For it says, "The earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the abyss," and these words seem to signify the formlessness of bodily substance. Or do these later words also signify the formlessness of both? The formlessness of bodily substance by the words "the earth was invisible and unformed", and that of spiritual substance by the words "and darkness was over the abyss", so that by a metaphor we understand the dark abyss as the nature of life, which is formless unless it turns to the Creator. Only in this way can it be formed, so as no longer to be an abyss, and enlightened, so as no longer to be dark. And how is it said that "darkness was over the abyss"? Is it because there was no light? For if there had been light, it would certainly have been over it, and as it were poured out over it. This is what happens in spiritual creation when it turns to the unchangeable and incorporeal light, which is God.

And how did God say, "Let there be light"? Was it in time, or in the eternity of the Word? And if in time, then certainly in a changeable way. How, then, can God be understood to have said this except through a creature? For he himself is unchangeable. And if God said "Let there be light" through a creature, how is light the first creature, if there was already a creature through which God could say "Let there be light"? Or is light not the first creature, since it had already been said, "In the beginning God made heaven and earth"? And could a voice have been produced in time and in a changeable way through the heavenly creation, so that "Let there be light" was spoken? If so, the light that was made is this bodily light which we see with bodily eyes. God would have said "Let there be light" through the spiritual creation which he had already made when in the beginning he made heaven and earth; and he would have said it in the way in which "Let there be light" could be spoken by God through the inner and hidden movement of such a creature.

Or did the voice of God saying "Let there be light" sound bodily, just as the voice of God saying "You are my beloved Son" sounded bodily? And did this happen through a bodily creature which God had made when in the beginning he made heaven and earth, before the light was made that came to be through this sounding voice? And if so, in what language did this voice sound when God said "Let there be light", since there was not yet a diversity of languages, which arose later, at the building of the tower after the flood? What was that one and only language in which God said "Let there be light"? And who was there who needed to hear and understand, to whom a voice of this kind might be addressed? Or is this an absurd and carnal way of thinking and conjecturing?

What, then, shall we say? Is it rightly understood that the voice of God is what is understood in the sound of the words "Let there be light", and not the bodily sound itself? And does this belong to the nature of his Word, of whom it is said, "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God"? For when it is said of him, "All things were made through him," it is shown clearly enough that light too was made through him when God said, "Let there be light." If this is so, then God's saying "Let there be light" is eternal, because the Word of God, God with God, the only Son of God, is coeternal with the Father, even though, when God says these things in the eternal Word, what is created is temporal. For although "when" and "at some time" are words of time, yet when something ought to be made is eternal in the Word of God; and it is made at the time when, in that Word, it is fixed that it ought to have been made. In that Word there is no "when" or "at some time", since that Word is wholly eternal.

And what is this light that was made? Is it something spiritual or something bodily? If it is spiritual, it may be the first creature itself, now perfected by this utterance, which was first called "heaven" when it was said, "In the beginning God made heaven and earth." Then the words "God said, Let there be light, and there was light" would be understood to mean that this creature was turned and enlightened as the Creator called it back to himself.

And why is it said, "In the beginning God made heaven and earth," and not, "In the beginning God said, Let there be heaven and earth, and heaven and earth were made," as is narrated of the light: "God said, Let there be light, and there was light"? Was it because what God made first had to be summed up and presented as a whole under the name of heaven and earth, and then it had to be set out part by part how he made it, by saying for each one, "God said", that is, that he made whatever he made through his Word?

Or was it that when the formlessness of matter, whether spiritual or bodily, was first being made, it was not right to say "God said, Let there be"? For imperfection does not imitate the form of the Word, who always cleaves to the Father, and through whom God eternally speaks all things, neither by the sound of a voice nor by a thought that runs through the stretches of time occupied by sounds, but by the light, coeternal with himself, of the Wisdom begotten of him. Imperfection does not imitate him while, unlike that which supremely and primordially is, it tends toward nothingness through a kind of formlessness. But it does imitate the form of the Word, who always and unchangeably cleaves to the Father, when it too, by a turning suited to its own kind toward that which truly and always is, that is, toward the Creator of its substance, takes on form and becomes a perfect creature. So in what Scripture narrates, "God said, Let there be," we should understand the incorporeal speaking of God in the nature of his coeternal Word, calling back to himself the imperfection of creation, so that it may not be formless but may be formed in each of the particular things which Scripture goes on to set out in order. In this turning and forming, the creature imitates in its own measure God the Word, that is, the Son of God, who always cleaves to the Father in full likeness and equal essence, by which he and the Father are one; but it does not imitate this form of the Word if it turns away from the Creator and remains formless and imperfect. For this reason, when it is said, "In the beginning God made heaven and earth," the Son is mentioned not as the Word but only as the Beginning, since what is being conveyed is the outset of creation, still in the formlessness of imperfection. But the Son, who is also the Word, is mentioned in what is written, "God said, Let there be." Thus, through his being the Beginning, Scripture conveys the outset of creation, which exists from him while still imperfect; and through his being the Word, it conveys the perfecting of creation called back to him, so that it might be formed by cleaving to the Creator and by imitating, according to its own kind, the Form that eternally and unchangeably cleaves to the Father, from whom he has it immediately that he is what the Father is.

For the Son, the Word, does not have a formless life. For him, not only is being the same as living, but living is also the same as living wisely and blessedly. A creature, however, even a spiritual and intellectual or rational one, which seems to be nearer to that Word, can have a formless life. For although for such a creature being is the same as living, living is not the same as living wisely and blessedly. When it is turned away from unchangeable Wisdom, it lives foolishly and wretchedly, and that is formlessness. But it is formed when it turns to the unchangeable light of Wisdom, the Word of God; for it turns to him from whom it came into existence, so as to be and live in some fashion, in order that it may live wisely and blessedly. For the beginning of intellectual creation is eternal Wisdom. This Beginning, abiding unchangeably in itself, would never cease to speak, by the hidden inspiration of its call, to the creature of which it is the beginning, so that the creature might turn to that from which it came, since otherwise it could not be formed and perfected. And so, when he was asked who he was, he answered, "The Beginning, because I also speak to you."

What the Son speaks, the Father speaks, because when the Father speaks, the Word who is the Son is spoken. This happens in an eternal manner, if "manner" is the right word: God speaks the coeternal Word. For in God there is supreme goodness, holy and just, and a love for his works that comes not from need but from generosity. That is why, before it was written, "God said, Let there be light," Scripture first said, "And the Spirit of God was borne over the water." By the name "water" Scripture may have meant the whole of bodily matter, so as to suggest the source from which all things were made and formed that we can now distinguish in their kinds; it would call this "water" because we see that everything on earth is formed and grows in various species out of a moist nature. Or it may have meant a kind of spiritual life, fluid as it were, before the form given by its turning. Either way, the Spirit of God was indeed borne over it, because whatever it was that he had begun, to be formed and perfected, lay subject to the good will of the Creator. Thus, when God said in his Word, "Let there be light," what was made would abide in his good will, that is, in his good pleasure, according to the measure of its kind. And so it is right that it pleased God, as Scripture says, "And there was light. And God saw the light, that it was good." At the very outset of creation as it was begun, which was mentioned under the name of heaven and earth because of what was to be perfected from it, the Trinity of the Creator is conveyed. For when Scripture says, "In the beginning God made heaven and earth," we understand the Father in the name "God" and the Son in the name "Beginning"; he is the beginning not of the Father, but of the spiritual creation, which was created first and foremost through him, and so also of all creation. And when Scripture says, "And the Spirit of God was borne over the water," we recognize that the mention of the Trinity is complete. In the same way, in the turning and perfecting of creation, by which the forms of things are set in order, the same Trinity is conveyed: the Word of God and the Begetter of the Word when it is said, "God said," and the holy goodness when it is said, "God saw that it was good"; for in that goodness God is pleased with whatever pleases him as perfected according to the small measure of its nature.

But why is creation mentioned first, imperfect as it was, and the Spirit of God afterward? Scripture first says, "The earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the abyss," and then adds, "and the Spirit of God was borne over the water." Is it because a needy and indigent love loves in such a way that it is subjected to the things it loves? And so, when the Spirit of God was mentioned, in whom his holy benevolence and love are understood, he was said to be borne over, so that no one would think that God loved the works he was to make out of the necessity of need rather than out of the abundance of his generosity. The apostle was mindful of this when, about to speak of charity, he said he would show a way that surpasses all others, and in another place speaks of "the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge." Since, then, the Spirit of God had to be presented in such a way that he was said to be borne over, it was more fitting that something already begun should be presented first, over which he could be said to be borne, not in place, but by a power that surpasses and excels all things.

In the same way, when things had been perfected and formed from that beginning, "God saw that it was good"; for what had been made pleased him in that same kindness in which it pleased him that it should be made. For there are two reasons why God loves his creation: that it may exist and that it may endure. So that there might be something to endure, "the Spirit of God was borne over the water"; and so that it might endure, "God saw that it was good." And what was said of the light is said of all things. For some things endure in the fullest holiness under God, having risen above all the turning of time, while others endure according to the measures of their own time, as the beauty of the ages is woven together through the passing away and succession of things.

When God said, "Let there be light, and there was light," did he say it on some particular day, or before any day? For if he said it through the Word coeternal with himself, he certainly said it outside of time; but if he said it in time, he said it not through the coeternal Word but through some temporal creature. In that case light will not be the first creature, since there was already a creature through which "Let there be light" could be said in time. And what is meant by "In the beginning God made heaven and earth" is understood to have been made before any day. By the name "heaven" we would then understand the spiritual creation, already made and formed, as the heaven, so to speak, of this heaven which is the highest of bodily things. For on the second day the firmament was made, which he again called "heaven". By the name "earth", invisible and unformed, together with the dark abyss, the imperfection of bodily substance is signified, from which those temporal things were to be made, the first of which was to be light.

But how "Let there be light" could be said in time through a creature that God made before time is hard to discover. For we do not understand it to have been said by the sound of a voice, since anything of that sort is bodily. Or did he make out of that imperfect bodily substance some bodily voice, through which "Let there be light" might sound? Then some body capable of sound was created and formed before the light. But if so, there was already time, through which the voice could run and the stretches of successive sounds could pass by. And if there was already time before light was made, a time in which a voice could arise and sound out "Let there be light", to which day did that time belong? For one day, and that the first, begins to be counted from when light was made. Or does the whole stretch of time belong to that same day, both the time in which the sounding body was made, through which "Let there be light" would sound, and the time in which the light itself was made? But every voice of this kind is uttered by a speaker for the bodily sense of a hearer, for that sense was made so as to perceive when the air is struck. Did that thing, whatever it was, which was invisible and unformed, have hearing of this kind, so that God might sound out to it and say, "Let there be light"? Let such an absurdity be banished from the mind of anyone who reflects on these things.

Was it, then, a spiritual movement, yet still a temporal one, by which we understand "Let there be light" to have been said, expressed by the eternal God through the coeternal Word in the spiritual creation which he had already made when it was said, "In the beginning God made heaven and earth", that is, in that heaven of heaven? Or is this utterance to be understood as being not only without any sound, but also without any temporal movement of the spiritual creature, being in some way fixed and impressed in its mind and reason by the Word coeternal with the Father? Then, in accordance with it, that lower, dark imperfection of bodily nature would be moved and turned toward form, and light would be made. But it is a great and very difficult thing to grasp how this is said. God does not command in time, and the creature that by contemplating truth transcends all times does not hear in time; rather, that creature transmits intellectually to the things beneath it the principles impressed upon it by the unchangeable Wisdom of God, as though they were intelligible utterances, and so temporal movements arise in temporal things, whether in forming them or in governing them. But if the light which was first commanded to be, and was made, is to be understood as also holding the first place in creation, then it is intellectual life itself, which would float about formlessly unless it turned to the Creator to be enlightened. And when it was turned and enlightened, what was said in the Word of God was done: "Let there be light."

Yet just as it was said without time, since time has no place in the Word coeternal with the Father, someone may perhaps ask whether it was also done without time. But how can this be understood, when, after light had been made and divided from the darkness and the names of day and night had been given, Scripture says, "And there was evening, and there was morning, one day"? From this it seems that this work of God was done over the span of a day, and when that span was over, evening came, which is the beginning of night. Likewise, when the span of night was over, the whole day was complete, so that morning came for a second day, on which God would go on to do another work.

Indeed, this very point is quite remarkable. God, by the eternal reason of his Word and with no interval of syllables, said, “Let there be light.” Why, then, did the light take so long to be made that the space of a day passed and evening came? Or perhaps the light was in fact made quickly, but the length of a day could have been spent while it was being separated from the darkness and each, once separated, was marked with its own name? . It would be strange if even this took God as long as it takes us to say it. For the separation of light and darkness certainly followed within the very work, when the light was made, since there could be no light unless it were separated from darkness.

As for God's calling the light day and the darkness night, how long could that have taken, even if he had done it syllable by syllable with the sound of a voice? No longer than it takes us to say, “Let the light be called day and the darkness be called night.” Unless perhaps someone is so foolish as to think that, because God is great above all things, even a very few syllables uttered by God's mouth could have been stretched out over the whole length of a day. Moreover, God called the light day and the darkness night by his Word, which is coeternal with him, that is, by the inner and eternal reasons of unchangeable Wisdom, not by the bodily sound of a voice. For the question arises again: if he named them with words such as we use, in what language did he name them? And what need was there for passing sounds where there was no one with bodily hearing? No answer can be found.

Or should we say that, although this work of God was finished quickly, the light remained, with no night following it, until the length of a day had run its course, and that the night that followed the light lasted until the length of night-time had passed, and morning came on the next day after the one and first day was over? But if I say this, I fear I shall be laughed at both by those who know with complete certainty, and by those who can very easily observe, that at the time when it is night with us, the presence of light is shining on those parts of the world through which the sun returns from its setting to its rising. Thus, through all twenty-four hours, around the circuit of the whole sphere it is always day somewhere and night somewhere else. Are we then to place God in some particular region where evening would come for him when the light departed from that region to another? For in the book called Ecclesiastes it is written: “The sun rises and the sun sets, and it is led back to its place,” that is, to the place from which it rose. For the text goes on to say: “Rising, it goes there toward the south and circles round to the north.” So when the southern region has the sun, it is day for us, and when the sun circles round and reaches the region of the north, it is night for us. Yet in the other region, where the sun is present, it is still day. Unless perhaps we are to incline our hearts to the fictions of the poets and believe that the sun plunges into the sea and, having bathed there, rises in the morning from the other side. Even if that were so, the deep itself would be lit up by the sun's presence, and it would be day there; for the sun could light up the waters as well, since they could not put it out. But it is monstrous to suspect such a thing. And what is more, the sun did not yet exist.

Therefore, if it was a spiritual light that was made on the first day, did it set, so that night might follow it? But if it was a bodily light, what light is this that we cannot see after sunset, since there was as yet neither moon nor any stars? Or suppose it is always in the same part of the sky as the sun, so that it is not the sun's light but a kind of companion joined to it so closely that it cannot be distinguished or told apart from it. Then we come back to the same difficulty in solving this question. For this light too, like the sun, as its companion, circles round and returns from setting to rising, and it is in the other part of the world at the time when this part, where we are, grows dark into night. From this we would be forced, God forbid, to believe that God was in one particular region, a region that this light abandoned, so that evening could come for him. Or perhaps it brought light to the region where he was going to make man, and so, when the light had departed from that region, evening is said to have come, even though that light which had departed from there was in another region, to rise in the morning when it had completed its circuit?

Why, then, was the sun made to rule the day and to shine upon the earth, if that light, which had also been called day, had been enough to make day? Or did that earlier light illuminate the higher regions far from the earth, so that it could not be perceived on earth, and was it therefore necessary for the sun to be made, through which day might appear in the lower parts of the world? It may also be said that the brightness of day was increased by the addition of the sun, so that we may believe the day was less bright with that light than it is now. I also know that someone has said that the nature of light was first introduced into the Creator's work when it was said, “Let there be light. And there was light,” but that afterward, in what is said about the lights, the text records what was made from that light, following the order of days in which the Creator saw fit to make all things. But where that nature of light went when evening came, so that night might run its course in turn, he did not say, nor do I think it can easily be found. For we must not believe that it was extinguished so that the darkness of night might follow, and then rekindled so that morning might come, before this was done by the sun's office, which the same Scripture testifies began from the fourth day.

Before that happened, it is difficult both to discover and to explain by what circuit three days and nights could have followed one another while the nature of the light first made remained, if we are to understand that a bodily light was made at that time. Unless perhaps someone were to say that God called “darkness” the mass of earth and water before the two were separated from each other, which is recorded as done on the third day. He would call it so either because of its denser bulk, which light could not penetrate, or because of the very deep shadow cast by so great a mass, which must have occurred if the body was on one side and the light on the other. For wherever the mass of any body prevents light from reaching a place, there is shadow in that place, since a place lacking the light that would illuminate it if an opposing body did not block it is all that we mean by shadow. If this shadow is so large, owing to the size of the body, that it covers as great an area of the earth as the day covers on the other side, it is called night. For not all darkness is night. In large caves too, into whose hidden depths light is not allowed to break because of the mass in the way, there is certainly darkness, because there is no light there and that whole space is a place lacking light. Yet such darkness has not received the name of night; that name belongs to the darkness that follows on in that part of the earth from which the day withdraws. In the same way, not every light is called day, for there is the light of the moon, of the stars, of lamps, of lightning flashes and of anything else that shines in this way. Only that light is called day which follows night when night has gone before and withdraws.

But if that primal light had been poured all around the mass of the earth and covered it on every side, whether it stood still or moved round, there was no side on which it would let night follow it, because it never withdrew from anywhere to make room for night. Or was it made on one side only, so that as it circled round it would allow night likewise to circle round on the other side? For since water still covered the whole earth, nothing prevented that watery, spherical mass from having day on one side through the presence of the light, and night on the other through its absence. Night would then follow, from evening on, in the part from which the light was moving on to another.

Where, then, were the waters gathered, if they had previously covered the whole earth? Into what region were those waters gathered that were drawn off so that land might be given? For if there was some bare portion of earth where they could be gathered, dry land was already appearing and the deep did not cover everything. But if they had covered everything, what place was there where they could be collected so that the dry land might appear? Were they gathered upward, as happens when threshed grain is piled up on the threshing floor for winnowing, and, heaped into a mound, it leaves bare the place it had covered when spread out? Who would say this, when one sees the expanses of the sea spread out evenly everywhere? For even when the surging water rises up into what look like mountains, it is levelled again once the storms die down. And if some shores are left bare over a wider area, it cannot be said that there are no other stretches of land to which the water that leaves one place may come, and from which it may come back again to the place it had left. But when the whole earth without exception was covered by the watery element, where could it withdraw so as to lay some parts bare? Or perhaps a thinner water covered the earth like a mist, and was thickened by being gathered together, so as to lay bare many of those parts where dry land could appear? Yet the earth too, sinking far and wide, could have provided other hollow regions into which the waters might flow together and rush down and be received, and the dry land might appear in those parts from which the moisture withdrew.
But matter is not altogether formless where even a misty appearance has shown itself.

And so it may still be asked when God created these visible forms and qualities of waters and lands, for this is not found in any of the six days. Suppose, then, that he did this before any day, as it is written before these first days are recounted: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” We would then understand by the word “earth” the form of earth, already shaped, with waters poured over it, these being already declared in their own visible form. In what Scripture goes on to say, “But the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the deep, and the Spirit of God was borne over the water,” we would then suppose no formlessness of matter, but earth and water without light, which had not yet been made, yet already created with their own very familiar qualities. The earth would be understood to be called invisible because, covered by waters, it could not be seen, even if there had been someone able to see; and unformed because it was not yet separated from the sea, bounded by shores, and adorned with its offspring and living creatures. If this is so, why were these forms, which are undoubtedly bodily, made before any day? Why is it not written, “God said: Let there be earth. And earth was made,” and likewise, “God said: Let there be water. And water was made”? Or both together, if they are held together by one law, so to speak, of the lowest place: “God said: Let there be earth. And so it was done”?
Why, when this had been done, was it not said, “God saw that it was good”?

For it is clear that everything changeable is formed out of some formlessness. At the same time, the Catholic faith prescribes and the most certain reason teaches that there could be no matter of any natures except from God, the originator and creator of all things, not only of things formed but also of things capable of being formed. Of this matter a certain scripture says to him: “You who made the world out of formless matter.” These considerations have led to the view that this matter was referred to in words suited, with spiritual prudence, even to slower readers or hearers: the words spoken before the days are numbered, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” and the rest, up to the point where it says, “And God said,” so that the ordered sequence of formed things might follow from there.

This is not because formless matter is prior in time to formed things, since both were created together: that from which something was made and that which was made. Voice is the matter of words, and words signify voice that has been formed; yet the speaker does not first emit a formless voice that he can afterward gather up and form into words. In the same way God the Creator did not first make formless matter at an earlier time and afterward, as if on second thought, form it in order into the various natures; for he created matter already formed. Rather, it is because that from which something is made, though not prior in time, is nevertheless prior in a certain order of origin to what is made from it. So Scripture could divide in the times of speaking what God did not divide in the times of making. For if one asks whether we make voice from words or words from voice, hardly anyone is found so slow-witted as not to answer that words are made from voice. So although the speaker makes both at once, what he makes from what is plain enough to natural attention. Therefore, since God made both at once, the matter that he formed and the things into which he formed it, and since Scripture had to mention both but could not mention both at once, who would doubt that it ought first to mention that from which something was made, and then what was made from it? For even when we say “matter and form,” we understand both to exist together, yet we cannot pronounce both together. Just as in the brief moment of uttering these two words we say one before the other, so in the length of a narrative one had to be told before the other, although, as has been said, God made both at once. Thus what is prior only in origin in the making is also prior in time in the telling. For if two things, neither of which is in any way prior, cannot be named at the same time, how much less can they be narrated at the same time! There is, then, no doubt that this formless matter, however close to nothing, is such that it was made only by God and was created together with the things that were formed from it.

But suppose it is credibly said that this matter is signified by the words, “But the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the deep, and the Spirit of God was borne over the water.” Then, apart from what is said there about the Spirit of God, we would understand the other terms as names of visible things, but used to suggest that formlessness in a way slower minds could grasp. For these two elements, earth and water, are more easily handled than the others by the hands of those who work to make something, and so that formlessness was more fittingly suggested by these names. If this is a plausible account, there was no formed mass that light could illuminate on one side and so cause darkness on the other, from which night could follow as day departed.

If we wish to understand day and night as the sending out and drawing back of that light, we see no reason why this should have happened, for there were not yet any living creatures for whom this alternation would be provided for their benefit, as we see it provided for them by the sun's circuit after they came into being. Nor does any example occur to us by which we could prove this sending out and drawing back of light so as to produce the alternation of day and night. The casting of rays from our eyes is indeed the casting of a certain light. It can be drawn in when we look at the air that is closest to our eyes, and sent out when we look in the same line at things placed far away. When it is drawn in, it certainly does not stop seeing distant things altogether, but it sees them more dimly than when the gaze is sent out toward them. Yet the light that is in the sense of the one who sees is shown to be so slight that, unless it is helped by light from outside, we can see nothing. And since it cannot be distinguished from that outside light, it is difficult, as I said, to find an example that could demonstrate the sending out of light to make day and its drawing back to make night.

But if it was a spiritual light that was made when God said, “Let there be light,” we must not understand it to be that true Light, coeternal with the Father, through which all things were made and which enlightens every man. It is rather the light of which it could be said, “Wisdom was created before all things.” For when that eternal and unchangeable Wisdom, which was not made but begotten, passes into spiritual and rational creatures, as into holy souls, so that once enlightened they can shine, there arises in them a certain disposition of bright reason. This can be taken as the light that was made when God said, “Let there be light,” if spiritual creation already existed, signified by the name “heaven” in the words, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” This is not the bodily heaven, but the incorporeal heaven of the bodily heaven, that is, set above every body, not by degrees of place but by the loftiness of its nature. As for how what was to be illuminated and the illumination itself could be made at the same time, and yet had to be narrated at different times, we explained a little earlier when discussing matter.

But how are we to understand the night that followed this light, so that evening came? And from what sort of darkness could such a light be divided, when Scripture says, “And God divided between the light and the darkness”? Were there already sinners and fools falling away from the light of truth, so that God divided between them and those who remained in that same light, as between light and darkness, and, by calling the light day and the darkness night, showed that he is not the author of sins but the one who orders them by distributing what is deserved? Or is this day the name for the whole of time, embracing all the ages within this word, and was it therefore called not the first day but one day? For “there was evening,” it says, “and there was morning, one day,” so that by the evening's coming the sin of the rational creature, and by the morning's coming its renewal, would seem to be signified.

But this is a discussion of prophetic allegory, which we have not undertaken in this treatise. For we have set out to speak of the Scriptures now according to the proper sense of the things that happened, not according to the enigmas of things to come. How, then, with regard to the account of the natures that were made and established, do we find evening and morning in spiritual light? Perhaps the dividing of light from darkness is the distinction of what is already formed from what is formless, while the naming of day and night suggests an ordering. This would signify that God leaves nothing disordered; that even formlessness itself, through which things change by passing in a certain way from form to form, is not without arrangement; and that the failings and advances of creation, by which temporal things follow one another, are not without their contribution to the beauty of the universe. For night is darkness put in order.

Now the reason it was said, as soon as the light was made, “God saw the light, that it was good,” though he could have said it after everything belonging to that same day, is this. He could have set out, “God said: Let there be light. And there was light. And God divided between the light and the darkness, and God called the light day and the darkness he called night,” and then said, “And God saw that it was good,” and next added, “And there was evening and there was morning,” as he does in the other works to which he gives names. He did not do so here because that formlessness was distinguished from the formed thing in such a way that it was not the end point but still remained to be formed through the other creatures, which were now bodily. So if, after these had been distinguished by that division and by names, it had then been said, “God saw that it was good,” we would take it to mean things made to which nothing more was to be added in their own kind. But since he had completed only the light in that way, the text says, “God saw the light, that it was good,” and he separated it from the darkness by division and by names. He did not then say, “God saw that it was good,” for that formlessness had been distinguished so that other things might still be formed from it. Our own very familiar night, by contrast, is produced over the lands by the sun's circuit. When it is divided from the day by the arrangement of the lights, it is said after that very division of day and night, “God saw that it was good.” For this night was not some formless substance from which other things were still to be formed, but a space full of air, lacking the light of day. Nothing more had to be added to this night in its own kind to make it more beautiful or more distinct. Throughout those three days before the lights were made, evening may perhaps reasonably be understood as the end of a completed work, and morning as a sign of the work to come.

But above all let us remember what we have already said a great deal about: God does not work through temporal movements, as it were, of his mind or body, as a man or an angel works. He works through the eternal, unchangeable and stable reasons of his Word, coeternal with him, and by a kind of brooding warmth, if I may put it so, of his Holy Spirit, likewise coeternal. For what is said in Greek and Latin about the Spirit of God, that he was borne over the waters, is, according to the sense of the Syriac language, which is close to Hebrew, said to mean not “was borne over” but rather “was brooding over.” This explanation is reported to have been given by a learned Syrian Christian. It is not meant in the way that swellings or wounds in the body are bathed with cold water or water warmed to the right temperature, but in the way that eggs are brooded by birds. There the warmth of the mother's body somehow assists even in forming the chicks, through a certain affection of love proper to its kind. So let us not think in a carnal way of God's utterances, through each of the days of these divine works, as though they were temporal. For the very Wisdom of God, having taken on our weakness, did not come to gather the children of Jerusalem under his wings as a hen gathers her chicks so that we might always remain little ones, but so that, while being infants in malice, we might cease to be children in mind.

And in matters that are obscure and very far removed from our eyes, if we read anything about them, even in the divine Scriptures, that can give rise to different opinions without harm to the faith in which we have been instructed, let us not rush headlong into firmly asserting any one of them. Otherwise, if the truth is examined more carefully and rightly overturns that opinion, we will fall with it. We would then be fighting not for the teaching of the divine Scriptures but for our own, wanting our opinion to be the Scriptures' opinion, when we ought rather to want the Scriptures' opinion to be ours.

Let us suppose, then, that in the words of Scripture, “And God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light,” one person has understood that corporeal light was made, and another that spiritual light was made. Our faith does not doubt that there is spiritual light in spiritual creation. But the view that there is a corporeal light, a heavenly one, or even one above or before the heaven, which night [?] could follow, is not contrary to the faith so long as it is not refuted by most certain truth. If that should happen, then it was not divine Scripture that contained this; it was human ignorance that had supposed it. But if sure reasoning should show this to be true, it will still be uncertain whether the writer of the holy books meant it to be understood in those words, or something else no less true. And if the rest of the passage's context proves that he did not mean this, the other meaning, which he himself intended, will not be false on that account; it will be both true and more profitable to know. If, however, the context of Scripture does not rule out that the writer meant this, it will still remain to ask whether he might not also have meant something else. And if we find that he could also have meant something else, it will be uncertain which of the two he intended; and it is not unfitting to believe that he meant both, if the rest of the surrounding context supports both interpretations.

For it often happens that even a non-Christian knows something about the earth, the heaven and the other elements of this world, about the motion and revolution, or even the size and distances, of the stars, about the predictable eclipses of the sun and moon, the cycles of years and seasons, the natures of animals, shrubs, stones and other such things, and knows it so well that he holds it by most certain reasoning or experience. Now it is a thing far too shameful and harmful, and one to be guarded against above all, that he should hear a Christian talking such nonsense about these matters, supposedly in accordance with Christian writings, that he can scarcely keep from laughing when he sees him, as the saying goes, wrong by the whole sky. And what is vexing is not so much that a man in error is laughed at, but that those outside believe our authors to have held such views, and our authors are criticized and rejected as unlearned, to the great ruin of the very people whose salvation we are anxious about. For when they catch some member of the Christian body in error on a subject they know very well, and hear him asserting his foolish opinion on the basis of our books, how are they going to believe those books about the resurrection of the dead, the hope of eternal life and the kingdom of heaven, when they think those books were written falsely about matters they have already been able to experience for themselves or grasp by indisputable calculations? It cannot be adequately expressed how much trouble and grief rash and presumptuous people bring upon prudent brethren. Whenever they begin to be rebuked and refuted for their perverse and false opinion by those who are not bound by the authority of our books, then, to defend what they have said with the most frivolous rashness and the most obvious falsehood, they try to bring forward those same holy books to prove it, or they even recite from memory many words from them that they think support their case, understanding neither what they are saying nor the things about which they make assertions.

It is with this in view, so that this might be considered and observed, that I have unfolded the book of Genesis in many ways, as far as I could, and have set out interpretations of words placed obscurely for our exercise. I have not rashly affirmed any one thing to the prejudice of another explanation that might perhaps be better, so that each person may choose, according to his own small capacity, what he is able to grasp; and where he cannot understand Scripture, let him give the honor to God and keep the fear for himself. But since the words of Scripture that we have treated can be explained in so many ways, let those at last restrain themselves who, puffed up with secular learning, attack as something unskilled and unpolished these words that were set down so as to nourish all devout hearts. They crawl on the ground without wings and mock the nests of birds that are going to fly. More dangerous, however, is the error of certain weak brethren. When they hear these impious men discoursing subtly and at length about the measurements of the heavenly bodies, or about any questions concerning the elements of this world, they lose heart; sighing, they rank these men above themselves and think them great, and they return with distaste to the books of most wholesome piety. What they ought to drink in with delight they can scarcely bear to touch, recoiling from the roughness of the grain and gaping after the flowers of thorns. For they have no leisure to see how sweet the Lord is, nor do they hunger on the sabbath; and so they are too lazy, though they have received permission from the Lord, to pluck the ears of grain and keep rubbing them in their hands and cleaning them until they come to food.

Someone will say: “With all this threshing in your discussion, what grain have you husked? What have you winnowed? Why does nearly everything still lie hidden in questions? Affirm one of the many things you have argued can be understood.” To him I reply that I have come with pleasure to this very food. I have learned that a person should not be at a loss in answering, in accordance with the faith, those who try to slander the books of our salvation. Whatever they can demonstrate about the nature of things by true proofs, we should show is not contrary to our Scriptures. But whatever they bring forward from any of their own volumes that is contrary to these Scriptures of ours, that is, to the Catholic faith, we should either show by some means to be utterly false, or else believe it to be so without any doubt. And so let us hold fast to our Mediator, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, so that we are neither led astray by the glib talk of false philosophy nor frightened by the superstition of false religion. And when we read the divine books, amid so great a multitude of true meanings that are drawn out of a few words and fortified by the soundness of the Catholic faith, let us choose above all the one that it is clear the author we are reading intended. If this is hidden, then let us choose one that the context of Scripture does not rule out and that agrees with sound faith. And if even the context of Scripture cannot be examined and discussed, then at least let us choose only what sound faith prescribes. For it is one thing not to discern what the writer chiefly meant, and another to stray from the rule of piety. If both are avoided, the reader's harvest is complete; but if both cannot be avoided, then even if the writer's intention remains uncertain, it is not without profit to have drawn out a meaning consistent with sound faith.
BOOK TWO

“And God said, ‘Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide between water and water.’ And so it was done. And God made the firmament, and God divided between the water that was below the firmament and the water that was above the firmament. And God called the firmament heaven. And God saw that it was good. And there was evening, and there was morning, the second day.” There is no need here to discuss again in the same way the word of God, by which God said, “Let there be a firmament,” and so on, or his good pleasure, by which he saw that it was good, or the evening and the morning. From here on, whenever these things are repeated, we advise that they be considered for the present in accordance with the earlier inquiry. But it may rightly be asked whether what is now made is the heaven that lies beyond all the spaces of the air and all its height, where the lights and stars are also set on the fourth day, or whether the air itself is called the firmament.

For many assert that waters of this nature cannot be above the starry heaven, because their weight is so ordered that they either flow over the earth or are carried as vapor in the air nearest the earth. Nor should anyone refute these people by saying that, in view of the omnipotence of God, to whom all things are possible, we ought to believe that waters as heavy as those we know and perceive are poured over the heavenly body in which the stars are. For our task now is to inquire, according to his Scriptures, how God established the natures of things, not what he might wish to work in them or out of them as a miracle of his power. If God wished oil ever to remain beneath water, it would happen; yet that would not make the nature of oil unknown to us, for it was made such that, seeking its own place, it breaks through the water even when poured underneath and settles itself on top. So we are now asking whether the Creator of things, who disposed all things in measure and number and weight, assigned to the weight of the waters not just one proper place around the earth, but also one above the heaven, which has been spread around and made solid beyond the boundary of the air.

Those who deny that this should be believed argue from the weights of the elements. They deny that the heaven is in any way made solid above like a kind of floor, so that it could support the weight of waters, since such solidity can belong only to earth, and whatever is of that kind is not heaven but earth. For the elements, they say, are distinguished not only by their places but also by their qualities, so that in accordance with their proper qualities they have also been allotted proper places. Water, namely, lies above earth; and even when it stands or flows beneath the earth, as in hidden caves and caverns, it is held up not by the part of the earth that is above it but by the part that is below it. For if any part of the earth should fall from above, it does not stay on top of the water but breaks through it, sinks, and makes its way to the earth; and when it gets there it comes to rest as in its own place, so that the water is above and the earth below. From this it is recognized that even when it was above the waters it was not being carried by the waters themselves but was held by the structure of the earth, as is the case with the vaults of caves.

Here I must give warning against the error I warned against in the first book. Because it is written in the Psalms, “He founded the earth upon the water,” someone of ours may perhaps think that he ought to rely on this testimony of Scripture against these men who discourse subtly on the weights of the elements. But they are not bound by the authority of our writings and do not know in what sense this was said, and so they will more readily laugh at the holy books than give up what they have grasped by sure reasoning or proved by the most evident experiments. That passage in the Psalms can rightly be taken figuratively. Since the spiritual and the carnal are often signified in the Church by the names heaven and earth, the psalm showed that the heavens pertain to the serene understanding of truth when it said, “who made the heavens in understanding”; and that the earth pertains to the simple faith of little ones, a faith not uncertain and deceptive because of fabulous opinions, but most firm through prophetic and evangelical preaching, and made solid through baptism; and therefore it added, “He founded the earth upon the water.” Or, if anyone insists on a literal understanding, it can quite fittingly be taken of the high places of land, whether continents or islands, which rise above the waters, or of the very roofs of caves, which are made firm above the waters with a hanging solidity. Hence no one, even reading literally, can understand the words “He founded the earth upon the water” in such a way as to think that by the natural order the weight of water is placed beneath, as it were, to support the weight of earth.

That air is above water, even though because of its greater extent it also covers the dry land, is understood from the fact that no vessel pressed down mouth first can be filled with water; this shows clearly enough that the nature of air seeks the higher place. The vessel seems empty, but it is proved to be full of air when it is pushed into water mouth downward. Since the air finds no place to escape through the upper part, and its nature does not allow it to go downward by breaking through the water beneath, it pushes the water back by its fullness and does not let it enter the vessel. But when the vessel is placed with its mouth not downward but tilted to the side, the water enters below as the air goes out above. Likewise, if the mouth of an upright vessel is open to the sky, when you pour water in, the air escapes upward through the other parts where you are not pouring, and room is made for the water to enter downward. But if the vessel is pushed down with greater force, so that the water suddenly flows in from the side or from above and covers the mouth of the vessel all around, the air, striving upward, bursts through the water to make room for it below; and this very bursting is the gurgling of vessels, as the air escapes in parts, since it cannot all get out so quickly because of the narrowness of the mouth. So if air is forced to go up above water, it scatters the water even as it flows together: the water, driven by the air's rush, leaps up and bubbles, and lets the air out in popping bubbles as it hastens to its own region and gives the water access to fall to the bottom. But if air is forced to go out of a vessel beneath the water, so that you want the vessel, pressed down mouth first, to be filled as the air gives way, the vessel is more easily covered by waves on every side than a tiny drop finds room to enter through its mouth from below.

Who, moreover, does not perceive that fire, leaping upward, wants to rise even beyond the nature of air itself? For if someone holds a burning torch upside down, the plume of flame nonetheless strains upward. But because fire is soon extinguished by the overpowering density of the air around and above it, and, overcome by its abundance, is soon changed and turned into the air's quality, it cannot last long enough to leap through the whole height of the air. And so, it is said, beyond the air the heaven is pure fire, and they conjecture that the stars and lights were also made from it, the nature of that fiery light being gathered into globes and arranged into the forms we see in the sky. And accordingly, just as both air and water give way to the weight of earth so that it may reach the earth, so air itself gives way to the weight of water so that it may reach either earth or water. From this they want it understood that air too, if anyone could release a particle of it in those lofty spaces of the heaven, would necessarily fall by its own weight until it reached the spaces of air below. Hence they conclude that there can be much less room for waters above that fiery heaven, since air, which is much lighter than water, cannot remain there.

Yielding to such arguments of theirs, a certain writer made a praiseworthy attempt to demonstrate that there are waters above the heavens, so as to uphold the trustworthiness of Scripture from those very natures that are visible and plain to see. First, which was very easy, he showed that this air of ours is also called heaven, not only in common speech, in which we speak of a clear or cloudy sky, but also in the usage of our own Scriptures, when they speak of the birds of heaven, since it is evident that birds fly in this air; and the Lord, speaking of clouds, said, “You know how to judge the face of the sky.” And we often see clouds massing even in the air next to the earth, when they lie along the slopes of ridges in such a way that the mountain peaks often rise above them. Having proved, then, that this air too is called heaven, he wanted it to be thought that it was called the firmament for no other reason than that the space it occupies divides certain watery vapors from the waters that flow in more bodily form on the earth. For clouds, as those who have walked among them in the mountains have found by experience, take on their appearance through the gathering and massing together of very tiny drops; and if these become denser, so that many very small drops join into one large one, the air does not allow it to be held within itself but gives way to its weight, letting it fall to the bottom, and this is rain. So from the air that lies between the moist vapors, out of which the clouds gather above, and the seas spread beneath, he wanted to show that there is a heaven between water and water. This diligence and reflection I judge most worthy of praise. For what he said is not contrary to the faith, and it can be believed on the basis of evidence readily at hand.

And yet it might seem that the proper weights of the elements do not prevent waters from being even above that lofty heaven, in the form of those minute particles by which they were able to be above this space of air. Although this air is heavier than the highest heaven and lies lower, beneath it, it is undoubtedly lighter than water, and yet no weight prevents those vapors from being above it. In the same way, then, a lighter exhalation of moisture in tinier drops could be spread above that heaven too, without being forced by its weight to fall. For these men themselves argue by very subtle reasoning that there is no body, however tiny, at which division comes to an end, but that all things can be divided infinitely, because every part of a body is a body, and every body must have a half of its quantity. And so, if water can be reduced, as we see, to such minute drops that it is carried as vapor above this air, which by nature is lighter than water, why could it not also remain above that lighter heaven in tinier drops and lighter vapors?

Some of our own writers also try to refute those who deny, on account of the weights of the elements, that there can be waters above the starry heaven, by appealing to the qualities and courses of the stars themselves. For these same men assert that the star they call Saturn is very cold, and that it takes thirty years to travel round the circle of the zodiac because it moves in a higher and therefore wider orbit. For the sun completes the same circle in a year, and the moon in a month, more quickly by as much, they say, as it is lower, so that the length of time corresponds to the length of the course. They are asked, therefore, why that star is cold, when it ought to be all the hotter the higher the heaven by which it is swept along. For without doubt, when a round mass is moved with a circular motion, its inner parts move more slowly and its outer parts more swiftly, so that the larger distances and the shorter ones complete the same revolutions together; and what moves more swiftly certainly becomes hotter. Accordingly that star ought to have been hot rather than cold. For although by its own motion, since the distance is great, it travels its whole orbit in thirty years, yet it is whirled more swiftly in the opposite direction by the motion of the heaven, which it must undergo every day (for in this way, they say, each revolution of the heaven makes up a single day), and so it ought to have taken on greater heat from the more rapidly moving heaven. Evidently, then, what makes it cold is the nearness of the waters placed above the heaven, which those who argue the things I have briefly described about the motion of the heaven and the stars refuse to believe in. With these conjectures some of our writers argue against those who will not believe that there are waters above the heaven and yet hold that the star circling next to the highest heaven is cold, so that they are compelled by this to accept that the waters there hang not in the thinness of vapor but in the solidity of ice. But in whatever way and of whatever kind the waters there may be, let us not doubt in the least that they are there; for the authority of this Scripture is greater than all the capacity of human intelligence.

But some have noticed, and I do not think it should be passed over, that it is not without reason that, when God had said, “Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let there be a division between water and water,” it did not seem enough to add, “And so it was done,” without also adding, “And God made the firmament; and God divided between the water that was above the firmament and the water that was under the firmament.” They take this to mean that the person of the Father is declared in what is written, “And God said, ‘Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let there be a division between water and water.’ And so it was done.” And they think that the words “And God made the firmament, and God divided,” and so on, were then added so that the Son might be understood to have made what the Father said should be made.

But earlier we read, "And so it was done." By whom do we understand it to have been done? If by the Son, what need was there to go on to say, "And God made," and the rest? But if we take the words "And so it was done" to mean that it was done by the Father, then it is no longer the Father who speaks and the Son who makes. The Father could then make something without the Son, and afterward the Son would make, not this, but something else like it. That is contrary to the Catholic faith. But suppose the thing of which it is said, "And so it was done," is the very same thing that is made when it is said in the same way, "And God made." What then prevents us from understanding that the one who said it, so that it might be made, is the same one who makes what he said? Or do they want us to set aside the words "And so it was done," and to find the persons of the Father and the Son only in the words "And God said, Let there be" and the later words "And God made"?

But it may still be asked whether we ought to take the words "And God said, Let there be" as though the Father had given an order to the Son. In that case, why did Scripture not take care to show the person of the Holy Spirit as well? Or is the Trinity to be understood this way: "And God said, Let there be"; "And God made"; "And God saw that it was good"? But it does not fit the unity of the Trinity that the Son should be understood to have made things as if under orders, while the Holy Spirit, with no one ordering him, freely saw that what had been made was good. Besides, with what words would the Father order the Son to make something, when the Son is himself the Father's primordial Word, through whom all things were made? Or is it that in the very words "Let there be a firmament" this utterance is itself the Word of the Father, the only-begotten Son? In him are all the things that are created, even before they are created, and whatever is in him is life, because whatever was made through him is life in him, and indeed creative life, while the creature is beneath him. The things made through him, then, are in him in one way, because he rules and contains them; and in another way the things that he himself is are in him. For he himself is life, and that life is in him in such a way that it is he himself, since he himself is the life that is the light of men. Nothing could be created, whether before time began (though even that is not coeternal with the Creator), or at the beginning of time, or at some point in time, unless the reason for creating it (if "reason" is the right word) lived as coeternal life in the Word of God, who is coeternal with the Father. Therefore, before Scripture introduces each creature in the order in which it says each was established, it looks back to the Word of God and first sets down: "And God said, Let this be made." For it finds no cause for creating anything other than this: that it finds in the Word of God that the thing ought to be created.

So God did not say "Let this or that creature be made" as many times as "And God said" is repeated in this book. He begot one Word, and in that Word he said all things before the individual things were made. But the language of Scripture comes down to the capacity of little ones. As it introduces the kinds of creatures one by one, it looks back in each case to the eternal reason for each kind in the Word of God. God did not repeat those things, though Scripture repeats "And God said." Suppose Scripture had chosen to say first, "The firmament was made in the midst of the waters, so that there might be a division between water and water," and someone had asked it how this was made. It would rightly answer, "God said, Let it be made"; that is, it was in the eternal Word of God that it should be made. So Scripture begins its account of each thing made with the answer it would have to give, in rendering the reason, even after narrating the making, to anyone who asked how the thing was made.

So when we hear, "And God said, Let it be made," we understand that it was in the Word of God that the thing should be made. When we hear, "And so it was done," we understand that the creature that was made did not go beyond the limits of its kind laid down in the Word of God. And when we hear, "And God saw that it was good," we understand that in the kindness of his Spirit the thing did not please him as though he had first come to know it after it was made. Rather, in the same goodness in which it pleased him that it should be made, it pleased him that what was made should endure.

And so there is still reason to ask why, after saying "And so it was done," where the work is already shown to be complete, Scripture added "And God made." By the very words "And God said, Let this be made. And so it was done," we already understand that God said this in his Word and that it was done through his Word, and there the person not only of the Father but also of the Son can already be seen. If "And God made" is repeated in order to show the person of the Son, did God then not gather the water through the Son on the third day so that the dry land might appear? For there it does not say "And God made the water gather" or "God gathered the water." Yet even there, after saying "And so it was done," it then repeated, "And the water that is under heaven was gathered." And was light not made through the Son either, where there is no repetition at all? There too it could have said, "And God said, Let there be light. And so it was done. And God made light. And he saw that it was good." Or at least, as with the gathering of the waters, it could have left out "And God made" and still repeated: "And God said, Let there be light. And so it was done. And light was made. And God saw the light, that it was good." But it repeats nothing at all. After setting down "And God said, Let there be light," it adds only "And light was made," and then goes on, without any repetition, to tell how the light pleased God, how it was divided from the darkness, and how each was called by its name.

What, then, does that repetition mean in the other cases? Perhaps it shows this. On the first day, when light was made, the name "light" signifies the creation of the spiritual and intellectual creature, a nature in which all the holy angels and powers are understood to be included. Scripture did not repeat the making after saying "light was made" because the rational creature did not first know its own formation and then become formed. It knew its formation in the very act of being formed, that is, in being enlightened by the Truth, and it was formed by turning toward that Truth. The other things, which are below it, are created in such a way that they come into being first in the knowledge of the rational creature and then in their own kind. So the creation of light exists first in the Word of God, according to the reason by which it was established, that is, in the Wisdom coeternal with the Father; and then in the actual creation of light, according to the nature that was established. There it is not made but begotten; here it is made, because it is formed out of formlessness. That is why "God said, Let there be light. And light was made": so that what was there in the Word might be here in the work. The creation of heaven, however, was first in the Word of God according to the begotten Wisdom. Then it was made in the spiritual creature, that is, in the knowledge of the angels, according to the wisdom created in them. Then heaven was made, so that the created heaven itself now existed in its own kind. So too with the separation or form of the waters and the lands, with the natures of trees and plants, with the lights of heaven, and with the living creatures that sprang from the waters and the earth.

For the angels do not see these things that the senses perceive by bodily sense alone, as cattle do. If they use some such sense at all, they recognize through it things they already know better inwardly, in the very Word of God. By that Word they are enlightened so as to live wisely, since the light that was made first is in them, if we understand that a spiritual light was made on that day. So the reason by which a creature is established exists in the Word of God before the creature that is established. In the same way, knowledge of that reason comes about first in the intellectual creature that has not been darkened by sin, and only then does the creature itself come to be. For the angels did not make progress toward wisdom as we do, by perceiving the invisible things of God, understood through the things that have been made. From the moment they were created, they have enjoyed the very eternity of the Word in holy and devout contemplation. From there they look upon these things according to what they see within, and they approve what is rightly done and condemn sins.

Nor is it surprising that God showed his holy angels, formed in the first creation of light, what he was going to create next. They could not have known God's mind except as far as he had shown it to them. "For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor? Or who has given to him first, so that he should be repaid? For from him and through him and in him are all things." So the angels learned from him. Knowledge of the creature to be made next came about in them, and then the creature was made in its own kind.

So once light has been made, and in it we understand the rational creature formed by the eternal Light, we should read the account of the other creatures in this way. When we hear "And God said, Let it be made," we should understand that Scripture is turning back to the eternity of the Word of God. When we hear "And so it was done," we should understand that the intellectual creature came to know the reason for establishing the creature, a reason that is in the Word of God. In this way the creature was in a sense made first in that nature, which by a prior movement knew beforehand, in the Word of God itself, that it was to be made. Last, when we hear it repeated that God made it, we should understand that the creature itself is now made in its own kind. And when we hear "And God saw that it was good," we should understand that what was made pleased the kindness of God. What it had pleased him to make, when the Spirit of God was borne over the water, should therefore endure according to the measure of its kind.

People also often ask what form and shape of heaven we should believe in according to our Scriptures. Many argue at length about matters that our authors, with greater wisdom, left out, because these matters would not help learners toward the happy life. Worse still, they use up a great deal of time that is precious and ought to be spent on things that bring salvation. What does it matter to me whether heaven encloses the earth on every side like a sphere, with the earth balanced in the middle of the universe, or covers it from above on one side only, like a disk? But the trustworthiness of the Scriptures is at stake. As I have said more than once, someone who does not understand the divine words may find something of this kind in our books, or hear it from them, that seems to contradict reasonings he has grasped for himself. Then he will refuse to believe them at all when they give other useful advice, or narrate, or foretell. For this reason I must say briefly that our authors knew the truth about the shape of heaven, but the Spirit of God, who spoke through them, did not wish to teach people these things, since they would do nothing for anyone's salvation.

"But," someone says, "how is the verse in our Scriptures, 'who stretches out heaven like a skin,' not contrary to those who say that heaven has the shape of a sphere?" Let it be contrary, certainly, if what they say is false. What divine authority says is true, rather than what human weakness guesses. But perhaps they can prove their view with evidence so strong that it cannot be doubted. In that case we must show that what our books say about the skin is not contrary to their true reasonings. Otherwise it will also be contrary to our own Scriptures in another place, where heaven is said to be hung up like a vault. For what could be more different, more opposed, than the flat stretching of a skin and the curved dome of a vault? We must understand these two passages so that they are found to agree and not to conflict with each other, as indeed we must. In the same way, neither of them must conflict with the arguments that teach that heaven is curved on every side in the shape of a sphere, if sure reasoning should show those arguments to be true, provided it is actually proven.

Our comparison of heaven to a vault, even taken literally, is no obstacle to those who say it is a sphere. It is reasonable to believe that Scripture meant to speak of the shape of heaven only with respect to the part that is above us. If, then, heaven is not a sphere, it is a vault on one side, the side on which it covers the earth. But if it is a sphere, it is a vault on every side. The saying about the skin, however, presents a harder problem. It may be contrary, not to the sphere, which is perhaps a human invention, but to our own vault. What allegorical sense I have found here is set out in the thirteenth book of my Confessions. Whether heaven stretched out like a skin should be understood as I explained it there or in some other way, I say this for the sake of those tiresome people who demand too much literal interpretation, and I think it is plain to everyone's senses. Both images, the skin and the vault, can perhaps be understood figuratively, but we must consider how both can be understood literally. If a vault can rightly be called not only curved but also flat, then surely a skin too can be stretched not only flat but also into a rounded hollow. After all, both a wineskin and a bladder are made of skin.

Some brothers also raise the question of the movement of heaven: does it stand still or does it move? "If it moves," they say, "how is it a firmament? But if it stands still, how do the stars, which are believed to be fixed in it, travel around from east to west, while the northern stars trace shorter circles near the pole? Heaven seems to rotate like a sphere, if there is another pole hidden from us at the opposite end, or like a disk, if there is no other pole." I answer them that these questions call for much subtle and laborious reasoning if we are really to discover which way it is. I no longer have time to take up and work through such reasoning, and neither should they, since we want them to be instructed for their own salvation and for the needs of the holy Church. Let them at least know this. The name "firmament" does not force us to think that heaven stands still. We may understand that it is called a firmament not because it stands still but because of its firmness, or because it is the boundary between the upper and the lower waters that cannot be crossed. And if the truth should convince us that heaven does stand still, the circling of the stars does not prevent us from understanding this. Indeed, the very people who have studied these questions with the greatest curiosity and the most leisure have found that, even if heaven did not move and only the stars moved, everything that has been observed and understood about the revolutions of the stars could still have happened.

"And God said, Let the water that is under heaven be gathered into one gathering, and let the dry land appear. And so it was done.
