And the water that is under heaven was gathered into its gathering, and the dry land appeared. And God called the dry land earth, and the gathering of the water he called sea. And God saw that it was good." We have already discussed this work of God at sufficient length in our first book, because we needed to look into another question. Here, then, we offer some brief advice. Some readers may not feel any need to ask when the form of the waters and the lands was created. They should take it that nothing was done on this day except the separation of these two lower elements. Others may be troubled by two questions. Why were light and heaven made within the days, but water and earth outside the days, or before all the days? And why were light and heaven made at God's word, when God said "Let it be made," while water and earth were separated when God spoke but not made when God spoke? Such readers have an explanation available that does no harm to the faith. Before the days were counted, Scripture said, "The earth was invisible and unformed," when it was explaining what kind of earth God had made, having said just before, "In the beginning God made heaven and earth." By these words it meant only to point to the formlessness of bodily matter, and it chose to name it in familiar rather than obscure terms. But a slow mind must not be led astray here. Because Scripture separates matter and form in words, such a mind may try to separate them in time as well, as though matter came first and form was added to it later, after an interval of time. In fact God created both together and established matter already formed. As I said, Scripture first announced the formlessness of that matter by the familiar word "earth" or "water." Earth and water exist with their own qualities, as we see them, yet because they are easily corrupted they are closer to that formlessness than the heavenly bodies are. In counting the days, Scripture counts things already formed out of what was formless, and it had already told how heaven was made out of this bodily matter, heaven whose form is very different from earthly things. So it did not wish to place what remained to be formed from that matter, in the lowest part of the universe, among created things with the words "Let it be made." The remaining formless matter was not going to receive a form like the form heaven had received, but a lower and weaker one, nearest to formlessness. Instead, with the words "Let the waters be gathered" and "Let the dry land appear," these two received their own forms, forms very familiar to us and within our handling: water that moves and earth that does not move. That is why of the one it is said, "Let it be gathered," and of the other, "Let it appear." For water slips and flows, and earth stands firm and fixed.

"And God said, Let the earth bring forth grass for fodder, bearing seed according to its kind and according to its likeness, and the fruit-bearing tree producing fruit whose seed is in it, according to its likeness, upon the earth. And so it was done. And the earth brought forth grass for fodder, having seed according to its kind and according to its likeness, and the fruit-bearing tree producing fruit whose seed is in it, according to its kind, upon the earth. And God saw that it was good. And evening came, and morning came, the third day." Here we should notice how carefully the one who ordered all things kept to his plan. Plants and trees are a kind of creature distinct from the form of earth and water, so they cannot be counted among the elements. For this reason it was said of them separately that they should come forth from the earth. The usual formulas were also given to them separately: "And so it was done" was said, then what was made was repeated, and it was also stated separately that God saw that it was good. Yet because plants and trees are fixed by their roots, continuous with the earth and joined to it, he wished them also to belong to the same day.

"And God said, Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven, so that they may shine upon the earth, to begin the day and the night and to divide between day and night; and let them be for signs and for seasons and for days and for years; and let them be for splendor in the firmament of heaven, so that they may shine upon the earth. And so it was done. And God made two great lights, the greater light to begin the day and the lesser light to begin the night, and the stars; and God set them in the firmament of heaven, so that they may shine upon the earth, and begin the day and the night, and divide between light and darkness. And God saw that it was good. And evening came, and morning came, the fourth day." On this fourth day we must ask what this order means. Why were water and earth made or separated, and why did the earth sprout, before the stars were made in heaven? We cannot say that the better things were chosen to mark out the series of days so that the end and the middle would stand out most splendidly, since the fourth day is the middle of the seven. For this objection at once presents itself: no creature was made on the seventh day. Or does the light of the first day correspond instead to the rest of the seventh, so that the order of things is woven together with matching ends, while the lights of heaven stand out in the middle? But if the first day matches the seventh, then the second ought to match the sixth. Yet what does the firmament of heaven have in common with man, made in the image of God? Is it that heaven fills the whole upper part of the world, and man was given the power to rule over the whole lower part? But then what are we to do with the cattle and wild beasts that the earth brought forth according to their kinds on that same sixth day? How can they be compared with heaven?

Or should we rather say this? The forming of spiritual creation is understood to have been made first, under the name of light. It followed that bodily creation should also be made, that is, this visible world, and it was made in two days because of its two greatest parts, of which the whole consists: heaven and earth. This follows the reasoning by which the whole of creation, spiritual and bodily, is often called "heaven and earth." On that view, this sphere of more turbulent air is counted with the earthly part, since it takes on body from moist exhalations, while any calm air, where windy and stormy motions cannot arise, belongs to the heavenly part. Once this whole mass of bodily matter had been built, a mass that is entirely in the one place where the world has been set, it followed that it should be filled with parts within the whole that would move from place to place with fitting motions. Plants and trees are not of this kind. They are fixed to the earth by their roots, and although they have the motion of their own growth, they do not move from their own places by their own effort; they are nourished and grow where they are fixed. They therefore belong more to the earth than to the kinds of things that move in the waters and on the land. Since two days were assigned to establishing the visible world, that is, heaven and earth, it remains that the three remaining days should be assigned to the mobile and visible parts created within it. And since heaven was made first, it must also be the first to be furnished with such parts of its own. So on the fourth day the stars are made, so that by their shining over the earth the lower dwelling place too might be lit up, and its inhabitants might not be brought into a dark dwelling. Further, the weak bodies of the lower inhabitants are restored by rest following their exertions. So it came about that, as the sun goes round, they should have the alternation of day and night for the alternation of sleeping and waking. Yet the night was not left without its beauty: by the light of the moon and the stars it would comfort human beings, who often must work at night as well, and it would be tempered enough to suit certain animals that cannot bear the light of the sun.

Then there is the saying: "And let them be for signs and for seasons and for days and for years." Who does not see how obscurely it is stated that time began on the fourth day, as if the three preceding days could have passed without time? Who can grasp with the mind how those three days passed before time began, when time is said to begin on the fourth day? Or whether those days passed at all? Perhaps "day" was the name given with reference to the form of the thing made, and "night" with reference to its privation. Then the matter from which everything else was to be formed would have been called "night" while it was not yet shaped by form. The formlessness of matter can be understood in this way even in things already formed, from their very mutability, for it cannot be distinguished as more remote in place or earlier in time. Or rather, within the thing made and formed, that same mutability, that is, its possibility of failing, if I may put it so, may have been called "night," because created things have the capacity to change even if they do not change. And "evening" and "morning" may refer not to the passing and coming of time, but to a kind of boundary by which we understand how far the proper measure of one nature extends, and where the beginning of another nature follows. Or is there some other meaning of these words that should be searched out more carefully?

Who could easily break into so deep a secret and say what signs are meant when Scripture says of the stars, "And let them be for signs"? It certainly does not mean the signs which it is vanity to watch for, but useful signs, necessary for the needs of this life: those that sailors watch in steering their ships, or that everyone watches to foresee the weather through summer and winter and the mild seasons of autumn and spring. And surely by "seasons" it means those brought about by the stars: not stretches of duration, but the changing conditions of this sky of ours. For if any motion, bodily or spiritual, came before the creation of these lights, so that something passed from future expectation through the present into the past, it could not have been without time. And who could maintain that there was no time except from the moment the stars were created? But the fixed hours, days and years that we commonly know would not come about except by the motions of the stars. So we may understand seasons, days and years in this way. Seasons are certain divisions that we reckon by clocks, or that are very well marked in the sky: the sun rises from the east to its noonday height and then sinks again toward the west, so that one can next observe the moon or some star rising in the east right after sunset; when that star in turn reaches the height of the sky at its meridian, it marks midnight, and it will set when the sun returns and morning comes. Days are the whole circuits of the sun from east to west. Years are either the familiar windings of the sun, counted not from its return to the east, which it makes daily, but from its return to the same position among the stars, which it does only after three hundred and sixty-five days and six hours, that is, a quarter of a whole day (this portion, taken four times, requires one day to be inserted, which the Romans call the bissextile day, so that the same cycle may come round again); or else greater and more hidden years, for when the courses of other stars are completed, greater years are said to be formed. If we understand seasons, days and years in this way, no one doubts that they are produced by the stars and the lights. But the text is so worded that it is uncertain whether the words "let them be for signs and for seasons and for days and for years" refer to all the stars, or whether signs and seasons refer to the others, and days and years only to the sun.

Many people also ask, at great length, what state the moon was in when it was made. If only they spoke as inquirers, and not instead as people trying to teach! Some say it was made full, because it was not fitting for God to make anything imperfect among the stars on the day on which it is written that the stars were made. Their opponents say: "Then it should have been called the first moon, not the fourteenth. For who starts counting like that?" I stand between the two, so that I assert neither. But I say plainly that whether God made the moon new or full, he made it perfect. For God is the author and founder of natures themselves. Whatever a thing brings forth and unfolds by natural progress over fitting periods of time, it held hidden within itself beforehand, if not in the form or bulk of its body, then in the power and principle of its nature. Unless, perhaps, a tree is to be called imperfect in winter, when it is empty of fruit and stripped of leaves, or its nature was imperfect at its very beginnings, when it had not yet borne any fruit. That could not rightly be said of the tree, nor even of its seed, in which everything that comes forth in some way over the course of time lies hidden in invisible ways. And yet, if God were said to have made something imperfect which he himself then brought to perfection, what fault could be found with that view? It would rightly be objectionable if what he had begun were said to have been perfected by someone else.

These people raise no complaint about the earth which God made when in the beginning he made heaven and earth, though it was invisible and unformed, and only on the third day was made visible and put in order. Why, then, do they create for themselves such dark questions about the moon? Or if they understand what was said of the earth as referring not to an interval of time, since God created matter together with the things made from it, but to the arrangement of the narrative, why do they not see in the moon, as can be seen even with the eyes, that it has a whole body, perfect in its complete roundness, even when it shines with a horned light, whether it is beginning to shine on the earth or ceasing to? If, then, the light in it grows, becomes full, or wanes, it is not the luminary itself that varies but what is lit up in it. If, on the other hand, it always shines on one side of its sphere, but appears to grow while it turns that side toward the earth until it has turned it wholly (which happens from the first day to the fourteenth), then it is always full, though it does not always appear so to the inhabitants of the earth. The same reasoning holds if it is lit by the sun's rays. In that case too, when it is nearest the sun it can appear only with bright horns, because the rest of it, which is lit all round, does not face the earth so as to be seen, except when it is opposite the sun, so that the whole of its lit part appears to the earth.

There are some, however, who say that their reason for thinking God originally made the moon on its fourteenth day is not that it must be believed to have been made full, but that the words of God in Scripture run like this: the moon was made "for the beginning of the night." And it is at the beginning of night that it is seen when it is full; at other times, before it is full, it begins to be seen even by day, and as it wanes it appears further and further into the night. But whoever understands "the beginning of the night" to mean nothing but rule over it (and the Greek word archē points to this more clearly, as does the plainer wording of the Psalms: "the sun to rule the day, the moon and the stars to rule the night") is not forced to count from the fourteenth day and to believe that the moon, when first made, was not new.

It is also often asked whether these visible lights of heaven, that is, the sun, the moon and the stars, shine equally, and appear to our eyes with greater or lesser brightness only because they stand at different distances from the earth. Those who say this have no doubt that the moon shines less than the sun, by which, they also claim, it is lit. But they dare to say that many stars are equal to the sun or even greater, but look small because they are farther away. For us, perhaps, it may be enough to know that, however the matter stands, the stars were founded by God the craftsman. Yet we hold to what was said on apostolic authority: "There is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory." But they can still reply, without contradicting the apostle: "They differ in glory, but only to the eyes of those on earth." Or, since the apostle said this to illustrate those who will rise again, who will certainly not be one thing to the eye and another in themselves: "The stars do indeed differ in glory in themselves, but some are nonetheless even greater than the sun." Then let them consider how they can give the sun such great dominion that, as they claim, it holds back certain stars with its rays and drives them backward from their own course, and these the chief ones too, to which these people pay more devotion than to the rest. For it is not likely that greater or even equal stars could be overpowered by the force of its rays. Or if they claim that the higher stars of the constellations, or those of the north, are greater, and these suffer nothing of the kind from the sun, why do they venerate more highly the stars that travel through the signs [?], and why do they declare them to be the lords of the signs? For even if someone argues that those retrograde motions of the stars, or perhaps their slowings, are caused not by the sun but by other, more hidden causes, it is still clear from their own books that in their ravings, by which, having strayed from the truth, they imagine the power of fate, they give the sun the chief power.

But let those who are strangers to the Father who is in heaven say what they like about the heavens. For us it is neither profitable nor fitting to inquire more minutely into the distances and sizes of the stars, and to spend on such an inquiry time needed for weightier and better things. We do better to believe that those lights are greater than the rest which holy Scripture commends in these words: "And God made two great lights." Yet they are not equal. For having set them above the rest, it goes on to say that they differ [?] from each other: "the greater light for the beginning of the day, and the lesser light for the beginning of the night." Surely they will grant this much to our eyes: it is plain that these two shine on the earth more than the others, that the day is not bright except by the light of the sun, and that the night, with all its visible stars, is not as bright when the moon is absent as it is lit up when the moon is present.

As for fate, let us utterly reject from the soundness of our faith all their subtleties of whatever kind, and the so-called experiments with astrological proofs, which they call apotelesmata. For by such arguments they try to take away from us even any reason for praying, and with impious perversity, in the case of evil deeds that are most rightly condemned, they press us to accuse God, the author of the stars, rather than man, the author of the crimes. But that our souls are not by nature subject to bodies, not even heavenly ones, let them hear even from their own philosophers. And that those higher bodies are not more powerful over earthly bodies in the ways they claim, let them at last learn from this at least: many bodies of different kinds, whether animals or plants and shrubs, are sown at one and the same moment, and countless numbers are born at one and the same moment, not only in different places but in the very same places; yet there is such variety in their development, in what they do and what they undergo, that these people would truly, as the saying goes, lose their stars if they considered it.

And what could be more foolish and dull than for them, when refuted by these facts, to say that the fatal power of the stars applies only to human beings, as subject to it? Even here they are refuted by twins. Twins often live different lives, meet with different good or bad fortune, and die different deaths, yet they generally receive the same constellations. For even if there was some interval when they were brought forth from the womb, in some cases the interval is so small that these people cannot take account of it in their calculations. As Jacob was being born, his hand was found holding the foot of his brother who came before him, so that they were born as if a single infant of double length were being born. Their constellations, as they call them, certainly could not have been different in any way. What then could be more absurd than for an astrologer, looking at those constellations, with the same horoscope and the same moon, to say that one of them was loved by his mother and the other not? If he said otherwise, he would certainly be saying what is false; if he said this, he would be saying what is true, but not in accordance with the silly little ditties of his books. If they will not believe this story because it comes from our Scriptures, can they also abolish the nature of things? Since they claim they are never mistaken if they find the hour of conception, let them at least not disdain, as human beings, to consider the conception of twins.

We must therefore admit that when these people say true things, they say them by some very hidden prompting which human minds undergo without knowing it. When this is done to deceive people, it is the work of seducing spirits. They are permitted to know certain truths about temporal things, partly by the keenness of their finer senses, since they are strong in finer bodies; partly by their shrewder experience, owing to the great length of their lives; and partly because the holy angels, at the command of almighty God, reveal to them what they themselves learn from him, who apportions to human beings what they deserve with the purity of his most hidden justice. Sometimes, too, these wicked spirits predict, as if by divination, what they themselves intend to do. So a good Christian must beware of astrologers and all impious diviners, especially when they speak the truth, lest they deceive his soul and ensnare it in fellowship with demons by some kind of pact of partnership.

It is also often asked whether these visible lights of heaven are bodies only, or whether they have certain spirits of their own to govern them; and, if they do, whether they are also given life by them, as flesh is animated by the souls of animals, or whether the spirits are simply present without any mingling. Although this is not easily understood, I think that as we proceed in treating the Scriptures we may come upon more suitable places where, according to the rules of holy authority, we will be allowed, if not to prove something certain about this matter, at least to believe something. For now, always keeping to the restraint of a devout seriousness, we ought to believe nothing rashly about an obscure matter. Otherwise, out of love for our own error, we might come to hate what the truth later reveals, even though it can in no way be contrary to the holy books of either the Old Testament or the New. Let us now pass on to the third book of our work.
BOOK THREE

"And God said: Let the waters bring forth creeping things with living souls, and flying things above the earth along the firmament of heaven. And so it was done. And God made great sea monsters, and every living creeping thing which the waters brought forth according to their kind, and every winged flying thing according to its kind. And God saw that they were good. And God blessed them, saying: Increase and multiply and fill the waters in the sea, and let the flying things multiply upon the earth. And there was evening and there was morning, the fifth day." Now in the lower part of the world the things that move by the spirit of life are made, and first those of the waters, since water is the element nearest to the quality of air. For air is so near to this heaven in which the lights are that it too has received the name "heaven," though I do not know whether it can also be called "firmament." Moreover, "heavens" in the plural is said of one and the same thing that is called one heaven. For although in this book "heaven" is used in the singular for that which divides the waters above from those below, in the psalm it says, "And let the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord." And if we rightly understand "the heavens of heavens" as the starry heavens of the airy ones, the higher above the lower, and take them in that sense in the same psalm where it says, "Praise him, you heavens of heavens," it is clear enough that this air is called not only "heaven" but also "heavens," just as we also speak of "lands" and mean nothing other than what is called "land" in the singular, when we say both "the world of lands" and "the world of land."

We read in one of the letters called canonical that these airy heavens once perished in the flood. For that watery element, which had risen so high that it went fifteen cubits above the tops of the highest mountains, could not have reached the stars. But because it had filled all or nearly all the space of this moister air in which birds fly, that letter writes that the heavens which then existed perished. I do not see how this can be understood unless the quality of this denser air was changed into the nature of water. Otherwise these heavens did not perish at that time, but were lifted higher when the water took their place. So, following the authority of that letter, we more readily believe that they perished and that others were put in their place, as is written there, namely by exhalations spreading out, than that they were lifted up in such a way that the nature of the higher heaven gave up its place to them.

It was fitting, therefore, that in the creation of the inhabitants of this lower part of the world, which is often referred to as a whole under the name "earth," animals should first be produced from the waters and afterward from the land. For air is so like water that it is shown to grow thick with water's exhalations, so as to produce the breath of the storm, that is, the wind, to gather clouds, and to be able to bear up the flight of birds. So even if one of the secular poets spoke truly in saying, "Olympus rises above the clouds," and, "The heights keep peace" (for it is reported that on the summit of Olympus the air is so thin that it is neither darkened by clouds nor stirred by wind, nor can it support birds, nor sustain with the breath of a thicker air any people who happen to climb there, as they are used to in this air of ours), still that too is air, from which it spreads down with a quality close to that of the waters. And for that reason it too is believed to have been turned into a watery nature at the time of the flood. For we must not suppose that the water usurped any of the space of the starry heaven, even though it had risen above all the mountains, even the highest.

Yet even among those who have examined these matters most minutely with idle care, the transformation of the elements is no small question. Some say that all things can be changed and turned into all things; others hold that each element has something entirely its own that can in no way be turned into the quality of another element. We will perhaps discuss this more carefully in its proper place, if the Lord wills. For now, as far as the present discussion is concerned, I thought these points worth mentioning so that we may understand that the order of things was kept, by which the creation of the water animals had to be narrated before that of the land animals.

We must by no means suppose that this scripture has left out any element of this world, which we are convinced is made up of the four best-known elements, merely because heaven, water and earth seem to be mentioned here while nothing is said of air. For it is the custom of our scriptures either to call the world by the name of heaven and earth, or sometimes to add the sea as well. Air, then, is understood to belong either to heaven, if there are any utterly calm and peaceful regions in its upper parts, or to earth, because of this turbulent and murky region which grows thick with moist exhalation, although this region too is quite often called by the name of heaven. And for this reason it is not written, “Let the waters bring forth creeping things of living souls, and let the air bring forth flying things that fly above the earth.” Rather, both these kinds of living creatures are said to have been brought forth from the waters. Water may be fluid and flowing in waves, or it may be thinned into vapour and held aloft, so that the first is plainly assigned to the creeping things of living souls and the second to the flying things. Yet both are to be counted as belonging to the moist nature.

That is why there are also some who, by a very subtle analysis, match these five most evident bodily senses to the four usual elements, saying that the eyes belong to fire and the ears to air. The senses of smell and taste they attribute to the moist nature: smell to those moist exhalations that thicken this space in which the birds fly, and taste to the flowing, bodily fluids. For whatever has taste in the mouth is mixed with the mouth's own moisture so that it can be tasted, even if it seemed dry when it was taken in. Fire, however, penetrates all things so as to produce motion in them. For moisture freezes when deprived of heat, and while the other elements can grow hot, fire cannot grow cold; it is more easily put out, so that it is no longer fire, than it can stay cold or be made less hot by touching something cold. Touch, the fifth of the senses, corresponds more closely to the earthy element; hence things that are touched are felt through the whole body of a living creature, which is made chiefly of earth. They also say that nothing can be seen without fire, nor touched without earth, and that therefore all the elements are present in all things, but each thing has taken its name from the element it has most of. And they say that when the body grows excessively cold through lack of heat, sensation is dulled, because the motion that heat gives the body grows sluggish; for fire acts on air, air on moisture, and moisture on everything earthy, the finer things, of course, penetrating the grosser.
Now the finer anything is in bodily nature, the nearer it is to spiritual nature, though it is far removed from it in kind, since the one is body and the other is not.

Sensing belongs not to the body but to the soul acting through the body. So although it may be acutely argued that the bodily senses are distributed according to the variety of the bodily elements, the soul, which has the power of sensing, is not bodily, and it exercises that power through the finer kind of body. It begins the motion in all the senses from the fineness of fire, but it does not reach the same point in all of them. In sight, with the heat held back, it reaches as far as fire's light; in hearing, the heat of fire penetrates as far as the clearer air; in smell, it passes through pure air and reaches the moist exhalation of which this thicker atmosphere consists; in taste, it passes through this as well and reaches as far as the more bodily moisture; and when it has penetrated and passed through this too and reached the heaviness of earth, it produces the last sense, touch.

So the writer was not ignorant of the natures of the elements and their order. In introducing the creation of the visible things that by nature move within the world among the elements, he told first of the heavenly lights, then of the living creatures of the waters, and last of those of the earth. This is not because he left out the air. Rather, if there are any regions of the purest and calmest air, where birds are said to be unable to fly, these are joined to the upper heaven, and in the scriptures they are understood, under the name of heaven, to belong to the upper part of the world. The name of earth, then, signifies in general this whole region which begins, going downward, with “fire, hail, snow, ice, stormy wind” and all the deeps, and runs down to the dry land, which is called earth in the proper sense. That upper air may belong to the heavenly part of the world, or it may simply have no visible inhabitant of the kind the narrator is now speaking of. Either way, it is not left out, since heaven has been named, nor is it counted in the creation of animals. But this lower air, which receives the moist exhalations of sea and land and is in a way thickened so as to support birds, receives its animals only from the waters. For it is the moisture in it that bears up the bodies of birds, which lean on their wings as they fly, just as fish lean on their own kind of wings as they swim.

Accordingly it is with knowledge, as befits the Spirit of God who was present to the writer, that he says the flying creatures were brought forth from the waters. The nature of the waters has been allotted a twofold place: a lower one in the gliding wave and an upper one in the breathing air, the first assigned to swimming creatures, the second to flying ones. In the same way we see that animals have been given two senses suited to this element: smell for exploring vapours, and taste for exploring liquids. We also feel waters and winds by touch, and that is because the solidity of earth is mixed into all the elements; but it is felt more in these grosser ones, so that they can even be handled by touch. And therefore these too are included under the general name of earth when the world is divided into its two greatest parts, as that psalm shows. It lists all the higher things from one beginning: “Praise the Lord from the heavens,” and all the lower things from another beginning: “Praise the Lord from the earth.” There stormy winds are named, and all the deeps, and this fire which burns whoever touches it, because it arises from earthy and moist motions in such a way that it is soon turned into another element. And although by striving upward it shows the inclination of its nature, it cannot escape into the higher, heavenly calm, because it is overpowered by the mass of air, changed into it, and put out. And so in this more corruptible and sluggish part of the universe it is driven about by turbulent motions, to temper the region's cold and to serve both the needs of mortals and their fears.

The surging of waves and the blowing of breezes can be felt by touch, which belongs properly to earth. For this reason the bodies of water animals also feed on earthly things, and birds especially also rest on the earth and raise their young there; for the part of the moisture that is breathed out as vapour also extends over the lands. And so, when scripture had said, “Let the waters bring forth creeping things of living souls, and flying things,” it says, “above the earth,” and then it adds, “along the firmament of heaven.” Here what seemed obscure before can appear somewhat more plainly. For it does not say “in the firmament of heaven,” as it did of the lights, but “flying things above the earth along the firmament of heaven,” that is, next to the firmament of heaven. This murky and moist space in which birds fly borders on the space where they cannot fly, and that space, because of its stillness and calm, rightly belongs already to the firmament of heaven. So birds do fly in heaven, but in this heaven which that psalm also includes under the name of earth. That is why in many places they are called “birds of heaven”: yet they are not in the firmament, but along it.

Some think that because of their slowness of sense these creatures are called not “living soul” but “creeping things of living souls.” But if that were the reason, the name “living soul” would be given to birds. Since, however, they too are called “flying things,” as the others are called “creeping things,” with “of living souls” understood in both cases, we must admit, I think, that the phrase means “those among living souls that creep or fly.” In the same way one could say “the base of men,” meaning whoever among men are base. For although there are also land animals that creep on the earth, far more of them move on feet, and perhaps as few creatures creep on land as walk in the waters.

Some, however, have thought that fish are called not “living soul” but “creeping things of living souls” because they have no memory and no life that comes, as it were, nearer to reason. But they are misled by lack of experience. For certain writers have recorded many remarkable things that they were able to observe in fishponds. And even if those writers happened to put down falsehoods, it is quite certain that fish have memory. I have tested this myself, and let anyone who can and will test it too. There is a great spring in the region of Bulla that is almost full of fish. People looking down from above usually throw them something, which they either crowd together to snatch for themselves or fight to tear from one another. Grown used to this feeding, when people walk along the edge of the spring, the fish swim in a shoal alongside them, going and coming back with them, waiting for something to be thrown by those whose presence they sense. So it does not seem to me without reason that water animals are called creeping things, just as birds are called flying things. For if lack of memory or slowness of sense had kept the name “living soul” from fish, it would certainly have been given to birds, whose life, as we see with our own eyes, has memory and chatter and great skill in building nests and rearing young.

Nor am I unaware that certain philosophers have assigned its own animals to each element. They said that the earthly creatures include not only those that creep and walk on the earth but birds as well, because birds too rest on the earth when tired from flying. The animals of the air, they said, are demons, and those of heaven are gods, some of whom we call lights and others angels. Yet these same philosophers assign fish and monsters of that kind to the waters, so that no element lacks its own animals. As if there were no earth under the waters, or as if they could prove that fish do not rest on it and restore their strength for swimming, as birds do for flying! Fish may perhaps do this more rarely, because water is stronger than air for bearing up bodies, so much so that it even carries land animals that swim, whether they have learned by practice, as humans have, or know by nature, as four-footed animals and snakes do. Or if the philosophers do not count fish as earthly because fish have no feet, then [neither sea-calves] nor seals belong to the waters, nor snakes and snails to the land. For seals have feet, while snakes and snails have no feet at all and yet, far from merely resting on the earth, hardly or never leave it. Dragons, too, are said to have no feet and yet both to rest in caves and to rise into the air. Though they are not easily known, literature, both ours and that of the Gentiles, has by no means been silent about this kind of creature.

Demons may indeed be animals of the air, since they flourish with the nature of airy bodies. On that view, they are not dissolved by death because the element that prevails in them is better suited to acting than to being acted on. Air has two elements beneath it, namely water and earth, and one above it, namely the fire of the stars; for the elements are divided into two suited to being acted on, water and earth, and two suited to acting, air and fire. Even if all this is so, the distinction does not hinder our scripture, which says that flying things were brought forth not from air but from the waters. For the place given to flying things is one of moisture, a finer moisture, breathed out and spread into the breezes, but moisture nonetheless. Air reaches from the border of the shining heaven down to the flowing waters and the bare lands. Yet moist exhalations do not darken all of it. They reach only up to the boundary from which the region begins to be called earth, according to that psalm where it says, “Praise the Lord from the earth.” The upper part of the air, because of its pure calm, shares a common peace with the heaven that borders it, and is called by the same name. Perhaps the angels who transgressed were in this part before their transgression, together with their prince, who is now the devil and was then an archangel; for some of our writers do not think they were heavenly or super-heavenly angels. If so, it is no wonder that after their sin they were thrust down into this murk. Yet there is air here too, interwoven with thin moisture. When stirred, it makes winds; when stirred more violently, fire and thunder; when drawn together, clouds; when condensed, rain; when the clouds freeze, snow; when denser clouds freeze more turbulently, hail; and when spread out, fair weather. All this happens by the hidden commands and the work of God, who governs everything he has created, from the highest to the lowest. Hence in that psalm, after it had mentioned “fire, hail, snow, ice, stormy wind,” it at once added, “which do his word,” so that no one would think such things happen and move without divine providence.

But if those transgressors had heavenly bodies before they transgressed, it is no wonder either if those bodies were changed, as a punishment, into an airy quality, so that they can now suffer something from fire, that is, from the element of a higher nature. And they were not allowed to occupy even the higher and purer regions of the air, but only this murky region, which is for them, given their kind, a sort of prison until the time of judgment. If anything about these transgressing angels needs more careful inquiry, there will be another passage of scripture better suited to it. For now this is enough. These turbid and stormy regions can support airy bodies, because air by its nature extends down to the waves and the lands. In the same way they can support the bodies of birds, which were brought forth from the waters, because of the thin breath that rises from the waters. This breath is mingled as vapour into the air that surrounds the waves and lands, which is therefore counted as part of the lowest, earthly region. It is woven into the breezes, which, weighed down by the chill of night, fall as dew even when the sky is clear, and when the cold is sharper, turn white and bright as frost.

“And God said, ‘Let the earth bring forth the living soul according to its kind: four-footed creatures and creeping things and beasts of the earth according to kind, and cattle according to kind.’ And so it was done. And God made the beasts of the earth according to kind, and cattle according to kind, and all the creeping things of the earth according to kind. And God saw that they were good.” It now followed that God should adorn with its own animals the other part of this lowest region, the part properly called earth. Elsewhere, scripture includes this whole lowest region, with all the deeps and the cloudy air, under the general name of earth. The kinds of animals that the earth brought forth at the word of God are plain enough. But since all animals without reason are often understood by the name of cattle or of beasts, it is fair to ask which ones the text now calls beasts in the proper sense and which cattle. As for the crawling or creeping things of the earth, there is no doubt that he meant all serpents to be understood, although they could also be called beasts; but the name cattle is not normally applied to serpents. Again, the word beasts is normally applied to lions, leopards, tigers, wolves and foxes, and also to dogs and apes and others of that sort. But the name cattle is more fittingly applied to animals that are of use to human beings, either to help with labour, like oxen and horses and the like, or for wool or food, like sheep and pigs.

What, then, are the four-footed creatures? Apart from certain serpents, all these animals walk on four feet. Yet unless he wanted certain animals to be understood properly by this name, he would surely not have named four-footed creatures here as well, though he said nothing of them in the repetition. Perhaps deer, fallow deer, wild asses and boars are the ones properly called four-footed. They cannot be grouped with the beasts that include lions, for they are like cattle, and yet they are not under human care. On this view they would be the remaining animals, and this name, which is general and which they share with many others because of the number of their feet, would be given to them in a specific sense. Or, since he said “according to kind” three times, is he inviting us to attend to three particular kinds? The first is “four-footed creatures and creeping things according to kind.” Here I think he showed which four-footed creatures he meant, namely those in the class of creeping things, such as lizards, geckos and the like. That is why in the repetition he did not repeat the name four-footed, because perhaps he included them under the word creeping things. Hence there he does not say simply “creeping things” but adds “all the creeping things of the earth”: “of the earth” because there are also creeping things of the waters, and “all” so that it would include those which also stand on four feet and were properly meant above by the name four-footed. The beasts, of which he likewise says “according to kind,” are whatever animals are savage with mouth or claws, serpents excepted. The cattle, of which he says “according to kind” the third time, are those that tear with neither of these, but either with horns or not even that. I said earlier that how widely the name four-footed extends is easily seen from the very number of feet, and that every irrational animal is sometimes included under the name of cattle or beasts. Indeed in Latin the word ferae (“wild animals”) usually has the same range. Still, that was no reason to neglect the question of how these names, which were not put in this passage of scripture for nothing, can also be told apart in a more specific sense, as can easily be seen in everyday speech.

The reader is also right to wonder whether “according to kind” is said at random, as if by chance, or for some reason, as though the creatures had existed before, when in fact the text is telling of their first creation. Or is their kind to be understood in the higher reasons, spiritual ones of course, according to which they are created here below? But if that were so, it would be said of light, of heaven, of the waters and the lands, and of the lights of heaven. For which of these does not have its eternal and unchangeable reason living in the very wisdom of God, which “reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly”? Yet the phrase begins to be used with plants and trees and continues up to these land animals. For even with the creatures made from the waters, although it was not said when they were first mentioned, it was said in the repetition: “And God made the great sea monsters and every soul of creeping animals which the waters brought forth according to their kind, and every winged bird according to kind.”

Or are they said to be made “according to kind” because they came into being in such a way that others would be born from them and keep the form of their origin through succession? On this view the phrase would refer to the propagation of offspring, through which they were created to endure. But then why is it said of trees and plants not only “according to kind” but also “according to likeness,” when animals too, whether of the waters or of the lands, generate according to their likeness? Or, since likeness follows from kind, did he not want to repeat it everywhere? After all, he did not mention seed everywhere either, although seed is present in plants and trees as in animals, though not in all animals. For it has been observed that certain creatures are born from the waters or the earth in such a way that they have no sex, and therefore their seed is not in them but in the elements from which they arise. This, then, is what “according to kind” means: both the power of seeds and the likeness of those that succeed to those that pass away. For none of these creatures was created to exist only once and then either endure or pass away with nothing to succeed it.

Why, then, was this not said of man as well: “Let us make man in our image and likeness according to kind,” when human propagation is also plain to see? Is it because God had not made man so as to die, if he had been willing to keep the commandment, and so there was no need for a successor to one passing away? But after sin he was compared to senseless cattle and became like them, so that now the children of this age beget and are begotten, and the mortal race can continue by keeping up succession. What, then, is the meaning of the blessing given after man was made, “Increase and multiply and fill the earth,” which surely could only happen by begetting? Or should nothing be said rashly on this until we reach the passage of scripture where these questions must be examined and discussed more carefully? For now it may perhaps be enough to say that “according to kind” was not said of man because a single man was being made, from whom the woman too was made. For there are not many kinds of human beings, as there are of plants, trees, fish, birds, serpents, cattle and beasts. Otherwise we would take “according to kind” as if it meant “kind by kind,” so that things that resemble one another and come from one origin of seed might be set apart from the rest.

Another question is what the creatures of the waters did to deserve so much from the Creator that they alone were blessed as human beings are. For God blessed them too, saying: "Increase and multiply and fill the waters of the sea, and let the birds be multiplied upon the earth." Or did it need to be said of only one kind of creature, so that it would be understood as following for the others that increase by generation? In that case it should have been said first of what was first created in that way, namely plants and trees. Or perhaps he judged that things with no desire to propagate offspring, which generate without any sensation, were unworthy of the words of blessing "Increase and multiply". Did he say it first where such a desire was present, so that it would be understood of the land animals even though it was not said of them? It was necessary, however, to repeat it in the case of human beings, so that no one would say there is any sin in the duty of begetting children, as there is in lust, whether in fornication or in an immoderate abuse of marriage itself.

There is also some question about certain very tiny animals: were they created in the first establishment of things, or did they arise afterward from the decay of mortal things? For most of them are generated from the ailments of living bodies, from their excretions or exhalations, or from the rotting of corpses. Some arise from the decay of wood and plants, and some from the decay of fruits. Of none of these can we rightly say that God is not the creator. For in all of them there is a certain beauty of nature proper to its kind. Anyone who considers them well finds greater wonder in them, and the almighty Craftsman receives fuller praise, who made all things in wisdom. That wisdom reaches from end to end and orders all things sweetly. It does not leave even the very lowest of things without form, though they are dissolved according to the order of their kind and we shudder at their dissolution because of the penalty of our mortality. Instead it creates animals tiny in body but keen in sense, so that we are more amazed at the agility of a fly in flight than at the size of a pack animal on the move, and marvel more at the works of little ants than at the loads of camels.

But the question, as I said, is this. Should we believe that these tiniest creatures too were established in the first creation of things, which is narrated in that order of six days? Or did they come later, from the subsequent dissolution of corruptible bodies? It can indeed be said that the tiniest creatures that arise from the waters or the earth were created then. Among these we may also reasonably count those born from the things that sprang up when the earth put forth its growth. Those plants preceded the creation not only of the animals but also of the lights, and they are joined to the earth by the connection of their roots. That is why they sprang up on the day the dry land appeared: they are to be understood as belonging to the furnishing of the dwelling rather than to the number of its inhabitants. But as for the others, which are generated from the bodies of animals, and especially dead ones, it is utterly absurd to say that they were created then, when the animals themselves were created. The only exception would be this: all living bodies already contained a certain natural power, the pre-sown and, in a sense, interwoven beginnings of future animals. These were to arise from the decay of such bodies, each according to its kind and its differences, through the ineffable governance of the Creator, who moves all things while remaining unchanged himself.

A question is also commonly raised about the venomous and harmful kinds of animals. Were they created after man's sin to punish him? Or were they created harmless, and did they only later begin to harm sinners? Nor is this surprising. No one in this toilsome and wretched life is so righteous as to dare call himself perfect, as the apostle faithfully testifies when he says: "Not that I have already received it or am already perfect." Temptations and bodily troubles are still necessary to exercise virtue and to perfect it in weakness, as the same apostle again makes clear. He says that a thorn in the flesh was given him, an angel of Satan to buffet him, so that he would not be exalted by the greatness of the revelations. He asked the Lord three times to take it away, and the Lord answered him: "My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness." Even in such a time, holy Daniel lived safe and unafraid among the lions, though in his prayer he confesses, and certainly does not lie to God, not only the sins of his people but also his own. And a deadly viper fastened on the apostle's own hand and did not harm him. So these creatures, even once created, could have done no harm, had there been no reason either to frighten and punish vices or to test and perfect virtue. Examples of patience must be shown for the progress of others. Man comes to know himself more surely in temptations. And it is just that the everlasting salvation that was shamefully lost through the will should be bravely regained through pain.

Someone will say: "Why then do wild beasts harm one another? They have no sins, so this cannot be called punishment, and they gain no virtue from such exercise." Clearly, it is because some are food for others. Nor can we rightly say that there should not have been some animals for others to feed on. For all things, as long as they exist, have their measures, numbers and orders. When all of these are properly considered, they are praised. Even as things change by passing from one into another, they are not without a hidden governance of temporal beauty proper to their kind. If this is hidden from the foolish, it glimmers for those who are making progress and is clear to the perfect. And certainly all such movements of the lower creation offer salutary admonitions to man. He sees all those creatures, from the largest elephants down to the smallest worms, doing whatever they can, by resisting or by guarding themselves, for the bodily and temporal well-being allotted to them according to the lower ordering of their kind. From this he may see how much he must strive for his spiritual and eternal salvation, by which he surpasses all irrational animals. Their striving becomes visible only when some seek to refresh their own bodies from the bodies of others, while others protect themselves by fighting back with strength, by the safety of flight, or by the shelter of hiding places. For even bodily pain itself in any animal is a great and wonderful power of the soul. By an ineffable mingling, the soul holds that bodily structure together in life and draws it into a kind of unity according to its own measure, since it does not suffer it to be corrupted and dissolved with indifference but, so to speak, with indignation.

This too may perhaps trouble someone. Harmful animals injure living people as punishment, or exercise them for their salvation, or test them for their benefit, or teach them without knowing it. Why, then, do they also tear apart the bodies of the dead for food? As though it made any difference to our welfare what passages this flesh travels through, once lifeless, into the deep hidden places of nature, from which the wonderful omnipotence of the Creator will draw it back again to be refashioned. Yet even from this the prudent receive a certain admonition. They should entrust themselves to the faithful Creator, who governs all things, greatest and least, by his hidden will, and by whom even the hairs of our head are numbered. Then they will not shudder at any kind of death out of empty concern for their lifeless bodies, but will not hesitate to steel the sinews of devout courage for anything.

A similar question often arises about thorns and thistles and certain unfruitful trees: why or when were they created, since God said, "Let the earth bring forth the plant of pasture bearing seed, and the fruit-bearing tree producing fruit"? But those who are troubled in this way do not understand, at least from the common formulas of human law, what is called usufruct. For the word "fruit" has in view a certain benefit to those who enjoy it. As for how great the uses are, whether evident or hidden, of everything the earth brings forth and nourishes through its roots, let them observe some for themselves and ask experienced people about the rest.

About thorns and thistles a more straightforward answer can be given, since after the sin it was said to man concerning the earth: "Thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you." Yet we should not readily say that they began to spring from the earth only then. Perhaps, since many uses are found in these kinds of seed-bearing plants too, they could have had their place without any punishment of man. But that they should also grow in the fields where he now labored as a punishment may be believed to serve to increase his punishment, since they could have grown elsewhere, as pasture for birds and cattle or for some uses of human beings themselves. Yet another sense also fits these words. On this reading, "Thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you" means that the earth brought these forth even before, but not for man's toil. It brought them forth as suitable food for all kinds of animals, for there are animals that feed conveniently and pleasantly on these kinds of plants, both the softer and the drier. Then, when man began to labor on the earth after the sin, it began to bring them forth for him as a wearisome business. This does not mean that they grew in other places before and later in the fields that man cultivated to obtain crops. They grew in the same places both before and after, but before not for man, and afterward for man. This is what is signified by the added words "for you". For it is not said, "Thorns and thistles it shall bring forth," but "it shall bring forth for you". That is, these things will now begin to grow for you, to your toil, which before grew only as pasture for other animals.

"And God said: Let us make man in our image and likeness; and let him rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of the sky and all the cattle and all the earth and all the creeping things that creep upon the earth. And God made man; in the image of God he made him; male and female he made them. And God blessed them, saying: Increase and multiply and fill the earth and have dominion over it, and rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of the sky and all the cattle and all the earth and all the creeping things that creep upon the earth. And God said: Behold, I have given you every seed-bearing plant of pasture yielding seed that is upon all the earth, and every tree that has in itself the fruit of seed-bearing seed. It shall be food for you and for all the beasts of the earth and all the birds of the sky and every creeping thing that creeps upon the earth that has in itself the breath of life, and every green plant shall be for food. And so it was done. And God saw all the things that he had made, and behold, they were very good. And there was evening, and there was morning, the sixth day." There will be a fuller opportunity later to consider the nature of man again and again and to discuss it more carefully. For now, so that our inquiry and treatment can conclude the works of the six days, we will say briefly, first of all, that a difference should be noted. In the other works it is said, "God said: Let there be," but here, "God said: Let us make man in our image and likeness." This was said to suggest, if I may put it so, a plurality of persons, on account of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Yet the text immediately reminds us that we must understand the unity of the Godhead, when it says, "And God made man in the image of God." This does not mean that the Father made him in the image of the Son, or the Son in the image of the Father. Otherwise "in our image" would not have been truly said, if man was made in the image of the Father alone or of the Son alone. Rather, "God made him in the image of God" was said as though it were said, "God made him in his own image." Now it says "in the image of God", whereas earlier it said "in our image". This signifies that the plurality of persons does not lead us to speak of, believe in or understand several gods. Rather, we are to take the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit as one God. On account of this Trinity it was said "in our image", and on account of the one God it was said "in the image of God".

Here we must not pass over this point either. Having said "in our image", he immediately added, "and let him have power over the fish of the sea and the birds of the sky" and the other animals that lack reason. Clearly, we are to understand that man was made in the image of God in that respect in which he surpasses the irrational animals. That is reason itself, or mind, or understanding, or whatever other word may name it more suitably. So the apostle too says: "Be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who is being renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of him who created him." This shows clearly where man was created in the image of God: not in the features of the body, but in a certain intelligible form of the enlightened mind.

Consider, then, that first light, if that name rightly refers to the creation of an intellectual light sharing in the eternal and unchangeable wisdom of God. There it was not said, "And so it was done," followed by the repeated statement, "And God made." As we have already argued as well as we could, in that first creature there was no knowledge of the Word of God that would be followed by the creation, at a lower level, of what was being created in that Word. Rather, the light itself was created first, so that in it the knowledge of the Word of God, through whom it was created, might come about. For that light, this very knowledge was its turning from its own formlessness to the God who forms it, and its being created and formed. Afterward, in the case of the other creatures, it is said, "And so it was done." This signifies that the knowledge of the Word came about first in that light, that is, in the intellectual creature. Then, when it is said, "And God made," it is shown that the kind of creature itself came into being which had been spoken in the Word of God so that it might come to be. The same pattern is kept in the creation of man. For God said, "Let us make man in our image and likeness," and so on. Then it is not said, "And so it was done"; instead it goes on at once, "And God made man in the image of God." For this nature too is intellectual, like that light, and so for it, coming into being is the same as knowing the Word of God, through whom it is made.

For if it said, "And so it was done," and afterward added, "And God made," it would be understood as though it was done first in the knowledge of the rational creature, and then in some other creature that was not rational. But since this creature too is rational, it was also perfected by that same knowledge. For just as after the fall into sin man is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of him who created him, so he was created in that very knowledge before he grew old through sin, which is why he could be renewed again in the same knowledge. But other things were not created in that knowledge, since what was being created was either bodies or irrational souls. For them, the knowledge of them was first produced in the intellectual creature by the Word through whom it was said that they should come to be. Because of this knowledge it was said first, "And so it was done," to show that the knowledge itself had come about in that nature which was able to know this beforehand in the Word of God. Then the bodily and irrational creatures themselves came into being, which is why the words "And God made" were added next.

But it is difficult to say how man was made immortal and yet, along with the other animals, received as food the seed-bearing plant of pasture, the fruit-bearing tree and the green plant. For if he became mortal through sin, then before sin he certainly did not need such food, since that body could not have been worn down by hunger. Then there is the command "Increase and multiply and fill the earth." It seems that this could happen only through the intercourse of male and female, which also points to mortal bodies. Even so, it can be said that there could have been another way in immortal bodies. Children might have been born from devout affection alone, without any desire belonging to corruption. They would not succeed parents who had died, nor would they die themselves, until the earth was filled with immortal human beings. Once a just and holy people had thus been established, such as we believe there will be after the resurrection, there would also have been an end to being born. That can indeed be said, and how it could be said is another matter for consideration. But no one will dare to say this as well: that any but mortal bodies could need food to restore them.

Some have even supposed that it was the inner man that was made at this point, and that the body of man was made later, when Scripture says, "And God formed man from the slime of the earth." On this view, "made" refers to the spirit and "formed" to the body. They did not notice that male and female could have been made only with respect to the body. One may indeed argue very subtly that the mind of man itself, in which he was made in the image of God, a kind of rational life, is divided between the truth of eternal contemplation and the management of temporal things. In this way it becomes, as it were, male and female, the one part taking counsel and the other obeying. Yet in this division only the part that clings to the contemplation of unchangeable truth is rightly called the image of God. As a figure of this, the apostle Paul calls only the man the image and glory of God; "but the woman," he says, "is the glory of the man." So although this is represented outwardly, according to the body, in two human beings of different sex, while it is also understood inwardly in the single mind of a human being, the woman, who is a woman in body, is herself also renewed in the spirit of her mind in the knowledge of God according to the image of him who created her, where there is neither male nor female. Women are not excluded from this grace of renewal and from the re-forming of the image of God, even though something different is represented in the sex of their bodies, by which the man alone is said to be the image and glory of God. Just so, in the first creation of man, the woman, since she too was a human being, certainly had her own mind, and a rational one, in respect of which she too was made in the image of God. But because of the unity of their union, Scripture says, "God made man in the image of God." And so that no one would think that only the spirit of man was made, although it was only in respect of the spirit that he was made in the image of God, it says, "He made him male and female he made them," so that we understand that the body too was now made. Again, so that no one would suppose that he was made in such a way that both sexes were expressed in a single individual, as sometimes happens with those called androgynes, it shows that it used the singular number because of the unity of their union, and because the woman was made from the man, as will become clear later when what is said briefly here begins to be explained more carefully. That is why it immediately added the plural, saying, "He made them, and blessed them." But, as I have already said, we will examine the creation of man more carefully in the passage of Scripture that follows.

Now we must notice that after saying "And so it was done," it immediately added, "And God saw all the things that he had made, and behold, they were very good." Here we understand that human nature was given the power and ability to take the plants of the field and the fruit of the trees as food. For "And so it was done" refers to what began at the words "And God said: Behold, I have given you the seed-bearing plant" and so on. If we referred "And so it was done" to everything said before that, it would follow that we must admit that on that same sixth day they had already increased and multiplied and filled the earth, which, as the same Scripture testifies, we find happened many years later. So, since this ability to eat had been given, and man had come to know it when God spoke, "And so it was done" is said with reference to the fact that man knew it when God spoke. For if he had also acted on it then, that is, if he had actually eaten what had been given him as food, Scripture's usual practice would have been kept. After "And so it was done," which serves to express the knowledge that came first, the action itself would have been added, with the words "And they took and ate." It could have been said this way even without naming God again. In that earlier passage, after the words "Let the water that is under the sky be gathered into one gathering, and let the dry land appear," it adds, "And so it was done." Then it does not say "And God made," but it does repeat: "And the water was gathered into its gathering," and so on.

With the other creatures, Scripture said of each one separately, "And God saw that it was good," but it did not say this separately of the human creature. Instead, after man was made and given the power both to rule and to eat, it added, concerning everything, "And God saw all the things that he had made, and behold, they were very good." There is good reason to ask why. It could first have said of man individually what was said individually of the other things made before him, and only then have said of everything God made, "Behold, they were very good." Or perhaps, since everything was completed on the sixth day, it had to be said of everything, "God saw all the things that he had made, and behold, they were very good," and not separately of the things made on that day? Why, then, was it said of the cattle, the beasts and the creeping things of the earth, which belong to that same sixth day? Unless perhaps they deserved to be called good both separately in their own kind and universally with the rest, while man, made in the image of God, deserved to have this said of him only together with the rest. Or was it because he was not yet complete, since he had not yet been placed in paradise? As though what was left out here had been said after he was placed there!

What, then, shall we say? Was it because God foreknew that man would sin and would not remain in the perfection of his image that he chose to call him good not individually but together with the rest, as if hinting at what was to come? For when the things that have been made remain in what they were made, as far as they have received it (as do those that have not sinned, or those that cannot sin), they are both good individually and all very good as a whole. The word "very" was not added for nothing. The members of the body, too, even if each is beautiful by itself, are all much more beautiful in the framework of the whole body. An eye, for example, may be pleasing and admired, yet if we saw it separated from the body we would not call it as beautiful as it is in that joining of members, seen set in its place in the whole body. But the things that lose their proper beauty by sinning in no way make it the case that they too, rightly ordered with the totality and the universe, are not good. Man, then, before sin was certainly good in his own kind as well; but Scripture passed over saying this so as to say instead something that would foretell what was to come. What was said of him is not false. For whatever is good individually is all the more good together with everything else. But it does not follow that when something is good together with everything else it is also good individually. So the wording was measured to say what was both true at present and a sign of foreknowledge of the future. For God is the best founder of natures and the most just orderer of sinners, so that even if some things individually become deformed by wrongdoing, the universe with them in it is always beautiful. But let us now treat what follows in the next book.
BOOK FOUR

"Thus heaven and earth were finished, and all their array. And on the sixth day God finished his works that he had made; and on the seventh day God rested from all his works that he had made. And God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it, because on it he rested from all his works which God had begun to make." It is indeed an arduous and very difficult thing, with the powers of our attention, to penetrate with a lively mind what the writer meant by these six days. Have those days passed, so that, with the seventh added, they are now repeated through the ages of time not in reality but only in name? For in the whole of time many days come that are like those gone by, but none returns the same. So have those days passed? Or, while these days, which are reckoned by their names and number, run by daily in the order of time, do those days remain in the very conditions of created things? In that case we would understand "day", not only in the three days before the luminaries were made but in the remaining three as well, as the form of the thing created, and its "night" as privation or deficiency, or whatever better name may signify it, when some form is lost through change, declining and tending from form toward formlessness. This change is present in every creature: either as a possibility, even if it never takes effect, as in the higher heavenly things; or else it is carried out, to complete a temporal beauty in the lowest things, through ordered alternations in which all changeable things give way and succeed one another, as is evident in earthly and mortal things. "Evening", then, would be in all things a kind of limit of a completed creation, and "morning" the beginning of one starting, since every created nature is held within its own fixed beginnings and ends. Which of these is true is difficult to investigate. But whether this or that, or some third and more probable account can be found of how night, evening and morning are to be understood in those days (which will perhaps become clear as the discussion goes on), it is still not beside the point to consider the perfection of the number six in the inner nature of numbers itself. It is by gazing on that nature with the mind that we count even the things that lie before the senses of the body, and arrange them in numerical order.

We find, then, that six is the first perfect number, on the ground that it is made up of its parts; for there are other numbers that are perfect for other causes and reasons. We have said that six is perfect for this reason, that it is completed by its parts, meaning only such parts as can, by being multiplied, make up the number of which they are parts. Of such a part it can be said what fraction of the number it is. Three can be called a part not only of six, of which it is the half, but of all numbers larger than three itself. Three is the greater part of four and of five, for four can be divided into three and one, and five into three and two. And of seven and eight and nine and all numbers beyond, three is a part that is neither greater nor a half, but smaller. For seven can be divided into three and four, eight into three and five, and nine into three and six; but for none of these can it be said what fraction three is, except for nine, of which it is the third part, just as it is the half of six. And so of all the numbers I have mentioned, none is made up of a certain number of threes except six and nine: the former consists of two threes, the latter of three.

Six, then, as I had begun to say, is completed by its own parts when they are counted together and summed. For there are other numbers whose parts taken together make a smaller sum, and others whose parts make a larger one. Fewer are found, at certain fixed intervals, that are completed by their parts, so that the sum neither stops short nor overshoots but comes to exactly as much as the number of which they are parts. The first of these is six. For one has no parts among numbers: in the numbers by which we count, one is so called because it has no half or any part, but is truly, purely and simply one. Of two, one is a part, namely its half, and there is no other. Three has two parts: one that can be named as a fraction, namely one, for it is its third; and another, greater, which cannot be named as a fraction, namely two. So the parts of three cannot be counted among those we are dealing with, that is, those that can be named as fractions. Next, four has two such parts: one is its fourth and two its half; but both summed, one and two together, make three, not four. So its parts do not complete it, because they stop at a smaller sum. Five has only one such part, namely one itself, which is its fifth part; for although two is a lesser part of it and three a greater, neither can be named as a fraction of it. Six, however, has three such parts: a sixth, a third and a half. Its sixth is one, its third two, its half three. And these parts summed, that is, one and two and three together, make up and complete that same six.

Seven has no such part except its seventh, which is one. Eight has three: its eighth, its fourth and its half, that is, one, two and four. But these, summed in the same way, make seven, which stops short, and so they do not fill out eight. Nine has two: its ninth, which is one, and its third, which is three.
