Together these make four, far less than nine. Ten has three such parts: one, its tenth; two, its fifth; five, its half. These numbers summed come to eight, not ten. Eleven has only its eleventh, just as seven has only its seventh, five only its fifth, three only its third and two only its half, which in every case is one. But twelve, when such parts of it are summed, is not completed but exceeded: they make a number larger than twelve, reaching sixteen. For it has five such parts: its twelfth, sixth, fourth, third and half. Its twelfth is one, its sixth two, its fourth three, its third four and its half six; and one, two, three, four and six summed make sixteen.

Not to dwell on this at length: in the infinite series of numbers more numbers are found that either have only one such part, like three and five and others of that kind, or have several such parts in such a way that, added together and brought to a sum, they either fall short, like eight and nine and very many others, or overshoot, like twelve and eighteen and many such. So more numbers are found of either of these kinds than of those called perfect, because they are completed by such parts of theirs added together. After six, twenty-eight is found, which likewise consists of such parts. It has five: its twenty-eighth, fourteenth, seventh, fourth and half, that is, one, two, four, seven and fourteen. Added together these complete that same twenty-eight, for they make twenty-eight. And the further the series of numbers advances, the longer, proportionately, are the intervals at which these numbers are found whose such parts, when summed, come back to the numbers themselves; and these are called perfect. Numbers whose such parts, added together, do not fill out the numbers of which they are parts are called imperfect; those whose parts even exceed them are called more than perfect.

So it was in a perfect number of days, that is, six, that God perfected his works that he made. For so it is written: "And on the sixth day God finished his works that he had made." I become all the more intent on this number when I also consider the order of the works themselves. For this number rises step by step through its parts into a triangle: one, two, three follow one another so that no other can be put between them, and each of these is one of the parts of six of which it consists, one being its sixth, two its third, three its half. In just the same way, on one day light was made, and on the next two days the structure of this world: on one the upper part, that is, the firmament, and on the other the lower part, that is, sea and land. But the upper part he did not fill with any kind of bodily food, because he was not going to place there bodies that needed such nourishment. The lower part, however, which he was going to adorn with animals suited to it, he first enriched with the food they would need. In the remaining three days, then, were created the things within the world, that is, within this visible universe made of all the elements, that would move visibly with their own fitting motions: first the luminaries in the firmament, because the firmament had been made first; then living creatures in the lower part, as the order itself required, those of the waters on one day and those of the land on another. And no one is so mad as to dare to say that God could not have made everything in one day if he wished, or in two if he wished, the spiritual creation on one day and the bodily on another, or heaven with all that belongs to it on one day and earth with all that is in it on another; and indeed whenever he wished, for as long as he wished, and in whatever way he wished. Who is there to say that anything could have resisted his will?

So when we read that he completed all things in six days, and on considering the number six find that it is perfect, and that the order of creatures runs in such a way that a kind of graded distinction appears even among the parts by which this number is completed, let us also call to mind what is said to him elsewhere in Scripture: "You have ordered all things in measure and number and weight." And let the soul that is able, having called on God for help as he grants and breathes strength into it, consider whether these three, measure, number and weight, in which it is written that God ordered all things, existed somewhere before the whole of nature was created, or whether they too were created. And if they existed before, where were they? For before creation there was nothing but the Creator. They were in him, then. But how? For we read that the things that were created are in him too. Are those three in him as he himself is, and these created things in him as in the one by whom they are ruled and governed? And how are those three he himself? For God is not measure or number or weight, or all of these together. Is it that in the sense in which we know measure in the things we measure, number in the things we count and weight in the things we weigh, God is not these; but in the sense that measure sets a limit for every thing, number gives every thing its form, and weight draws every thing to rest and stability, he is these things primordially, truly and uniquely, he who bounds all things, forms all things and orders all things? And is nothing else meant, so far as a human heart and tongue could say it, by "You have ordered all things in measure and number and weight" than "You have ordered all things in yourself"?

It is a great thing, and granted to few, to rise above all that can be measured so as to see measure without measure; to rise above all that can be counted so as to see number without number; to rise above all that can be weighed so as to see weight without weight.

For measure and number and weight can be observed and conceived not only in stones and wood and masses of that kind, and in bodily things of any size, whether earthly or heavenly. There is also a measure in acting, so that one's course may not be irrevocable and unrestrained. There is a number of the soul's affections and of the virtues, by which the soul is drawn together out of the deformity of folly into the form and beauty of wisdom. And there is a weight of will and love, in which it appears how much each thing is weighed in seeking, avoiding, preferring and setting aside. But this measure of souls and minds is held in check by another measure, this number is formed by another number, and this weight is drawn by another weight. Measure without measure is that to which whatever comes from it is made equal, while it itself comes from nowhere. Number without number is that by which all things are formed, while it itself is not formed. Weight without weight is that to which those whose rest is pure joy are drawn back so that they may rest, while it itself is not drawn on to anything else.

But whoever knows the names of measure, number and weight only in their visible sense knows them in a servile way. Let him therefore rise above everything he knows in that way; or if he cannot yet do so, let him not cling to the names themselves, since he can only think of them in a base way. For these things are dearer to each person in the higher realm the less he himself is flesh in the lower. But if someone does not wish to transfer words he learned among weak and very lowly things to those sublime things he is trying to clear his mind to contemplate, he is not to be pressed to do it. As long as what is to be understood is understood, there is no great need to worry about what it is called. Still, one ought to know what kind of likeness lower things bear to higher ones. Otherwise reason does not rightly reach out and strive from here to there.

Now if anyone says that measure and number and weight, in which Scripture testifies that God ordered all things, were created, then, if he ordered all things in them, where did he order these very things? If in others, how then did he order all things in these, when these themselves are in others? So there is no doubt that the things in which all things were ordered lie outside the things that were ordered.

Or shall we perhaps suppose that "You have ordered all things in measure and number and weight" was said as though it meant "You have ordered all things so that they should have measure and number and weight"? For if it were said, "You have ordered all bodies in colours," it would not follow that the Wisdom of God itself, through which all things were made, should be understood to have first had colours within itself in which to make bodies. Rather, "You have ordered all bodies in colours" would be taken as though it meant "You have ordered all bodies so that they should have colours." As if bodies ordered in colours by God the Creator, that is, ordered so as to be coloured, could be understood in any other way than that some principle for distributing colours to the several kinds of bodies was not lacking in the very Wisdom of the one who ordered them, even if it is not called colour there! This is what I said: once the reality is granted, there is no need to labour over words. Let us suppose, then, that "You have ordered all things in measure and number and weight" was said as though it meant that they were so ordered as to have their own proper measures, their own proper numbers and their own proper weight, which would change in them according to the changeableness of each one's kind, by increase and decrease, abundance and scarcity, lightness and heaviness, according to God's ordering. Do we then say that, just as these change, so the very counsel of God in which he ordered them is changeable? May he himself keep us from such madness!

When, then, these things were being ordered so as to have their measures and numbers and weights, where did he who ordered them see them? Not outside himself, as we see bodies with our eyes, for they certainly did not yet exist when they were being ordered so that they might come to be. Nor did he see them within himself in the way we see with the mind images of bodies that are not present to our eyes, when we picture in thought the things we have seen or things drawn from what we have seen. In what way, then, did he see them so as to order them? In what way, but the one in which he alone can?

Yet we are mortals and sinners, whose souls are weighed down by corruptible bodies, and whose understanding, busy with many thoughts, is pressed down by its earthly dwelling. And even if we had the purest hearts and the most single minds and were already equal to the holy angels, the divine substance would certainly not be known to us as it is known to itself.

Even so, we see this perfection of the number six neither outside ourselves, as we see bodies with our eyes, nor within ourselves in the way we see images of bodies and pictures of visible things, but in another, far different way. For although certain likenesses, as it were of little bodies, present themselves to the mind's gaze when we think of the composition or order or division of the number six, a stronger and more powerful reason from above does not assent to them, and looks more inwardly upon the power of number. By that inward look it says with confidence that what is called one among numbers cannot be divided into any parts, while no body can be divided except into countless parts; and that heaven and earth, which were made according to the number six, would pass away more easily than it could come about that six should not be completed by its parts. Let the human mind, then, always give thanks to its Creator, by whom it was so created that it can see this, which no bird, no beast can see, although they see with us the sky and the earth, the luminaries, the sea and the dry land, and all that is in them.

We cannot, therefore, say that six is a perfect number because God completed all his works in six days, but rather that God completed his works in six days because six is a perfect number. So even if these works did not exist, that number would be perfect; but if it were not perfect, these works would not have been made perfect according to it.

Now as to what is written, that God rested on the seventh day from all his works that he had made, and that he therefore blessed and sanctified that day because on it he rested from all his works: in order to try to grasp this with our understanding as far as we can, with his help, let us first drive from our minds the carnal suspicions of men on this point. For is it right to say or believe that God toiled in working when he founded the things written above, when he spoke and they came to be? Not even a man toils if something that is to be done comes about as soon as he has spoken. Human words, carried by sounds, are indeed uttered in such a way that long speaking tires us. But when they are as few as the few we read in what is written, when God said "Let there be light," "Let there be a firmament," and the rest up to the end of the works he completed on the sixth day, it is utterly absurd raving to think this a labour even for a man, let alone for God.

Or perhaps someone might say that God did not labor in speaking, so that the things that were made came into being at once, but perhaps in thinking out what ought to be made. Then, freed as it were from this care by the completion of things, he rested, and for that reason chose to bless and sanctify the day on which he was first free of this mental effort? But if to think this is great folly — for with God both the power and the ease of creating things are beyond comparison and beyond words — what remains for us to understand? Perhaps this: that after the rational creature, in which he also created man, had been completed, he granted it rest in himself through the gift of the Holy Spirit, through whom charity is poured out in our hearts. So we are carried by the longing of desire toward the place where, once we have arrived, we may rest, that is, seek nothing further. For just as God is rightly said to do whatever we do when he is working in us, so God is rightly said to rest when we rest by his gift.

This much we understand rightly, because it is true and needs no great effort to see: God is said to rest when he makes us rest, just as he is said to know when he brings it about that we know. For God does not come to know in time what he did not know before, and yet he says to Abraham: "Now I know that you fear God." What else do we take this to mean but "Now I have made you know"? By these figures of speech, when we speak of things that do not happen to God as though they happened to him, we recognize that he causes them to happen to us — at least those things that are praiseworthy, and only so far as the usage of the Scriptures allows. For we ought not rashly to say anything of this kind about God that we do not read in his Scripture.

I believe it is by this figure of speech that the Apostle said: "Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption." For the very substance of the Holy Spirit, by which he is whatever he is, cannot be grieved, since he possesses eternal and unchangeable blessedness, or rather is himself eternal and unchangeable blessedness. But he dwells in the saints in such a way that he fills them with charity. Because of this charity people must rejoice, in the course of time, at the progress and good works of the faithful, and so they must also be grieved at the fall or sins of those in whose faith and devotion they used to rejoice. This sorrow is praiseworthy, because it comes from the love that the Holy Spirit pours in. For this reason the Spirit himself is said to be grieved by those who act in such a way that the saints are grieved at their deeds, for no other reason than that they have the Holy Spirit. By this gift they are so good that the wicked sadden them, above all those whom they knew or believed to have been good. Such sorrow is certainly not to be blamed; on the contrary, it is especially to be praised and commended.

The same Apostle again made wonderful use of this kind of expression when he says: "But now, knowing God, or rather being known by God." For it was not only then that God came to know them, since he foreknew them before the foundation of the world. But because they had then come to know him, by his gift and not by their own merit or ability, he preferred to speak figuratively, saying that they had then been known by him when he granted them to know him. He preferred to correct his word, as though he had spoken less correctly what he had said properly, rather than allow them to claim for themselves the power to do what he had given them the ability to do.

This understanding of the statement that God rested from all his works, which he made very good — namely, that he makes us rest when we have done good works — may perhaps satisfy some. But having taken up the study of this sentence of the Scriptures, we are pressed to ask how he himself could also rest, even though, by making his rest known to us, he urged us to hope that our future rest will be in him. For he himself made heaven and earth and the things that are in them, and completed everything on the sixth day. It cannot be said that we created anything among them, as though he had given us the power to create, and that this is why it is said, "God completed on the sixth day his works which he had made," because he enabled them to be completed by us. In the same way, the words "God rested on the seventh day from all his works which he had made" must certainly be understood first not of our rest, which we shall obtain by his grant, but of his own rest, by which he rested on the seventh day when his works were completed. In this way it may first be shown that all that has been written actually took place, and then, if need be, it may also be shown that it signified something. It is indeed rightly said that, just as God rested after his good works, so we too shall rest after our good works. But for this very reason it is also rightly demanded that, just as the works of God have been discussed, which plainly are his own, so too there should be a sufficient discussion of the rest of God, which is shown to be properly his own.

Therefore we are compelled by the soundest of reasons to investigate, if we can, and to explain how both statements are true: what is written here, that on the seventh day God rested from all his works which he had made, and what he himself, through whom all things were made, says in the Gospel: "My Father is working until now, and I am working." He gave this answer to those who complained that he did not keep the Sabbath, which had been enjoined long ago on the authority of this Scripture because of God's rest. It can indeed plausibly be said that the keeping of the Sabbath was commanded to the Jews as a shadow of what was to come, prefiguring the spiritual rest that God, by the example of this rest of his, was promising in a hidden way to the faithful who do good works. The Lord Jesus Christ, who suffered only when he willed, also confirmed the mystery of this rest by his burial. For on the very day of the Sabbath he rested in the tomb and spent that whole day in a kind of holy repose, after he had completed all his works on the sixth day, that is, the day of preparation, which they call the sixth day of the week, when the things written about him were fulfilled on the very gibbet of the cross. Indeed, he used this very word when he said: "It is finished"; and bowing his head he gave up his spirit. What wonder, then, if God, wishing to foretell in this way too the day on which Christ would rest in the tomb, rested from his works for one day, and thereafter continued to work out the order of the ages, so that this too might be said truly: "My Father is working until now"?

It can also be understood that God rested from creating kinds of creatures, because he did not thereafter create any new kinds. From then until now and beyond, however, he works at governing those same kinds which were established at that time. It is not that even on the seventh day itself his power ceased from governing heaven and earth and all the things he had created; otherwise they would immediately have fallen apart. For the power of the Creator, the might of the Almighty who holds all things together, is the cause of every creature's continued existence. If that might ever ceased to rule the things that have been created, their forms would cease at the same moment, and all nature would collapse. A builder of houses goes away once he has built, and his work stands when he has stopped and left. The world is not like this: it could not stand for even the blink of an eye if God withdrew his governance from it.

Accordingly, when the Lord says, "My Father is working until now," he shows a certain continuation of his work, by which he holds together and governs the whole creation. It could have been understood otherwise if he had said, "and he is working now," for then we would not necessarily have to take it as a continuation of work. But when he says "until now," he compels us to understand it otherwise: from the time, that is, when he worked in creating all things. Scripture also says of his Wisdom that "she reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly," and again that her motion is more nimble and swift than all motions. To those who consider this rightly it is clear enough that Wisdom gives this incomparable and ineffable motion of hers, which is, if it can be understood, a motionless one, to the sweet ordering of things; and that if it were withdrawn, if she ceased from this work, they would perish at once. The Apostle too, when preaching God to the Athenians, said: "In him we live and move and have our being." If this is clearly considered, as far as the human mind is able, it supports the view by which we believe and say that God works unceasingly in the things he has created. For we are not in him in the way of being his substance, as it is said that he has life in himself. Rather, since we are something other than he, we are in him for no other reason than that he works this. And this is his work, by which he holds all things together, and by which his Wisdom reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly; through this ordering we live and move and have our being in him. From this it follows that, if he withdrew this work of his from things, we would neither live nor move nor be. It is clear, then, that God has not ceased even for a single day from the work of governing what he created. Otherwise they would immediately lose their natural motions, by which they are moved and kept alive, so that they may be natures at all and remain, each according to its kind, in what they are; and they would cease to be anything at all if that motion of God's Wisdom by which he orders all things sweetly were withdrawn from them. We therefore take God's resting from all his works which he had made to mean that he did not thereafter create any new nature, not that he ceased to hold together and govern what he had created. Hence it is true both that God rested on the seventh day and that he is working until now.

His works we do indeed see to be good, but his rest we shall see after our own good works. To signify this he commanded the Hebrew people to keep one day. They observed it so carnally that when they saw our Lord and Savior working on that day they accused him. So he answered them most fittingly about the work of the Father, with whom he himself also worked equally, not only in governing the whole creation but also in bringing about our very salvation. Now, however, in the time of grace revealed, that observance of the Sabbath, which was prefigured by resting for one day, has been removed from the observance of the faithful. For in this grace a person keeps a perpetual Sabbath who does whatever good he does in hope of the rest to come, and who does not boast of his good works as though he had some good that he had not received. Thus, receiving and understanding the sacrament of baptism as a kind of Sabbath day, that is, the day of the Lord's rest in the tomb, he rests from his former works. Walking now in newness of life, he recognizes that God is working in him, God who both works and rests at once, giving fitting governance to his creation while possessing eternal tranquility in himself.

In short, he was neither wearied when he created nor refreshed when he ceased. But through his Scripture he wished to stir in us a desire for rest by making known to us that he sanctified the day on which he rested from all his works. For nowhere in all the six days on which all things were created do we read that he sanctified anything. Nor before those six days, where it is written, "In the beginning God made heaven and earth," is it added, "and he sanctified." But he chose to sanctify this day, on which he rested from all his works which he had made, as if even with him, who has no toil at all in his work, rest counts for more than activity. The Gospel teaches us this in the case of human beings, where our Savior says that Mary, who sat at his feet resting in his word, had the better part, rather than Martha, though she was busy about many things in the service she rendered him, and though she was doing a good work. But how this holds true of God, or how it may be understood, is hard to say, even if thought can reach to some small extent why God sanctified the day of his rest when he sanctified none of the days of his work, not even the sixth, on which he made man and completed all things. And first of all, what is this resting of God? Whose human mind can keenly grasp it? Yet if it were not real, this Scripture would certainly not have stated it. I will say plainly what I think, but first I state two things beyond doubt: that God did not take pleasure in some temporal rest as if after toil, or after a longed-for end of his business; and that these writings, which rightly stand out with such great authority, did not say idly or falsely that God rested on the seventh day from all his works which he had made, and for that reason sanctified that day.

It is a fault and a weakness of the soul to take such delight in its own works that it rests in them rather than resting in itself away from them; for without doubt there is something better in the soul, by which those works were made, than the works themselves. Clearly, then, God makes known to us through this Scripture, which says that he rested from all his works which he had made, that he took no such delight in any work of his, as though he had needed to make it, or would have been less had he not made it, or became more blessed when he had made it. For whatever comes from him exists from him in such a way that it owes to him the fact that it exists, while he owes to nothing that comes from him the fact that he is blessed. So in his love he set himself above the things he made. He did not sanctify the day on which he began to make them, nor the day on which he completed them, lest his joy seem to have been increased either by making them or by their having been made. He sanctified instead the day on which he rested from them in himself. He himself, indeed, was never without this rest, but he showed it to us through the seventh day. In this way he also signified that his rest is attained only by the perfected, since to make it known he assigned no day other than the one that followed the completion of all things. For he who is always at rest rested for us at the time when he showed that he had rested.

We must also note that God's rest, by which he is blessed in himself, had to be made known to us so that we might understand how he is also said to rest in us. This is said only when he grants us too rest in himself. To those who understand rightly, then, God's rest is that by which he needs no good from anyone. Therefore our rest in him is also secure, because we are made blessed by the good that he is, not he by the good that we are. For we too are some good, from him who made all things very good, among which he made us also. Moreover, there is no good thing besides himself that he did not make; and so he needs no good other than himself, since he does not need the good that he made. This is his rest from all his works which he had made. But what goods could he praiseworthily be said not to need if he had made none? For even then he could be said to need no goods, not by resting in himself from what he had made, but by making nothing at all. Yet if he could not make good things, he would have no power; and if he could but did not, his envy would be great. Because, then, he is almighty and good, he made all things very good; and because he is perfectly blessed in himself, his own good, he rested in himself from all the things he made, with that rest, of course, from which he never departed. But if it were said that he rested from making things, this would be understood to mean nothing other than that he had not made them; and if it were not said that he rested from the things made, the fact that he does not need the things he made would be less clearly commended to us.

On what day, then, should this have been commended to us if not the seventh? Anyone understands this who recalls the perfection of the number six, of which we spoke above, and how fittingly it was applied to the perfection of the creation. For if the creation was to be completed in the number six, as it was completed, and if that rest of God was to be commended to us by which it would be shown that he is not made blessed even by his completed creatures, then without doubt the day to be sanctified in commending this was the one that follows the sixth. By it we were to be roused to long for this rest, so that we too may rest in him.

For it would not be a devout likeness if we wished to be like God in such a way that we too would rest from our works in ourselves, as he rested in himself from his works. We ought to rest in an unchangeable good, and that good for us is he who made us. This, then, will be our highest rest, one in no way proud and truly devout: just as he rested from all his works, because his works are not his good but he is his own good, by which he is blessed, so we too should hope that we shall rest from all works, not only our own but even his, only in him. And we should desire this after our good works, which we recognize in ourselves to be his rather than ours, so that in this way too he himself rests after his good works, when, after the good works we have done once justified by him, he grants us rest in himself. For it is a great thing for us to have come into being from him, but it will be greater to have rested in him; just as he is not blessed because he made these things, but because, not needing even the things he made, he rested in himself rather than in them. Hence he sanctified the day not of work but of rest, because he made known that he is blessed not by making these things but by not needing the things he made.

What, then, is so lowly and easy to say, and what so lofty and hard to think, as God resting from all his works which he had made? And where does he rest, if not in himself, since he is blessed only in himself? When, if not always? But among the days on which the completion of the things he created is narrated, and on which the order of God's rest is set apart from them, when does he rest, if not on the seventh day, which follows their completion? For he rests from the completed works, since he does not need even them, completed as they are, to be more blessed.

With God himself, his rest has neither morning nor evening, for it is neither opened by a beginning nor closed by an end. Yet in relation to his completed works it has a morning and no evening. The reason is that the completed creation has a certain beginning of its turning toward the rest of its Creator, but that rest has no end as a limit of its perfection, as the things that were made do. Accordingly, God's rest begins not for God himself but for the perfection of the things he created. What is perfected by him thus begins to rest in him and has a morning in him; in its own kind it has been brought to a close as if by an evening. But in God it can no longer have an evening, because there will be nothing more perfect than that perfection.

In those days when all things were being created, we took evening to mean the end of the creation that had just been made, and morning the beginning of the next creation to be made. So the evening of the fifth day is the end of what was created on the fifth day, and the morning that came after that evening is the beginning of what was to be created on the sixth day. Once that was made, evening came as its end. And because nothing else remained to be made, the morning that came after that evening did not begin another creation. Instead it began the rest of the whole creation in the rest of the Creator. For heaven and earth and all that is in them, that is, the whole of creation, both spiritual and bodily, do not abide in themselves but in him of whom it is said: "For in him we live and move and have our being." Each part can exist in the whole of which it is a part, but the whole itself exists only in him by whom it was made. So it is not absurd to understand that, when the sixth day was completed, the morning that came after its evening did not signify the beginning of another creation, as it did on the other days. It signified the beginning of the abiding and resting of everything that had been made in the rest of the one who made it. For God this rest has neither beginning nor end. For the creature it has a beginning but no end. And so for that same creation the seventh day began with a morning but is closed by no evening.

If evening and morning on the other days signified the same kind of alternation of time that now passes in our daily cycles, I do not see what would have prevented an evening and its night from closing the seventh day too, so that Scripture might likewise have said: "And there was evening, and there was morning, the seventh day." After all, the seventh is itself one of the days, and there are seven of them in all, whose repetition makes up the months, years and ages. Then the morning placed after the evening of the seventh day would have been the beginning of an eighth day. Nothing more needed to be said about that day, because it is the same as the first, to which the cycle returns and from which the series of the week begins again. It is therefore more probable that our seven days, which bear the names and number of those days, measure out the spans of time as they run on, each succeeding the other. The first six days, however, unfolded in the very founding of things in a form unknown to our experience and unfamiliar to us. In them evening and morning, like light and darkness themselves, that is, day and night, did not alternate in the way our days do through the circuit of the sun. We are certainly forced to admit this about the first three days, which are recorded and counted before the lights of heaven were made.

Whatever kind of evening and morning there was in those days, we must in no way suppose that God's rest began with the morning that came after the evening of the sixth day. We must not rashly and foolishly suspect that some temporal good befell that eternal and unchangeable being. God's own rest, by which he rests in himself and is blessed in the good that he is to himself, has neither beginning nor end for him. Yet this same rest of God has a beginning for the completed creation. For the perfection of each thing is established, according to the measure of its kind, not so much in the universe of which it is a part as in him from whom it comes and in whom the universe itself exists. It is established so that it may rest, that is, keep the order proper to its own weight. So the whole of creation, completed in six days, has one thing in its own nature and another in the order by which it exists in God. It does not exist as God does, but it has no rest or stability of its own except in the rest of him who desires nothing beyond himself, as though he needed to attain something in order to rest. Therefore, while he abides in himself, he turns back to himself whatever comes from him. Every creature thus has in itself the limit of its nature, by which it is not what he is, but in him it has a place of rest, by which it preserves what it is. I know that I have not used the word "place" in its proper sense, since it properly refers to spaces occupied by bodies. But bodies themselves remain in a place only when they have reached it by what is, so to speak, the desire of their weight, and there, having found it, they rest. So it is not unfitting to transfer the word from bodily things to spiritual ones and speak of a "place," even though the reality is very different.

I think, then, that the morning that came after the evening of the sixth day signified the beginning of creation's rest in the Creator, for creation could not rest in him unless it were complete. So when all things had been completed on the sixth day and evening had come, morning came too, and with it the completed creation began to rest in him who made it. From that beginning it found him resting in himself, and found there a place where it too could rest. Its rest was all the more stable and firm because it needed him for its rest, and he did not need it. Through all its changes, whatever the whole creation comes to be, it will certainly never be nothing. Therefore the whole creation will always abide in its Creator, and for this reason no evening followed that morning.
This is what we have to say about why the seventh day, on which God rested from all his works, had a morning after the evening of the sixth day but had no evening.

There is another way in which this matter can, I think, be understood more properly and better, though it is somewhat harder to explain: that God's rest, not only for the creature but also for himself, had on the seventh day a morning without an evening, that is, a beginning without an end. For if it were said, "God rested on the seventh day," without the addition "from all his works which he had made," we would look in vain for a beginning of this rest. God does not begin to rest, for his rest is everlasting, without beginning and without end. But since he rested from all his works which he had made, in the sense that he did not need them, we understand that God's rest itself neither began nor ended, while his rest from all his works which he had made began from the moment he completed them. He could not have rested by not needing his works before they existed, since he would not need them even once they were completed. And because he never needed them at all, and this blessedness by which he does not need them will not be perfected as though by progress, no evening was added to the seventh day.

But one may clearly ask, and it is a question that deserves consideration, how we are to understand that God rested in himself from all his works which he had made, when it is written, "And God rested on the seventh day." It does not say "in himself" but "on the seventh day." What, then, is the seventh day? Is it some creature, or only a span of time? But even a span of time was created along with temporal creation, and so it too is undoubtedly a creature. For there neither are, nor have been, nor can be any times of which God is not the creator. So if this seventh day is a time, who created it but the creator of all times? The earlier passage of holy Scripture shows with which creatures, or in which, those six days were created. So, among these seven days whose form we know, which actually pass away but somehow hand their names on to the days that follow, so that the six days keep being named, we know when the first of them were created. But we do not see when God created the seventh day, which is called the sabbath. On that day he made nothing. Rather, on that same seventh day he rested from the things he had made in six days. How, then, did he rest on a day he had not created? Or how did he create it right after the six days, when on the sixth day he completed everything he created and created nothing on the seventh day, but instead rested on it from all that he had created? Or did God create only one day, so that by its repetition the many that are called days passed by and ran their course? Then there was no need for him to create a seventh day, since the seventh repetition of the day he had created produced it. For of the light it is written, "And God said, Let there be light, and there was light," and he separated it from the darkness, called it day, and called the darkness night. At that point, then, God made a day. Scripture calls its repetition the second day, then the third, and so on to the sixth, on which God completed his works. From then on, the seventh repetition of that first-created day received the name of the seventh day, on which God rested. And so the seventh day is no creature other than that same one, returning a seventh time, which was established when God called the light day and the darkness night.

So we slip back once more into the question we seemed to have left behind in the first book, and must ask again how the light could circle round to produce the alternation of day and night. This was not only before the lights of heaven were made, but before heaven itself, which was called the firmament, was made, and in short before there was any form of land or sea that would allow the light to circle round, with night following in the place it had left. Driven by the difficulty of this question, we ventured to bring our discussion to roughly this conclusion: the light that was made first was the forming of spiritual creation, while the night was the matter still to be formed in the remaining works. That matter had been established when in the beginning God made heaven and earth, before he made the day by his Word. But now the seventh day reminds us to consider things again, and it is easier for us to admit that we do not know what lies far beyond our senses. We do not know how that light which was called day produced the alternation of day and night. If it is bodily, it may have done so by circling, or by contracting and sending itself out. If it is spiritual, it may have been present to all the creatures to be established, making day by its presence, night by its absence, evening by the beginning of its absence, and morning by the beginning of its presence. Admitting this is easier than going against the words of divine Scripture in a plain matter by saying that the seventh day is something other than the seventh repetition of the day God made. Otherwise, either God did not create the seventh day, or he created something after those six days, namely the seventh day itself. Then what is written would be false: that on the sixth day he completed all his works, and on the seventh rested from all his works. Since that certainly cannot be false, it remains that the presence of that light which God made to be day was repeated through all his works, as often as "day" is named, and also on the seventh day itself, on which he rested from his works.

The heaven called the firmament, in which the lights were also made, did not yet exist. Before it was made, we cannot discover by what circling, or by what advance and withdrawal, bodily light could have produced the alternation of day and night. So we ought not to leave this question without offering some opinion of our own. Suppose the light that was created first is not bodily but spiritual. It was made after darkness, which we understand to mean that it was turned from a certain formlessness of its own toward its creator and was formed. In the same way, then, morning comes after evening when, having come to know its own nature, by which it is not what God is, it turns back to praise the light which God himself is, by contemplating whom it is formed. And because the other creatures made below it are not made without its knowledge, the same day is repeated throughout, so that by its repetition there are as many days as there are distinct kinds of created things, all to be completed in the perfection of the number six. So the evening of the first day is also its knowledge of itself, that it is not what God is. The morning after this evening, which concludes the first day and begins the second, is its turning, by which it refers what it was created to be to the praise of the creator, and receives from the Word of God the knowledge of the creature that is made after it, that is, the firmament. The firmament is made first in that light's knowledge, when it is said, "And so it was done"; then it is made in the nature of the firmament itself as it is established, when, after "And so it was done" has already been said, there is added, "And God made the firmament." Then comes the evening of that light, when it knows the firmament not in the Word of God, as before, but in the firmament's own nature. Since this knowledge is lesser, it is rightly signified by the name of evening. After that comes the morning, which concludes the second day and begins the third. In this morning, likewise, this light, that is, this day, turns to praise God for having made the firmament, and to receive from his Word knowledge of the creature to be established after the firmament. So when God says, "Let the water that is under heaven be gathered into one gathering, and let the dry land appear," that light knows this in the Word of God by which it is said, and therefore there follows, "And so it was done," that is, in its knowledge, from the Word of God. Then, when there is added, "And the water was gathered," and so on, although "And so it was done" had already been said, the creature itself is made in its own kind. The light had already known in the Word of God that this creature was to be made. When it in turn knows the creature as made in its own kind, evening comes for the third time. From there the rest proceeds in the same way, up to the morning after the evening of the sixth day.

There is a great difference between knowing anything in the Word of God and knowing it in its own nature, so that the former rightly belongs to day and the latter to evening. Compared with the light that is seen in the Word of God, all the knowledge by which we know any creature in itself may fairly be called night. Yet this knowledge in turn differs so greatly from the error or ignorance of those who do not even know the creature itself that, compared with that, it may fittingly be called day. In the same way, the life of the faithful, lived in this flesh and in this world, is quite reasonably called light and day when compared with an unbelieving and ungodly life. As the apostle says, "For once you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord," and, "Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light, so that we may walk decently as in the day." Yet this day too is night compared with that day on which, made equal to the angels, we shall see God as he is. If it were not, we would not need the lamp of prophecy here. That is why the apostle Peter says, "We have the more certain prophetic word, to which you do well to attend, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts."

The holy angels, to whom we shall be made equal after the resurrection if we hold to the end to the way that Christ has become for us, always see the face of God. They enjoy his Word, the only-begotten Son, as he is equal to the Father, and in them wisdom was created first of all things. Therefore they undoubtedly knew the whole creation, in which they themselves were the first established, first in the Word of God himself. In him are the eternal reasons of all things, even of those made in time, since through him all things were made. Then they knew it in the creation itself, which they knew as though looking down on it from above. They refer it to the praise of him in whose unchangeable truth they see, primarily, the reasons according to which it was made. There it is as though by day, which is also why their most harmonious unity, through sharing in the same truth, is the day that was created first. Here it is as though by evening. But morning comes at once, as can be seen in all six days, because angelic knowledge does not rest in what has been created without at once referring it to the praise and love of him in whom it is known, not as made but as to be made. By standing in that truth it is day. For if angelic nature were to turn even toward itself, and delight in itself more than in him by sharing in whom it is blessed, it would swell with pride and fall, like the devil. We must speak of him in the proper place, when we come to the discussion owed to the serpent who seduced man.

The angels, then, know the creature in that creature itself, but by choice and love they rank above this knowledge the fact that they know it in the truth through which all things were made, of which they have been made sharers. For this reason night is not named through all six days. Instead, after evening and morning there is one day; likewise after evening and morning the second day; then after evening and morning the third day; and so on to the morning of the sixth day, from which begins the seventh, the day of God's rest. Although these days have their nights, it is days and not nights that are recounted. For night belongs to day, and not day to night, when the exalted and holy angels refer what they know of the creature in the creature itself to the honor and love of him in whom they contemplate the eternal reasons by which it was created. In that most harmonious contemplation they are the one day which the Lord has made. To that day the Church too will be joined when it is freed from this pilgrimage, so that we too may rejoice and be glad in it.

So it was by the sixth repetition of this day, whose evening and morning can be understood in the way explained above, that the whole of creation was completed. Morning came, to end the sixth day and begin the seventh, which would have no evening, because God's rest is not a creature. When creation was being established during the other days, it was known as made in itself differently from the way it was known in him in whose truth it was seen as something to be made. The faded appearance, as it were, of this knowledge made the evening. In this account of how things were established, then, we should not take "day" to mean the form of the work itself, "evening" its end, and "morning" the beginning of another work. Otherwise we would be forced to say, against Scripture, that the seventh day was a creature established outside the six days, or else that the seventh day itself is no creature. Rather, that day which God made is itself repeated through his works, not by bodily circling but by spiritual knowledge. That blessed society of angels first contemplates in the Word of God the work of which God says, "Let it be," and so the work is first made in their knowledge, when it is said, "And so it was done." Afterwards they know the thing itself as made in itself, and this is signified by "evening came." Then they refer that knowledge of the thing made to the praise of the truth in which they had seen the reason for making it, and this is signified by "morning came." So through all those days there is one day. It is not to be understood after the manner of the days we know, which we see marked off and counted by the sun's circuit, but in some other way, and the three days mentioned before these lights were made must also be understood in that way. This manner continues not just up to the fourth day, as though from then on we should think of our ordinary days, but through to the sixth and seventh. So the day and night between which God divided must be understood quite differently from this day and night between which he said the lights he created should divide, when he said, "And let them divide between day and night." He established our day when he established the sun, whose presence produces it. But that first-established day had already completed three days when these lights were created at its fourth repetition.

In this earthly mortality of ours we cannot experience or perceive that day, or the days numbered by its repetition. If we can make any attempt to understand them, we ought not to rush into a rash opinion, as though nothing more fitting or more probable could be thought about them. Our seven days make up the week that stands in for those days, and by its course and recourse the seasons are swept along. In it one day is the circuit from sunrise to sunrise. Let us believe that these days present some likeness of those, while having no doubt at all that they are not like them but very unequal to them.

I have spoken about spiritual light; about the day established in the spiritual, angelic creation; about the contemplation it has in the Word of God; about the knowledge by which the creature is known in itself; and about the referral of this knowledge to the praise of the unchangeable truth, where the reason for making the thing, now known as made, had first been seen. Let no one think that all this fits the meaning of day, evening, and morning not properly but only in a figurative or allegorical sense. It fits them differently, of course, from our everyday experience of this daily, bodily light, yet not as though the words are used properly here and figuratively there. For where the light is better and more certain, there the day is also truer. Why, then, should there not also be a truer evening and a truer morning? In our days the light has a kind of decline toward its setting, which we call evening, and a return toward its rising, which we call morning. Why then should we not speak of evening there too, when the creature is looked at from below, after the contemplation of the creator, and of morning, when one rises from the knowledge of the creature to the praise of the creator? Christ too is not called light in the same way that he is called a stone: the first is said properly, the second certainly figuratively. So if anyone, in the counting of those days, looks not for the view that we have been able to investigate or conjecture within our small capacity, but for another, one that can be understood not figuratively, as in prophecy, but properly and better, as an account of the creation of things, let him seek it and, with God's help, find it. It may be that I too shall perhaps find another view better suited to these words of divine Scripture. I do not affirm this view in such a way as to insist that no other could be found that should be preferred to it. It is otherwise with my affirmation that holy Scripture did not mean to suggest to us that God's rest came as if after weariness or the burden of care: that I do affirm.

So perhaps someone may argue against me. He may say that the angels of the highest heavens do not look first at the reasons of creatures, unchangeably present in the unchangeable truth of the Word of God, then at the creatures themselves, and third refer their knowledge of the creatures in themselves to the praise of the creator, taking these in turn. Rather, he may say, their mind can do all these things at once with wonderful ease. But will he say, or if anyone does say it, should he be listened to, that the heavenly city, with its thousands of angels, either does not contemplate the eternity of the creator, or is ignorant of the changeableness of the creature, or does not praise the creator on the basis of its somewhat lower knowledge of the creature too? Granted that they can do all this at once and do all this at once, they can still do it, and they do. So they have day and evening and morning all at once.

Nor need we fear that someone already capable of grasping these things might think this cannot happen there because it cannot happen in our days, which are completed by the circuit of this sun. It cannot, indeed, happen in the same parts of the earth. But who, if he cares to pay attention, does not see that the whole world has at one and the same time day where the sun is, night where it is not, evening where it is departing, and morning where it is approaching? We on earth, plainly, cannot have all these at once. Yet we should not for that reason put this earthly condition, and the temporal and spatial circuit of bodily light, on a level with that spiritual homeland. There it is always day in the contemplation of unchangeable truth, always evening in the knowledge of the creature in itself, and always morning as well, rising from this knowledge to the praise of the creator. For there evening comes not by the withdrawal of the higher light but by the distinctness of a lower knowledge. Morning comes not as though a morning knowledge succeeded a night of ignorance, but because it lifts even the evening knowledge up to the glory of the creator. Finally, the psalmist too, without naming night, says, "At evening and morning and noon I will tell and declare, and you will hear my voice." Here he perhaps speaks in terms of the alternation of times, yet I think he signifies what goes on without any alternation of times in the homeland for which he sighed in his pilgrimage.

Perhaps that angelic society, the unity of the day which God first established, does and has all these things at once now. But did it also have them all at once then, when these things were being established? Throughout all six days, as the things God was pleased to establish on each day were being established, did it not first receive them in the Word of God, so that they were first made in its knowledge when it was said, "And so it was done"? Then, when they had been made in their own proper nature, by which they exist, and had pleased God because they are good, did it not know them in turn by another, lower knowledge, which is signified by the name of evening? And then, after evening had come, did not morning come, when God was praised for his work and knowledge of another creature, which was to be made next, was received from the Word of God before it was made? Then it was not all at once, day and evening and morning, but one at a time, in the order that Scripture records.

Or were they all at once even then? For this happened not through the delays of time, as our days come about when the sun rises and sets and returns to its place to rise again. It happened through the spiritual power of the angelic mind, which grasps all it wishes at once with the easiest knowledge. Yet it was not without order on that account, an order in which the connection of preceding and following causes appears. For knowledge cannot come about unless the things to be known come first, and these in turn exist in the Word, through whom all things were made, before they exist in all the things that were made. The human mind, therefore, first experiences through the bodily senses the things that have been made, and grasps knowledge of them in the small measure that human weakness allows. Then it seeks their causes, to see whether it can somehow reach them, since they abide primarily and unchangeably in the Word of God, and so behold his invisible things, understood through the things that have been made. Everyone knows how slowly and with what difficulty it does this, and with how much delay, because of the corruptible body that weighs down the soul, even a soul driven by the most fervent zeal to do it earnestly and perseveringly. But the angelic mind, cleaving to the Word of God in pure love, was created in such an order as to come before the rest. So it first saw in the Word of God the things that were to be made before they were made. Thus they were made in its knowledge, when God said that they should be, before they were made in their own proper nature. Once they were made, it also knew them in themselves, with a lesser knowledge certainly, which is called evening. The things being made did indeed come before that knowledge, because whatever can be known comes before the knowledge of it. Unless the thing to be known exists first, it cannot be known. After this, if the angelic mind had been so pleased with itself as to delight in itself more than in its creator, morning would not have come; that is, it would not have risen from its own knowledge to the praise of its creator. But when morning had come, another thing was to be made and known, with God saying, "Let it be." So it was likewise made first in the knowledge of the angelic mind, and again it could be said, "And so it was done." Then it was made in its own nature, where it would be known in the evening that followed.

And so, even if there are no intervals of temporal delay here, the principle of the creature to be made nevertheless came first in the Word of God when he said, "Let there be light," and then the light itself followed. By this light the angelic mind was formed and made in its own nature, but the light did not follow somewhere else in order to be made. That is why it was not first said, "And so it was done," and only afterward, "And God made the light." Rather, light was made immediately after God's word, and the created light clung to the creating Light, seeing that Light and itself in it, that is, the principle by which it was made. It also saw itself in itself, that is, what was made as distinct from the one who made it. So when God, seeing what had been made, was pleased that it was good, and the light had been divided from the darkness, and the light called day and the darkness night, evening also came. This knowledge was necessary too, because by it the creature was distinguished from the Creator, being known in itself differently than in him. Then came morning, and something else to be known beforehand that was to be made by the Word of God: first in the knowledge of the angelic mind, then in the nature of the firmament itself. And so God said, "Let there be a firmament." And so it was done, in the knowledge of the spiritual creature, which knew this beforehand, before it was made in the thing itself. Then God made the firmament, now meaning the actual nature of the firmament, and knowledge of that nature would be lesser, an evening knowledge as it were. And so it went on to the end of all the works and up to God's rest. That rest has no evening, because it was not made as a creature is made, in such a way that knowledge of it too could be doubled, an earlier and greater knowledge in the Word of God, as in daytime, and a later and lesser one in itself, as in the evening.

But if the angelic mind can grasp all at once what language distinguishes one item at a time through the order of connected causes, were the things being made also all made at once? Were the firmament itself, the gathering of the waters and the laying bare of the land, the sprouting of shrubs and trees, the forming of the lights and stars, and the living things of water and land all made at once, and not rather through intervals of time according to the appointed days? Or perhaps we should not think of them, when they were first established, the way we now experience them in their natural motions. Perhaps we should think of them according to the wonderful and inexpressible power of the Wisdom of God, which reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly. For that Wisdom does not reach by degrees or arrive by steps, as it were. The most effective motion is easy for it, and just as easily God created all things, since they were created through it. So what we now see, things being moved through intervals of time to carry out what suits each kind, comes from those implanted principles that God scattered like seeds in the instant of creating, when he spoke and they were made, when he commanded and they were created.

So it was not slowly established that slow things should be slow, and the ages were not founded with the same delay with which they run their course. For times work out those numbers which things did not receive in time when they were created. Otherwise, suppose we think of the natural motions of things and the usual lengths of the days we know when these things were first made by God's word. Then many days would have been needed, not one. The things that sprout from roots and clothe the earth would first have to germinate below ground, and then after a certain number of days, each according to its kind, break out into the air, even if things went only as far as Scripture says was done regarding their created nature in one day, the third. Then how many days were needed for birds to fly, if they came into existence from their first beginnings and arrived at feathers and wings through the numbers of their nature? Or perhaps only eggs were created when it was said on the fifth day that the waters brought forth every winged bird according to its kind? But perhaps this could rightly be said because everything that coalesces and in a way unfolds through fixed numbers of days was already present in the fluid of the eggs, since those numerical principles were already there, woven incorporeally into bodily things. If so, why could the same thing not rightly be said even before the eggs, when the same principles were already coming to be in the moist element, principles by which birds could arise and be brought to completion through the time spans proper to each kind? For this Scripture narrated that the Creator completed his works in six days, and of that same Creator it is written elsewhere, certainly without contradiction, that he created all things at once. And so he who made all things at once also made these six or seven days at once, or rather one day repeated six or seven times. Why then did six days need to be narrated so distinctly and in such order? Because those who cannot see what was said, "He created all things at once," cannot reach the point the text is leading them to unless the discourse walks more slowly with them.

How then do we say that the presence of that light was repeated seven times from evening to morning through angelic knowledge? It was enough for that light to have these three, day, evening and morning, together and once. For it contemplated the whole creation at once, just as it was made at once. It contemplated creation in the first and unchangeable principles through which creation was founded, and that is why there is day. It knew creation in its own nature, and that is why there is evening. It praised the Creator even on the basis of that lower knowledge, and that is why there is morning. Or how did morning come first, so that the angelic mind knew in the Word what God was afterward to make, and would then know the same thing in the evening, if nothing was made earlier and later because all things were made at once? In fact, the things mentioned were both made earlier and later across six days and all made at once. Both are true: this Scripture, which narrates the works of God through the days it mentions, and the other, which says that he made all things at once. And both are one Scripture, because they were written under the inspiration of the one Spirit of truth.

In matters where intervals of time do not show what is earlier or later, both things can be said: "at once" and "earlier and later." Still, "at once" is easier to understand than "earlier and later." For example, when we look at the rising sun, it is plain that our gaze could not reach it without crossing the whole space of air and sky between us and the sun. Who could estimate how great that distance is? And if we are somewhere inland, our gaze, the ray of our eyes, would certainly not cross the air above the sea without first crossing the air above the land, from where we are to the seashore. Then, if there are more lands beyond the sea along the same line of sight, our gaze cannot cross the air above those lands overseas without first covering the air that stretches above the sea it meets first. Now suppose that beyond those lands overseas there is nothing left but the Ocean. Can our gaze cross the air spread over the Ocean without first crossing whatever air lies above the land on this side of the Ocean? The Ocean is said to be incomparably vast, but however great it is, the rays of our eyes must first cross the air above it, and then whatever lies beyond, and only then reach the sun that we see. Just because we have said "first" and "afterward" so many times here, does our gaze not cross everything at once, in a single instant? Suppose we shut our eyes and turn our face toward the sun to look at it. As soon as we open them, will we not think that we found our gaze already there rather than brought it there? Our eyes will not even seem to have opened before our gaze reached what it was aimed at. And this is certainly a ray of bodily light, flashing out from our eyes and touching things so far away with a speed that cannot be estimated or compared. Clearly, then, all those vast and immense spaces are crossed at once in a single instant, and it is no less certain which is crossed first and which afterward.

So when the apostle wanted to express how fast our resurrection will be, he rightly said that it happens in the twinkling of an eye. Nothing faster can be found among the motions or strokes of bodily things. But if the gaze of fleshly eyes can move so fast, what about the gaze of the mind, even the human mind? How much faster is the angelic mind? And what is to be said of the speed of the supreme Wisdom of God itself, which reaches everywhere because of its purity, and into which nothing defiled can enter? So in these things that were made at once, no one sees what had to be made earlier or later except in that Wisdom through which all things were made, in order and at once.

That day, then, which God made first, if it is the spiritual and rational creation, that is, the angels and powers above the heavens, was presented to all the works of God in this order of presence. This was the order of knowledge by which that creation knew beforehand in the Word of God the things to be made and knew in creation the things that had been made. It did not do this through the delays of temporal intervals. Earlier and later belonged to the connection among creatures, while in the effective power of the Creator all things were at once. For he made the things that were to be in such a way that he did not make temporal things temporally. Rather, the times he made ran their course. And so these seven days, which the light of the heavenly body unfolds and folds back as it goes round, are a kind of shadow and sign. They prompt us to seek those days in which the created spiritual light could be presented to all the works of God through the perfection of the number six, and then, in the seventh, God's rest, have morning but no evening. God's resting on the seventh day does not mean that he needed the seventh day for his rest. It means that in the sight of his angels he rested from all the works he had made, and he rested nowhere but in himself, who was not made. That is, his angelic creation was presented like a day with its evening for knowing all his works, both in him and in themselves. After all his very good works, it was to know nothing better than this: that he rests from all of them in himself and needs none of them to be more blessed.
BOOK FIVE

This is the book of the creation of heaven and earth, when the day was made: God made heaven and earth and every green thing of the field before it was on the earth, and every grass of the field before it had sprung up. For God had not sent rain on the earth, and there was no man to work the earth. But a spring rose up from the earth and watered the whole face of the earth. Now the view that God made one day becomes firmer still, the view that the six or seven days could be counted by repeating this one day. For Holy Scripture now says it more openly. It sums up, as it were, everything it had said from the beginning up to this point and adds: This is the book of the creation, or making, of heaven and earth, when the day was made. No one is going to say that heaven and earth are mentioned here in the same way as in the words spoken before the creation of the day was introduced: In the beginning God made heaven and earth. That passage can be understood to mean that God made something without day before he made the day. In its proper place I said what I thought should be said about how it can be taken, without denying anyone the freedom to understand it better. But now Scripture says: This is the book of the creation of heaven and earth, when the day was made. In my opinion this shows clearly enough that heaven and earth are not mentioned here as they were in the beginning, before the day was made, when darkness was over the abyss. They are mentioned as heaven and earth were made when the day was made, that is, with the parts and kinds of things already formed and distinguished. Through these the whole creation, set in order and composed, presents this appearance which is called the world.

So the heaven mentioned here is the one God called the firmament when he had created it, together with everything in it. And the earth is the one that held the lowest place along with the abyss, together with everything in it. For Scripture goes on to add: God made heaven and earth. It places the words "heaven and earth" before mentioning that the day was made and repeats them after mentioning it. In this way it does not allow us to suspect that it now names heaven and earth in the same sense as in the beginning, before the day was created. For it wove the words together like this: This is the book of the creation of heaven and earth, when the day was made, God made heaven and earth. Someone might want to understand the first phrase, the book of the creation of heaven and earth, in the sense of the words In the beginning God made heaven and earth, spoken before God founded the day, on the grounds that here too heaven and earth are mentioned first and the day is made afterward. That person would be corrected by the words that follow, because even after the making of the day is mentioned, the words "heaven and earth" are added again.

And yet the very fact that "when" was placed there and joined with the day was made would force even a contentious person to admit that no other understanding is possible. Suppose it had been put this way: This is the book of the creation of heaven and earth. The day was made; God made heaven and earth. Then someone might perhaps think that the book of the creation of heaven and earth was so called in the same sense as In the beginning God made heaven and earth, before the day was founded. He might think that the day was made was added next, just as Scripture afterward narrated there that God made the day, and that God made heaven and earth was then said again, now referring to the way these were made after the day was founded. But it was put this way: when the day was made. You may connect this with the preceding words to make one sentence: This is the book of the creation of heaven and earth, when the day was made. Or you may connect it with the following words, so that the complete sentence is: When the day was made, God made heaven and earth. Either way, it undoubtedly compels us to understand that heaven and earth are mentioned as they were made when the day was made. Then, after the words God made heaven and earth, Scripture added: and every green thing of the field, and these were clearly made on the third day. This shows still more plainly that it is the same one day that God made, and that the second and third days and the rest up to the seventh were made by repeating it.

But since Scripture wanted the whole creation to be understood here under the name of heaven and earth, as the Scriptures usually do, one may ask why it added: and every green thing of the field. It seems to me that this was put there to show more pointedly which day was meant by the words when the day was made. For someone might quickly assume that the day meant here is the day of bodily light, whose circuit brings us the alternation of daytime and nighttime. But we can recall the order of the created things and find that every green thing of the field was created on the third day, before the sun was made. The sun was made on the fourth day, and its presence completes the ordinary day we know every day. So when we hear: When the day was made, God made heaven and earth and every green thing of the field, we are prompted to think about that day itself and to try to track it down with our understanding. It may be a bodily day in some light unknown to us, or a spiritual day in the fellowship of the angelic unity, but in any case not a day like the one we know here.

It is also worth noticing that Scripture could have said: This is the book of the creation of heaven and earth, when God made heaven and earth. Then we would understand under heaven and earth whatever is in them. Divine Scripture usually speaks that way. Very often it indicates the whole creation by the words "heaven and earth," sometimes adding "and the sea," and sometimes adding the words: and all that is in them. Whichever of these it used, we would understand the day as included there too, whether the day God first created or the one that the presence of the sun makes. But Scripture did not speak that way. Instead it inserted the day, saying: when the day was made. Nor did it say: This is the book of the creation of day and heaven and earth, as if following the order in which they are narrated as made. Nor did it say: This is the book of the creation of heaven and earth, when day and heaven and earth were made, when God made heaven and earth and every green thing of the field. Nor: This is the book of the creation of heaven and earth, when God made day and heaven and earth and every green thing of the field. Nor: This is the book of the creation of heaven and earth. God made day and heaven and earth and every green thing of the field. Ordinary usage would rather have called for these ways of speaking. But Scripture says: This is the book of the creation of heaven and earth, when the day was made, God made heaven and earth and every green thing of the field. It is as if it were suggesting that God made heaven and earth and every green thing of the field at the time when the day was made.

Moreover, the earlier narrative indicates that the day was made first and counts it as one day. After it the narrative counts a second day, on which the firmament was made, and a third, on which the forms of land and sea were set in order and the earth brought forth trees and plants. Or is this perhaps what we were working to show in the previous book, that God made all things at once? For that narrative sequence first recounted that all things were created and completed in the order of six days, and now it brings everything back to one day under the name of heaven and earth, adding the kind of shrubs as well. No doubt this is for the reason I gave above. If the day were perhaps understood according to our familiar usage, the reader would be corrected on remembering that God told the earth to bring forth the green things of the field before there was this solar day. So the testimony that God created all things at once is not brought in from some other book of Holy Scripture.
