The nearby testimony of the very next page reminds us of it, saying: When the day was made, God made heaven and earth and every green thing of the field. This lets you understand that this day was repeated seven times to make seven days. And when you hear that all things were made then, when the day was made, you may grasp, if you can, that the sixfold or sevenfold repetition took place without intervals of delay and spans of time. If you cannot yet do so, leave these things for those who are able to contemplate them. Make progress yourself with Scripture, which does not abandon you in your weakness but walks more slowly with you at a mother's pace. Scripture speaks in such a way that its loftiness mocks the proud, its depth fills the attentive with awe, its truth feeds the great, and its kindness nourishes the little ones.

What, then, does the next passage mean? For the text runs on like this: When the day was made, God made heaven and earth and every green thing of the field before it was on the earth, and every grass of the field before it sprang up. What does this mean? Must we not ask where God made these things before they were on the earth and before they sprang up? Who would not more readily believe that God made them when they sprang up, not before? He would believe that unless this divine utterance reminded him that God made them before they sprang up. So even if he cannot find where they were made, anyone who believes this Scripture with piety still believes that they were made before they sprang up. For it is the impious who do not believe it.

What then shall we say? That, as some have thought, all things were made in the very Word of God before they sprang up on the earth? But if they were made in this way, they were made not when the day was made but before the day was made. Yet Scripture says plainly: When the day was made, God made heaven and earth and every green thing of the field before it was on the earth, and every grass before it sprang up. If, then, they were made when the day was made, they were certainly not made before the day was made. They were therefore not made in the Word, who is coeternal with the Father, before the day and before anything at all was made, but when the day was made. For the things that are in the Word of God before all creation are certainly not made. These things, however, were made when the day was made, as the words of Scripture declare, and yet before they were on the earth and before they sprang up. That is what is said of the green things and the grass of the field.

Where, then? Were they in the earth itself, causally and in their reasons, as all things are already present in seeds before they in some way unfold and display their growth and their forms through the measured courses of time? But the seeds we see are already on the earth; they have already sprung up. Or were they not on the earth but beneath it, and so made before they sprang up, since they sprang up only when the seeds germinated and, as growth was added, broke out into the air? We now see this happen over stretches of time allotted to each kind. Were seeds, then, made when the day was made? Was every green thing of the field and every grass contained in them, not yet in the form they have once they have sprung up above the earth, but in the power they have in the seminal reasons? Did the earth, then, produce seeds first? But that is not how Scripture spoke when it said: And the earth brought forth the herb of pasture, or herb of grass, sowing seed according to its kind and according to its likeness, and the fruit-bearing tree producing fruit, whose seed is in itself according to its kind upon the earth. From these words it appears rather that the seeds arose from the herbs and trees, and that these arose not from seeds but from the earth. This is all the more so because the words of God themselves run the same way. For he does not say: Let the seeds in the earth sprout the herb of grass and the fruit-bearing tree. He says: Let the earth sprout the herb of grass sowing seed, to indicate that seed comes from the herb, not the herb from seed. And so it was done. And the earth brought forth: that is, it was first done so in the knowledge of that day, and then the earth brought forth, so that this might come about also in the very creation that had been established.

How, then, were they made before they were on the earth and before they sprang up? Is it as though being made together with heaven and earth was one thing for them, when that day was made which God made first, a day unusual and unknown to us, and springing up on the earth was another? The latter happens only through these days that the circuit of the sun produces, over stretches of time suited to each kind. If that is so, and if that day is the fellowship and unity of the angels and powers above the heavens, then beyond doubt God's creation is known to the angels in a very different way than it is known to us. Even apart from the fact that they know it in the Word of God, through whom all things were made, I say that it is known to them very differently than to us even in itself. They know it primordially, so to speak, or originally, as God first established it, after which he rested from his works and established nothing further. We know it according to the governance of things already established, through the sequences of time. In this governance God works until now, those things having already been completed in the perfection of the number six.

So it was said that the earth then brought forth herb and tree causally, that is, it received the power of bringing them forth. In the earth, as in the roots of time, so to speak, the things that were to come about through time had already been made. For afterward God certainly planted a paradise toward the east and made every tree that was beautiful to look at and good for food spring up there out of the earth. Yet we must not say that he then added to creation something he had not made before, as if something had to be added afterward to that perfection in which he completed all things very good on the sixth day. All the natures of shrubs and trees had already been made in the first establishing, and from that establishing God rested. Since then he moves and governs through the courses of time the very things he established and from which he rested once they were established. So he not only planted paradise then, but also plants now all things that are born. For who else creates these things even now but he who works until now? But now he creates them from things that already exist. Then, however, they were created by him when they did not exist at all, when that day too was made, which itself did not exist at all: that is, the spiritual and intellectual creation.

So with the movements of creation, once it was made, times began to run. It is therefore pointless to look for times before creation, as if times could be found before times. For if there were no movement of either spiritual or bodily creation, by which future things succeed past ones through the present, there would be no time at all. But creation certainly could not move if it did not exist. Time, then, began from creation rather than creation from time, but both are from God; for from him and through him and in him are all things. Nor should the statement that time began from creation be taken to mean that time is not a creature. Time is the movement of a creature from one thing to another, as things follow one another according to the ordering of God, who governs everything he created. Therefore, when we think of the first establishing of creatures, the works from which God rested on the seventh day, we must not think of those days as like these solar days. Nor should we think of that working as like the way God now works something in time. We should think of it as the working from which times were to begin, by which he made all things at once. He gave them an order, not by intervals of time but by a connection of causes, so that the things made at once were also brought to completion as that day was presented six times.

Thus formless and formable matter, both spiritual and bodily, was made first, not in the order of time but in the order of causes. From it was to be made whatever was to be made, though it too had not existed before it was established. It was established by none other than that supreme and true God from whom are all things. Is it signified by the name of heaven and earth, which God made in the beginning before that one day which he established, and was it already called by that name because heaven and earth were made from it? Or is it signified by the name of the invisible and unformed earth and the dark abyss? This has already been discussed in the first book.

Among the things that were formed out of formlessness, which are more evidently called created, made or established, the day was made first. It was fitting that the first place in creation should be held by that nature which could know the creature through the Creator, not the Creator through the creature. Second came the firmament, where the bodily world begins. Third came the forms of sea and land, and in the land, potentially, so to speak, the nature of herbs and trees. For in this way the earth, at God's word, produced them before they had sprung up, receiving all their numbers, which it would put forth through time according to its kind. Then, after this dwelling-place of things, as it were, had been established, the lights and stars were created on the fourth day, so that the upper part of the world might first be furnished with visible things that move within the world. On the fifth day the nature of the waters, since it is joined to sky and air, brought forth at God's word its native inhabitants, that is, everything that swims and flies. These too were brought forth potentially, in numbers that would be put forth through fitting movements of time. On the sixth day came the land animals, in the same way: the last creatures, as it were, from the last element of the world. They too were made potentially, and time would afterwards visibly unfold their numbers.

That day knew this whole order of ordered creation. Through this knowledge it was, in a sense, presented six times, and so it displayed what looked like six days, though it is one day. It recognized the things that were made first in the Creator and then in themselves. It did not remain in them, but referred even its later knowledge of them to the love of God. In this way it presented evening and morning and midday in all of them, not through stretches of time but because of the order of the things established. Finally it presented the knowledge of its Creator's rest, since he rests in himself from all his works. In this knowledge it has no evening, and for this reason it was found worthy to be blessed and sanctified. That is why Scripture commends the number seven, and the Church knows it, as dedicated in some way to the Holy Spirit.

This, then, is the book of the creation of heaven and earth. In the beginning God made heaven and earth with respect to a certain formability, so to speak, of matter, which was afterward to be formed by his Word, and which preceded its own formation not in time but in origin. For certainly, when it was being formed, the day was made first. When the day was made, God made heaven and earth and every green thing of the field before it was on the earth, and every grass of the field before it sprang up. So we have discussed it, unless something clearer and more fitting could be seen and said, or ever may be.

Then follows: For God had not rained upon the earth, and there was no man to work the earth. What this refers to and what it intimates to us is hard to work out. It is as though God made the grass of the field before it sprang up precisely because he had not yet rained upon the earth. If he had made the grass after rain, it would seem to have sprung up by the rain rather than to have been made by him. But what of that? Is what springs up after rain made by anyone other than the same God? And why was there no man to work the earth? Had God not already made man on the sixth day and rested on the seventh from all his works? Or does Scripture mention this by way of recapitulation, because when God made every green thing and every grass of the field it had not yet rained on the earth and there was not yet a man? For he made these on the third day, but man on the sixth. But when God made every green thing and every grass of the field before it sprang up on the earth, it was not only that there was no man to work the earth. The grass itself was not yet on the earth, since Scripture says it was made before it sprang up. Or did God make these things on the third day because there was not yet a man to produce them by working the earth? As if so many trees and so many kinds of herbs did not spring from the earth without any human work at all!

Or are both statements made for this reason, that it had not yet rained on the earth and that there was not yet a man to work the earth? Where there is no human labour, these things grow by rain. But there are some that do not grow even by rain unless human labour is added. So now both helps are needed for everything to grow, but at that time both were lacking. Therefore God made these things by the power of his Word, without rain and without human work. Even now he himself makes them, but now through rain and through human hands, although neither he who plants is anything nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase.

What, then, does Scripture mean when it adds: But a spring went up from the earth and watered the whole face of the earth? Such a spring, flowing as abundantly as the Nile does for Egypt, could serve the whole earth in place of rain. Why, then, is it held up as something great that God made those growing things before it rained, when a spring watering the earth could help as much as rain? Even if it helped somewhat less, those things might perhaps grow smaller, but they would still grow. Or here too, as is its custom, does Scripture speak weakly as to the weak, and yet hint at something for whoever is able to understand it? Surely it does. A little earlier it mentioned that day, and so signified that one day was made by God and that God made heaven and earth when the day was made. This was so that we might think, as far as we can, that God made all things at once, although the earlier enumeration of six days seemed to show intervals of time. In the same way, having said that along with heaven and earth God made every green thing of the field before it was on the earth and every grass of the field before it sprang up, Scripture added: For God had not yet rained upon the earth, and there was no man to work the earth. It is as if to say: God did not make them in the way he now makes such things, when it rains and when people work. These things now come about through stretches of time, and these did not exist when he made all things at once, so that times too might begin from it.

What follows, then, is: But a spring went up from the earth and watered the whole face of the earth. From here on, I think, Scripture intimates what comes about over intervals of time out of that first establishing of creatures, in which all things were made at once. It rightly began with that element from which all kinds are born, whether of animals or of herbs and trees, so that they may carry out their temporal numbers as these are distributed to their own natures. For all the first beginnings of seeds are moist and grow from moisture, whether those from which all flesh is produced or those from which all shrubs are produced. And in them are most effective numbers, which draw in their train the powers that follow from those perfect works of God from which he rested on the seventh day.

Still, it is fair to ask what this spring was that could water the whole face of the earth. If it existed and was then stopped up or dried up, we must look for the cause. For now we see that there is no spring by which the whole face of the earth is watered. Perhaps, then, human sin deserved this penalty too: that the great abundance of that spring was held back and took away from the lands their very easy fruitfulness, so that the labour of their inhabitants might be increased. Human conjecture could assert this, though no scripture has recorded it, were it not for an objection. Human sin, on which the penalty of labour was imposed, came about after the delights of paradise. Yet paradise had its own very great spring, of which we must speak more carefully later in its place. From its single source four great rivers, known to the nations, are said to flow. Where, then, were this spring and these rivers when that one very great spring went up from the earth and watered the whole face of the earth? For certainly the Gihon, which is called the Nile and is one of those four, was not watering Egypt at the time when a spring went up from the earth and saturated not Egypt alone but the whole face of the earth.

Should we believe that God at first willed to water the whole earth with one very great spring? Then the things he had established in it in their principles, having received the help of moisture, might now be produced also over spans of time, with different numbers of days according to the diversity of their kinds. Afterward, when paradise was planted, he would have held back that spring and filled the earth with many springs, as we now see it. But from the one spring of paradise he would have divided four huge rivers. In this way the rest of the earth, full of the kinds of its creatures carrying out the fitting numbers of their times, would also have its own springs and rivers. And paradise, planted in a choicer place, would send forth those four rivers from the source of its spring. Or did God first water the whole earth from that one spring of paradise, then overflowing much more abundantly? Did he make the earth fruitful to bring forth, through the numbers of time, the kinds he had created in it without intervals of time? Did he afterward hold back the vast outburst of waters in that place, so that they would flow from various sources of rivers and springs throughout the whole earth? And did he then plant paradise in the region of that spring, which no longer watered the whole earth but sent out only those four memorable rivers, so that he might place there the man he had made?

For not everything has been written down about how times ran on after that first establishing of things, or how the governance of creatures followed, the creatures first made and completed on that sixth day. Only as much was written as the Spirit who was in the writer judged sufficient, things that would serve not only for knowledge of what had been done but also as a prefiguring of what was to come. So we, who do not know, conjecture what could have happened that he, who did know, left out. In our small measure and so far as we are helped, we attempt only this: that no absurdity or contradiction may be thought to exist in the Holy Scriptures that might offend the reader's judgment. Otherwise, thinking that what Scripture records as done could not have been done, the reader may either recoil from the faith or never come to it.

So we are asking about this spring, and how the statement that it went up from the earth and watered the whole face of the earth may not seem impossible. If what we have said seems impossible to anyone, let him look for some other explanation by which this Scripture may still be shown to be truthful. It is beyond doubt truthful even if it is not shown to be. If he wants to argue so as to prove it false, either he will say nothing true about the establishing and governance of creatures, or, if he does say true things, he will think this Scripture false because he does not understand it. Suppose, for instance, he contends that the whole face of the earth could not be watered by one spring, however great. For if it did not water the mountains, it did not water the whole face of the earth. But if it watered the mountains too, it was no longer a bestowal of nourishment but a flood. And if the earth was like that at the time, it was all sea, and the dry land had not yet been separated.

The reply to him is that this could happen through the alternation of seasons, as the Nile at one season overflows across the plains of Egypt and at another returns to its banks. Or if the Nile is believed to gather its yearly rise from the waters and winter frosts of some unknown and distant part of the world, what can be said of the alternating tides of the ocean, or of certain shores that are laid bare by the waves far and wide and covered again in turn? I say nothing of what is reported about the remarkable alternation of certain springs: at a fixed interval of years they flood so as to water the whole region around them, though at other times they supply it with enough water for drinking only from deep wells. Why, then, should it be incredible if the whole earth was then watered from one source of the abyss, flowing and ebbing in alternate floods? Leave aside the part of the abyss called the sea, which surrounds the lands with its evident breadth and bitter waves. There remains the part that the earth holds in hidden hollows, from which all springs and rivers distribute themselves through various tracts and veins and burst out each in its own place. Suppose Scripture chose to call the vastness of the abyss in that part alone a spring rather than springs, because of the unity of its nature. Suppose it says that this spring went up from the earth through countless passages of caves and fissures and, spread out everywhere like strands of hair, watered the whole face of the earth. It did so not in a continuous expanse like a sea or a pool, but as we see waters run through riverbeds and the windings of streams and soak the nearby land when they overflow. Who would not accept this, except someone labouring under a contentious spirit? The whole face of the earth can also be understood to have been watered in the sense in which the whole face of a garment is said to be coloured, even if the colour is not continuous but in patches. This is especially so since it is credible that at that time, when the lands were new, most of them, if not all, were flat, so that the streams bursting out could spread and extend more widely.

Therefore, as to the size or the multitude of this spring, let us labour over it no longer. Perhaps it had a single outburst from somewhere. Perhaps it was called one spring because of some unity in the hidden hollows of the earth, from which all the waters of all springs, great and small, gush forth over the earth, so that it went up from the earth through all its divisions and watered the whole face of the earth. Or perhaps, and this is more credible, Scripture put the singular for the plural, since it does not say, "One spring went up from the earth," but, "But a spring went up from the earth." We should then understand many springs throughout the whole earth, each watering its own places or regions. In the same way one says "the soldier" and many soldiers are understood, and "the locust" and "the frog" were spoken of in the plagues with which the Egyptians were struck, though the locusts and frogs were countless.

But let us consider again and again whether the view we were stating can hold good in every respect: that God worked in one way in the first founding of all creatures, the works from which he rested on the seventh day, and in another way in his administration of them, by which he works until now. That is, then he made all things at once, without any intervals of temporal delay, but now he works through the lapse of time. Through these lapses of time we see the stars move from rising to setting and the sky change from summer to winter. We see seeds sprout, grow, turn green and wither at fixed moments of days. We see animals, too, conceived, completed and born within appointed limits and courses of time, then running through the stages of life to old age and death, and other temporal things of this sort. For who works these things but God, even without any such motion of his own? Time does not happen to him. Between those works of God from which he rested on the seventh day and these which he works until now, Scripture inserted a kind of joint in its narrative. It indicated that it had finished setting out the former and was now beginning to weave together the account of the latter. The conclusion of the former was marked thus: “This is the book of the creation of heaven and earth: when day was made, God made heaven and earth and every green thing of the field before it was upon the earth, and every plant of the field before it sprang up. For God had not rained upon the earth, and there was no man to work the earth.” The account of the latter began thus: “But a spring went up from the earth and watered the whole face of the earth.” From this mention of the spring onward, the things narrated were done through the lapse of time, not all at once.

So there are three things, each of a different kind: the unchangeable reasons of all creatures in the Word of God, those works of his from which he rested on the seventh day, and these which he works from them until now. Of these three, the last I have named is known to us in some measure through the bodily senses and our ordinary experience of this life. The other two, however, are remote from our senses and from the ordinary range of human thought. So they must first be believed on divine authority. Then they may be known in some measure through the things that are known, more or less, as far as each person is able according to the measure of his capacity, helped by God to be able.

Consider first those divine, unchangeable and eternal reasons. The very Wisdom of God, through whom all things were made, knew them before they were made, as Scripture testifies: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.” Who, then, would be so mad as to say that God did not make the things he knew? Further, if he knew them, where did he know them but within himself, with whom was the Word through whom all things were made? For if he knew them outside himself, who had taught him? “For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor? Or who has first given to him, that he should be repaid? For from him and through him and in him are all things.”

Indeed, what follows in the Gospel gives ample support to this view. The evangelist goes on to say: “What was made, in him is life, and the life was the light of men.” This is because rational minds, the kind in which man was made in the image of God, have no true light of their own except the very Word of God, through whom all things were made. They will be able to share in him once they are cleansed of all iniquity and error.

So the sentence “What was made in him is life” should not be read with a pause after “What was made in him,” followed by “is life.” For what was not made in him? In the psalm, after many earthly creatures as well have been listed, it is said: “In wisdom you have made all things.” And the Apostle says: “For in him were created all things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible.” If we punctuate in that way, then, it will follow that the earth itself and whatever is in it are life. It is absurd to say that all things are alive. How much more absurd to say that they are even life! This is especially so since he specifies what kind of life he is speaking of when he adds: “and the life was the light of men.” So the sentence should be punctuated this way: having said “What was made,” we then add “in him is life.” It is not life in itself, that is, in its own nature, by which it was made so as to be a founded thing and a creature. Rather, in him it is life, because he knew all the things made through him before they were made. For this reason they were in him not as the creature that he made but as life and the light of men, which is Wisdom itself and the Word itself, the only-begotten Son of God. What was made is life in him, then, in the way in which it was said: “As the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son to have life in himself.”

Nor should we pass over the fact that the more correct manuscripts read: “What was made, in him was life.” Then “was life” is to be understood in the same way as “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” What was made, then, already was life in him. And it was not life of just any sort, for cattle too are said to live, though they cannot enjoy any share in wisdom. Rather, “the life was the light of men.” For rational minds, purified by his grace, can attain to a vision of such a kind that there is nothing higher or more blessed.

But even if we read and understand it as “What was made, in him is life,” this view still stands. What was made through him is understood to be life in him, and in that life he saw all things when he made them. As he saw, so he made. He did not look at anything outside himself; within himself he numbered all the things he made. Nor is his vision different from the Father’s; it is one, just as the substance is one. The book of Job also proclaims that very Wisdom through which all things were made: “But wisdom,” it says, “where is it found? Or what is the place of understanding? Mortal man does not know its way, nor will it be found among men.” And a little later: “We have heard,” it says, “of its glory. The Lord has commended its way, and he knows its place. For he looks upon everything under heaven and knows all the things on earth that he made: the weights of the winds, the measures of the water. When he made them, as he saw, so he numbered them.” These and similar testimonies prove that all these things, before they were made, were in the knowledge of the Maker. Surely they were better there, where they were truer, where they were eternal and unchangeable. It ought to be enough for anyone to know, or firmly believe, that God made all these things. Still, I do not think anyone is so senseless as to suppose that God made things he did not know. And if he knew them before he made them, then surely before they were made they were known with him in the way in which they live eternally and unchangeably and are life. Once made, however, they exist in the way in which each creature exists in its own kind.

That eternal and unchangeable nature which is God has within itself its own being, as was said to Moses: “I am who I am.” It exists in a way far different from the things that were made. For that truly and primordially is which always is in the same way, and which not only is not changed but cannot be changed at all. He is none of the things he made, yet he holds all things primordially, just as he himself is. For he would not make them unless he knew them before he made them. He would not know them unless he saw them, nor see them unless he had them. And he could not have things not yet made except in the way in which he himself is unmade. That substance, I say, is ineffable. One human being cannot speak of it to another at all except by borrowing certain words of place and time, though it is before all times and before all places. Nevertheless, he who made us is nearer to us than many of the things that were made. For “in him we live and move and have our being.” Most of those things, however, are remote from our mind because their kind is unlike it, since they are bodily. Nor is our mind fit to see them with God in the very reasons by which they were made, and so to know how many they are, how great, and of what kind, even if we do not see them with the bodily senses. They are remote from our bodily senses because they are far away, or because other things placed between or in front of them cut them off from our sight and reach. So it happens that it is harder to discover them than to discover him by whom they were made. Yet to perceive him with a devout mind, even in the smallest part, is incomparably happier and more excellent than to comprehend all those things. That is why the investigators of this world are rightly blamed in the book of Wisdom: “For if they were able to know so much,” it says, “that they could assess the world, how did they not more easily find its Lord?” The foundations of the earth are unknown to our eyes, yet he who founded the earth draws near to our minds.

Now let us consider the things that God made all at once. He completed them on the sixth day and rested from them on the seventh. Afterwards we shall consider the works in which he works until now. For he himself is before the ages. We say that some things are “from the age,” namely those that exist from when the age began, such as the world itself. Other things we say are “in the age,” such as the things born in the world. So when Scripture had said, “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made,” a little later it says: “He was in this world, and the world was made through him.” Of this work of God it is written in another place: “You who made the world out of formless matter.” This world is very often called by the name of heaven and earth, as we have already mentioned. Scripture says that God made it “when day was made.” We have already discussed these words as far as seemed fitting. We showed how they agree with the founding of this world: that it was completed in six days with all the things in it, and that it was made when day was made. In this way they also agree with the statement that he created all things at once.

There is much in this whole creation of God that we do not know. Some things are in the heavens, too high for our senses to reach. Some are perhaps in uninhabitable regions of the earth. Others lie hidden below, either in the depth of the abyss or in the secret recesses of the earth. Before these things were made, they certainly did not exist. How, then, were things known to God which did not exist? And again, how could he make things that were not known to him? For he made nothing in ignorance. So he made things he knew; he did not come to know things after they were made. Accordingly, before they were made, they both were and were not. They were in God’s knowledge; they were not in their own nature. And for this reason that day was made, to which they might become known in both ways, both in God and in themselves. The first is a morning or daytime knowledge, so to speak; the second is an evening knowledge, so to speak. But as for God himself, I do not dare to say that they became known to him in any other way, once he had made them, than the way in which he knew them in order to make them. With him there is no change, nor shadow of a moment.

He certainly does not need messengers in order to know lower things, as if he became more knowing through them. Rather, he knows all things stably and unchangeably in that simple and wonderful way. He has messengers for our sake and for their own. For they consult him about lower things and comply with his heavenly precepts and commands. To obey and attend upon God in this way is good for them in the order of their own nature and substance. In Greek, messengers are called angels. This general name is applied to that whole heavenly city, which we judge was founded as the first day.

For not even that mystery of the kingdom of heaven was hidden from them, which was revealed at the fitting time for our salvation. By it we are freed from this pilgrimage and joined to their company. Nor could they be ignorant of it, since that very seed which came at the fitting time was “ordained through them in the hand of a mediator.” That is, it was ordained in the power of him who is their Lord, both in the form of God and in the form of a servant. The Apostle likewise says: “To me, the least of all the saints, this grace was given: to announce among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ, and to bring to light what is the dispensation of the mystery hidden from the ages in God, who created all things. This was so that the manifold wisdom of God might now be made known through the church to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places, according to the purpose of the ages which he accomplished in Christ Jesus our Lord.” So this was hidden from the ages in God in such a way that the manifold wisdom of God was nevertheless made known through the church to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places. For the church is there primordially, and after the resurrection this church of ours too is to be gathered there, so that we may be equal to the angels of God. It was made known to them, then, from the ages, because no creature exists before the ages; every creature exists from the ages. For the ages arose from creation, and creation is from the ages, since its beginning is the beginning of the ages. But the Only-begotten is before the ages, and through him the ages were made. And so Scripture says, speaking in the person of Wisdom: “Before the ages he founded me.” He did this so that he might make all things in Wisdom, to whom it was said: “In wisdom you have made all things.”

What is hidden is made known to the angels not only in God. It also appears to them here, when it is brought about and made public. The same Apostle testifies to this: “And without doubt,” he says, “great is the mystery of godliness, which was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, appeared to angels, preached among the Gentiles, believed in the world, taken up in glory.” Unless I am mistaken, there is a reason why God is said to come to know things, as if at some present moment. It would be surprising if he were not always said to know them in this sense: that he causes them to be known, whether by angels or by men. In this manner of speaking, what is brought about is signified by naming the one who brings it about. This is frequent in the holy Scriptures. It is especially common when something is said of God that does not fit him if the words are taken in their proper sense, as Truth itself, presiding over our minds, cries out.

Now, then, let us distinguish the works of God which he works until now from those works from which he rested on the seventh day. For some think that God made only the world itself, and that everything else is now made by the world, as he ordained and commanded, while God himself does nothing. Against them we bring forward that saying of the Lord: “My Father works until now.” And so that no one would think he works something within himself and not in this world, he says: “The Father, abiding in me, does his works.” He also says: “As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he will.” Further, God works not only great and preeminent things but also these earthly and lowest ones. So the Apostle says: “Fool! What you sow is not brought to life unless it dies. And what you sow is not the body that is to be, but a bare grain, perhaps of wheat or of some other kind. But God gives it a body as he wills, and to each of the seeds its own body.” So let us believe, or if we can, also understand, that God works until now. If his working were withdrawn from the things he has founded, they would perish.

But suppose we thought that he now establishes some creature whose kind he did not implant in that first founding. Then we would plainly contradict Scripture, which says that he completed all his works on the sixth day. It is evident that he makes many new things, which he did not make then, according to those kinds of things which he first founded. But it cannot rightly be believed that he establishes a new kind, since he completed all things then. So by a hidden power he moves his whole creation, and it is turned by that motion. Angels carry out his commands. Stars circle. Winds alternate. The deep of the waters is stirred by its currents and by its various massings even in the air. Green things sprout and unfold their seeds. Animals are begotten and lead their own lives by their varied appetites. The wicked are permitted to test the just. Through all this, creation unfolds the ages which he had laid within it, folded up as it were, when it was first founded. Yet they would not unfold in their courses if he who founded it ceased to govern them by his provident motion.

The things that are formed and born in time ought to remind us how we should consider them. For it is not written in vain of Wisdom that “she shows herself cheerfully to her lovers in the ways, and meets them with all providence.” Some have thought that the higher parts of the world, from the boundary of this denser air upward, are governed by divine providence. They also thought that this lowest part is driven rather by chance and random motions. This lowest part includes the earthy and watery region and this nearer air, which grows moist with the exhalations of land and waters and in which winds and clouds arise. Such people should not be listened to at all. The psalm speaks against them. After setting forth the praise of heavenly things, it turns also to these lower things, saying: “Praise the Lord from the earth, you dragons and all deeps; fire, hail, snow, ice, stormy wind, which fulfill his word.” For nothing seems so much tossed about by chance as all these stormy and turbulent conditions. They vary and change the face of this lower sky, which is not without reason also counted under the name of earth. But when the psalm added, “which fulfill his word,” it showed clearly enough that the order of these things too is subject to divine command. That order is hidden from us; it is not absent from the nature of the universe. And what of this? The Savior said with his own mouth that not one sparrow falls to the ground without God’s will. He also said that God himself clothes the grass of the field, which shortly is to be thrown into the oven. Does he not confirm that divine providence rules this whole part of the world assigned to mortal and corruptible things? And does he not confirm that it rules even the most worthless and lowly particles of this part?

Certainly these people deny this and do not acquiesce in sacred utterances of such great authority. They think this part of the world is disturbed by random motions rather than ruled by the wisdom of the divine Most High. To prove this, as they suppose, they misuse a twofold argument: either the inconstancy of the weather, which I mentioned above, or the good and bad fortunes of men, which do not befall them according to the merits of their lives. But suppose they saw how great an order appears in the bodily members of any living creature. I do not mean the order seen by physicians, who for the needs of their art have carefully explored these members, laid them open and enumerated them. I mean the order seen by any person of ordinary mind and reflection. Would they not cry out that God does not cease from governing even for a moment of time? From him comes every measure, every equality of numbers, every order of weights. What, then, can be thought more absurd and foolish than to suppose that the whole of a thing is empty of the will and rule of providence, when you see its lowest and smallest parts formed with such careful arrangement? When those parts are considered a little more attentively, they strike us with an ineffable awe of wonder. The nature of the soul surpasses the nature of the body. So what is more insane than to think that divine providence makes no judgment about the conduct of human beings, when such clear evidence of its skill shines out and is displayed in their flesh? But these smallest things are readily available to our senses, and we easily trace them out, so the order of things shines out in them. Things whose order they cannot see, however, they suppose to be disordered. These are people who think nothing exists except what they can see, or who, if they do think something exists, imagine it to be like what they are accustomed to see.

The same divine providence guides our steps through holy Scripture, so that we do not fall into that perversity. With the same help, then, let us try to trace out from God’s works themselves where he created these things all at once, when he rested from his completed works. Their forms he still works through the order of times until now. Let us consider, then, the beauty of any tree in its trunk, branches, leaves and fruit. This form certainly did not arise suddenly at such a size and in such a shape. It arose in an order that we also know. For it rose from a root which the sprout first fixed in the earth, and from there all those parts grew, formed and distinct. That sprout, in turn, came from a seed. So all those things were in the seed primordially, not in the bulk of bodily size but in causal force and power. For the tree’s size was built up from an abundance of earth and moisture. But the tiny grain holds a more wonderful and more excellent power. By it the surrounding moisture, mixed with earth, was able to be turned like raw material into the quality of that wood, the spreading of the branches, the greenness and shape of the leaves, the forms and abundance of the fruit, and the most orderly distinction of all its parts. For what rises or hangs from that tree that has not been drawn out and brought forth from a kind of hidden treasury in that seed? But that seed came from a tree, though not that tree but another, and that tree came in turn from another seed. Sometimes, too, a tree comes from a tree, when a shoot is cut off and planted. So seed comes from tree, tree from seed, and tree from tree. But seed never comes from seed unless a tree intervenes first, whereas tree comes from tree even if no seed intervenes. So in alternating succession one comes from the other, but both come from the earth, and the earth does not come from them. The earth, therefore, is their first parent. So it is with animals too. It may be uncertain whether the seeds come from them or they from seeds. But whichever of these comes first, it most certainly comes from the earth.

In the seed itself there were present, invisibly and all at once, all the things that would rise up into a tree over time. In the same way we must think of the world itself. When God created all things at once, the world held all at once everything that was made in it and with it when the day was made. This was not only the heaven with the sun and moon and stars, whose form remains while they move in their rotation, and the earth and the deeps, which undergo what seem to be unsteady motions and, joined below, supply the other part of the world. It also included the things that water and earth produced potentially and causally, before they arose over the course of time in the way they are now known to us in the works that God works until now.

This being so, "this is the book of the creation of heaven and earth: when the day was made, God made heaven and earth and every green thing of the field before it was upon the earth, and every plant of the field before it had sprung up." He did not make them in the way he makes them by the work he works until now, through rain and human farming. That is why the words were added, "for God had not rained upon the earth, and there was no man to work the earth." He made them in the way he created all things at once and completed them in the number of six days, when he presented the day he had made to the things he had made six times over. This was not an interval alternating in time but an ordered knowledge, according to causes. From these works he rested on the seventh day, and he deigned to offer his rest also to the knowledge and joy of that same day. Therefore he blessed and sanctified that day not in any of his works but in his rest. From then on he established no further creature. Instead he governs and rules, by an act of administration, the things he made all at once, and so he works without ceasing, at once resting and working, as has already been discussed. Scripture takes up what is, as it were, the beginning of its account of these works he works until now, which unfold through the long course of time, and says: "But a spring rose up from the earth and watered the whole face of the earth." We have said what we thought should be said about this spring, so let us consider what follows by making a fresh beginning.
BOOK SIX

"And God formed man as dust from the earth and breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul." Here we must first see whether this is a recapitulation, so that we are now told how the man was made whom we read was made on the sixth day. Or did God, when he made all things at once, also make man among them in a hidden way, like the plant of the earth before it had sprung up? In that case man too, having already been made in a different way in some secret place of nature, like the things God created at once when the day was made, would in the course of time also be made in this way, in which he lives his life in this visible form, whether badly or well. Similarly, the plant that was made before it sprang up upon the earth sprang up when the time came, watered by that spring, so that it might be upon the earth.

First, then, let us try to take it as a recapitulation. For perhaps man was made on the sixth day in the same way that the day itself was first made, and the firmament, and the earth and sea. We should not say that these were first made and lay hidden in certain primordial beginnings, and then in the course of time came to light, as if sprouting into the appearance in which the world has been built. Rather, the world was established from the beginning of the age, when the day was made, and in its elements were established all at once the things that would later arise in the course of time, whether shrubs or animals, each according to its kind. Nor should we believe that even the stars were first made and stored away in the elements of the world, and afterward in the course of time came forth and shone out in the forms that gleam in the heavens. Rather, all things were created at once in that number six of perfection, when the day was made. Was man made in this way too, already in the form in which he lives in his own nature and does good or evil? Or was he also made in a hidden way, like the plant of the field before it sprang up, so that his being made from dust was the way he would later spring forth in the course of time?

Let us suppose, then, that he was formed from the clay on that very sixth day in this clear and visible form, but that this was not mentioned then and is now brought in by way of recapitulation. Let us see whether scripture itself agrees with us. This is certainly what is written while the works of the sixth day are still being recounted: "And God said: Let us make man in our image and likeness, and let him have power over the fish of the sea and the birds of the sky and all the cattle and all the earth and all the creeping things that creep upon the earth. And God made man; in the image of God he made him; male and female he made them. And God blessed them, saying: Increase and multiply and fill the earth and have dominion over it, and have power over the fish of the sea and the birds of the sky and all the cattle and all the earth and all the creeping things that creep upon the earth." On this view he had already been formed from the clay, and the woman had already been made from his side while he slept. But this had not been mentioned, and it is now mentioned by way of recapitulation. For it was not the case that the male was made on the sixth day and the female made later in the course of time. Scripture says, "he made him; male and female he made them, and blessed them." How, then, was the woman made for him after the man had already been placed in paradise? Or did scripture go back to this too as something it had passed over? For on that sixth day paradise must also have been planted, the man placed there and put to sleep so that Eve might be formed, and when she had been formed he must have woken and given her a name. But these things could only happen over intervals of time. So they were not made in the way that all things were created at once.

However easily one may imagine God making these things at once with all the rest, we certainly know that human words can only be uttered by the voice over brief intervals of time. We hear the man's words when he gave names to the animals or to the woman, and also when he went on to say, "For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two will be in one flesh." Whatever syllables these words were spoken in, not even two of their syllables could sound at once. How much less could all these things happen at once together with the things that were created at once! It follows that one of two things is true. On the first view, all those other things too were made not at once from the very first beginning of the ages but over delays and intervals of time. In that case that day was first established not as a spiritual but as a bodily substance, and it made morning and evening somehow, either by the circling of light or by its going out and drawing back. On the second view, we have considered everything discussed in the earlier books, and a probable reasoning has persuaded us of several things: that the day was spiritual, established on a high plane and before all else, a certain wise light called "day"; that its presence was offered to the establishment of things through ordered knowledge in the number six; that the words of scripture agree with this view when it says later, "When the day was made, God made heaven and earth and every green thing of the field before it was upon the earth, and every plant of the field before it sprang up"; and that what is written elsewhere also bears witness to it: "He who lives forever created all things at once." If this second view is right, there is no doubt that man's being formed from the clay of the earth, and his wife's being formed for him from his side, no longer belongs to the establishment in which all things were made at once, which God completed and then rested. It belongs to the working that now goes on through the long course of the ages, by which he works until now.

There is a further point. The very words that tell how God planted paradise, placed in it the man he had made, and brought the animals to him to name, and how, when no helper like him was found among them, God took out one of his ribs and formed the woman for him, make it clear enough that these things do not belong to the work of God from which he rested on the seventh day. They belong rather to the work by which he works until now through the course of time. For when paradise was planted, scripture tells it this way: "And God planted a paradise in Eden toward the east, and he placed there the man whom he had formed. And God further brought forth from the earth every tree beautiful to look at and good for food."

So when scripture says, "he further brought forth from the earth every tree beautiful to look at," it certainly shows that he brought forth trees from the earth in one way now and in another way then, on the third day, when the earth produced plants for fodder that bore seed according to their kind, and fruit-bearing trees according to their kind. For this is the meaning of "he further brought forth": in addition, that is, to what he had already brought forth. Then he brought them forth potentially and causally, in the work belonging to the creation of all things at once, from which he rested on the seventh day once it was completed. But now he brought them forth visibly, in the work belonging to the course of time, just as he works until now.

Someone might perhaps say that not every kind of tree was created on the third day, but that some kind was held back to be created on the sixth, when man was made and placed in paradise. But scripture declares very plainly what was created on the sixth day: the living soul, that is, according to each kind of four-footed creature, creeping thing and beast, and man himself, male and female, in the image of God. Scripture could therefore pass over how man was made, while still saying that he was made on that day, so that later, by recapitulating, it might make known how he was made: from the dust of the earth, and the woman for him from his side. But it could not pass over any kind of creature, whether where God said "let there be" or "let us make," or where it is said "so it was done" or "God made." Otherwise all things were distinguished day by day with such care to no purpose, if any suspicion can remain that the days were mixed together, so that, although plants and trees were assigned to the third day, we should believe that some trees were also created on the sixth day, though scripture said nothing of them on that day.

Finally, what shall we say about the beasts of the field and the birds of the sky that God brought to Adam to see what he would call them? This is how it is written: "And the Lord God said: It is not good for the man to be alone; let us make for him a helper like himself. And God further formed from the earth all the beasts of the field and all the birds of the sky, and he brought them to Adam to see what he would call them; and whatever Adam called each living soul, that was its name. And Adam gave names to all the cattle and to all the birds of the sky and to all the beasts of the field. But for Adam no helper like himself was found. And God cast a trance upon Adam, and he fell asleep; and he took one of his ribs and filled up the flesh in its place. And the Lord God built the rib that he took from Adam into a woman." Since no helper like the man had been found among the cattle, the beasts of the field and the birds of the sky, God then made him a helper like himself from a rib of his side. And this happened after he had further formed those same beasts of the field and birds of the sky from the earth and brought them to him. How, then, can this be understood to have happened on the sixth day? On that day the earth produced the living soul at the word of God, while the waters had produced the birds on the fifth day, likewise at the word of God. So scripture would not say here, "And God further formed from the earth all the beasts of the field and all the birds of the sky," unless the earth had already produced all the beasts of the field on the sixth day, and the water all the birds of the sky on the fifth. He formed them in one way then, that is, potentially and causally, as befitted the work by which he created all things at once and from which he rested on the seventh day. He formed them in another way now, as we see the things he creates over the spans of time, just as he works until now. It follows that Eve was made from her husband's side in these very familiar days of bodily light, which are made by the circling of the sun. For it was then that God further formed the beasts and birds from the earth, and when no helper like Adam himself was found among them, she was formed. So it was in days like these that God also formed Adam himself from the clay.

Nor should we say that the male was made on the sixth day and the female on later days, since on the sixth day itself it is said most plainly, "male and female he made them, and blessed them," along with the other things said about both and to both. So both were made in one way then, and both in another way now. Then they were made according to the power placed in the world by the word of God, as if in seed, when he created all things at once, from which he rested on the seventh day. From these all things would come to be, each in its own time, through the order of the ages. Now they were made according to the working that is supplied to the times, by which he works until now. In this way it was fitting that Adam should come to be in his own time from the clay of the earth, and his wife from her husband's side.

We have divided the works of God in this way. Some belong to those invisible days in which he created all things at once. Others belong to these days of ours, in which he works daily whatever unfolds in time from those things, as if from primordial wrappings. If we have followed the words of scripture that led us to make this distinction neither inappropriately nor absurdly, we must still take care. These matters are rather difficult to grasp, and slower minds are not able to attain them, so we must not be thought to hold and say something that we know we neither hold nor say. In the earlier books I prepared the reader as far as I could. Yet I think many are still in the dark on these passages. They think that man first existed in that work of God in which all things were created at once in such a way that he was already living some kind of life, so that he could discern, believe and understand the speech God addressed to him when he said, "Behold, I have given you every seed-bearing plant." Whoever thinks this should know that I neither held nor said it.

On the other hand, suppose I say that in that first establishment of things, in which God created all things at once, man did not exist as he exists now. He was not only not a man of full age; he was not even an infant. He was not only not an infant; he was not even a fetus in his mother's womb. Nor was he even the visible seed of a man. Then that reader will think he did not exist at all. So let him go back to scripture. He will find that man was made on the sixth day in the image of God, and that they were made male and female. Let him also ask when the woman was made, and he will find that it was outside those six days. For she was made when God further formed the beasts of the field and the birds of the sky from the earth, not when the waters produced the birds and the earth produced the living soul, among which are also the beasts. Yet man, both male and female, was made at that time. So he was made both then and later. It was not then and not later, or later and not then. Nor were others made later. The same two were made in one way then and in another way later. He will ask me, "How were they made later?" I will answer: visibly, in the form of the human makeup that we know, though not born of parents; he was made from the clay, and she from his rib. He will ask, "How were they made then?" I will answer: invisibly, potentially, causally, in the way that things to come are made, not yet having been made.

Perhaps he will not understand this. For everything he knows is taken away from him, even down to the bodily substance of seeds. Man was not even anything of that kind when he was made in that first establishment of the six days. Seeds do offer some likeness for this matter, because of the future things that are woven together within them. But those causes come before all visible seeds. Still he does not understand. What then can I do but urge him, as far as I can and for his own good, to believe the scripture of God? Man was made then, when God, as the day was made, made heaven and earth, about which scripture says elsewhere, "He who lives forever created all things at once." He was also made later, when God was no longer creating all things at once but each in its own time, and formed him from the clay of the earth, and the woman from his bone. For scripture does not allow us to understand that they were made in this second way on the sixth day, nor yet that they were not made on the sixth day.

Perhaps, then, their souls were made on that sixth day, and the image of God itself is rightly understood to be in the spirit of their minds, so that their bodies were formed later? But the same scripture does not allow us to believe this either. First, there is the completion of the works. I do not see how that could be understood if something was missing then, not established in its causes, which was to be established visibly later. Second, the very sexes of male and female can exist only in bodies. Someone might think that both sexes should be understood within a single soul, as intellect and action. What then will he do with the food God gave that same day from the fruits of the trees, which is surely suited only to a man who has a body? If anyone chooses to take this food figuratively as well, he will depart from the literal reality of the events, which in narratives of this kind must first be firmly established with every care.

"How then," someone says, "did God speak to them when they could not yet hear or understand, since there was no one to take in the words?" I could answer that God addressed them in the way that Christ addressed us, who were not yet born and would come so long afterward. Nor did he address only us, but also all those who will come after us. For he said to all whom he saw would be his own, "Behold, I am with you until the end of the age." In the same way the prophet was known to God, to whom he said, "Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you"; and Levi paid tithes when he was still in the loins of Abraham. Why then should not Abraham himself have been in Adam in the same way, and Adam himself in the first works of the world, which God created all at once? But the Lord's words through the mouth of his flesh, and God's words through the mouths of the prophets, were uttered by a bodily voice in time, and with all their syllables they take up and use up their proper spans of time. God, however, said: "Let us make man in our image and likeness, and let him have power over the fish of the sea and the birds of the sky and all the cattle and all the earth and all the creeping things that creep upon the earth"; and, "Increase and multiply and fill the earth and have dominion over it, and have power over the fish of the sea and the birds of the sky and all the cattle and all the earth and all the creeping things that creep upon the earth"; and, "Behold, I have given you every seed-bearing plant that bears seed, which is upon all the earth, and every fruit-bearing tree that has in itself the fruit of seed that will be sown, to be food for you." When he said these things, his speech came before any sound in the air and before any voice from flesh or cloud. It was in his supreme Wisdom, through whom all things were made. It did not ring in human ears, as it were. Rather, it planted in the things that were made the causes of things yet to be made. By his almighty power it made things to come. It established man, to be formed in his own time, as if in the seed or root of the times. It did so when he was establishing the point from which the ages would begin, the ages established by him who is before the ages. Among creatures, some come before others in time and some in causes. But he comes before all the things he has made not only by his excellence, by which he is also the maker of causes, but also by his eternity. But perhaps this should be discussed more fully later, at more suitable places in the scriptures.

For now, let us finish what we began about man, keeping to this restraint: in the deep meaning of scripture we should show diligence in inquiring rather than rashness in asserting. It is not right to doubt that God knew Jeremiah before he formed him in the womb, for he says most plainly, "Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you." But where he knew him before he formed him in this way is difficult or impossible for our weakness to grasp. Was it in some nearer causes, as Levi paid tithes in the loins of Abraham? Was it in Adam himself, in whom the human race was established as if in its root? And if in Adam, was it once Adam had been formed from the clay, or when he was made causally in those works that God created all at once? Or was it rather before all creation, just as he chose and predestined his saints before the foundation of the world? Or was it rather in all the preceding causes, those I have mentioned and those I have not, before he was formed in the womb? I do not think we need to inquire into this too minutely. It is enough that one thing is settled. From the time Jeremiah was brought into this light by his parents, he lived a life of his own, by which, growing with the years, he could live either badly or well. Before that he did not do so at all: not before he was formed in the womb, and not even once he had been formed there but was not yet born. For the Apostle's statement about the twins in Rebecca's womb, who had not yet done anything good or evil, leaves no room for hesitation.

Yet it was not written in vain that not even an infant whose life on earth is one day old is clean from sin, nor that line in the psalm, "I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother nourished me in the womb," nor that in Adam all die, in whom all sinned. For now, though, let us hold this clearly: whatever merits of parents may pass to their offspring, and whatever grace of God may sanctify anyone before birth, there is no injustice with God, and no one does anything good or evil, so far as concerns his own person, before he is born. And that opinion by which some think that souls sinned more or less elsewhere and were thrust down into different bodies according to the merits of their different sins does not agree with the apostle's teaching, since it is said most plainly that those not yet born had done nothing, either good or evil.

There is therefore another question, to be taken up again in its proper place: what the whole lump of the human race contracted from the sin of its first parents, who were only two. Yet there is no question that man could have had no merits of that kind before he was fashioned from the dust of the earth, before he lived in his own time. For Esau and Jacob, of whom the apostle said that before they were born they had done nothing good or evil, could not be said to have drawn any merit from their parents if those parents themselves had done nothing good or evil. Nor could the human race have sinned in Adam if Adam himself had not sinned, and Adam would not have sinned unless he were already living in his own time, in which he could live either well or badly. In the same way it is pointless to look for his sin or his right conduct at the stage when he was still established causally among the things created all together, when he was not yet living a life of his own, nor was he in parents who were living in that way. For in that first establishment of the world, when God created all things together, man was made as the one who was to be: the principle of creating man, not the action of a man already created.

But these things exist in one way in the Word of God, where they are not made but eternal; in another way in the elements of the world, where all things that are to be were made together; in another way in things which, according to the causes created together, are created no longer together but each in its own time. Among these is Adam, now formed from the clay and given life by God's breath, like the grass that has sprung up. They exist in yet another way in seeds, in which primordial causes, as it were, are found again, derived from the things that came into existence according to the causes God first established, as the plant comes from the earth and the seed from the plant. In all these, the things already made have received the manner and activity proper to their own time, having come forth from hidden and invisible principles, which lie latent causally in creation, into manifest forms and natures: the plant sprung up on the earth, man made a living soul, and other such things, whether shrubs or animals, which belong to that working of God by which he works until now. But these too carry within themselves, as it were, themselves over again, invisibly, in a certain hidden power of generating. This power they drew from those first beginnings of their causes, in which they were implanted when the world was created, when day was made, before they sprang forth into the visible form of their kind.

For if those first works of God, when he created all things together, had not been complete in their own way, then without doubt whatever was lacking for their completion would have been added afterward, so that a kind of completeness of the universe would be made up of both, each being a half, as it were, like the parts of some whole whose joining completed the very whole of which they were parts. On the other hand, if they had been complete in the way they are completed when each is brought forth in its own time into manifest forms and activities, then surely either nothing would have come of them after those times, or else only what God never ceases to work from the things that now arise each in its own time. As it is, the very things which God originally created all together when he made the world, to be unfolded in the times that followed, are in one sense finished and in another sense begun. They are finished, because in their own natures, by which they run the course of their times, they have nothing that was not made causally in those first works. They are begun, because they were like seeds of things to come, to be brought out from hidden to manifest, in suitable places, through the course of the ages. And the words of Scripture itself stand out clearly enough to point this out, if one is alert to them. For it calls these things both finished and begun. Had they not been finished, it would not be written, "And the heavens and the earth were finished, and all their array. And God finished on the sixth day the works which he had made. And God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it." And again, had they not been begun, it would not go on to say, "because on that day he rested from all his works which God began to make."

If anyone asks here, then, how he finished them and how he began them (for he did not finish some and begin others, but these were surely the very same works from which he rested on the seventh day), the answer is clear from what we said above. We understand that God finished them when he created all things together so completely that nothing remained for him to create in the order of time which had not already been created by him here in the order of causes; and that he began them so that what he had fixed beforehand here in causes he might afterward fulfil in effects. Accordingly God formed man as dust of the earth, or as clay of the earth, that is, from the dust or clay of the earth, and breathed or blew into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul. He was not predestined at that moment, for that took place before the ages in the Creator's foreknowledge. Nor was he at that moment begun causally, or begun in a finished way, or finished in a begun way, for that took place from the beginning of the ages in the primordial principles, when all things were created together. Rather, he was created in his own time, visibly in body and invisibly in soul, made up of soul and body.

Let us now see, then, how God made him: first his body from the earth; afterward we shall see about his soul too, if we are able. To think that God fashioned man from clay with bodily hands is far too childish. Even if Scripture had said so, we ought rather to believe that the writer used a figure of speech than that God is bounded by such outlines of limbs as we see in our own bodies. For it is said, "Your hand destroyed the nations," and, "You led your people out with a strong hand and an uplifted arm." Who is so foolish as not to understand that the name of this member is used here for the power and might of God?

Nor should we listen to the view held by some, that man is God's chief work because God spoke and the other things were made, whereas man he made himself. Man is God's chief work rather because God made him in his own image. As for the things of which it is said that he spoke and they were made, it is written so because they were made through his Word, just as a man could speak to men in words that are thought in time and uttered aloud. But God does not speak in that way except when he speaks through a bodily creature, as he did to Abraham, as he did to Moses, as he did through the cloud concerning his Son. Before every creature, however, so that creation itself might exist, it was spoken by that Word which in the beginning was God with God. And since all things were made through him and without him nothing was made, man too was certainly made through him. Indeed God made heaven by his word, for he spoke and it was made; yet it is written, "And the heavens are the works of your hands." And of this lowest region, the floor of the world as it were, it is written, "For the sea is his, and he made it, and his hands formed the dry land." So let it not be counted to man's honour that God spoke and the other things were made, but made man himself; or that he made the rest by his word but man with his hands. What makes man excel is this: God made man in his own image because he gave him an intellectual mind, by which he surpasses the beasts, as we discussed earlier. If, placed in this honour, he does not understand so as to act well, he will be compared to those very beasts above which he was set. For so it is written: "Man, placed in honour, did not understand; he has been compared to the senseless beasts and has become like them." For God made the beasts too, but not in his own image.

Nor should it be said, "Man he made himself, but the beasts he commanded, and they were made." Both man and the beasts he made through his Word, through whom all things were made. But since that same Word is also his Wisdom and his Power, it is also called his hand, meaning not a visible member but the power to bring things about. For the same Scripture that says God fashioned man from the clay of the earth also says that he fashioned the beasts of the field from the earth, when he brought them with the birds of the sky to Adam to see what he would call them. For so it is written: "And God further fashioned from the earth all the beasts." If, then, he himself formed both man and the beasts from the earth, what does man have that is more excellent in this respect, except that he was created in the image of God? Yet this is not in respect of the body but of the understanding of the mind, of which we shall speak later. Even in his body, however, he has a certain distinctive feature that points to this: he was made with an upright stature, so that by this very fact he would be reminded not to pursue earthly things like the beasts, all of whose pleasure comes from the earth, which is why they are all bent forward and lie prone on their bellies. So his body too befits the rational soul, not in the outlines and shapes of its members, but rather in that it is raised up toward heaven to behold the things that are on high in the body of the world itself, just as the rational soul ought to be raised up toward those things that most excel in the spiritual order, so that it may set its mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth.

But how did God make him from the clay of the earth? Was it suddenly, at full maturity, that is, as a grown young man, or as he still forms people in their mothers' wombs? For no one else does this than he who said, "Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you."
