In that case Adam's only distinction would have been that he was not born of parents but made from the earth, yet in such a way that in bringing him to completion and growing him through the stages of life, those measures of time would be fulfilled which we see assigned to the nature of the human race. Or is this something we should not inquire into at all? For whichever he did, he did what it befitted God, being both almighty and wise, to be able to do and to do. For he assigned fixed laws of time to the kinds and qualities of things that are to be brought forth from hiddenness into the open in such a way that his will remains above all things. By his power he gave measures to creation; he did not bind that power itself by those measures. For his Spirit was borne above the world in making it in such a way that he is borne above it now that it is made, not by bodily location but by the pre-eminence of his power.

For who does not know that water mixed into the earth, when it reaches the roots of the vine, is drawn up to nourish its wood and there takes on a quality by which it passes into the grape as it gradually bursts forth, and becomes wine in the swelling grape, and grows sweet as it ripens; and that once pressed out it still ferments, and when settled by some aging it becomes more useful and more pleasant to drink? Did the Lord, then, look for a vine or soil or these delays of time when, with wonderful shortness, he turned water into wine, and such wine that even a guest who had drunk well would praise it? Did the Maker of time need the help of time? Does not every kind of serpent grow, take shape, come to birth and gain strength over a fixed number of days suited to each kind? Were those days waited for when the rod turned into a serpent from the hand of Moses and Aaron? Nor do such things, when they happen, happen against nature, except for us, to whom the course of nature has become known otherwise; not for God, for whom nature is whatever he has made.

But one may rightly ask how those causal reasons that God placed in the world when he first created all things together were set up. Were they set up so that they would pass through different spans of time in their formation and growth, according to the diversity of their kinds, as we see with everything that is born, whether plants or animals? Or were they set up so that they would be formed at once at the age of manhood, without any process of growth, as Adam is believed to have been made? But why should we not believe that they had both capacities, so that from them would come whatever pleased the one who was to act? For if we take the first view, then not only the turning of water into wine but all the miracles that happen against the usual course of nature begin to look as if they were done against those reasons. But if we take the second, it will be far more absurd that the everyday forms and appearances of nature should run through their spans of time against those primary causal reasons of all things that come to birth. It remains, then, that they were created fit for both ways: for the way in which temporal things most usually run their course, and for the way in which rare and wonderful things happen, as it pleases God to do what suits the time.

Even so, man was made just as those first causes held that the first man should be made. He was not to be born of parents, since there had been none before him, but formed from the mud according to the causal reason in which he had first been made. For if he was made otherwise, then God had not made him among the works of those six days. When man is said to have been made among them, God had certainly made the very cause by which man was to come to be in his own time, and according to which he was to be made by the one who at once both completed what he had begun, through the perfection of the causal reasons, and began what was to be completed, through the order of times. Suppose, then, that in those first causes of things which the Creator implanted in the world at the beginning he laid down not only that he would form man from the mud but also how he would form him, whether as in a mother's womb or in youthful form. In that case he undoubtedly made him as he had determined there in advance, for he would not act against his own arrangement. But suppose instead that he placed there only the power of possibility that man should come to be, in whatever way he came to be, so that he could come to be either this way or that. That is, this too was there: that he could come to be either way. The one particular way in which God was going to make him he kept in his own will and did not weave into the constitution of the world. In that case it is clear that even so man was not made contrary to what was in that first establishment of causes, because it was there that he could be made in this way, although it was not there that he must be made so. For this lay not in the condition of the creature but in the good pleasure of the Creator, whose will is the necessity of things.

For we too, within the limits of human weakness, can already know what is in the nature of each thing that has arisen in time, because we have perceived it by experience; but whether it will actually come about we do not know. It is in the nature of this young man, for example, to grow old; but whether this is also in God's will we do not know. Yet it would not be in his nature unless it had first been in the will of God, who founded all things. And certainly the reason of old age in a youthful body, or of youth in a child's body, is hidden. It is not seen with the eyes, as childhood itself is seen in a child or youth in a young man. But by another kind of knowledge we gather that there is something latent in nature by which the hidden numbers are drawn out into the open: those of youth from childhood, or of old age from youth. So this reason, by which it comes about that this can happen, is hidden, but only from the eyes; it is not hidden from the mind. But whether it must also necessarily happen, we do not know at all. And we know that the reason by which it comes about that it can happen is in the nature of the body itself; but the reason by which it comes about that it must happen is clearly not there.

But perhaps it is in the world that this man must grow old; and if it is not in the world either, then it is in God. For what God wills will necessarily come to be, and the things he has foreknown are truly going to happen. Many things are going to happen according to lower causes. If they stand the same way in God's foreknowledge too, they are truly going to happen; but if they stand otherwise there, they will rather happen as they stand there, where the one who foreknows cannot be deceived. For old age is said to lie ahead for a young man, yet it does not lie ahead if he is going to die first. And this will turn out according to how the other causes stand, whether those woven into the world or those kept in reserve in God's foreknowledge. For according to certain causes of future things Hezekiah was going to die, yet God added fifteen years to his life. In doing so God was certainly doing what he had foreknown before the foundation of the world that he would do, and had kept in his will. So he did not do something that was not going to happen; rather, what he foreknew he would do was all the more what was going to happen. Yet those years could not rightly be called added unless they were added to something that had stood otherwise in other causes. According to certain lower causes, then, Hezekiah had already come to the end of his life. But according to the causes that are in the will and foreknowledge of God, who knew from eternity what he would do at that time (and this was what was truly going to happen), he was to end his life when he did end it. For even though the years were granted to him because he prayed, the one whose foreknowledge could not be deceived certainly foreknew that Hezekiah would pray in such a way that such a prayer ought to be granted. And therefore what he foreknew was necessarily going to happen.

Therefore, if the causes of all future things were implanted in the world when that day was made on which God created all things together, then Adam, when he was formed from the mud (most credibly already in full manhood), was not made otherwise than he was in those causes where God made man among the works of the six days. For it was there not only that he could be made so, but also that he must necessarily be made so. God no more acts against the cause that he undoubtedly established in advance by his will than he acts against his will itself. But suppose he did not fix all causes in advance in the creation he founded at the beginning, but kept some in his own will. Then the causes he kept in his will do not depend on the necessity of those he created. Yet the causes he kept in his will cannot be contrary to those he established by his will, because God's will cannot be contrary to itself. So he founded the created causes in such a way that the thing they are causes of could come from them, but need not; and he hid the others in such a way that from them must necessarily come what he had made possible through the created ones.

It is also commonly asked whether the body first formed for man from the mud was an animal body, such as we have now, or a spiritual body, such as we shall have when we rise. One will indeed be changed into the other, for it is sown an animal body and rises a spiritual body. Yet what was first made for man is still debated, because if it was made animal, we shall not receive back what we lost in him, but something better, by as much as the spiritual is to be preferred to the animal, when we shall be equal to the angels of God. But angels may rank above others in righteousness too; can they also rank above the Lord? Yet of him it was said: "You made him a little less than the angels." Why, unless because of the weakness of the flesh that he took from the virgin when he received the form of a servant, in which by dying he would redeem us from servitude? But why discuss this at greater length? The Apostle's view on this matter is not obscure. He wanted to bring forward a testimony to prove that there is an animal body, and for this he did not draw so much on his own body, or on the body of any person that could be seen at the time, as on this very passage of this scripture, which he recalled and cited, saying: "If there is an animal body, there is also a spiritual one. Thus also it is written: The first man Adam became a living soul; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit. But it is not the spiritual that comes first, but the animal, and afterwards the spiritual. The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man is from heaven, heavenly. As was the earthly man, so are those who are earthly; and as is the heavenly man, so are those who are heavenly. And just as we have put on the image of the earthly man, let us also put on the image of the one who is from heaven." What can be said against this? So we now bear the image of the heavenly man by faith, and we shall have in the resurrection what we believe; but the image of the earthly man we have worn from the very beginning of the human race.

Here another question arises: how are we renewed, if through Christ we are not called back to what we formerly were in Adam? Many things are indeed renewed not to their former state but to something better; yet they are renewed from a lower state than the one they were in before. How, then, was that son dead and come back to life, lost and found? How is the first robe brought out for him, if he does not receive back the immortality that Adam lost? But how did Adam lose immortality if he had an animal body? For the body will be not animal but spiritual when this corruptible thing has put on incorruption and this mortal thing has put on immortality. Some people have been hemmed in by these difficulties. They wanted two things to hold together. First, that statement should stand in which an example of the animal body is taken from this passage: "The first man Adam became a living soul [the last Adam became a life-giving spirit]." Second, this renewal and recovery of immortality should not absurdly be called a return to the former state, that is, to what Adam lost. So they supposed that man at first had an animal body, but that when he was placed in paradise he was changed, just as we too shall be changed in the resurrection. The book of Genesis does not mention this. But they believed it followed almost by necessity, so that the two testimonies of scripture could agree with each other: what was said about the animal body, and the many passages about our renewal found in the holy writings.

But if that is so, it is in vain that we try to take paradise, with those trees and their fruits, first in the proper sense of things that actually happened, before taking them as figures. For who would believe that food of that kind, the fruit of trees, could have been necessary for immortal and spiritual bodies? Still, if no other answer can be found, we would rather understand paradise spiritually than either suppose that man is not renewed, when scripture mentions this so often, or think that he recovers something he is not shown to have lost. There is a further point. Many divine testimonies declare that man incurred death itself by sin, and this shows that he would have been without death had he not sinned. How, then, could he be mortal yet without death? Or how could he not be mortal, if his body was animal?

Hence some think that what he incurred by sin was not the death of the body but the death of the soul, which iniquity brought about. They believe that because of his animal body he would have departed from this body, namely into the rest that the saints who have already fallen asleep now enjoy, and that at the end of the age he would have received the same members back to live immortally. On this view the death of the body did not come from sin but happened naturally, as with the other animals. But the Apostle confronts these people in turn when he says: "The body is dead because of sin, but the spirit is life because of righteousness. And if the Spirit of him who raised Christ from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you." Accordingly, the death of the body too comes from sin. If, then, Adam had not sinned, he would not have died in the body either, and so he would have had an immortal body as well. How, then, could it be immortal, if it was animal?

But again, those who think his body was changed in paradise from animal to spiritual fail to see that nothing stood in the way of a different course. If he had not sinned, he would have lived the life of paradise justly and obediently, and after it he could have received that same change of body into eternal life, where he would no longer need bodily food. Why, then, must we be forced on this account to understand paradise figuratively rather than literally, simply because the body could not die except through sin? It is true that he would not have died even in the body had he not sinned, for the Apostle plainly says: "The body is dead because of sin." Yet the body could have been animal before sin, and then, after a life of righteousness, have become spiritual when God willed.

How then, they ask, are we said to be renewed, if we do not receive back what the first man, in whom all die, lost? We plainly do receive it back in one sense, and in another sense we do not. We do not receive back the immortality of a spiritual body, which man did not yet have; but we do receive back righteousness, from which man fell through sin. We shall be renewed, then, from the oldness of sin, not into the former animal body in which Adam was, but into something better: a spiritual body, when we are made equal to the angels of God and fit for the heavenly dwelling, where we shall not need food that perishes. We shall be renewed, then, in the spirit of our mind according to the image of him who created us, the image Adam lost by sinning. And we shall be renewed in the flesh too, when this corruptible thing puts on incorruption and becomes a spiritual body. Adam had not yet been changed into such a body, but he would have been, had he not by sinning incurred the death even of his animal body.
In short, the Apostle does not say "The body is mortal because of sin," but "The body is dead because of sin."

Before sin, that body could be called mortal for one reason and immortal for another: mortal because it was able to die, immortal because it was able not to die. It is one thing to be unable to die, which is how God created certain immortal natures; it is another to be able not to die, which is how the first man was created immortal. This immortality was granted to him by the tree of life, not by the constitution of his nature. He was separated from that tree when he sinned, so that he became able to die, he who would have been able not to die had he not sinned. He was mortal, then, by the condition of an animal body, but immortal by the kindness of his Creator. If the body was animal, it was certainly mortal, since it was able to die; yet it was also immortal, in that it was also able not to die. For nothing will be immortal in the sense of being wholly unable to die unless it is spiritual, as the body promised to us in the resurrection will be. So that body was animal and therefore mortal, and through righteousness it was to become spiritual and therefore wholly immortal. Through sin it was made not mortal, which it already was before, but dead, which it need not have become had man not sinned.

For how can the Apostle call our body dead when he is still speaking of the living, unless the very condition of dying has, through our first parents' sin, clung to their offspring? This body too is an animal body, as the first man's was. But within the animal kind itself it is now much worse, for it is under the necessity of dying, which that body was not. It is true that his body still had to be changed and, once made spiritual, receive full immortality, where it would not need corruptible food. Even so, if man had lived justly, his body would have been changed into a spiritual condition rather than going into death. In us, however, the body is going to die even if we live justly. Because of this necessity, which comes from the first man's sin, the Apostle called our body not mortal but dead, since in Adam we all die. He also says: "As the truth is in Jesus, put off the old man of your former way of life, who is corrupted by deceitful desires." That is, put off what Adam became through sin. See, then, what follows: "But be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who was created according to God in righteousness and holiness of truth." There you have what Adam lost through sin!

So in this respect we are renewed according to what Adam lost, that is, according to the spirit of our mind. But in the body, which is sown animal and will rise spiritual, we shall be renewed into something better, something Adam had not yet been.

The Apostle likewise says: "Stripping off the old man with his deeds, put on the new man, who is being renewed unto the knowledge of God according to the image of him who created him." This image, imprinted on the spirit of the mind, Adam lost through sin, and we receive it back through the grace of righteousness. We do not receive back the spiritual and immortal body, for he had not yet been in such a body, though all the saints will be in it when they rise from the dead. That body is the reward of the merit which he lost. Accordingly, that first robe is either righteousness itself, from which he fell, or, if it signifies the garment of bodily immortality, then he lost this too in the sense that because of sin he could not attain it. For a man is said to have lost a wife or lost an honor when he has not received what he hoped for because he has offended the one from whom he hoped to receive it.

According to this view, then, Adam had an animal body not only before paradise but even after he had been placed in paradise, although in the inner man he was spiritual, according to the image of him who created him. That image he lost by sinning, and he also incurred the death of the body, whereas by not sinning he would have earned the change into a spiritual body as well. For if he had lived as an animal man inwardly too, we could not be said to be renewed to what he was. When people are told, "Be renewed in the spirit of your mind," they are told this so that they may become spiritual. But if he was not spiritual even in his mind, how are we renewed to what man never was? The apostles and all the righteous certainly still had an animal body, yet they lived spiritually within, renewed unto the knowledge of God according to the image of him who created them. That did not mean, however, that they could no longer sin, if they consented to iniquity. For the Apostle shows that even spiritual people can fall into the temptation of sin when he says: "Brothers, even if someone is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual should instruct such a person in a spirit of gentleness, looking to yourself, lest you too be tempted." This has been said so that no one may think it impossible for Adam to have sinned if he was spiritual in mind though animal in body. Even so, we do not yet affirm anything too hastily, but rather wait to see whether the rest of scripture also allows this understanding.

For next comes a very difficult question about the soul. Many have toiled over it, and they have left us something to toil over too. I confess that no one has yet persuaded me to hold such a view of the soul that I think nothing more needs to be asked. Perhaps this is because I have not been able to read everything by everyone who, following the truth of our scriptures, managed to reach something clear and free from doubt on this matter. Or perhaps the question is so great that even those who truly solve it are not easily understood by people like me. Whether I shall now find and define anything certain, I do not know. But whatever I can manage, if the Lord helps my effort, I shall take care to set out in the following book.
BOOK SEVEN

"And God formed man, dust from the earth, and blew into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul." We had set these words of scripture before ourselves for consideration at the beginning of the previous book as well. There we discussed the making of man himself, and especially his body, as far as we thought sufficient and as it seemed to us according to the scriptures. But because the question of the human soul is no small one, we thought it should be put off until this book. We did not know how far the Lord would help us in our desire to speak rightly, but we did know that we would speak rightly only as far as he helped us. To speak rightly is to speak truthfully and fittingly. It means refuting nothing boldly and affirming nothing rashly while it is still doubtful whether it is true or false, whether the matter belongs to faith or to Christian knowledge. And it means asserting without hesitation whatever can be taught, either by the plainest reasoning about things or by the most certain authority of the scriptures.

First let us look at what is written: "He blew," or "blew upon, into his face the breath of life." For some manuscripts have "He breathed" or "breathed into his face." But since the Greek has ἐνεφύσησεν, there is no doubt that we should say "blew" or "blew upon." In the previous discussion we were inquiring about the hands of God, as we thought about man being formed from the mud. What, then, should be said now about the words "God blew"? Surely this: just as he did not form man with bodily hands, so he did not blow with throat or lips.
Nevertheless, by this word, in my opinion, scripture has helped us a great deal with a most difficult question.

Some people have taken this word to mean that the soul is something of God's very substance, that is, of the same nature as he is. They think so because when a man breathes out, he expels something of himself in the breath. This should rather prompt us to reject that opinion, which is hostile to the Catholic faith. For we believe that the nature and substance of God, which many believe in the Trinity but few understand, is wholly unchangeable. But who doubts that the nature of the soul can change for the worse or for the better? So it is a sacrilegious opinion to believe that the soul and God are of one substance. What else would that amount to but believing that he too is changeable? We must therefore believe and understand, and in no way doubt, what the right faith holds: that the soul is from God as a thing he has made, and not as something of his own nature, whether begotten or brought forth in any other way.

"How, then," they say, "is it written, He breathed into his face, and man became a living soul, if the soul is not a part of God, or wholly God's substance?" On the contrary, this very word shows clearly enough that it is not so. When a man breathes out, the soul moves the nature of the body that is subject to it, and it makes the breath from the body, not from itself. Perhaps these people are so slow that they do not know that the breath we blow out when we choose to is made from the same alternating respiration by which we draw in the surrounding air and give it back. Even if, in breathing out, we expelled something that was not taken in from the outside air and returned, but came from the very nature of the body we consist of, the nature of body and soul would still not be the same, and they themselves certainly agree with this. So even then, the substance of the soul, by which it rules and moves the body, is one thing. The breath is another, which the soul makes by ruling and moving the body subject to it, and not from itself, since the body is subject to it. The soul rules the body subject to it, and God rules the creation subject to him, in an incomparably different way, to be sure, but still both rule. Why, then, should we not rather understand that God made the soul from the creation subject to him, in the sense that he is said to have breathed? After all, the soul does not have such mastery over its body as God has over the universe he founded, yet it makes breath by moving the body, not out of its own substance.

We could indeed say that God's breath is not itself the soul of man, but that God made the soul in man by breathing. But someone might then think that what God made by his word is better than what he made by breath, since in us too a word is better than a breath. So for the present, on the reasoning given above, there is no reason to hesitate to call the soul itself God's breath, provided it is understood that the soul is not God's nature and substance. Rather, to breathe is the same as to make breath, and to make breath is the same as to make the soul. This view agrees with what God says through Isaiah: For the spirit shall go forth from me, and I have made every breath. What follows shows that he does not mean just any bodily breath. For after saying, I have made every breath, he says: Because of sin I grieved him a little and struck him. What, then, does he call breath, if not the soul, which was struck and grieved because of sin? And what does I have made every breath mean, if not I have made every soul?

Suppose, then, we said that God was, as it were, the soul of this bodily world, and that the world itself was to him like the body of a single living being. Then we would be right to say that he made the soul of man by breathing only if that soul were bodily, made from the air that lies subject to him, out of his own body. Even then we ought not to think that what he gave by breathing he gave from himself. He would have given it from the air of his body that is subject to him, just as the soul makes breath from something similarly lying next to it, that is, from the body, not from itself. As it is, however, we say not only that the body of the world is subject to God, but that he is above all creation, whether bodily or spiritual. So we must not believe that in breathing he made the soul either from himself or from the bodily elements.

But one may rightly ask whether he made it from what did not exist at all, that is, from nothing, or from something that he had already made spiritually but that was not yet a soul. We do not believe that God still creates anything from nothing after he created all things together. That is why we believe he rested from all the works he had begun to make once they were completed, so that whatever he made afterward he would make from these. If so, I do not see how we are to understand that he still makes souls from nothing. Or should we say this? In those works of the first six days he made that hidden day, or, if this is what we should rather believe, the spiritual and intellectual nature, namely that of the angelic unity. He also made the world, that is, heaven and earth. And in those natures, which already existed, he created the reasons of other natures still to come, not the natures themselves. Otherwise, if those natures had already been created there as they were going to be, they would no longer be still to come. If this is so, there was not yet any nature of the human soul among created things, and it began to exist when God made it by breathing and put it into man.

But that does not settle the question still being asked. Did he create from nothing the nature that is called the soul and did not exist before? In that case his breath itself was not made from some underlying substance, as we said of the breath the soul makes from its body. Instead, the breath was made wholly from nothing at the moment God willed to breathe, and that same breath became the soul of man. Or did something spiritual already exist, though whatever it was, it was not yet the nature of a soul? In that case the breath of God, which was to be the nature of the soul, was made from this. In the same way, the nature of the human body did not yet exist before God formed it from the mud or dust of the earth. Dust or mud was not human flesh, yet it was something from which the flesh, which did not yet exist, could be made.

Is it credible, then, that in those first works of the six days God established not only the causal reason of the future human body but also the matter from which it would be made, that is, earth, from whose mud or dust it would be shaped, while for the soul he established there only the reason according to which it would be made, and not also some matter of its own kind from which to make it? If the soul were something unchangeable, we would have no reason to look for anything like its matter. As it is, however, its changeableness shows clearly enough that at times it is deformed by vices and falsehoods, and formed by virtues and the teaching of truth. But this happens within its own nature, by which it is already a soul. In the same way, flesh too, within its own nature, by which it is already flesh, is adorned by health and disfigured by diseases and wounds. Apart from the fact that flesh is already flesh, the nature in which it either advances so as to be beautiful or declines so as to be deformed, it also had matter, that is, earth, from which it was made so as to be flesh at all. So perhaps the soul too, before it was made into the very nature called the soul, whose beauty is virtue and whose deformity is vice, could have had some spiritual matter of its own kind which was not yet a soul. In just this way the earth from which the flesh was made was already something, though it was not flesh.

But the earth filled the lowest part of the world before the body of man was made from it, and it contributed its whole being to the universe. So even if no flesh of any living creature had been made from it, it would still complete the structure and mass of the world by its own form, and in this sense the world is called heaven and earth.

But what about that spiritual matter, if there was any, from which the soul was to be made, or if there is any, from which souls are made? What is it? What name, what form, what function does it hold among created things? Does it live or not? If it lives, what does it do? What does it contribute to the workings of the universe? Does it lead a happy life, or a miserable one, or neither? Does it give life to anything? Or is it free even from this work, resting idle in some hidden corner of the universe without wakeful sense or vital motion? If there was as yet no life at all, how could there be a bodiless and lifeless matter of a life still to come? Either this is false or it is very obscure. But if it was already living, neither happily nor miserably, how was it rational? And if it became rational only when the nature of the human soul was made from that matter, was an irrational life, then, the matter of the rational, that is, the human, soul? In that case, what difference was there between it and the soul of a beast? Or was it already rational in possibility, but not yet in capacity? We see that an infant's soul, which is certainly already a human soul, has not yet begun to use reason, and yet we already call it rational. Why, then, should we not believe that in the matter from which the soul was made even the motion of sensation lay dormant, just as in this infant soul, which is certainly already a human soul, the motion of reasoning still lies dormant?

If the life from which the soul of man was made was already happy, then the soul was made worse. In that case that life would not be the matter of this soul; this soul would rather be an outflow from it. For when any matter is formed, especially by God, it is without doubt formed for the better. But even if the human soul could be understood as an outflow from some life that God had made in a state of happiness, we still should not believe that it began in any action deserving merit or blame until it began to lead its own life. That happened when it became a soul giving life to flesh, using the flesh's senses as messengers, and perceiving itself living within itself by its own will, understanding and memory. Suppose there is something from which God breathed this outflow into the flesh he had formed, as though making the soul by breathing, and suppose that something is happy. Then it is in no way moved or changed, and it loses nothing when the outflow that becomes the soul flows from it. For it is not a body, to be diminished as though by breathing out.

But suppose an irrational soul is in some way the matter from which the rational, that is, the human, soul is made. Then the question arises again where the irrational soul itself comes from, since it too is made by none other than the creator of all natures. Is it made from bodily matter? Then why not the rational soul too? Perhaps someone will deny that God can do at a stroke what everyone grants he can do by degrees. Whatever intermediate step is brought in, if body is the matter of the irrational soul and the irrational soul is the matter of the rational soul, then beyond doubt body is the matter of the rational soul. I know of no one who has ever dared to hold this, except those who place the soul itself in nothing but some kind of body.

Next, if we grant that an irrational soul underlies the rational soul as a kind of matter from which it is made, we must take care that no one comes to believe that a soul can somehow pass from a beast into a man. That is wholly contrary to the truth and to the Catholic faith. For then it would follow that if this soul is changed for the better and becomes a man's, the other is also changed for the worse and becomes a beast's. Even the later successors of certain philosophers were ashamed of this absurd teaching. They said that their masters had not held it but had been misunderstood, and I believe this is so. It is as if someone were to draw this meaning from our own scriptures too, where it is said: Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and became like them; or again where we read: Do not hand over to the beasts the soul that confesses you. For all heretics read the Catholic scriptures, and they are heretics for no other reason than that they do not understand them rightly and stubbornly assert their own false opinions against the truth of those scriptures. But whatever the truth of the philosophers' opinion about the cycles of souls, it does not befit the Catholic faith to believe that the souls of beasts migrate into men, or those of men into beasts.

That men do become like beasts by their way of life is something human affairs themselves cry out and scripture testifies. Hence the verse I mentioned: Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared to senseless cattle and became like them. But this certainly happens in this life, not after death. So the one who said, Do not hand over to the beasts the soul that confesses you, did not want his soul to be given into the power of such beasts. These may be the kind the Lord warns us against when he says they are clothed in sheep's clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves. Or they may be the devil himself and his angels, for the devil too has been called both a lion and a dragon.

What argument do the philosophers offer who think that human souls can be transferred into beasts after death, or the souls of beasts into men? Surely this: that likeness of character draws them there, so that the greedy go into ants, the rapacious into kites, the cruel and proud into lions, the followers of unclean pleasure into swine, and so on. This is what they assert. They do not notice that on this reasoning it is quite impossible for the soul of a beast to be transferred into a man after death. A pig will never be more like a man than like a pig, and when lions are tamed, they become more like dogs or even sheep than like men. Beasts do not depart from the ways of beasts. Those that become somewhat unlike the rest are still more like their own kind than like the human race, and they differ far more from men than from beasts. If what is more alike draws souls to itself, these souls will never be human souls. But if this argument is false, how can that opinion be true, since they offer nothing else that would make it, if not true, at least plausible? So I too would more readily believe, as their later followers also do, that the men who first put these things in their books meant rather that in this life men become like beasts through some perversity and baseness of character, and so are in a way changed into beasts. By holding up this disgrace before people, they meant to call them back from the depravity of their desires.

There are stories of certain people who seemed to remember which animals' bodies they had once been in. These are either false accounts, or the experience was produced in their minds by the tricks of demons. In dreams a man may seem, through a deceptive memory, to remember having been what he was not, or having done what he did not do. So why be surprised if, by some just and hidden judgment of God, demons are allowed to do something of this kind in people's hearts even while they are awake?

The Manichees, who either think themselves Christians or want to be thought so, are worse and more detestable in this opinion about the transfer or cycling of souls than those pagan philosophers, or any other foolish men who think this. The philosophers distinguish the nature of the soul from the nature of God. The Manichees, however, say that the soul is nothing other than the very substance of God and wholly what God is, and yet they do not shrink from calling it so shamefully changeable that, in their extraordinary madness, they suppose there is no kind of plant or little worm in which it is not mingled or into which it cannot be cycled. They turn over questions about the most obscure matters with a fleshly heart, and so they inevitably slip and tumble into false, harmful and monstrous opinions. If they would put these questions out of their minds and hold most firmly to the one truth that is naturally and truly implanted in every rational soul, without the twists of any argument, namely that God is wholly unchangeable and incorruptible, their whole thousand-shaped fable would suddenly fall apart. They have painted it in their foolish and sacrilegious minds out of nothing but the idea that God is changeable, which is a most shameful thing to say.
Therefore not even an irrational soul is the matter of the human soul.

What, then, did the breath of God make the soul from? Was it some body, earthy and moist? By no means; that is rather what the flesh was made from. For what else is mud but moist earth? Nor should we believe that the soul was made from moisture alone, as if the flesh were made from earth and the soul from water. It is quite absurd to think that the soul of man was made from the same thing as the flesh of fish and birds.

Perhaps, then, it was made from air? Breath, after all, belongs to this element, but our breath, not God's. That is why we said above that this could fittingly be thought if we believed God to be the soul of the world, as of one vast living being. Then he would have breathed out the soul from the air of his body, as our soul breathes from the air of its own body. But it is established that God is above every body in the world and above every spirit he created, at an utterly incomparable distance. How, then, can this rightly be said? Or perhaps, since God is present to his whole creation by his unique omnipotence, he could all the more make from air a breath that would be the soul of man? But the soul is not bodily, whatever is made from the bodily elements of the world must be bodily, and this air too is counted among the elements of the world. So we ought not to believe it even if someone said the soul was made from the element of that pure, heavenly fire. There have been people who asserted that every body can be changed into every other body. But I know of no one who has held that any body, whether earthly or heavenly, can be turned into a soul and become a bodiless nature, and the faith does not hold it either.

Next, there is what physicians not only say but also claim they can prove, and it should not be disregarded. Although all flesh plainly has the solidity of earth, it also contains something of air, which is held in the lungs and spread from the heart through the veins they call arteries. It also contains something of fire: not only its burning quality, which has its seat in the liver, but also its bright quality. They show that this bright quality is refined, as it were, and rises up to the high region of the brain, as if to the heaven of our body. From there the rays of the eyes flash out. From the brain's middle, as from a kind of centre, fine tubes lead not only to the eyes but also to the other senses, namely to the ears, the nostrils and the palate, for hearing, smelling and tasting. The sense of touch itself extends through the whole body, and they say that it too is directed from the same brain. It runs through the marrow of the neck and the marrow held in the bones that make up the spine of the back, and from there certain very fine streams, which produce the sense of touch, spread through all the limbs.

The soul, then, receives through these as through messengers whatever it perceives of bodily things. Yet the soul itself is so different from them that when it wishes to understand divine things, or God, or indeed itself, and to consider its own powers so as to grasp something true and certain, it turns away even from this light of the eyes. It senses that this light is no help for the task, and is even something of a hindrance, and it lifts itself up into the gaze of the mind. How, then, can the soul be something of that kind? The highest thing of that kind is simply the light that flashes from the eyes, and that light helps the soul only to perceive bodily shapes and colours. The soul, however, holds countless things utterly unlike every kind of body, and it beholds them only by understanding and reason, which no sense of the flesh can reach.

So the nature of the human soul is not made of earth, or water, or air, or any kind of fire. Nevertheless, it governs the matter of its grosser body, that is, a kind of moist earth which has been turned into the quality of flesh, by means of a finer bodily nature, namely light and air. Without these two there is no sensation in the body and no voluntary movement of the body by the soul. Just as knowing must come before doing, so sensing comes before moving. Since the soul is an incorporeal thing, it acts first on the kind of body that is close to the incorporeal, such as fire, or rather light, and air. Through these it acts on the other, grosser parts of the body, such as moisture and earth, from which the bulk of the flesh is made solid. These are more suited to being acted upon than equipped for acting.

So it seems to me that the words "man became a living soul" mean only that he began to have sensation in the body, which is the surest sign of flesh that is animated and alive. Trees and shrubs move too, and not only by a force pushing them from outside, as when the winds shake them. They also move with an inner motion, which drives everything that belongs to the growth and form of the tree: sap is drawn into the root and is turned into the substances that make up a plant or a tree. None of this happens without inner motion. But this motion is not voluntary, like the motion joined to sensation for governing the body, as in every kind of animal, which Scripture calls a living soul. If we too did not have that inner motion, our bodies would not grow, nor would they put out nails and hair. But if this alone were in us, without sensation and voluntary motion, it would not be said that man became a living soul.

The front part of the brain, from which all the senses are distributed, is placed toward the forehead, and the organs of sensation themselves, so to speak, are in the face. The sense of touch is an exception, since it extends through the whole body. Even so, it is shown to have its own path from that same front part of the brain, a path that runs back over the crown and the neck to the spinal marrow I spoke of a little earlier. This is why the face, like the whole body, has the sense of touch, apart from the senses of sight, hearing, smell and taste, which are placed in the face alone. For this reason, I think, it is written that God breathed the breath of life into the man's face when he became a living soul. The front part is rightly ranked above the back, because the front leads and the back follows. Sensation comes from the front and movement from the back, just as planning comes before action.

No bodily movement that follows sensation happens without intervals of time, and we cannot carry out intervals of time by voluntary movement except with the help of memory. For this reason, they point out three ventricles, as it were, in the brain. One is at the front, toward the face, and all sensation comes from it. Another is at the back, toward the neck, and all movement comes from it; another is at the back, toward the neck, and all movement comes from it. The third lies between the two, and they show that memory is active there. Without it, when movement follows sensation, a person would not connect what he has to do, if he had forgotten what he had done. They say this has been proved by sure evidence. When these parts have been affected by some disease or defect, and the functions of sensing, or of moving the limbs, or of remembering the body's movements have failed, this has shown clearly enough what each part does. And when treatment was applied to them, it was found out which function the treatment had helped restore. But the soul acts in these as in organs and is none of them itself. It gives life to them all and governs them all, and through them it cares for the body and for this life in which man became a living soul.

So when we ask where the soul comes from, that is, from what material, so to speak, God made this breath that is called the soul, nothing bodily should come to mind. Just as God surpasses all creation, so the soul surpasses all bodily creation in the dignity of its nature. Yet it governs the body through light and air, which are the highest bodies even in the world itself. They have more power to act than the heavy bulk that is acted upon, like moisture and earth, and so the soul governs the body through things that are more like spirit. Bodily light reports something, but what it reports to is not the same as light itself. The soul is what light reports to; it is not the light that does the reporting. When the soul feels the afflictions of the body as troublesome, it is distressed because its work of being present to the body and governing it is hindered when the body's balance is disturbed, and this distress is called pain. The air poured into the nerves obeys the will so as to move the limbs, but it is not itself the will. The middle part of the brain reports the movement of the limbs so that it may be held in memory, but it is not itself memory. Finally, when these servants of the soul, so to speak, fail completely through some defect or disorder, so that the messengers of sensation and the servants of movement cease to work, the soul departs, as if it had no reason to remain. If they do not fail so completely, as they usually do in death, the soul's attention is disturbed, like someone trying to restore what is slipping away and unable to do it. And the way it is disturbed reveals which of its servants is the cause, so that medicine may come to the rescue if it can.

The soul is one thing, and these bodily servants of it, or vessels, or organs, or whatever better name they may be given, are another. This is clearly seen from the following. The soul often turns away from everything through intense concentration in thought. It then fails to notice many things set before eyes that are open and perfectly healthy. If the concentration is greater, a person who was walking may suddenly stop, because the soul has turned its command away from the servant of movement by which the feet were being driven. If the concentration in thought is not so great as to fix the walker to the spot, but is still great enough that he has no attention to spare for the middle part of the brain that reports the body's movements, he sometimes forgets where he is coming from and where he is going, and passes the farm he was heading for without noticing. His body is perfectly healthy, but his soul has been called away to something else. Consider, then, the bodily particles of the bodily heaven, namely of light and air, which are the first to receive the commands of the life-giving soul because they are closer to incorporeal nature than moisture and earth are, so that the whole mass of the body is governed through their immediate service. Whether God mixed or joined them into the living body from this heaven that surrounds and overspreads us, or made them too from clay, as he made the flesh, is a question of no importance here. It is credible that any body can be changed into any other body, but it is absurd to believe that any body can be changed into a soul.

For the same reason we should not listen to the view some have held, that there is a fifth kind of body from which souls come. On this view, it is neither earth nor water nor air nor fire, whether the more turbulent, earthly fire or the pure and bright fire of heaven, but some other thing without a familiar name, which is nevertheless a body. If those who hold this mean by body what we mean, namely any nature that occupies a space in length, breadth and height, then the soul is not such a thing, nor should we believe it was made from such a thing. To put it briefly, anything of that kind can be divided or bounded by lines in any part of itself. If the soul were subject to this, it could in no way know lines that cannot be cut lengthwise. Yet it knows such lines, while also knowing that they cannot be found in a body.

Nor does the soul find anything of this kind in itself, since it cannot be ignorant of itself, even when it searches in order to know itself. When it searches for itself, it knows that it is searching for itself, and it could not know this if it did not know itself. For it does not search for itself from anywhere else than from itself. So when it knows itself searching, it certainly knows itself, and whatever it knows, it knows as a whole. Therefore when it knows itself searching, it knows itself as a whole, and so it also knows its whole self. For it knows nothing other than itself; it knows itself, as a whole. Why then does it still search for itself, if it knows itself searching? If it did not know itself, it could not know that it was searching for itself. But this concerns the present. What it searches for about itself is what it was before or what it will be. So for the time being let it stop suspecting that it is a body. If it were anything of that kind, it would know itself to be such, since it knows itself better than it knows heaven and earth, which it knows through the eyes of its body.

I will not dwell on the fact that the power of the soul which even cattle and the birds of the air are understood to have, when they return to their dens or nests, the power in which images of all bodily things are captured, is not like any body at all. Yet this power, above all, ought to be like a body, since the likenesses of bodily things are contained in it. But if this is not a body, as it certainly is not, since these likenesses of bodies are not only held there in memory but also shaped at will in countless numbers, how much less can the soul be like a body in any other of its powers!

Suppose, however, that they give the word "body" some other meaning, and call everything that exists a body, that is, every nature and substance. We should not accept such usage, or we will find no way of speaking that distinguishes things that are not bodies from bodies. Still, we need not argue too much about a word. For we too say that whatever the soul is, it does not consist of these four best-known elements, which are obviously bodies, and that it is not what God is either. As for what it is, nothing better can be said than "soul" or "spirit of life." The words "of life" are added because this air of ours is also often called spirit. Indeed, people have even called that same air soul, so that no name can now be found to mark off this nature properly. It is neither body nor God. It is not life without sensation, such as may be believed to exist in trees, nor life without a rational mind, such as is found in cattle. It is a life now lower than that of the angels, and it will be what the angels are, if it lives here according to the commandment of its Creator.

There is doubt and inquiry about where the soul comes from: from what material, so to speak, it was made, or from what perfect and blessed nature it flowed, or whether it was made entirely from nothing. Even so, we must not doubt in the least that if anything existed before, what existed was made by God, and that the soul has now been made by God to be a living soul. Either nothing existed before, or what existed was not what the soul now is. But we have already dealt sufficiently with the part of the question in which we asked about its material, so to speak, the thing from which it was made.

Now, if the soul did not exist at all before, we must ask how we can understand the statement that its causal reason existed in God's first works of the six days, when God made man in his own image, which cannot rightly be understood except with reference to the soul. We must be careful, however, that we are not thought to be talking nonsense when we say that when God created all things at once, he did not then create the actual natures and substances that were to come, but certain causal reasons of those future things. What are these causal reasons, according to which it could already be said that God made man in his own image, when he had not yet formed man's body from clay or made his soul by breathing? In the case of the human body, even if there was some hidden reason by which it would come to be formed, there was also the material from which it would be formed, namely earth, in which that reason can be seen to have lain hidden as in a seed. But in the case of the soul that was to be made, that is, the breath that was to be made as the soul of man, what causal reason was first established there when God said, "Let us make man in our image and likeness"? That cannot be rightly understood except with reference to the soul. And if there was no nature in which it could be established, where was it established?

If this reason was in God and not in a creature, then it had not yet been created. How, then, was it said, "God made man in the image of God"? But if it was already in a creature, that is, among the things God had created all at once, in which creature was it? Was it in a spiritual creature or a bodily one? If it was in a spiritual creature, was that creature doing anything in the bodies of the world, whether heavenly or earthly? Did this reason lie idle in it before man was established in his own nature, just as the reason for begetting lies hidden and idle in a man already leading his own life, and does not operate except through intercourse and conception? Or did that spiritual creature, in which this reason lay hidden, do no work of its own at all? And then why was it created? Was it created to contain the reason of the future human soul, or of future souls, as though these could not exist in themselves but only in some creature already living a life of its own, just as the reason for begetting can exist only in natures that already exist and are complete? On that view, some spiritual creature was established as the parent of the soul, containing the reason of the future soul. The soul would not come forth from it until God made the soul to be breathed into man. For even from a human being, God alone creates and forms the offspring, whether as seed or as an actual child. He does this through Wisdom, which reaches everywhere because of its purity, so that nothing defiled enters into it, while it stretches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly. But I do not see how we can understand that some spiritual creature or other was created for this purpose alone, and yet was not mentioned among God's works made in those six days. Scripture says that God made man on the sixth day, when he had not yet made him in his own nature, but only in his causal reason in that creature which is not mentioned. That creature ought rather to have been mentioned, since it had been completed in such a way that it did not still have to be made according to a reason that preceded it.

Or perhaps God placed this causal reason of the soul to be made in the nature of the day he first established, if that day is rightly taken to be intellectual spirit. On this view, when he made man in his own image on the sixth day, he fixed beforehand the cause and reason according to which he would make him after those seven days. So we would believe that he created the causal reason of man's body in the nature of the earth, and that of his soul in the nature of that day. But what does this amount to, if not that the angelic spirit is a kind of parent of the human soul? The reason for creating the human soul would be pre-established in the angel just as the reason of his future offspring is in a man. Then human beings would be the parents of human bodies and angels the parents of souls, while God would be the Creator of both bodies and souls. But he would create bodies from human beings and souls from angels; or rather the first body from the earth and the first soul from the angelic nature, where he had fixed their causal reasons beforehand when he first made man among the things he created all at once, and from then on human beings from human beings, body from body and soul from soul! It is hard to say that the soul is the daughter of an angel or of angels. It is much harder to say it is the daughter of the bodily heaven, and how much harder still to say it is the daughter of the sea and the earth! So it is even less likely that the causal reason of the soul was pre-established in some bodily creature when God made man in his own image, before he formed him from clay in due time and gave him life by his breath, if it is absurd to believe that he established the soul causally in the angelic nature.

So let us see whether the following might be true. It certainly seems to me easier for human opinion to accept. In those first works, which he created all at once, God also created the human soul, which he would breathe in due time into the limbs of the body formed from clay. Among those things established all at once, he created causally the reason of that body, according to which the human body would come to be when the time came for it to be made. For we rightly understand the words "in his own image" only of the soul, and the words "male and female" only of the body. Let it be believed, then, unless some authority of Scripture or some reasoning of truth contradicts it, that man was made on the sixth day in such a way that the causal reason of the human body was created in the elements of the world, while the soul itself was actually created, just as the day was first established. Once created, the soul lay hidden among God's works until, in due time, he placed it by breathing, that is, by inspiring it, into the body formed from clay.

But here again a serious question arises. If the soul had already been made and lay hidden, where could it be better off than there? What reason was there, then, for a soul living in innocence to be placed in the life of this flesh, where by sinning it would offend the very one who created it, and so would deservedly incur the hardship of toil and the torment of condemnation? Should we say that it was drawn by its own will to govern the body? In the life of the body one can live either justly or unjustly, so the soul would receive whatever it chose, either reward for justice or punishment for injustice. This would not contradict the apostle's statement that those not yet born had done nothing good or evil. For that inclination of the will toward the body is not yet an act of justice or injustice, of which an account must be given at the judgment of God, when each will receive according to what he has done in the body, whether good or evil. Why, then, should we not believe instead that the soul came to the body at God's command? There, if it chose to act according to his commandment, it would receive the reward of eternal life and the company of the angels; but if it disdained his commandment, it would pay the most just penalty, either long toil or eternal fire. Or is obeying God's will already, in itself, a good act, so that this too would contradict the statement that those not yet born had done nothing good or evil?

If this is so, we will admit that the soul was not first created in a condition where it foreknew its future works, whether just or unjust. For it is utterly incredible that it could have been drawn by its own will to the life of the body if it had foreknown that it would sin in certain things and so be justly punished with everlasting torment. The Creator is rightly praised in all things, for he made all things very good. Nor is he to be praised only for the creatures to whom he gave foreknowledge. He is rightly praised also for creating cattle, and human nature is superior to them even in those who sin. For man's nature is from God, but not the injustice in which he entangles himself by misusing free will. Yet if he did not have free will, he would rank lower in the natural order. We must think of a man who lives justly even without foreknowing the future. Here we must see how excellent a good will is, since it is not hindered from living rightly and pleasing God by the fact that it lives by faith without knowing the future. So whoever would wish that such a creature did not exist opposes the goodness of God, and whoever would not have it pay the penalty for its sins is an enemy of justice.

But if the soul is made in order to be sent into a body, one may ask whether it is compelled if it is unwilling. It is better to believe that it wills this by nature, that is, that it is created with a nature such that it wills it, just as it is natural for us to will to live. But living badly no longer belongs to nature; it belongs to a perverse will, which punishment justly follows.

So it is pointless to keep asking from what material, so to speak, the soul was made, if it can rightly be understood to have been made in those first works, when the day was made. Just as those things which did not exist were made, so the soul too was made among them. But suppose there was also some formable matter, both bodily and spiritual, though even that was established only by God, from whom all things come. This matter would come before its own formation not in time but in origin, as sound comes before song. In that case, what is more fitting to believe than that the soul was made from spiritual matter?

But if someone refuses to think that the soul was made at any time other than when it was breathed into the formed body, let him consider how he will answer when he is asked what it was made from. Either he will say that God made, or makes, something out of nothing after the completion of his works. In that case he must work out how to explain that man was made in the image of God on the sixth day, which cannot rightly be understood except with reference to the soul. That is, he must explain in what nature the causal reason of this thing, which did not yet exist, was made. Or else he will say that the soul was made not from nothing but from something already existing. Then he will have to labour to find out what that nature is, whether bodily or spiritual, along the lines of the questions we turned over above. And the difficulty will still remain: he must still ask in what substance, among the creatures first established in the six days, God made that causal reason of the soul, when he had not yet made the soul either from nothing or from something.

Suppose he wants to escape this difficulty by saying that man was also made from the clay on the sixth day, and that this was only mentioned later by way of recapitulation. Then let him consider what he will say about the woman, for Scripture says: "Male and female he made them, and he blessed them." If he answers that she too was made from the man's bone on that day, let him consider how he can maintain that the birds brought to Adam were made on the sixth day, when Scripture indicates that every kind of bird was created from the waters on the fifth day. Likewise, how can he maintain that the trees planted in paradise were made on the sixth day, when the same Scripture assigned this kind of creature to the third day? Let him also weigh the words themselves. What is meant by "God brought forth still further out of the earth every tree beautiful to look at and good for food"? It sounds as though the trees the earth had brought forth on the third day were not beautiful to look at and good for food, when they were among the works that God made, all of them very good. And what is meant by "God formed still further out of the earth all the beasts of the field and all the birds of the sky"? It sounds as though the creatures produced first were not all of them, or rather as though none had been produced before. For it does not say, "And God formed further out of the earth the rest of the beasts of the field and the rest of the birds of the sky," as if these were creatures that the earth on the sixth day or the water on the fifth day had failed to produce. It says "all the beasts" and "all the birds." Let him also reflect on how God made all things in six days: on the first the day itself, on the second the firmament, on the third the form of sea and land and, from the land, grass and trees, on the fourth the lights and the stars, on the fifth the creatures of the waters, and on the sixth those of the land. Yet afterwards it is said: "When the day was made, God made heaven and earth and every green thing of the field," although when the day was made he made nothing but the day itself. Let him consider too how God made every green thing of the field before it was on the earth, and every plant before it sprang up. Who would not say that it was made when it sprang up, and not before, if the words of Scripture did not call him back? Let him remember also that it is written: "He who lives for ever created all things at once." Then let him see how things can be said to have been created at once when their creation is separated by intervals of time, not only of hours but even of days. Let him also take care to show how two statements that may seem to contradict each other are both true: that God rested on the seventh day from all his works, as the book of Genesis says, and that he is working until now, as the Lord says. And let him consider how the very things said to have been completed are also said to have been begun.

Only an unbeliever or an impious person doubts that divine Scripture is truthful, and all these testimonies of Scripture have led us to this view. From the beginning of the world, God first created all things at once, some with their natures already established and some in causes established beforehand. In this way the Almighty made not only things present but also things to come, and then rested from what he had made, so that from then on, by administering and governing them, he might also create the orders of the ages and of temporal things. For he had both completed them, since every kind had received its limit, and begun them, so that the ages might unfold. Because they were completed he rested, and because they were begun he is working until now. But if these things can be understood better, I not only do not resist, I welcome it.

For now, however, I affirm nothing about the soul, which God breathed into man by blowing into his face, except these things. It is from God in such a way that it is not the substance of God, and it is incorporeal. That is, it is not a body but a spirit. It is not begotten of God's substance nor does it proceed from God's substance, but it was made by God. Nor was it made by turning some nature of a body or of an irrational soul into its nature, and therefore it was made from nothing. It is immortal with respect to a certain mode of life which it can in no way lose. Yet with respect to a certain changeableness, by which it can become worse or better, it may not unreasonably be understood to be mortal as well, since only he has true immortality of whom it was said in the proper sense: "who alone has immortality." As for the other things I have said in this book by way of discussion, let them serve the reader in one of two ways. Either he will learn how to investigate, without rash assertion, matters that Scripture does not speak of openly. Or, if this way of inquiring does not please him, I may learn how he has inquired himself. Then, if he can teach me, I will not refuse; and if he cannot, let him join me in seeking someone from whom we may both learn.
BOOK EIGHT

"And God planted a paradise in Eden toward the east, and put there the man whom he had formed." I am aware that many people have said many things about paradise. There are, however, three general views on the matter. The first belongs to those who want paradise to be understood only in a bodily sense. The second belongs to those who understand it only spiritually. The third belongs to those who take paradise in both ways, sometimes bodily and sometimes spiritually. To put it briefly, I confess that the third view pleases me. In keeping with it I have now undertaken to speak about paradise, as far as the Lord will deign to grant. My aim is to show that the man made from the clay, which is certainly the human body, should be understood as placed in a bodily paradise. Adam himself may signify something further, since the Apostle said he was a type of the one to come. Yet he is understood as a man in his own proper nature, who lived a definite number of years, fathered many offspring and died as other people die, even though he was not born of parents as others are but was made from the earth, as was fitting at the beginning. In the same way, the paradise in which God placed him should be understood as nothing other than a certain place, namely a place on earth where an earthly man might live.

For the narrative in these books is not written in the figurative mode of speech, as in the Song of Songs. It is wholly a narrative of things that happened, as in the books of Kings and others of the same kind. But in those books the things described belong to the most familiar experience of human life, so they are readily, indeed very easily, taken first in the literal sense, and afterwards one can draw out what the events themselves also signified about things to come. Here, by contrast, the things described do not match the ordinary course of nature as people observe it. So some do not want them understood literally but figuratively, and want history, that is, the narrative of things that actually happened, to begin at the point where Adam and Eve, sent out of paradise, came together and had children. As if it were ordinary for us that people lived so many years, or that Enoch was taken up, or that a woman both very old and barren gave birth, and other things of that sort!

"But," they say, "a narrative of wonderful deeds is one thing, and a narrative of the establishment of creatures is another. In the first, the unusual events themselves show that there are, so to speak, natural ways in which things happen and other ways that belong to miracles, which are called mighty works. Here, by contrast, it is the very establishment of natures that is being described." We answer them: these things too are unusual precisely because they were the first. For in the constitution of worldly things, what is so without precedent and without parallel as the world itself? Should we refuse to believe that God made the world because he no longer makes worlds, or that he made the sun because he no longer makes suns? This answer should really have been given to those troubled about man himself rather than about paradise. But as it is, since they believe that man was made by God in a way no one else has been made, why do they refuse to believe that paradise was made in the way they now see woods being made?

I am speaking, of course, to those who follow the authority of these writings, some of whom want paradise to be understood not literally but figuratively. As for those who are entirely opposed to these writings, I have dealt with them elsewhere and in another way. Even so, in this very work of ours we defend these things according to the letter as well as we can. In that way, those who refuse to believe them, moved not by reason but by a stubborn or dull mind, may still find no argument by which to prove them false. But as for our own people, who have faith in these divine books and yet do not want paradise understood in the proper sense of the letter, I am amazed at them. By paradise I mean a most delightful place, shaded with fruitful groves, large, and made fertile by a great spring. They see so many great green woods springing up without any human labour, through God's hidden work, and I wonder how they can believe that man himself was made in a way they have never seen. Or if man too is to be understood figuratively, who fathered Cain, Abel and Seth? Were they too merely figures, and not also human beings born of human beings? Let them therefore look closely at where this presumption leads, and let them try with us to take everything narrated as having happened first of all in its proper and literal sense. Who would not then gladly support them as they go on to understand what these things also teach by figurative signification, whether about spiritual natures and dispositions themselves or about things to come? Certainly, if the things named here in bodily terms could in no way be taken in a bodily sense without compromising the true faith, what would remain except to understand them as spoken figuratively, rather than impiously finding fault with Holy Scripture? But if these things, understood in a bodily sense as well, not only do not hinder the narrative of the divine word but actually support it more firmly, then no one, I think, will be so faithlessly stubborn that, once he has seen them explained in their proper sense according to the rule of faith, he would prefer to remain in his former opinion, if he happened to think they could only be taken figuratively.

Shortly after my conversion I wrote two books against the Manichaeans. They do not err by interpreting these writings of the Old Testament wrongly; they blaspheme by rejecting and detesting them altogether. I wanted to refute their ravings quickly, or else to rouse them to seek the Christian and evangelical faith in the very writings they hate. At that time it did not occur to me how all these things could be taken in their proper sense. It seemed rather that they could not be, or only barely and with difficulty. So that I would not be held up, I explained as briefly and clearly as I could what the passages I could not work out literally signified figuratively. I did not want my readers to be put off by a long text or obscure argument and so not bother to take the books in hand. Still, I was mindful of what I had chiefly wanted and been unable to do, namely to have everything understood first of all not figuratively but in its proper sense. Nor did I entirely despair that it could be understood that way, and I said as much at the beginning of the second book: "Certainly, if anyone wants to take everything that has been said according to the letter, that is, to understand it no differently from how the letter sounds, and can avoid blasphemy and proclaim everything in agreement with the Catholic faith, he is not only not to be begrudged but is to be regarded as an outstanding and very praiseworthy interpreter. But if no way out is given for understanding what is written in a manner that is reverent and worthy of God, except by believing that these things are set forth figuratively and in riddles, then let us hold to the method we have set out. We have the authority of the apostles, by whom so many riddles in the books of the Old Testament are solved. With the help of him who urges us to ask, seek and knock, let us explain all these figures of things in accordance with the Catholic faith, whether they belong to history or to prophecy, without prejudice to a better and more careful treatment, whether by us or by others to whom the Lord deigns to reveal it." That is what I said then.
