But now the Lord has willed that, looking at and considering these things more carefully, I should judge, not in vain, I think, that I too could show these things were written in the proper and not the allegorical mode of speech. So, just as with what we sought to show above, let us likewise examine what follows about paradise.

So God planted a paradise in delights, for that is what "in Eden" means, toward the east, and put there the man whom he had formed. It is written this way because it happened this way. Then Scripture recapitulates, to show how what it had stated briefly was done, that is, how God planted paradise and set there the man he had formed. For it continues: "And God brought forth still further out of the earth every tree beautiful to look at and good for food." It did not say, "And God brought forth out of the earth another tree" or "the rest of the trees." It says, "he brought forth still further out of the earth every tree beautiful to look at and good for food." So the earth had already, on the third day, produced every tree both beautiful to look at and good for food. For on the sixth day God had said: "See, I have given you every seed-bearing plant that yields seed, which is on the face of all the earth, and every fruit-bearing tree that has in it the fruit of its seed, which will be food for you." Did he then give them one thing at that time and intend to give them another now? I do not think so. Rather, since these trees set in paradise were of the same kinds the earth had already produced on the third day, the earth produced them "still further" in their own time. For when it was written that the earth produced them, this had been done causally in the earth. That is, the earth had then secretly received the power to produce them, and by that power it now brings forth such things visibly and in their own time.

So on the sixth day God said: "See, I have given you every seed-bearing plant that yields seed, which is on the face of all the earth," and so on. These words were not uttered by a sounding voice in time; they are words in the way that the power of creating is in his Word. But what God said without sounds in time could only be told to human beings through sounds in time. For it was going to happen that man, once formed from the clay and given life by God's breath, and the whole human race that would come from him, would use as food the things that would spring up on the earth from the power of generation the earth had already received. When God established the causal reasons of this future in creation, he spoke as though it already existed. He spoke by an inner and inmost truth, which eye has not seen nor ear heard, but which his Spirit revealed to the writer.

What follows, however, needs to be considered more carefully: "and the tree of life in the middle of paradise, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil." Otherwise it may force us into allegory, as though these were not trees but signified something else by the name of a tree. For it was said of wisdom: "She is a tree of life to all who embrace her." Yet although there is an eternal Jerusalem in heaven, a city that signified it was also founded on earth. Sarah and Hagar signified the two covenants, but they were also two actual women. And although Christ waters us with a spiritual stream through his passion on the wood, there was also the rock that poured out water for the thirsty people when it was struck with a rod, of which it could be said: "And the rock was Christ." All these things signified something other than what they were, but they nevertheless existed bodily themselves. And when the narrator recorded them, this was not figurative speech but the plain narrative of things that served as figures going before. So there was a tree of life just as the rock was Christ, and God did not want man to live in paradise without mysteries of spiritual things presented in bodily form. In the other trees, then, man had nourishment, but in that one a sacrament. What did it signify if not wisdom, of which it was said, "She is a tree of life to those who embrace her," just as it might be said of Christ, "He is a flowing rock to those who thirst for him"? A thing that went before to signify him is rightly called by his name. He is the lamb sacrificed at the Passover; yet that too was prefigured not only by words but also by a deed. That lamb really was a lamb: it certainly was a lamb, and it was killed and eaten. And yet by that real event something else was also prefigured. It was not like the fatted calf that was killed for the feast when the younger son returned. There the narrative itself consists of figures, not of events that carry a figurative meaning. For it was not the evangelist who told that story but the Lord himself; the evangelist told that the Lord told it. So what the evangelist narrated really happened, namely that the Lord said such things. But the Lord's own narrative was a parable, and no one ever demands that the things told in a parable be shown to have happened literally. Christ is both the stone anointed by Jacob and the stone rejected by the builders, which has become the cornerstone. But the first actually took place among real events, while the second was only foretold in figures. The first was written by one who narrated past events, the second by one who only foretold things to come.

In the same way wisdom, which is Christ himself, is the tree of life in the spiritual paradise, into which he sent the thief from the cross. But to signify wisdom, a tree of life was also created in the bodily paradise. For so says that Scripture which, narrating events in their own times, related that man was made in bodily form and placed there to live in the body. Or if anyone thinks that souls, after leaving the body, are held in bodily visible places even though they are without bodies, let him defend his view. There will be no lack of people to support him, who will argue that the thirsting rich man was in a bodily place, and will not hesitate to declare that the soul itself is entirely bodily because of the parched tongue and the drop of water he longed for from Lazarus's finger. I will not rashly fight with them over so great a question. It is better to be in doubt about hidden things than to quarrel about uncertain ones. I do not doubt that the rich man must be understood to be in the burning of punishment and the poor man in the refreshment of joy. But how we are to understand that flame of hell, that bosom of Abraham, that tongue of the rich man, that finger of the poor man, that thirst of torment, that drop of refreshment, can perhaps scarcely be found even by those who seek gently, and never by those who argue contentiously. I must answer briefly, so that this deep question, which needs a long discussion, does not hold us up. If souls are held in bodily places even when stripped of their bodies, then the thief could have been brought into the paradise where the body of the first man had been. In a more suitable passage of Scripture, if any need demands it, we will set out somehow what we inquire or think about this matter too.

For now, I do not doubt, and I do not think anyone doubts, that wisdom is not a body and therefore not a tree. But someone may think it incredible that wisdom could have been signified in a bodily paradise by a tree, that is, by a bodily creature, as by a kind of sacrament. Such a person either does not see the many bodily sacraments of spiritual things in the Scriptures, or else he insists that the first man ought not to have lived with any sacrament of this kind. Yet the Apostle says that even what was said about the woman, who was certainly made from the man's side, "For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two will be one flesh," is a great sacrament in Christ and in the Church. It is strange and hardly bearable that people are willing for paradise to have been spoken of figuratively but unwilling for it also to have been made as a figure. If they grant that these things, like the accounts of Hagar and Sarah or of Ishmael and Isaac, both really happened and were also figures, I do not see why they should not also admit that the tree of life was truly a tree and yet also figured wisdom.

I add this too: although that tree was bodily food, it nevertheless provided a food by which the human body was strengthened in lasting health. It did not do this as other food does, but by a certain hidden infusion of health. Surely there was something more than ordinary bread in the bread by which, with a single cake, God kept a man from the want of hunger for forty days. Shall we hesitate to believe that God, for the sake of some higher signification, granted man through the food of a certain tree that his body should not change for the worse through weakness or age, nor sink even to death? This is the God who gave ordinary human food so wonderful a state that the flour and oil in earthen jars, as they ran low, were replenished and did not run out. Now let someone of the contentious sort stand up and say that God ought to have done such miracles in our lands but ought not to have done them in paradise. As if he did not work a greater miracle there in making man from dust or woman from the man's side than when he raised the dead here!

Next we must consider the tree of the knowledge of discerning good and evil. This tree too was certainly visible and bodily, like the other trees. So there is no doubt that it was a tree; what we must ask is why it was given this name. As I consider the matter again and again, I cannot say how strongly I am drawn to the view that the tree was not harmful as food (for he who had made all things very good would not have placed anything evil in paradise), but that what was evil for the man was his breaking of the commandment. For it was fitting that the man, placed under the Lord God, should be forbidden something, so that obedience itself would be the virtue by which he earned his Lord's favour. I can say with complete truth that obedience is the one virtue for every rational creature acting under God's authority, and that the first and greatest vice, the swelling pride that leads to ruin, is to want to use one's own power. The name of that vice is disobedience. The man would therefore have had no way of thinking and feeling that he had a Lord unless something was commanded of him. So that tree was not evil. It was called the tree of the knowledge of discerning good and evil because, if the man ate from it after it had been forbidden, the breaking of the commandment would lie in it, and through that breach he would learn by experiencing punishment the difference between the good of obedience and the evil of disobedience. Accordingly, this too is not said figuratively. It must be taken as a real tree, which received its name not from any fruit or produce that grew on it, but from what would follow if it were touched against the prohibition.

"A river went out from Eden to water paradise, and from there it divided into four branches. The name of one is Pishon; it is the one that flows around the whole land of Havilah, where there is gold. The gold of that land is good, and there is carbuncle there, and the green stone. The name of the second river is Gihon; it is the one that flows around the whole land of Ethiopia. The third river is the Tigris; it is the one that flows over against the Assyrians. The fourth river is the Euphrates." Why should I labour any further to show that these are real rivers and not figures of speech for things that do not exist, as though the names alone signified something? They are very well known in the lands they flow through and famous among almost all nations. Indeed, two of them have had their names changed over time, just as the river now called the Tiber was once called the Albula: the Gihon is the river now called the Nile, and the river that was called Pishon is now called the Ganges, while the other two, the Tigris and the Euphrates, have kept their ancient names. Since it is quite certain that these rivers exist, they should remind us to take the rest of the account first in the proper, literal sense of the words. We should not suppose that it is figurative language, but rather that the things narrated both really existed as described and also signify something further. I do not say this because a parable could not borrow something from a thing that also exists in the literal sense. Take the man of whom the Lord speaks, who was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among robbers. Who does not perceive and clearly see that this is a parable and that the whole passage is figurative? Yet the two cities named there are still pointed out today in their own places. We would take these four rivers in that way too if some necessity forced us to take everything else told about paradise figuratively rather than literally. But as it is, since no reason forbids us to understand the things themselves first in their literal sense, why should we not rather simply follow the authority of Scripture in its narrative of events, understanding first that the events really happened, and only then searching out whatever else they signify? Or shall we be troubled because it is said that the sources of some of these rivers are known while those of others are entirely unknown, and conclude that the passage cannot be taken literally when it says they divide from a single river of paradise? We should rather believe that, since the place of paradise itself is very far removed from human knowledge, the waters do divide there into four branches, as most trustworthy Scripture testifies. The rivers whose sources are said to be known must somewhere have gone under the earth, and after passing beneath wide stretches of country broken out in other places, where they are said to be known as if at their sources. Who does not know that some waters commonly do this? But it is known only where they do not run underground for long. So a river went out from Eden, that is, from the place of delights, and watered paradise, that is, all the beautiful and fruitful trees that shaded the whole ground of that region.

"And the Lord God took the man whom he had made and placed him in paradise to work and to keep it. And the Lord God commanded Adam, saying: From every tree that is in paradise you shall eat for food, but from the tree of knowing good and evil you shall not eat. On the day you eat from it you shall die the death." Having said briefly above that God planted paradise and set there the man whom he had formed, Scripture went back over the matter to tell how paradise was established. Now, going back again, it also recalls how God placed there the man whom he had made. Let us see, then, what is meant by "to work and to keep." What was he to work, or what was he to keep? Did the Lord perhaps want the first man to work at farming? Or is it not credible that he condemned him to toil before sin? We would indeed think so, if we did not see that some people farm with such delight of mind that it is a heavy punishment for them to be called away from it to anything else. Whatever delights farming holds, then, they were certainly far greater at a time when nothing adverse befell either the earth or the sky. There was no affliction of toil, only the gladness of a willing spirit, since the things God had created yielded more richly and abundantly with the help of human work. And so the Creator himself would be praised more fully, for he had given a soul placed in an animal body the skill and the ability to work, as much as a willing mind would wish, not as much as the needs of the body would force on it against its will.

For what greater or more wonderful sight is there, or where can human reason more nearly converse, as it were, with the nature of things, than when seeds are sown, shoots planted, saplings transplanted and cuttings grafted? It is as though each power of root and bud is being questioned about what it can and cannot do, and why it can or cannot do it, what is achieved by the invisible inner power of numbers and what by care applied from outside. And in that very study one can see that "neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth," since even the work that is added from outside is added through one whom God likewise created, and whom God invisibly rules and directs.

From here the mind's eye is raised to the world itself, as to a kind of great tree of all things, and in it too a twofold working of providence is found, partly natural and partly voluntary. The natural working is carried out through God's hidden governance, by which he gives growth even to trees and plants; the voluntary through the works of angels and of human beings. By the first, the heavenly things are ordered above and the earthly below; the lights and stars shine; day and night alternate; the earth, founded upon the waters, is washed through and around by them; the air is spread above it; plants and animals are conceived and born, grow, age and die; and whatever else happens in things by an inner and natural movement. By the second, signs are given, things are taught and learned, fields are tilled, communities are governed, arts are practised, and whatever else is done, whether in the society above or in this earthly and mortal one, in such a way that the good are provided for even through the wicked, who do not know it. In man himself the same twofold power of providence is at work. Toward the body it acts naturally, through the movement by which the body comes to be, grows and ages; and voluntarily, by which it is provided with food, clothing and care. Likewise toward the soul it acts naturally, so that the soul lives and perceives; and voluntarily, so that it learns and gives its assent.

In a tree, farming acts from outside so that what goes on inside may flourish. In the same way, in a human being, as regards the body, medicine serves from outside what nature works within; and as regards the soul, teaching is supplied from outside so that our nature may be made happy within. What neglect of cultivation is to a tree, lack of medical care is to the body, and sloth in learning is to the soul. What harmful moisture is to a tree, deadly food is to the body, and persuasion to wickedness is to the soul. So God, who is above all things, who founded all things and rules all things, in his goodness creates every nature and in his justice orders every will. Then what is contrary to truth in believing that man was placed in paradise to work at farming, not with servile toil but with honourable delight of mind? What is more innocent than this work for those at leisure, or more full of deep reflection for the wise?

But to keep what? Paradise itself? Against whom? Certainly no neighbouring invader was feared, no one to disturb the boundaries, no thief, no attacker. How, then, are we to understand that a bodily paradise could have been kept by a man in a bodily way? But Scripture did not say "to work and to keep paradise"; it said "to work and to keep." Although, if the Greek is rendered more carefully word for word, it is written like this: "And the Lord God took the man whom he had made and placed him in paradise to work him and to keep." But whether he placed the man to work himself (this is how the translator who wrote "that he might work" understood it) or to work paradise, that is, so that the man might work paradise, is ambiguous. And the wording seems rather to require that it be taken not as "to work paradise" but "to work in paradise."

However, in case it was said "to work paradise" in the same way as it was said earlier, "there was no man to work the ground" (for "to work paradise" is the same expression as "to work the ground"), let us consider the ambiguous sentence both ways. If we need not take it as "to keep paradise" but as "in paradise," what was he to keep in paradise? We have already discussed, as seemed best, what he was to work in paradise. Was it that what he worked in the ground by farming he should keep in himself by discipline? That is, just as the field obeyed him when he cultivated it, so he too should obey his Lord when he gave a command, so that, having received the command of obedience, he would yield fruit and not the thorns of disobedience. In the end, because he refused to keep in himself, as a subject, the likeness of the paradise he cultivated, he was condemned and received a field like himself: "Thorns and thistles," it says, "it shall bring forth for you."

But if we understand it to mean that he was to work paradise and keep paradise, he could indeed work paradise by farming, as we said above. But he could keep it not against wicked men or enemies, for there were none, but perhaps against beasts. How so? Or why? Were beasts already savage toward man? That could only have happened because of sin. For he himself gave names to all the beasts when they were brought to him, as is related later, and on the sixth day, by the law of God's word, he received food in common with all of them. Or if there was already something to fear in the beasts, how could one man fortify that paradise? It was no small place, watered by so great a spring. He would have had to keep it, if he could, by enclosing paradise with a wall of such a kind and size that the serpent could not get in. And it would be astonishing if he could have driven all the serpents out of it before he built the wall.

Why, then, do we pass over the meaning that lies before our eyes? The man was placed in paradise to work that paradise, as was argued above, by a farming that was not toilsome but delightful, and that would remind a wise mind of great and useful things; and to keep that same paradise for himself, by not committing anything for which he would deserve to be expelled from it. In the end he also received a command, so that there would be something by which he might keep paradise for himself, that is, by observing which he would not be cast out of it. For a person is rightly said not to have kept his property if he acted in such a way as to lose it, even if it remains safe for someone else who either found it or earned the right to receive it.

There is another sense in these words which I think may well be preferred: that God was to work the man himself and to keep him. Just as a man works the ground, not to make it be ground but to make it cultivated and fruitful, so, and much more so, God works man, whom he himself created so that he would be a man, in order that he may be righteous, provided that man does not withdraw from him through pride. For that is what it is to apostatize from God, which Scripture calls the beginning of pride: "The beginning of man's pride," it says, "is to apostatize from God." Since God is the unchangeable good, while man is a changeable thing in both soul and body, man cannot be formed so as to be righteous and happy unless he turns to the unchangeable good, which is God, and abides in him. And therefore the same God who creates man so that he may be a man himself works man and keeps him, so that he may also be good and happy. So in the same way of speaking by which a man is said to work the ground, which was already ground, so that it may be fertile and well-tended, God is said to work man, who was already a man, so that he may be devout and wise; and to keep him, because man cannot be safe if he delights in his own power over himself rather than God's power above him, and scorns God's lordship.

I therefore believe that it is by no means without purpose, but that it reminds us of something, and something important, that from the very opening of this divine book, which begins "In the beginning God made heaven and earth," up to this point, it nowhere says "the Lord God" but only "God." Now, however, when it comes to his setting the man in paradise and working and keeping him by means of a commandment, Scripture speaks like this: "And the Lord God took the man whom he had made and placed him in paradise to work him and to keep." This is not because God was not the Lord of the creatures mentioned earlier. It is because this was written not for the sake of the angels or of the other created things, but for the sake of man, to remind him how much it is to his advantage to have the Lord God, that is, to live obediently under his lordship rather than to abuse his own power licentiously. So Scripture chose not to use this phrase anywhere before it came to placing him in paradise, working him and keeping him. It did not say, as it said of everything else above, "And God took the man whom he had made," but rather: "And the Lord God took the man whom he had made and placed him in paradise to work him," so that he would be righteous, "and to keep," so that he would be safe, by that very lordship of his which is useful not to him but to us. For he has no need of our service, but we need his lordship, so that he may work and keep us. And that is why he alone is truly Lord: because we serve him not for his advantage but for our own advantage and salvation. If he needed us, he would by that very fact not be truly Lord, since we would be helping him in his need, and he himself would be a servant to that need. Rightly does the psalmist say: "I said to the Lord, You are my God, for you have no need of my goods." Nor should our statement that we serve him for our own advantage and salvation be taken to mean that we expect anything from him other than himself, who is our highest good and our salvation. For in this way we love him freely, in keeping with that saying: "But for me it is good to cling to God."

For man is not the kind of thing that, once made, can do anything good as if of himself when he abandons the one who made him. His whole good action is to turn to the one by whom he was made, and to be made by him always righteous, devout, wise and happy, not to be made so and then depart, as one is healed by a physician of the body and then goes away. For the physician of the body was a worker from outside, serving nature as it works within under God, who brings about all health by that twofold work of providence of which we spoke above. So man ought not to turn to God in such a way that, once he has been made righteous by him, he goes away; he should turn to him so as to be made so by him always. For by this very fact, that he does not depart from him, he is justified, enlightened and made happy by God's presence, as God works and keeps him, ruling over one who is obedient and submissive.

For, as we were saying, God does not work a man to be righteous, that is, justify him, in the way a man works the ground so that it may be tilled and fertile. A man, when he has worked the ground, goes away and leaves it ploughed or sown or watered, or whatever else, and the work that was done remains after the worker has gone. But God does not justify a man in such a way that, if the man departs, what God did remains in him as he departs. Rather, just as the air, when light is present, has not been made bright but is being made bright (for if it had been made bright, rather than being made so continually, it would stay bright even when the light was absent), so man is enlightened when God is present to him, and at once falls into darkness when God is absent. And one departs from God not by distances of place but by turning the will away.

Let him, then, who is unchangeably good work man to be good and keep him so. We must always be made by him and always be perfected by him, clinging to him and remaining in that turning which is toward him, of whom it is said, "But for me it is good to cling to God," and to whom it is said, "I will keep my strength for you." For we are his handiwork, created not only so that we might be human beings, but also so that we might be good. The apostle, too, commending to the faithful who had turned from ungodliness the grace by which we are saved, says: "For by grace you have been saved through faith; and this is not from yourselves, it is the gift of God; not from works, lest anyone should boast. For we are his handiwork, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared so that we might walk in them." And elsewhere, after saying, "Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling," he at once added, so that they would not think they should take the credit as though they made themselves righteous and good: "For it is God who works in you." So the Lord God took the man whom he had made and placed him in paradise to work him, that is, to work in him, and to keep him.

"And the Lord God commanded Adam, saying: From every tree that is in paradise you shall eat for food, but from the tree of knowing good and evil you shall not eat. On the day you eat from it you shall die the death." If the tree from which God forbade the man had been something evil, he would seem to have been poisoned to death by the very nature of that evil. But he who made all things very good had planted all the trees in paradise good, and there was no evil nature there, since there is no evil nature anywhere (a point we will discuss more carefully, if the Lord wills, when we come to speak of the serpent). The man was forbidden a tree that was not evil, so that keeping the commandment would in itself be good for him and breaking it would be evil.

Nor could it have been shown better or more carefully how great an evil disobedience alone is, since the man became guilty of wickedness precisely because he touched, against the prohibition, a thing which he would certainly not have sinned in touching if it had not been forbidden. For suppose someone says, for example, "Do not touch this plant," because it happens to be poisonous and threatens death if touched. Death will indeed follow for the one who disregards the command; but even if no one had forbidden it and he had touched it, he would die all the same. That thing would not be conducive to his health and life, whether he was forbidden it or not. Again, when someone forbids the touching of a thing that would harm not the one who touches it but the one who forbade it, as when a person lays hands on someone else's money after being forbidden by its owner, it is a sin for the one forbidden because it could cause loss to the one forbidding. But when the thing touched would not harm the one touching it, if it were not forbidden, nor anyone else, whenever it was touched, why was it forbidden, except to show the good of obedience in itself and the evil of disobedience in itself?

In short, the sinner sought nothing other than not to be under God's lordship, when he committed that act in which, to keep from committing it, he ought to have attended only to the command of his Lord. If he had attended to that alone, what else would he have attended to but God's will? What else would he have loved but God's will? What else would he have set above the human will but God's will? Why the Lord commanded it is his own concern. The servant must do what he commanded, and then perhaps, having earned it, he may see why he commanded it. But, so that we need not look any longer for the reason for this command: if it is in itself of great benefit to man to serve God, then by commanding, God makes useful whatever he chooses to command, and there is no need to fear that he could ever command anything useless.

It cannot be that a person's own will does not come crashing down on him with a heavy weight of ruin if he exalts it and sets it above the will of his superior. Man learned this by experience when he despised God's command, and through that experience he learned the difference between good and evil: the good, that is, of obedience, and the evil of disobedience, which is pride and stubbornness, a perverse imitation of God and a harmful freedom. The tree in connection with which this could happen took its name from the event itself, as was said above. For we would not feel evil except by experience, since there would be no evil if we had not done it. No nature is evil; it is the loss of good that has received this name. God is the unchangeable good. Man, as far as concerns the nature in which God created him, is indeed good, but not unchangeable as God is. A changeable good, which comes after the unchangeable good, becomes a better good when it clings to the unchangeable good, loving and serving it with a rational will that is its own. Indeed, this too is a nature of great good, because it has also received the power to cling to the nature of the supreme good. If it will not do so, it deprives itself of good, and this is evil for it, and from this, through God's justice, torment also follows. For what could be so unjust as that it should go well with one who deserts the good? There is no way this can be so. Yet sometimes the evil of losing the higher good is not felt, while the lower good that one has loved is still possessed. But divine justice requires that whoever has by his own will lost what he ought to have loved should lose with pain what he did love, so that the Creator of natures may be praised everywhere. For what grieves over a lost good is still good; if some good had not remained in the nature, there would be no grief in punishment over the good that was lost.

But one who takes pleasure in the good without any experience of evil, that is, who chooses to hold on to it so as not to lose it before he feels its loss, deserves to be proclaimed above all men. Unless this were a matter of singular praise, it would not have been ascribed to that child who, born of the race of Israel as Emmanuel, God with us, reconciled us to God: the man who is mediator between men and God, the Word with God, flesh with us, the Word made flesh between God and us. Of him the prophet says: "Before the child knows good or evil, he will scorn wickedness, so as to choose the good." How can he either scorn or choose what he does not know, unless these two things are known in one way through the understanding of good and in another through the experience of evil? Through the understanding of good, evil is known even if it is not felt, for the good is held fast so that its loss may not be felt as evil. Again, through the experience of evil, good is known, since whoever has fared badly from losing the good feels what he has lost. So before the child knew by experience either the good he would lack or the evil he would feel by losing the good, he scorned evil so as to choose good; that is, he refused to lose what he had, so that he might not feel, by losing it, what he ought not to lose. A singular example of obedience! For he came not to do his own will but the will of the one who sent him, unlike that other who chose to do his own will and not the will of the one who made him. Rightly, then, just as through one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so through one man's obedience many will be made righteous; for as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive.

Some people show a sharp kind of dullness, and to no purpose, when they ask how it could have been called the tree of the discerning of good and evil before man had transgressed the command in it and discerned by actual experience the difference between the good he had lost and the evil he had taken on. The tree received this name so that, by not touching it as the prohibition required, they might guard against what they would feel if they touched it against the prohibition. It was not because they ate from it against the command that the tree became the tree of the discerning of good and evil. Even if they had been obedient and had taken nothing from it against the command, it would still rightly have been called after what would happen to them there if they had taken from it. Suppose a tree were called the tree of fullness because people could be filled by it: would that name be unfitting if no one had ever gone near it? When they did go near it and were filled, they would then find out how rightly that tree had been so called.

"And how," they say, "could man understand what was said to him about the tree of the discerning of good and evil, when he had no idea at all what evil itself was?" Those who think this pay too little attention to the way most unknown things are understood from their known opposites, so that even when words for things that do not exist come up in speech, no hearer is left in the dark. What does not exist at all is called "nothing," and there is no one who hears and speaks Latin who does not understand these two syllables. How is that, unless the mind's perception looks at what is and, by its absence, recognizes also what is not? So too when "void" is said, we understand what "void" means by looking at the fullness of a body and at its absence as its opposite. Just as with the sense of hearing we judge not only sounds but silence as well, so from the life that was in man he could guard against its opposite, that is, the loss of life, which is called death. And the very cause by which he would lose what he loved, that is, any deed of his own that would bring about the loss of life, whatever syllables it might be called by, as in Latin it is called "sin" or "evil," he would understand as a sign of something his mind could discern. For how do we understand the word "resurrection," which we have never experienced? Is it not because we feel what it is to live, and we call the loss of this "death," and call the return from it to what we feel "resurrection"? And if the same thing is called by some other name in any language, a sign is conveyed to the mind through the speaker's voice, and when it sounds the mind recognizes what it would think even without a sign. It is wonderful how nature avoids the loss of the things it has, even without having experienced that loss. Who taught animals to avoid death if not their sense of life? Who taught a small child to cling to the one carrying him if he threatens to throw him down from a height? This begins at a certain age, but still before he has experienced anything of the kind.

So for those first human beings life was already sweet, and they certainly shrank from losing it, and they could understand God when he signified this very thing by whatever means or sounds. Nor could they have been persuaded to sin unless they had first been persuaded that they would not die from that deed, that is, that they would not lose what they had and rejoiced to have. But this must be discussed in its proper place. Let those who are troubled about how they could understand God when he named or threatened things they had not experienced take note, and see that we recognize the names of all things we have not experienced, without any agitation of doubt, only from opposites we already know, if they are privations, or from similar things, if they are kinds. Unless perhaps someone is troubled about how they could speak, or understand someone speaking, when they had not learned either by growing up among speakers or by any instruction. As if it were a great thing for God to teach speech to those whom he had made capable of learning it even from human beings, had there been any to learn from!

It is indeed reasonable to ask whether God gave this command to the man alone or to the woman as well. But it has not yet been told how the woman was made. Or perhaps she had already been made, and how this was done, though it was done earlier, is told later by way of recapitulation? For the words of Scripture are as follows: "And the Lord God commanded Adam, saying"; it did not say, "commanded them." Then follows: "Of every tree that is in paradise you shall eat for food"; it did not say, "you shall both eat." Then it adds: "But of the tree of knowing good and evil, you shall not eat of it." Here it now speaks in the plural, as if to both, and ends the command in the plural, saying: "But on the day you eat of it, you shall surely die." Or was it that, knowing he was going to make the woman for him, God gave the command in perfect order, so that the Lord's command might reach the woman through the man? The apostle keeps this discipline in the Church when he says: "If they wish to learn anything, let them ask their husbands at home."

Likewise one may ask how God spoke at this point to the man he had made, who was certainly already endowed with sense and mind so that he could hear and understand someone speaking. He could not have received a command, and so become its transgressor, unless he understood it when he received it. How then did God speak to him? Was it inwardly in the mind, through the intellect, so that he wisely understood God's will and command without any bodily sounds or likenesses of bodily things? I do not think God spoke to the first man in that way. Scripture tells things of such a kind that we should rather believe God spoke to man in paradise as he later spoke to the fathers, to Abraham and to Moses, that is, in some bodily form. This is why they heard his voice as he walked in paradise toward evening, and hid themselves.

A great subject therefore presents itself, and one not to be passed over: that we should contemplate, as far as we can and as far as he himself deigns to help and grant, the twofold work of divine providence. We touched on this briefly above, in passing, when we were speaking of agriculture, so that the reader's mind might begin from that point to grow used to contemplating it. This helps a great deal to keep us from thinking anything unworthy of God's very substance. We say, then, that the supreme, true, one and only God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, that is, God and his Word and the Spirit of both, the Trinity itself, neither confused nor separated, God who alone has immortality and dwells in unapproachable light, whom no man has seen or can see, is neither contained in any space of places, finite or infinite, nor varied by any course of times, finite or infinite. For in his substance, by which he is God, there is nothing smaller in a part than in the whole, as must be the case with things that are in places; nor was there anything in his substance that is no longer, nor will there be anything that is not yet, as there is in natures that can undergo the changeableness of time.

He, then, living in unchangeable eternity, created all things at once, from which times would run their course, places would be filled, and the ages would roll on through the temporal and local motions of things. Among these things he made some spiritual and some bodily. He formed matter, which no one else, indeed nobody at all, but he himself alone established as formless and capable of form, so that it preceded its own formation not in time but in origin. He set the spiritual creation above the bodily, because the spiritual could be changed only through times, while the bodily is changed through times and places. For example, the mind is moved through time when it remembers what it had forgotten, learns what it did not know, or wills what it did not will; but the body is moved through places, from earth to heaven, from heaven to earth, from east to west, or in some other similar way. Everything that is moved through place must at the same time be moved through time as well; but not everything that is moved through time must also be moved through place. So, just as the substance that is moved only through time comes before the substance that is moved through time and place, so that substance comes before it which is moved neither through place nor through time. And so, just as the created spirit, itself moved only through time, moves the body through time and place, so the Creator Spirit, himself moved neither through time nor through place, moves the created spirit through time. The created spirit moves itself through time, and moves the body through time and place; but the Creator Spirit moves himself without time and place, moves the created spirit through time without place, and moves the body through time and place.

Therefore, whoever tries to understand how the eternal God, truly eternal, truly immortal and unchangeable, himself moved neither through place nor through time, moves his creation in time and place, cannot succeed, I think, unless he has first understood how the soul, that is, a created spirit moved not through place but only through time, moves the body through time and place. For if he cannot yet grasp what goes on within himself, how much less can he grasp what is above him!

For the soul, influenced by its habit of relying on the bodily senses, thinks that it too is moved through place along with the body when it moves the body through place. But if it could carefully examine how the hinges, so to speak, of its body's limbs are arranged joint by joint, and on what the beginnings of movement take their purchase, it would find that things moved through spaces of place are moved only from things that are fixed in place. A finger alone is not moved unless the hand is held fixed, so that the finger is moved from the hand's joint as from an unmoving hinge. In the same way the whole hand moves from the joint of the elbow, the forearm from the joint of the shoulder, and the upper arm from the shoulder blade; when any of these is moved, the hinges on which the movement depends stay still, while the part that is moved travels through space. So too the foot has its joint at the ankle, which stays still while the foot is moved; the shin has its joint at the knee, and the whole leg at the hip. There is no movement whatever of a limb moved by the will except from the hinge of some joint which the command of that same will first holds fixed, so that what is moved may be moved from what is not moved through space. Even in walking, one foot is not lifted unless the other is fixed and bears the whole body, until the one that has been moved, carried from one place to another, comes to rest on the unmoving joint of its own hinge.

Now if, in the body, the will moves no limb through place except from a joint of the limb that it does not move, even though both the part of the body that is moved and the part held fixed so that it can be moved have their own bodily dimensions by which they occupy their spaces, then how much more is this true of the soul's own command, which the limbs obey so that whatever it pleases is held fixed for the part to be moved to rest upon! For the soul is not a bodily nature, nor does it fill the body by spatial extension as water fills a wineskin or a sponge, but it is mingled in wonderful ways, by that incorporeal command, with the body to which it gives life, and by it the soul rules the body through a kind of directed attention, not through bulk. How much more, I say, is the very command of its will not moved through place in order to move the body through place, since it moves the whole by means of parts, and moves none of them in place except through those that it does not move in place!

If this is hard to understand, let both things be believed: that the spiritual creature, not moved through place, moves the body through place, and that God, not moved through time, moves the spiritual creature through time. But suppose someone is unwilling to believe this about the soul. He would without doubt not only believe it but understand it too, if he could think of the soul as it is, incorporeal. For who would not readily see that what is not extended through spaces of place is not moved through place? Whatever is extended through spaces of place is a body; and so it follows that the soul should not be thought to be moved through place, if it is believed not to be a body. But, as I had begun to say, if anyone is unwilling to believe this about the soul, he should not be pressed too hard. But unless he believes that the substance of God is moved neither through time nor through place, he does not yet believe it to be perfectly unchangeable.

Because that nature of the Trinity is wholly unchangeable, and therefore so eternal that nothing can be coeternal with it, it abides with itself and in itself without any time or place; and yet it moves through time and place the creation subject to it, creating natures by its goodness and ordering wills by its power, so that among natures there is none that is not from him, and among wills there is no good one that he does not help, and no evil one that he cannot make good use of. But since he has not given free choice of will to all natures, and those to which he has given it are more powerful and higher, the natures that have no will must be subject to those that do. This is by the ordinance of the Creator, who never punishes an evil will in such a way as to destroy the dignity of its nature. Since, then, every body and every irrational soul lacks free choice of will, these are subject to the natures endowed with free choice of will; yet not all to all, but as the Creator's justice distributes them. So the providence of God, ruling and governing the whole creation, both natures and wills, natures so that they may exist, and wills so that the good may not be fruitless nor the evil go unpunished, first subjects all things to himself; then bodily creation to spiritual, irrational to rational, earthly to heavenly, female to male, weaker to stronger, needier to richer. Among wills, it subjects the good to himself, and the rest to those who serve him, so that the evil will may suffer what the good will has done at God's command, whether directly or through an evil will; this, at least, in things that are by nature subject even to evil wills, that is, in bodies. For within themselves evil wills have their own inner punishment, which is their very wickedness.

And so to the exalted angels, who enjoy God in subjection to him and serve God in blessedness, all bodily nature, all irrational life, and every will that is either weak or depraved is subject, so that they may do with their subjects, or concerning them, what the order of nature demands in all things, at the command of him to whom all things are subject. They therefore see in him the unchangeable truth and direct their wills according to it. Thus they become sharers in his eternity, truth and will, always, without time and place. Yet at his command they are moved in time as well, though he is not moved in time; and this is not in such a way that they spring back or slip away from contemplating him. Rather, at one and the same time they contemplate him without place and time and carry out his commands among lower things, moving themselves through time, and bodies through time and place, as befits their activity. And so God presides over his whole creation by the twofold work of his providence: over natures, so that they may come into being, and over wills, so that they may do nothing without his command or permission.

The nature of the bodily universe as a whole, then, is not helped from outside in a bodily way, for there is no body outside it; otherwise it would not be the universe. But it is helped from within in an incorporeal way, God bringing it about that it is a nature at all, since from him and through him and in him are all things. The parts of this universe, however, are helped both from within, incorporeally, or rather they are made so that they may be natures, and from outside, bodily, so that they may be in better condition: by food, for example, by agriculture, by medicine, and by whatever is done for adornment as well, so that they may be not only healthy and more fruitful but also more comely.

But created spiritual nature, if it is perfect and blessed, like that of the holy angels, is helped only from within and incorporeally, as far as concerns itself, that is, in order to exist and to be wise. For God speaks to it within in a wonderful and ineffable way: not through writing fixed on bodily materials, nor through voices sounding in bodily ears, nor through likenesses of bodies such as are formed as images in the spirit, as happens in dreams or in some going-out of the spirit, which in Greek is called ekstasis, a word we now use in place of a Latin one. For this kind of vision too, although it takes place more inwardly than the things reported to the mind through the bodily senses, is nevertheless like them, so that when it occurs it either cannot be told apart from them at all, or only with difficulty and very rarely; and it is more external than what the rational and intellectual mind beholds in the unchangeable truth itself, by whose light it judges all these things. I therefore think it should be counted among the things that happen externally. The spiritual and intellectual creature, then, perfect and blessed, such as that of the angels, is helped, as I said, as far as concerns itself, that is, in order to exist and to be wise and blessed, only from within, by the eternity, truth and love of the Creator. If it should be said to be helped from outside at all, perhaps it is helped only in this: that they see one another and rejoice in their fellowship in God, and that, having looked upon all creatures everywhere as well, it gives thanks and praises the Creator. But as regards the activity of the angelic creation, through which the providence of God provides for every kind of thing and above all for the human race, it gives help from outside, both through those visions that resemble bodily things and through bodies themselves, which are subject to angelic power.

Since this is so, God, almighty and all-sustaining, always the same in his unchangeable eternity, truth and will, is himself not moved through time or place, yet he moves the spiritual creation through time, and moves the bodily creation through time and place. By this movement he governs from without the natures he has established from within. He does so through wills subject to him, which he moves through time, and through bodies subject both to him and to those wills, which he moves through time and place, at the time and place whose rationale is, in God himself, life without time or place. When God does something of this kind, then, we must not suppose that his substance, by which he is God, is changeable in time and place or movable through times and places. We should recognize these things as the work of divine providence: not the work by which he creates natures, but the work by which he governs from without what he has created from within. For he himself, by no interval or extent of places but by his unchangeable and surpassing power, is both more inward than every thing, because all things are in him, and more outward than every thing, because he is above all things. Likewise, by no interval or extent of times but by his unchangeable eternity, he is both older than all things, because he is before all things, and newer than all things, because he is the same after all things.

So when we hear Scripture saying: "And the Lord God commanded Adam, saying: Of every tree that is in paradise you shall eat for food; but of the tree of knowing good and evil you shall not eat. On the day you eat of it, you shall surely die," and we ask in what manner God spoke these words, the manner itself cannot properly be grasped by us. Yet we ought to hold most firmly that God speaks either through his own substance or through a creature subject to him. Through his own substance he speaks only to create all natures, and, in the case of spiritual and intellectual natures, not only to create them but also to enlighten them, once they are able to receive his speech as it is in his Word, which was in the beginning with God, and the Word was God, through whom all things were made. But to those who cannot receive that speech, God speaks only through a creature. This is either a purely spiritual creature, in dreams or in ecstasy, in the likeness of bodily things, or else a bodily creature itself, when some form appears to the bodily senses or voices sound in the ears.

If, then, Adam was such that he could receive that speech of God which God offers to angelic minds through his own substance, we need not doubt that God moved Adam's mind through time in a wonderful and ineffable way, without himself being moved through time. He would have impressed on him a useful and wholesome precept of truth, and by that same ineffable truth would have shown him what penalty was due to a transgressor, just as all good precepts are heard or seen in that unchangeable Wisdom which passes into holy souls at some point in time, though it has no movement in time itself. But if Adam was righteous in such a way that he still needed the authority of another creature, holier and wiser, through whom to learn God's will and command, as we need the prophets and as the prophets themselves need the angels, why should we hesitate to say that God spoke to him through some such creature, with signs of speech that he could understand? For what is written later, that after they had sinned they heard the voice of the Lord God walking in paradise, was done not through God's very substance but through a creature subject to him. No one who has a sound grasp of the Catholic faith doubts this. I wanted to discuss this matter at somewhat greater length because some heretics think that the substance of the Son of God is visible in itself, without taking on any body. They therefore suppose that he himself was seen by the fathers before he received a body from the Virgin, as though it was of God the Father alone that it was said, "whom no man has seen or can see," since the Son, they say, was seen even in his own substance before he took the form of a servant. This impiety must be driven far from Catholic minds. But we shall discuss this more fully elsewhere, if it pleases the Lord. Now that this volume is ended, what follows, namely how the woman was created from her husband's side, is to be looked for in what comes next.
BOOK NINE

"And the Lord God said: It is not good for the man to be alone; let us make him a helper like himself. And God formed further from the earth all the beasts of the field and all the birds of the sky, and brought them to Adam to see what he would call them. And whatever Adam called each living soul, that is its name. And Adam gave names to all the cattle and to all the birds of the sky and to all the beasts of the field. But for Adam himself no helper was found like him. And God cast an ecstasy upon Adam, and he fell asleep. And he took one of his ribs and filled up flesh in its place. And the Lord God built the rib that he had taken from Adam into a woman, and brought her to Adam. And Adam said: This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called woman, because she was taken from her man. And for this reason a man shall leave father and mother and be joined to his wife, and the two shall be in one flesh." If what was considered and written in the earlier books is of any help to the reader, we need not linger long over the statement that God formed further from the earth all the beasts of the field and all the birds of the sky. We have already explained in the preceding books, as well as we could, why the word "further" was used: it refers to the first establishment of creatures, completed in six days, in which all things were made complete and begun together causally, so that the causes might then be brought to their effects. If anyone thinks this should be explained differently, let him only pay careful attention to all the considerations that led us to this view. If from them he can draw out a more probable interpretation, not only should we not resist it, we should even rejoice in it.

But someone may be troubled that Scripture did not say "God formed further from the earth all the beasts of the field and from the waters all the birds of the sky," but spoke as though he formed both kinds from the earth: "And God formed further from the earth," it says, "all the beasts of the field and all the birds of the sky." Let him see that this can be understood in two ways. Either Scripture here left unsaid what God formed the birds of the sky from, because this could occur to the reader even without being said: we are to take it that God formed only the beasts of the field from the earth, not both, and we understand where he formed the birds of the sky from even though Scripture is silent, since we know that in the first establishment of causal reasons they were brought forth from the waters. Or else "earth" is used in a universal sense that includes the waters, as it is in the psalm where, after the praises of heavenly beings are finished, the discourse turns to the earth and says, "Praise the Lord from the earth, you dragons and all depths," and so on, and it is not said afterwards, "Praise the Lord from the waters." For where are all the depths, which nevertheless praise the Lord from the earth? Where too are the creeping things and the winged birds, which likewise praise the Lord from the earth? According to this universal use of the word "earth", in which it is also said of the whole world, "God, who made heaven and earth," whatever was created, whether from earth or from the waters, is truly understood to have been created from the earth.

Now let us see how we should understand God's words: "It is not good for the man to be alone; let us make him a helper like himself." Did God say this in time, by uttering sounds and syllables? Or is what is recorded the very rationale, present primordially in the Word of God, by which the woman was to be made? Scripture was conveying that rationale also when it said, "And God said: Let there be" this or that, at the time all things were first established. Or did God perhaps say this in the mind of the man himself, as he speaks to some of his servants within those servants? Among servants of this kind was the one who said in the psalm: "I will hear what the Lord God will speak in me." Or was some revelation about this made to the man within himself by an angel, in likenesses of bodily speech, though Scripture does not say whether in dreams or in ecstasy? For this is how such things usually happen. Or was it in some other way, as revelation is made to the prophets? Hence the words: "And the angel who spoke in me said to me." Or did the voice itself sound through a bodily creature, as from the cloud: "This is my Son"? Which of all these happened we cannot clearly grasp. Yet let us hold most firmly both that God said this and that, if he said it with a bodily voice or through a likeness of a body expressed in time, he said it not through his own substance but through some creature subject to his command, as we discussed in the previous book.

For God was seen later by holy men too, at one time with a head white as wool, at another with the lower part of his body like brass, and at others in various other ways. Yet those who faithfully believe, or even excellently understand, that the substance of the Trinity is unchangeably eternal, moved neither through time nor through place, yet moving things through time and place, are entirely certain that he did not offer these visions to men through the substance by which he exists. He offered them through things he created and that are subject to him, and he showed and said what he willed through likenesses of bodily forms and voices. So let us no longer ask how God said this, but rather understand what he said. That a helper like himself had to be made for the man is contained in the eternal Truth itself, through which all things were created; and whoever is able to know in it what was created and why hears this in it.

But if it is asked for what purpose this helper had to be made, no other answer seems probable than the procreation of children, just as the earth is a helper to the seed, so that a plant may be born from both. For this had also been said at the first establishment of things: "Male and female he made them, and God blessed them, saying: Increase and multiply and fill the earth and have dominion over it." This rationale for the creation and union of male and female, and this blessing, did not fail even after man's sin and punishment. It is by virtue of it that the earth is now full of human beings who have dominion over it.

For although Scripture records that they came together and begot children only after they had been sent out of paradise, I do not see what could have prevented them from having, even in paradise, an honorable marriage and an undefiled bed. God would have granted this to them as they lived faithfully and righteously and served him obediently and holily, so that offspring might be begotten from their seed without any restless heat of lust and without any toil or pain in childbirth. Children would not have succeeded parents who died. Rather, those who had begotten would remain in some settled state of form, drawing bodily vigor from the tree of life that had been planted there, and those who were begotten would be brought to the same state. Then, once a fixed number had been reached, if all lived righteously and obediently, the change would come about by which, without that death, animal bodies would be turned into another quality. Because they would serve the spirit that ruled them at its every nod, and would live by the life-giving spirit alone without any bodily support from food, they would be called spiritual. This could have happened, had not the transgression of the command deserved the penalty of death.

Those who do not believe this could have happened pay attention to nothing but the customary course of nature as it now runs after human sin and punishment. But we ought not to be among those who believe nothing except what they are accustomed to see. For who can doubt that what we have described could have been granted to a man living obediently and devoutly, if he does not doubt that the clothes of the Israelites were granted a certain stable state of their own kind, so that for forty years they suffered no wear from age?

Why, then, did they not come together until they had left paradise? The answer can be given quickly: because soon after the woman was created, before they came together, that transgression took place, for which they were destined to death and also departed from that place of happiness. Scripture does not state how much time passed between their creation and the birth of Cain from them. It can also be said that God had not yet commanded them to come together. For why should divine authority not have been awaited for this, when no concupiscence, like the goad of disobedient flesh, was pressing them? And God had not commanded this because he arranged all things according to his foreknowledge, in which he undoubtedly foreknew their fall as well, by which the human race would from then on have to be propagated as mortal.

Or if the woman was not made for the man as a helper for begetting children, for what kind of help was she made? If it was to work the ground with him, there was as yet no toil requiring assistance; and if there had been need, a male would have made a better helper. The same can be said of companionship, if perhaps he was weary of solitude. For how much more fittingly would two friends live together for company and conversation than a man and a woman? And if it was necessary for them to live together with one commanding and the other obeying, so that conflicting wills would not disturb the peace of those living together, there would have been no lack of an order to maintain this, with one first and the other second, especially if the second were created from the first, as the woman was. Or will anyone say that God could make only a woman from the man's rib and not also a man, had he wished? So I do not find for what help the woman was made for the man, if the purpose of childbearing is taken away.

For if parents had to give way to their children from this life, so that the whole human race might be filled up to a fixed number through departures and successions, people could also, after begetting children and fully carrying out the righteousness of human duty, have been transferred from here to better things, not through death but through some change. This might be that highest change, by which the saints, having received back their bodies, will be like the angels in heaven; or, if that is not to be given except to all together at the end of the age, some change lower than that one. Yet it would still have a better state than either this body has or even those bodies had that were first made, the man's from the clay of the earth and the woman's from the man's flesh.

For we must not think that Elijah is already as the saints will be when, the day's work being done, they will all receive the denarius together, or that he is as people are who have not yet departed from this life, a life from which he departed not by death but by being taken up. So he already has something better than he could have in this life, although he does not yet have what he will have at the end for a life lived rightly here; for they foresaw better things for us, that they should not be made perfect without us. Or if anyone thinks Elijah could not have merited this had he married and fathered children (it is believed that he had none, because Scripture does not say so, though it says nothing of his celibacy either), what will he answer about Enoch, who, after begetting sons and pleasing God, did not die but was taken up? Why, then, could Adam and Eve too, had they lived righteously and fathered children chastely, not have given way to their successors by being taken up rather than by death? For Enoch and Elijah died in Adam and carry in their flesh the inherited stock of death; to pay that debt they are believed to be returning to this life and to die after so long a delay. Yet they are now in another life where, before the resurrection of the flesh and before the animal body is changed into a spiritual one, they do not waste away through disease or old age. How much more justly and probably, then, would it have been granted to those first human beings, living without any sin of their own or of their parents, that after begetting children they should give way to them by passing into some better state! From there, at the end of the age, together with all the posterity of the saints, they would have been changed into angelic form far more happily, not through the death of the flesh but through the power of God.

So I do not see for what other help the woman was made for the man, if the purpose of begetting is taken away. Nor do I know why it should be taken away. For why does faithful and devout virginity have great merit and great honor with God, unless because now, in this time for refraining from embracing, when there is an abundant supply from all nations to fill up the number of the saints, the desire for sordid pleasure does not claim for itself what the need to provide offspring no longer requires? Then, too, the weakness of both sexes, prone to fall into shameful conduct, is rightly caught by the honorable estate of marriage, so that what could have been a duty for the healthy becomes a remedy for the sick. For it does not follow that, because incontinence is an evil, marriage, even that by which the incontinent are joined, is not a good. On the contrary, this good is not blameworthy because of that evil; rather, that evil is pardonable because of this good. For the good that marriage has, by which marriage is good, can never be a sin. This good is threefold: fidelity, offspring, sacrament. In fidelity, care is taken that neither partner lie with another man or woman outside the marriage bond; in offspring, that children be received lovingly, nourished kindly, and brought up religiously; in the sacrament, that the marriage not be dissolved, and that a man or woman who has been put away not be joined to another, not even for the sake of offspring. This is, so to speak, the rule of marriage, by which either the fruitfulness of nature is adorned or the depravity of incontinence is governed. Since we have discussed this sufficiently in the book we recently published on the good of marriage, where we also distinguished widowed continence and the excellence of virginity according to the dignity of their ranks, our pen need not be occupied with it any longer here.

For our question now is for what help the woman was made for the man, if they were not permitted to unite in paradise to beget children. Those who hold this view perhaps think that all intercourse is sin. For it is hard for people, while perversely avoiding vices, not to rush headlong into their opposites. One who abhors avarice becomes a spendthrift, or one who abhors extravagance becomes a miser; the person whose sloth you rebuke becomes restless, or the one whose restlessness you rebuke becomes slothful; one who has been rebuked and comes to hate his own boldness flees into timidity, or one who tries not to be timid becomes rash, as though a bond had been snapped. They measure faults not by reason but by opinion. In the same way, because people do not know what is condemned by divine law in adultery and fornication, they detest even marital intercourse undertaken for the sake of procreation.

Others do not go this far, but still hold that the fruitfulness of the flesh was given by God for the succession of mortal generations. Yet they too think that those first human beings could not have lain together except that, being doomed to die because of the sin they had committed, they sought successors by begetting. They do not consider that if successors could rightly be sought by those who were to die, companions could much more rightly have been sought by those who were to live. Once the earth was filled with the human race, it would be right to seek offspring only to succeed those who were dying. But for the earth to be filled by two human beings, how could they fulfill the duty of forming a society except by begetting? Or is anyone so blind of mind as not to see what an ornament the human race is to the earth, even when only a few live rightly and praiseworthily, and how much the order of the commonwealth avails to restrain even sinners within the bond of a certain earthly peace? For human beings are not so depraved that even such as these do not surpass cattle and birds. Yet who does not delight to consider this lowest part of the world adorned, in keeping with its place, by all their kinds? And who would be so senseless as to think it could have been less adorned if it were filled with righteous people who did not die?

For because the heavenly city of the angels is exceedingly numerous, they would not rightly be joined in marriage unless they died. Foreseeing that this perfect number would also be joined to the angels at the resurrection of the saints, the Lord says: "In the resurrection they will neither marry nor take wives; for they will not begin to die, but will be equal to the angels of God." Here, however, the earth was to be filled with human beings, and because of the closer bond of kinship and to commend the bond of unity above all, it had to be filled from one man. For what other reason, then, was the female sex sought as a helper like him, except that woman's nature, like the fruitfulness of the earth, might help him as he sowed the human race?

Yet it is more fitting, and better, to believe that the body of those people, created as an animal body in paradise, was at that time not yet condemned by the law of death, so that they did not have the craving for carnal pleasure that these bodies of ours now have, descended as they are from a stock subject to death. For it is not the case that nothing happened in them when they ate from the forbidden tree. God had not said, "If you eat, you shall surely die," but, "On the day you eat, you shall surely die." That day was to bring about in them the very thing over which the apostle groans when he says: "I delight in the law of God according to the inner man, but I see another law in my members fighting against the law of my mind and making me captive to the law of sin which is in my members. Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from the body of this death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord." It would not have been enough for him to say, "Who will deliver me from this mortal body?" Instead he says, "from the body of this death." So too elsewhere he says, "The body indeed is dead because of sin." There too he does not say "mortal" but "dead," although it is certainly mortal as well, since it is going to die. We must not believe that those bodies were like that. Though they were animal and not yet spiritual, they were not dead, that is, they were not bodies that must necessarily die. That came about on the day they touched the tree against the prohibition.

In our own bodies we speak of a certain health appropriate to their condition. If this health is so disturbed that a deadly disease is already eating away the vital organs, and the doctors examine it and declare that death is imminent, the body is of course called mortal even then, but in a different sense from when it was healthy, though doubtless destined to die some day. In the same way those people had animal bodies, but bodies that would not die unless they sinned, and that were destined to receive an angelic form and a heavenly quality. As soon as they transgressed the command, death itself was conceived in their members like some deadly sickness. It changed that quality by which they so ruled the body that they would not say, "I see another law in my members fighting against the law of my mind." For although the body was not yet spiritual but animal, it was not yet the body of this death, from which and with which we are born. For what else have we contracted, I will not say at birth but at our very conception, if not a kind of sickness by which we must necessarily die? A man who has developed dropsy, consumption, or elephantiasis is not so certain to die of that disease as one who has begun to have this body, in which all people are by nature children of wrath. Only the penalty of sin has brought this about.

Since this is so, why should we not believe that before sin those people could command their genital members for the procreation of children just as they commanded the other members, which the soul moves in any task without any trouble and without any itch, so to speak, of pleasure? The almighty Creator, who is to be praised beyond words and who is great even in his smallest works, granted to bees that they should produce their offspring in the same way as they produce the form of wax and the liquid of honey. Why then should it seem incredible that he made such bodies for the first human beings that, if they had not sinned and so immediately contracted a kind of disease by which they would die, they would command the members from which offspring arise by the same nod with which they command their feet when walking? Then seed would not be sown with burning lust, nor would children be born with pain. But now, by transgressing the command, they deserved to have in their members, in which death had been conceived, the motion of that law which fights against the law of the mind. Marriage orders this motion, and continence restrains and bridles it, so that, just as punishment came from sin, merit may come from punishment.

The woman, then, was made for the man and from the man, in the sex and with the form and arrangement of members by which women are known. She bore Cain and Abel and all their brothers, from whom all human beings would be born.
