Among them she also bore Seth, through whom the line came to Abraham and to the people of Israel, a nation now very well known to all nations, and through Noah's sons to all the nations. Whoever doubts this makes everything we believe totter, and must be driven far from the minds of the faithful. So when we ask for what kind of help that sex was made for the man, I consider everything as carefully as I can, and the only answer that occurs to me is the begetting of offspring, so that the earth might be filled through their descendants. But this begetting was not to be in the way human beings are begotten now, when the law of sin is in our members, fighting against the law of the mind, even if by the grace of God it is overcome by virtue. For we must believe that this could not exist except in the body of this death, the body that is dead because of sin. And what punishment could be more just than that the body, the soul's own servant, should not obey its every nod, since the soul itself refused to serve its own Lord? This holds whether God creates both from the parents, body from body and soul from soul, or makes souls in some other way. In any case, the task is not impossible, nor is the reward small. For when the soul, subject to God in devotion, has by grace overcome this law of sin, which is in the members of the body of this death and which the first man received as a punishment, it will receive a heavenly reward with greater glory. It will show how great is the praise due to obedience, which by its virtue could overcome the penalty of another's disobedience.

Since we have, I think, sufficiently examined for what kind of help the woman was made for the man, let us now see why it came about that all the beasts of the field and all the birds of the sky were brought to Adam for him to give them names, so that a kind of necessity arose to create a woman for him from his side, since no helper like him had been found among those animals. It seems to me that this was done for the sake of some prophetic meaning, but it was nevertheless really done, so that, with the historical fact established, we remain free to interpret the figure. For what does it mean that Adam gave names to the birds and land animals, but not also to the fish and all the creatures that swim? If we consult human languages, all these things are called by the names that people have given them in speaking. And not only the creatures in the waters and on land, but the earth itself, the water, the sky, the things seen in the sky and those not seen but believed in, are called by different names according to the variety of the nations' languages. We have indeed learned that at first there was one language, before the pride of the tower built after the flood divided human society into different sounds of signs. But what does it matter which language that was? Certainly Adam spoke it then, and in that language, if it still survives, are the articulate words by which the first man named the land animals and the birds. Is it at all credible, then, that in the same language the names of the fish were established not by man but by God, and that man afterwards learned them with God teaching him? Even if that had happened, there would doubtless be a mystical meaning behind why it happened so. But we must believe that names were given to the kinds of fish gradually, as they became known. When, however, the cattle, beasts, and birds were brought to the man, so that he might give them names once they were gathered before him and sorted by kind, he could also have named these gradually, and much sooner than the fish, if this had not been done. What reason was there for it, then, if not the purpose of signifying something that would serve to foretell the future? This is above all what the order of this narrative keeps in view.

Besides, did God not know that he had created nothing among the kinds of animals that could be a helper like the man? Or was it necessary that the man himself should also learn this, and so value his wife the more because among all the flesh created under heaven and living, as he did, on this air, he found nothing like her? It would be strange if he could not know this unless all of them had been brought before him and examined. If he believed God, God could have told him this in the same way that he gave him the command, and in the same way that he questioned and judged him when he sinned. But if he did not believe God, he certainly could not know whether the one he did not believe had brought him every creature, or had perhaps hidden away, in some more remote parts of the earth, some creatures like him which he had not shown him. So I think there is no doubt that this was done for the sake of some prophetic meaning, but that it was nevertheless really done.

In this work we have not undertaken to search out prophetic riddles, but to commend the trustworthiness of the events as literal history. Where something may seem impossible to the frivolous and unbelieving, or seem to contradict the authority of holy Scripture itself as if by contrary testimony, I aim to show by discussion, as far as my strength allows and God helps, that it is neither impossible nor contradictory. Where something appears possible and has no appearance of contradiction, yet may seem to some superfluous or even foolish, I aim to show by argument that it was done outside the natural or usual order of events precisely so that, since the most trustworthy authority of the holy Scriptures holds first place in our hearts and cannot be foolish, it may be believed to be mystical. Its exposition or investigation, however, we have either already presented elsewhere or are postponing to another time.

What, then, is the meaning of the fact that the woman was made from the man's side? Granted, let us believe that it had to be done this way in order to commend the strength of their union. But did the same reason or necessity also demand that it be done while he slept, and that a bone be taken out and flesh put in its place? Could not the flesh itself have been taken, so that from it the woman, being the weaker sex, might be formed more fittingly? Or could God, who made man himself from dust, build a rib into a woman by adding so much to it, yet be unable to do so with flesh or muscle? Or if a rib had to be taken out, why was another rib not put back in its place? And why does it not say "formed" or "made," as with all the works above, but rather, "The Lord God built the rib," not as one would make a human body, but as one would build a house? There is no doubt, then, since these things were done and cannot be foolish, that they were done to signify something. From the very beginning of the human race God in his foreknowledge was mercifully proclaiming in his own works the fruit of the age to come, so that at a set time these things would be revealed to his servants, whether through successive generations of people, or through his Spirit, or through the ministry of angels, and written down, to bear witness both by promising things to come and by recognizing things fulfilled. This will become more and more evident in what follows.

Let us see, then, as we have undertaken in this work, how these things can be understood, not as prefiguring things to come, but in the proper, not allegorical, sense of what actually happened. "And God," it says, "formed further out of the earth all the beasts of the field and all the birds of the sky." We have already discussed this as we saw fit and as far as we saw. "And he brought them all to Adam to see what he would call them." How God brought these to Adam, so that we do not understand it in a fleshly way, should be clarified for us by what we discussed in the previous book about the twofold working of divine providence. For we must not believe that this was done the way hunters and fowlers track down and drive into their nets whatever animals they catch, or that some voice of command came from a cloud in words of the kind that rational souls usually understand and obey when they hear them. Beasts and birds have not received the capacity for this. Yet in their own way they obey God, not by the rational choice of the will, but as he moves all things at the proper times, though he himself is not moved in time. He does this through the ministry of angels, who grasp in his Word what ought to be done and when. Moved by him who is not moved in time, they themselves are moved in time, so as to carry out his commands among the things subject to them.

For every living soul, not only the rational soul as in human beings but also the irrational soul as in cattle, birds, and fish, is moved by things perceived. But the rational soul by the choice of its will either consents to what it perceives or does not consent. The irrational soul does not have this judgment; still, according to its kind and nature, when touched by something perceived, it is driven on. Nor is it in the power of any soul to decide what perceptions will come to it, whether to the bodily senses or inwardly to the spirit itself, perceptions by which the appetite of any living creature is moved. So when such perceptions are supplied from above through the obedience of angels, God's command reaches not only human beings, nor only birds and cattle, but also the creatures that hide beneath the waters, such as the whale that swallowed Jonah, and not only these larger creatures but even the little worm. For we read that it too was commanded by God to gnaw the root of the gourd under whose shade the prophet had rested. God so endowed man at his creation that even while carrying the flesh of sin he can not only subject cattle and beasts of burden to his use, nor only domestic fowl, but can also capture birds that fly freely and even fierce wild beasts, tame them, and command them wonderfully by the power of reason, not of the body. He seizes on their appetites and pains and gradually, by enticing, pressing, and relaxing, controls them, strips them of their wild habits and, as it were, clothes them with human ways. If God granted this to man, how much more can the angels do it! At God's command, having discerned it in his unchangeable truth, which they contemplate for ever, they move themselves in time, and move the bodies subject to them in time and place with wonderful swiftness. They are able to produce in every living soul both the perceptions by which it is moved and the appetite of bodily need, so that it is led, without knowing it, where it needs to go.

Let us now see how the formation of the woman itself, which is mystically also called a building, was carried out. The nature of the woman was created, although from the male nature that already existed, and not by some movement of natures already existing. Angels, however, cannot create any nature at all. For the one and only creator of any nature, great or small, is God, that is, the Trinity itself, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. It is a different question, then, how Adam was put to sleep and how his rib was taken from the framework of his body without any sensation of pain. Perhaps it might be said that these things could have been done through angels. But to form or build the rib so that it became a woman was something that only God, by whom all nature subsists, could do. So much so that I would not believe that even the flesh supplied in the man's body to take the place of that rib was made by angels, any more than man himself was made by them from the dust of the earth. Not that angels contribute no work when something is created, but they are not creators on that account, just as we do not call farmers the creators of crops and trees. "For neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth." To this growth belongs also the fact that in the human body, when the bone was removed, its place was filled with flesh, through that work of God by which he sustains natures so that they exist, and by which he also created the angels themselves.

So it is the farmer's work to channel water when he irrigates; but that the water flows down the slopes is not his work, but the work of him who has arranged all things in measure, number, and weight. Again, it is the farmer's work to pull a shoot from a tree and plant it in the ground; but it is not his work that it soaks up sap and puts forth a bud, that it fixes one part in the soil to establish its root and sends another up into the air to strengthen its trunk and spread its branches. That is the work of him who gives the growth. A doctor, too, applies food to a sick body and medicine to a wounded one. First, he applies them not from things he has created, but from things he found created by the Creator's work. Next, he could prepare food or drink and administer it, and could make a plaster, spread it with medicine, and apply it. But can he also, from the things he applies, produce and create strength or flesh? Nature does that, by an inner movement completely hidden from us. Yet if God were to withdraw from nature his innermost activity, by which he sustains and makes it, it would immediately be as if extinguished and nothing would remain.

God governs his whole creation by the twofold working of his providence, which we spoke of in the previous book, both in natural and in voluntary movements. Therefore no angel can create a nature, any more than he can create himself. But the angelic will, obediently subject to God and carrying out his command, can, by natural movements, supply from the things beneath it a kind of material, in the manner of farming or healing, so that something may be created in time according to those principal reasons that are uncreated in the Word of God, or according to those reasons created causally in the first works of the six days. Who, then, would dare to state what kind of ministry the angels rendered to God in the formation of the woman? But I would say with complete certainty that the flesh supplied in place of the rib, and the woman's own body and soul, the shaping of her members, all her inner organs, all her senses, and whatever else made her a creature, a human being, and a woman, were made only by that work of God which God performs not through angels but through himself. He did not work and then leave off; he works so continuously that neither the nature of anything else nor that of the angels themselves would subsist if he did not work.

As far as we have been able to experience the nature of things within the limits of human understanding, we know of no living, sentient flesh being born except either from what we might call the material elements, that is, water and earth, or from shrubs or the fruits of trees, or even from the flesh of animals, as with countless kinds of worms and creeping things, or else from the intercourse of parents. We know of no flesh born from the flesh of any living creature that was so like it as to differ only in sex. So we look among the things of this creation for something comparable to the woman's being made from the man's side, and we cannot find it. The only reason is that we know how human beings work on this earth, but we certainly do not know how angels do a kind of farming in this world. If the course of nature produced the various kinds of plants without any human effort, we would know nothing except that trees and grasses spring from the earth and from their seeds, which in turn fall from them to the earth. Would we ever have learned what grafting can do, so that a tree of one kind, on its own root, bears fruit of another kind, which by growing together has now become its own? We learned this through the work of farmers. Yet they were in no way the creators of trees; they merely rendered a certain service and ministry to the course of nature for God the Creator. Nothing would come into being through their work unless the inner principle of nature contained it in God's work. Why then be surprised that we do not know how a woman was made from a man's bone, when we do not know how angels serve God as he creates? We could not even have known that a tree is made from a tree's shoot on another's trunk if we were likewise ignorant of how farmers serve God as he creates these things.

Yet we have no doubt at all that the creator of both human beings and trees is none other than God, and we faithfully believe that the woman was made from the man without any intercourse, even if perhaps the man's rib was supplied by angels in the Creator's work. In the same way we faithfully believe that a man was made from a woman without any intercourse, when the seed of Abraham was ordained through angels in the hand of a mediator. Both are incredible to unbelievers. But why should believers find credible as literal fact what was done concerning Christ, and credible only as figurative meaning what was written about Eve? Or could a man be made from a woman without anyone's intercourse, but a woman not from a man? Did the virgin's womb have what was needed to make a man, while the man's side did not have what was needed to make a woman, when in the one case the Lord was born of a handmaid, and in the other a handmaid was formed from a servant? The Lord could also have created his flesh from a rib or some other member of the virgin. But he, who could have shown in his own body that he was doing again what had once been done, chose the more useful course of showing in his mother's body that nothing chaste is shameful.

Now someone may ask about the causal creation in which God first made man in his own image and likeness, for it was there that it was said, "Male and female he made them." Did that reason which God created together with the first works of the world, and in which he was present with them, already contain the necessity that the woman be made from the man's side? Or did it contain only the possibility that this could happen, while the necessity that it should happen in this way was not established there but hidden in God? If this is the question, I will say what seems right to me, without rashly asserting it. Yet when I have said it, perhaps those who consider these matters wisely and who have already been formed in the Christian faith will judge that it should not be doubted, even if they are learning these things now for the first time.

This whole, most familiar course of nature has certain natural laws of its own. By these laws the spirit of life, which is a creature, has certain appetites of its own that are in some way fixed, and even an evil will cannot go beyond them. By them, too, the elements of this bodily world have their own definite power and quality: what each can or cannot do, and what can or cannot come from what. From these, as from the first beginnings of things, all things that are begotten take, each in its own time, their rise and growth, and the ends and passing away proper to their kind. That is why a bean does not grow from a grain of wheat, nor wheat from a bean, nor a man from a beast, nor a beast from a man. But above this natural motion and course of things, the Creator's power holds within itself the ability to make out of all these things something other than what their seminal reasons, so to speak, contain. Yet it cannot be something he did not place in them as a possibility, to be made from them even by him. For he is almighty not by a reckless power but by the strength of wisdom, and he makes of each thing in its own time what he had already made it capable of becoming. There is, then, one mode of things by which this plant sprouts in this way and that one in that, by which one age bears offspring and another does not, by which a man can speak and a beast cannot. The reasons for these and similar modes are not only in God; he has also placed them in created things and fixed them there. Consider a piece of wood cut from the earth, dry and polished, without any root, soil or water, that suddenly blossoms and bears fruit; a woman barren all through her youth who bears a child in old age; a donkey that speaks; and anything else of this kind. God did indeed grant to the natures he created that these things too could come about from them, for not even he would make from them what he himself had determined could not be made from them, since he is not more powerful than himself. But he granted it in another way. They have these possibilities not in their natural motion, but in the fact that they were created so that their nature would be further subject to a more powerful will.

God, then, has hidden in himself the causes of certain deeds, which he did not implant in created things. He carries them out not by that work of providence by which he establishes natures so that they may exist, but by the work by which he governs as he wills the natures that he founded as he willed. There too is the grace by which sinners are saved. A nature depraved by its own wicked will has no way back by itself. It returns only through the grace of God, by which it is helped and restored. Nor should we despair of people because of the sentence in which it is written: "None who walk in it will return." This was said with respect to the weight of their iniquity, so that whoever does return should credit it not to himself but to the grace of God, "not from works, lest anyone be lifted up."

This is why the apostle said that the mystery of this grace was hidden, not in the world, where the causal reasons of all things that will arise naturally lie hidden, as Levi was hidden in the loins of Abraham when he too paid tithes, but "in God, who created all things." So the causes of all the things that were done to signify this grace, done not by the natural motion of things but miraculously, were also hidden in God. One of these was that the woman was made from the side of the man, and of a man asleep at that. She was made strong through him, as though strengthened by his bone, while he was made weak for her sake, since in place of the rib it was not a rib but flesh that was supplied. If this was one of them, then the first founding of things, when it was said on the sixth day, "Male and female he made them," did not contain the fact that the woman would be made in exactly this way. It contained only the possibility that she could be made this way, so that God would not act with a changeable will against the causes he had established by his will. But what would actually be done, so that nothing else would happen, was hidden in God, who created all things.

But the apostle said it was hidden in such a way that "the manifold wisdom of God might be made known through the church to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places." It is therefore reasonable to believe that angels ministered in all the things that were done miraculously in the natural world, beyond the usual course of nature, to foretell or announce the coming of that seed, just as "the seed to whom the promise was made was ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator." Yet everywhere the creator or restorer of creatures is none other than God, who alone gives the growth, whoever may plant and water.

So the ecstasy which God sent upon Adam, so that he fell into a deep sleep, is rightly understood to have been sent for this purpose: that through ecstasy his mind too might share, as it were, in the court of the angels, and might enter the sanctuary of God and understand the last things. Then, waking as though full of prophecy, when he saw his wife brought to him, he at once burst out with what the apostle commends as a great sacrament: "This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh. She shall be called woman, because she was taken from her man. And for this reason a man will leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two will be one flesh." Scripture itself testifies that these words were the first man's, yet the Lord in the Gospel declared that God said them. For he says: "Have you not read that he who made them from the beginning made them male and female? And he said: For this reason a man will leave father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two will be one flesh." From this we are to understand that, because of the ecstasy that had come upon Adam, he was able to say this by divine inspiration, as a prophet. But let this be the end of this book, so that what follows may renew the reader's attention with a fresh beginning.
BOOK TEN

The order of the work itself now seems to demand that we discuss the sin of the first man. But Scripture has told how the woman's flesh was made and has said nothing about her soul. This makes us all the more intent on inquiring carefully into the matter: can those who believe that soul comes from soul, as flesh comes from flesh, the seeds of both being passed down from parents to children, be refuted or not? Their first argument for this view runs as follows. God made one soul, which he breathed into the face of the man he had formed from dust, so that the other human souls might be created from it, just as all human flesh comes from his flesh, since Adam was formed first, then Eve. In his case we are told where his body came from and where his soul came from: his body from the dust of the earth, and his soul from the breath of God. But of her, although she is said to have been made from his side, it is not said that God likewise gave her life by breathing, as if both her body and her soul had been drawn from him who already had life. "Either Scripture should have been silent about the man's soul too," they say, "so that we might understand, or at least believe, as best we could, that it was given by God; or, if Scripture did not keep silent about it so that we would not think the soul was made from earth like man's flesh, it ought not to have been silent about the woman's soul either, so that it would not be thought to come by transmission, if that is not true. So the fact that God breathed into her face was passed over," they say, "because the truth is that the soul too was propagated from the man."

This suspicion is easily answered. If they think the woman's soul was made from the man's soul because it is not written that God breathed into the woman's face, why do they believe that the woman received life from the man, when not even that is written? So if God makes the souls of all human beings who are born as he made the first, Scripture said nothing about the others because what is recorded as done in one case could wisely be understood of the rest too. If, then, this scripture needed to advise us of anything on this matter, it would rather be the case where something was done in the woman that had not been done in the man: that her soul was drawn from his living flesh, instead of her body coming from one source and her soul from another, as with her husband. Scripture ought not to have kept silent about this very thing, done in a different way, so that we would not think it was done in the same way that we had already learned in his case. Since, then, it did not say that the woman's soul was made from the man's soul, it is more fitting to believe that by this very silence it meant to advise us to suppose nothing different here from what we had learned about the man's soul, that is, that a soul was given to the woman in the same way. This is all the more so since there was a most obvious opportunity: if not when she was formed, then certainly afterwards, it could have been said when Adam says, "This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh." How much more tenderly and lovingly he would have added, "and soul of my soul!" Yet this does not settle so great a question so far that we can hold either of these views as clear and certain.

We must therefore first see whether the holy scripture of this book, studied from its beginning, allows us to doubt on this point. Then perhaps we shall rightly ask either which opinion is to be preferred, or what measure we ought to keep while the matter remains uncertain. Certainly God made man in his image on the sixth day, where it was also said: "Male and female he made them." We took the first statement, where the image of God is mentioned, to refer to the soul, and the second, where the difference of sex is mentioned, to refer to the flesh. Many weighty testimonies were considered and discussed there, and they did not allow us to take it that on that same sixth day the man was also formed from clay and the woman from his side. Rather, this was done afterwards, after those first works of God in which he created all things together. So we asked what we should believe about the soul of man. When all sides of our debate had been examined, it seemed more credible, or more acceptable, to say that man's soul itself was made in those works, while the reason of his body was made in the bodily world as in a seed. This kept us from being forced to say any of the following. Against the words of Scripture, we would have had to say either that the whole man was made on the sixth day, that is, both the man from clay and the woman from his side; or that man was in no way made in those works of the six days; or that only the causal reason of the human body was made and none of the soul, when it is rather according to the soul that man is in the image of God. Or else, if not against the plain words of Scripture, we would have had to say something harsh and intolerable. One possibility was that the reason of the human soul was made in a spiritual creature created solely for this purpose, although no such creature, in which this reason was supposedly made, is mentioned among the works of God. The other was that the reason of the soul was made in some creature that is mentioned among those works, just as the reason of the children to be begotten lies hidden, already made, in human beings who now exist. We would then have believed the soul to be the daughter either of angels or, what is even more intolerable, of some bodily element.

But now suppose it is asserted that the woman received her soul not from the man but made by God, as his was, because God makes a soul for each person one by one. Then the woman's soul had not been made in those first works. Or, if a general reason of all souls had been made, as the reason of begetting exists in human beings, we return to that harsh and troublesome view that human souls are the daughters either of angels or, what is most unworthy, of the bodily heaven or even of some lower element. We must therefore see, even if the truth is hidden, what at least can be said more tolerably. Is it what I have just described? Or was one soul, that of the first man, made in those first works of God, so that all human souls would be created from his offspring? Or are new souls made from time to time, of which not even a reason was made beforehand in those first works of God in the six days? Of these three, the first two do not conflict with those first foundings, in which all things were created together. Suppose the reason of the soul was made in some creature as in a parent, so that all souls are generated from it but created by God when they are given to individual human beings, as bodies are generated from human parents. Or suppose it was not the reason of the soul, like the reason of offspring in a parent, but the soul itself that was made outright when day was made, like day itself, like heaven and earth and the lights of heaven. Either way, it is fitting to say: "God made man in his image."

But it is not so easy to see how this third view does not conflict with the statement by which man is understood both to have been made in the image of God on the sixth day and to have been visibly created after the seventh day. Suppose we say that new souls are made, and that neither they nor their reason, like offspring in a parent, were made on that sixth day along with those works, completed and begun, from which God rested on the seventh day. Then we must beware lest Scripture has stressed to no purpose, and so carefully, that God completed in six days all his works, which he made very good, if he was still going to create some natures that he did not make there, neither the natures themselves nor their causal reasons. There is one way out. We may understand that God has in himself, and did not establish in any creature, the reason for making souls one by one and giving them to each person as he is born. Then, since the soul is not a creature of a different kind from that according to which man was made in God's image on the sixth day, it is wrong to say that God now makes things he did not complete then. For even then he had already made a soul of the kind he makes now. So he does not now make some new kind of creature that he did not create then in his completed works. Nor is this work of his contrary to the causal reasons of future things that he then implanted in the universe. It accords with them, since it is fitting that such souls as he now makes and inserts should be inserted into human bodies, whose propagation extends from those first works in continuous succession.

We need no longer fear, then, that whichever of these three opinions proves most probable, we will seem to hold a view contrary to the words this book wrote about that first founding in six days. So let us undertake a more careful treatment of this question, as far as God helps us. Perhaps we may reach, if not a clear opinion that ought no longer to be doubted, then at least one so acceptable that it is not absurd to hold it until something certain comes to light. If we cannot manage even this, because the weight of evidence sways equally in every direction, at least our doubt will not appear to have shunned the labour of searching, only the rashness of asserting. Then anyone who is already rightly certain may be kind enough to teach me. And anyone who was made certain not by the authority of divine speech or of clear reasoning but by his own presumption may not disdain to doubt along with me.

First, let us hold most firmly that the nature of the soul is not changed into the nature of a body, so that what was a soul becomes a body. Nor is it changed into the nature of an irrational soul, so that what was the soul of a man becomes the soul of a beast. Nor is it changed into the nature of God, so that what was a soul becomes what God is. Conversely, neither a body, nor an irrational soul, nor the substance by which God is God, is changed so as to become a human soul. It should be no less certain that the soul is nothing other than a creature of God. Therefore, if God made man's soul neither from a body, nor from an irrational soul, nor from himself, it remains that he makes it either from nothing or from some spiritual but rational creature. But to try to show that something is made from nothing after the completion of the works in which he created all things together is to force the matter, and I do not know whether it can be established by clear proofs. Nor should we be required to do what a human being cannot grasp. Or if he can grasp it, it would be a wonder if he could persuade anyone of it, except someone who could understand such a thing for himself even if no one tried to teach him. It is safer, then, not to proceed in such matters by human conjecture, but to search the divine testimonies.

I know of no authority in the canonical books for saying that God creates souls from angels as from parents. Much less, then, is there any for saying he creates them from the bodily elements of the world. Someone might perhaps be moved by the passage in the prophet Ezekiel that shows the resurrection of the dead. There, once the bodies have been restored, the spirit is summoned from the four winds of heaven, and by its breathing they are given life so that they rise. For thus it is written: "And the Lord said to me: Prophesy to the spirit, prophesy, son of man, and say to the spirit: Thus says the Lord: Come from the four quarters of the winds of heaven and breathe into these dead, and let them live. And I prophesied as the Lord commanded me, and the spirit of life entered into them, and they came to life again and stood on their feet, a very great assembly." It seems to me that this was a prophetic sign that people will rise not only from the plain where the thing itself was being shown, but from the whole world, and that this was figured by the breath from the four quarters of the world. Likewise, the breath that came from the Lord's body when he breathed and said, "Receive the Holy Spirit," was not the substance of the Holy Spirit. It surely signified that the Holy Spirit proceeds from him, just as that breath proceeded from his body. But the world is not joined to God in unity of person, as that flesh was joined to his Word, his only-begotten Son. So we cannot say that the soul is from the substance of God in the way that the breath from the four winds was made from the nature of the world. Still, I think the breath was one thing and signified another, and this can rightly be understood from the example of the breath proceeding from the Lord's body. This holds even if, in that passage, the prophet Ezekiel foresaw by a figurative revelation not the resurrection of the flesh as it will actually take place, but the unexpected restoration of a despairing people through the Spirit of the Lord, which has filled the whole world.

Let us now see, then, which opinion the divine testimonies rather support. Is it the one that says God made one soul and gave it to the first man, so as to make the rest from it, as the other human bodies come from his body? Or is it the one that says God makes a soul for each person one by one, as he made one for Adam, and does not make the rest from it? Take what he says through Isaiah: "I have made every breath." What follows shows clearly enough that he is speaking of the soul, but it can be taken either way. For whether from the one soul of the first man or from some secret source of his own, it is beyond doubt he himself who makes all souls.

Then there is the verse, "He who fashioned their hearts one by one." If we choose to take "hearts" as meaning souls, this too does not conflict with either of the two views we are now unsure between. He may fashion each soul from the one he breathed into the face of the first man, just as he fashions bodies too. Or he may fashion each one and send it, or fashion them within the very people into whom he has sent them. Yet it seems to me that this was said only of our souls being formed by grace, through renewal to the image of God. Hence the apostle says: "For by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves, but it is the gift of God; not from works, lest anyone be lifted up. For we are his handiwork, created in Christ Jesus for good works." We cannot take this to mean that our bodies were created or fashioned through this grace of faith. It is meant in the sense of the psalm: "Create a clean heart in me, O God."

I think the saying "He who fashioned the spirit of man within him" also comes from this, as though it is one thing to send a soul already made, and another to make it within the man himself, that is, to remake and renew it. But even if we take this not of the grace by which we are renewed but of the nature in which we are born, it can be applied to either view. Either God himself fashions within the man something like a seed of soul drawn from that one soul of the first man, so that it may give life to the body. Or he likewise fashions, through the mortal senses of the flesh, the spirit of life that is poured into the body from elsewhere and not from that stock, so that the man becomes a living soul.

The passage from the book of Wisdom, however, calls for more careful consideration, where it says: "I was allotted a good soul, and since I was rather good, I came into an undefiled body." It seems rather to support the view that souls are not propagated from the one soul but come down to bodies from above. Yet what does "I was allotted a good soul" mean? It sounds as though, in that wellspring of souls, if there is one, some souls were good and others not good, and they came out by a kind of lot deciding which was given to which person; or else as though God, at the hour when people are conceived or born, made some souls good and others not good, and each person had whichever fell to him by lot. It would be surprising if this helped even those who believe that souls made elsewhere are sent one by one by God into each human body, rather than those who say that souls are sent into bodies according to the merits of the deeds they did before the body. For on what basis could some souls be thought to come to bodies good and others not good, except on the basis of their own deeds? Certainly not on the basis of their nature, in which they are made by him who makes all natures good. But far be it from us to contradict the apostle, who says that those not yet born had done nothing good or bad; from which he establishes that it could not have been said on the basis of works, but on the basis of him who calls, "The elder will serve the younger," when he was speaking of the twins still in Rebecca's womb. Let us therefore set aside for a little while this testimony from the book of Wisdom. For we must not neglect those who, whether they are mistaken or rightly understand it, think that this was said specially and uniquely of the soul of the mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus. What that view amounts to we will consider later if need be, so that, if it cannot fit Christ, we may ask how we ought to take it, lest we go against the apostolic faith by thinking that souls have some merits from their own deeds before they begin to live in bodies.

Now let us see in what sense it was said: "You will take away their spirit, and they will fail and return to their dust. You will send forth your spirit, and they will be created; and you will renew the face of the earth." This seems to tell in favor of those who think that souls are created from parents as bodies are, when it is understood thus: the psalmist said "their spirit" because people received it from people; and when they have died, it cannot be given back to them by people so that they may rise again, since it is not drawn again from parents as it was when they were born; rather God, who raises the dead, will give it back. And so he called the same spirit "theirs" when they die, but "God's" when they rise again. But those who maintain that souls come not from parents but by God's sending can understand it in favor of their own view thus: he called it "their spirit" when they die because it was in them and goes out from them, but "God's" when they rise again because it is sent by him and given back by him. So this testimony, too, opposes neither of them.

For my part, I think this saying is better understood of the grace of God by which we are renewed inwardly. For all the proud, who live according to the earthly man and presume on their own vanity, in a certain way have their own spirit taken away when they strip off the old man and are made weak, so that, once pride is driven out, they may be made perfect, saying to the Lord in humble confession, "Remember that we are dust"—they to whom it had been said, "Why is earth and ashes proud?" For when with the eye of faith they behold the righteousness of God, so that they no longer wish to establish their own, they despise themselves, as Job says, and waste away and regard themselves as earth and ashes; this is what is meant by "and they will return to their dust." But once they have received the Spirit of God, they say, "I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me." Thus the face of the earth is renewed through the grace of the new covenant, by the great number, indeed, of the saints [?].

Again, what is written in Ecclesiastes—"and let the dust return to the earth as it was, and the spirit return to God who gave it"—supports neither view against the other but stands between the two. For when these people say that it proves the soul is given not by parents but by God, because, once the dust has returned to its earth (that is, the flesh, which was made from dust), the spirit returns to God who gave it, the others reply: "Certainly it is so. For the spirit returns to God, who gave it to the first man when he breathed into his face, while the dust, that is, the human body, returns to its earth, from which it was originally made. The spirit was not going to return to the parents, even though it was created from them, out of that one spirit which was given to the first man, just as the flesh itself does not return after death to the parents from whom it was undoubtedly propagated. So just as the flesh does not return to the human beings from whom it was created, but to the earth from which it was formed for the first man, so too the spirit does not return to the human beings from whom it was passed on, but to God, by whom it was given to that first flesh."

This testimony, indeed, sufficiently reminds us that God made from nothing the soul he gave to the first man, and not from some already-made creature, as the body was made from earth. And therefore, when it returns, it has nowhere to return to except its author who gave it, and not to some creature from which it was made, as the body returns to the earth. For there is no creature from which it was made, since it was made from nothing; and so the soul that returns returns to its maker, by whom it was made from nothing. For not all return, since there are those of whom it is said: "a spirit that goes and does not return."

It is therefore difficult to gather all the testimonies of the holy Scriptures on this matter; and even if it could be done, so that they were not only cited but also thoroughly discussed, they would run to a great length of discourse. Yet unless something is put forward as certain as the passages that show that God made the soul, or that he gave it to the first man, I do not know how this question could be settled by the testimony of the divine word. For if it had been written that God likewise breathed into the face of the woman once she was formed and she became a living soul, a great deal of light would indeed have been shed, by which we could believe that a soul is given to each formed human flesh and not from parents. Even then, however, one would still wait to learn what properly holds for offspring, which is the usual way known to us of one human being coming from another. But the first woman was made in a different way, and so it could still be said that the soul was given to Eve by God and not from Adam for the reason that she did not arise from him as offspring. If, however, Scripture recorded that the first person born from those two received a soul given from above and not drawn from the parents, then that would have to be understood of all the rest as well, even though Scripture is silent.

So now let us also consider whether the following text confirms neither view but can be adapted to both: "Through one man sin entered into this world, and death through sin, and so it passed to all men, in whom all sinned"; and a little later: "As through the trespass of one, condemnation came upon all men, so also through the righteousness of one, justification of life came upon all men. For as through the disobedience of one man many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of one many will be made righteous." From these words of the apostle, those who defend the propagation of souls try to build up their view thus: "If sin or the sinner," they say, "can be understood with respect to the flesh alone, we are not compelled by these words to believe that the soul comes from the parents. But if, although it happens through the enticement of the flesh, it is nonetheless only the soul that sins, how is the saying 'in whom all sinned' to be understood, unless the soul too, like the flesh, was propagated from Adam? Or how were they made sinners through his disobedience if they were in him only according to the flesh and not according to the soul as well?"

"For we must beware," they say, "lest either God appear to be the author of sin, if he gives a soul to a flesh in which it must necessarily sin, or else there could be some soul besides Christ's own that does not need Christian grace to be set free from sin, because it did not sin in Adam—if it was said that all sinned in him only according to the flesh, which was created from him, and not according to the soul as well. This is so contrary to the faith of the Church that parents hurry with their little children and infants to receive the grace of holy baptism. If in them the bond of sin that is loosed belongs only to the flesh and not to the soul as well, one may rightly ask what harm it would do them if they left the body at that age without baptism. For if this sacrament provides for their body and not for their soul, then the dead ought to be baptized too. But since we see that the Church universally holds to this, that people hurry with the living and come to the aid of the living, lest after they have died nothing can be done to benefit them, we do not see what else can be understood except that every little child is nothing but Adam, in both body and soul, and therefore needs the grace of Christ. For that age has done nothing in itself, either good or bad; consequently the soul there is utterly innocent if it was not propagated from Adam. So anyone who holds this view of the soul and can show how it could justly go into condemnation, if it leaves the body without baptism, would be remarkable indeed."

It is most truly and most accurately written: "The flesh lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh." Yet I think no one, learned or unlearned, doubts that the flesh can lust after nothing without the soul. And so the cause of carnal lust itself does not lie in the soul alone, but still less does it lie in the flesh alone. For it arises from both: from the soul, because without it no pleasure is felt; and from the flesh, because without it carnal pleasure is not felt. So when the apostle speaks of the flesh lusting against the spirit, he undoubtedly means the carnal pleasure that the spirit has from the flesh and with the flesh, set against the pleasure it has by itself alone. For unless I am mistaken, it alone has that desire, unmixed with bodily pleasure or craving for carnal things, by which the soul longs and faints for the courts of the Lord; it alone also has the desire of which it is told: "You have desired wisdom; keep the commandment, and the Lord will grant it to you." For when the spirit commands the members of the body to serve this desire, by which it alone is kindled—as when a book is taken up, when something is written, read, debated, or listened to, or when bread is broken for the hungry and the other duties of humanity and mercy are performed—the flesh shows obedience and does not stir up lust. When these and similar good desires, which the soul alone has, are opposed by something that delights the same soul according to the flesh, then the flesh is said to lust against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh.

For when he says, "The flesh lusts," the flesh is so called with reference to what the soul does according to the flesh, just as it is said, "The ear hears and the eye sees"—for who does not know that it is rather the soul that both hears through the ear and sees through the eye? We speak the same way when we say, "Your hand helped someone," when something is given with outstretched hand to help someone. Now it was said even of the very eye of faith, whose task is to believe what is not seen through the flesh, "All flesh shall see the salvation of God"—which can only mean the soul, by which the flesh lives—even though to see Christ piously through this flesh of ours as well, that is, the form he put on for our sake, belongs not to lust but to the service of the flesh, lest perhaps someone should wish to take "All flesh shall see the salvation of God" in that sense. If so, how much more fittingly is the flesh said to lust when the soul not only supplies animal life to the flesh but also lusts after something according to the flesh itself—something it is not in its power not to lust after, so long as sin is present in the members, that is, a certain violent enticement of the flesh in the body of this death, which comes from the punishment of that sin from which we derive our descent, and by reason of which all are children of wrath before grace. Against this sin those who are established under grace do battle, not so that it may not be in their body, as long as that body is so mortal that it may rightly even be called dead, but so that it may not reign. And it does not reign when its desires, that is, the things lusted after according to the flesh against the spirit, are not obeyed. Does the apostle therefore say, "Let there be no sin in your mortal body"? No—he knew that the delight in sin is present, which he calls sin, since nature has been corrupted by the first transgression. Rather he says, "Let not sin reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its desires, and do not present your members to sin as weapons of iniquity."

According to this view, we neither assert the utterly absurd notion that the flesh lusts without the soul, nor do we agree with the Manichaeans, who, seeing that the flesh cannot lust without the soul, thought that the flesh had another soul of its own, from another nature opposed to God, by which it lusts against the spirit. Nor are we forced to say that some soul does not need the grace of Christ, when we are asked: "What has the soul of an infant deserved, that it should be harmful to it to leave the body without having received the sacrament of Christian baptism, if it has committed no sin of its own and does not come from the soul that first sinned in Adam?"

For we are not dealing with somewhat older children, to whom some, indeed, are unwilling to attribute sin of their own until the point of their fourteenth year, when they begin to reach puberty. We would rightly believe this if there were no sins except those committed with the genital members. But who would dare to claim that thefts, lies, and perjuries are not sins, except someone who wants to commit such things with impunity? Yet childhood is full of them, although in children they do not seem to deserve punishment as they do in adults, because it is hoped that with the coming years, as reason grows strong, they will be able to understand the commandments of salvation better and obey them more willingly. But we are not now dealing with children, who, if truth and justice oppose their carnal and childish will, whether of body or of mind, resist with all the force they can muster in word and deed. And on behalf of what, if not of falsehood and injustice, which they see will help them either to obtain what attracts them or to avoid what offends them? We are speaking of infants—and not because they are often born of adulterers; for the gifts of nature are not to be blamed for wicked behavior, nor should grain have refused to sprout because a thief's hand sowed it. Or indeed, will their iniquity harm even the parents themselves if they amend their lives by turning to God? How much less will it harm the children, if they live rightly!

But that age raises a pressing question. Since the soul of an infant has no sin arising from the free choice of its own will, it is asked how it can be justified through the obedience of the one man if it is not guilty through the disobedience of the other one man. This is what is said by those who hold that human souls are created from human parents—not, indeed, except by God the creator, but in the same way as bodies are. For bodies too are not created by the parents rather than by him who says, "Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you."

To them the reply is made that God does indeed give new souls one by one to human bodies, so that, in the flesh of sin that comes from original sin, they may earn merit by living rightly and by subduing carnal lusts under the grace of God, by which they may be transformed for the better together with that same body at the time of the resurrection and live forever with the angels in Christ. But, it is said, when they are wonderfully fitted to earthly and mortal members, especially members propagated from the flesh of sin, so that they may first give them life and later, as age advances, also govern them, they are necessarily weighed down, as it were, by forgetfulness. If this forgetfulness were somehow impossible to shake off [?], it would be attributed to the creator. But since the soul, gradually recovering from the torpor of this forgetfulness, can turn to its God and earn his mercy and truth, first by the very devotion of its conversion and then by perseverance in keeping his commandment, what harm is it to the soul to be plunged for a little while into this sort of sleep, from which, gradually awakening into the light of understanding for which the rational soul was made, it can choose a good life by a good will? This, indeed, it cannot do unless the grace of God helps it through the mediator. If a person neglects this, he will be Adam not only according to the flesh but also according to the spirit; but if he attends to it, he will be Adam only according to the flesh, while, living rightly according to the spirit, he will deserve to receive back, cleansed from the stain of sin, even that guilty part which was derived from Adam, through the transformation that the resurrection promises to the saints.

But before it is old enough to live according to the spirit, the soul needs the sacrament of the mediator, so that what it cannot yet do through its own faith may be done through the faith of those who love it. For by his sacrament the penalty of original sin is loosed even in infancy; and unless he helps, even a young man will not master carnal lust, nor, once it is subdued, will he lay hold of the merit of eternal life except by the gift of him whose favor he strives to earn. Therefore even an infant ought to be baptized while alive, so that its association with the flesh of sin may not harm the soul; for by sharing in it, the infant's soul comes to be unable to have any understanding according to the spirit. That very condition weighs on it even when it has been stripped of the body, unless, while it is in the body, it is expiated through the one sacrifice of the true priest.

"What then," someone says, "if its own people have not seen to this, whether through unbelief or through negligence?" This, of course, can be said of adults too. For they may die suddenly, or fall ill among people where no one comes to their aid by having them baptized. "But adults," he says, "also have sins of their own, which need forgiveness; and if these have not been forgiven, no one will rightly say that they are punished undeservedly for what they committed by their own will in their own lives. But that soul to which a certain contagion has been passed on from the flesh of sin—if it was not created from that first sinful soul, this contagion can in no way be imputed to it, for it was given to the flesh not by any sin but by the nature in which it was so made, and by God's giving. Why then will it be shut out from eternal life if no one comes to the aid of the infant by baptizing it? Or perhaps it will do no harm? Then what good does it do to the one who is helped, if it does no harm to the one who is not helped?"

I confess that I have not yet heard or read anywhere what those who try to maintain, on the basis of the holy Scriptures—either because it is found in them or because it is not contrary to them—that new souls not drawn from the parents are given to bodies, could answer here in support of their case. Still, the cause of those who are absent should not be abandoned if anything occurs to me by which it might seem to be helped. For they can still say that God, foreknowing how each soul would live if it lived longer in the body, provides the ministry of the saving washing to the one whose future devotion he foresees, had it reached the years capable of faith, if for some hidden reason it must now be overtaken by death. It is therefore hidden, and far removed from human understanding, or certainly from mine, why an infant is born who is going to die immediately or soon. But this is hidden in such a way that it helps neither of the two parties whose views we are now examining. For once we have rejected the opinion that souls are thrust down into bodies according to the merits of a previous life—so that the soul that had not sinned much would seem to have deserved to be released sooner—lest we contradict the apostle, who testifies that those not yet born had done nothing good or bad, then neither those who affirm the transmission of the soul nor those who hold that new souls are given one to each body can show in their own favor why the death of some is hastened and that of others delayed. This cause, then, is hidden, and as far as I can judge, it neither supports nor opposes either side equally.

Some people were pressed with the question of infants who die: why is the sacrament of baptism necessary for all, if their souls are not drawn from that one man through whose disobedience many were made sinners? They answer that all are indeed made sinners according to the flesh, but according to the soul only those who lived badly at a time when they could also have lived well. They add that all souls, including those of infants, need the sacrament of baptism, without which it is not good to depart from this life even at that age. The reason, they say, is that the contagion of sin from the sinful flesh, which overwhelms the soul when it is put into these members, will harm the soul after death unless it is cleansed by the sacrament of the Mediator while it is still in that flesh. They also say that God provides this help for a soul which he foreknew would have lived piously if it had lived here until the years suited to faith, and which, for some reason known to him, he both willed to be born in a body and quickly withdrew from the body. When they give this answer, what can be said against them? Only this: we would become uncertain about the salvation of those who lived good lives and died in the peace of the Church, if each person is to be judged not only by how he lived but also by how he would have lived if he could have lived longer. For then the evil deserts not only of past sins but even of future sins would count before God. Death would not free a person from guilt for them, even if it came before they were committed, and nothing would have been gained for the one who was snatched away lest wickedness change his understanding. For God foreknew that future wickedness. Why then would he not rather judge the man by it, if he judged that the soul of a dying infant must be helped by baptism, so that the filth it shared from the body of sin would not harm it, precisely because he foreknew that, if it lived, it would have lived piously and faithfully?

Or can this idea be refuted more readily because it is mine? Those who declare themselves certain of this view may perhaps bring forward other testimonies of scripture or proofs from reason. With these they might remove this ambiguity, or at least show that their view does not conflict with the apostle. Commending with great earnestness the grace by which we are saved, he says: "As in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive"; and: "As through the disobedience of one man many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one man many will be made righteous." And because he wants these same "many sinners" to be understood as all, with no exceptions, he says earlier about Adam: "in whom all sinned." So those who hold that souls are propagated from one man are not unreasonable in believing that the souls of infants cannot be set apart. They draw this both from the word "all" and from the fact that infants are helped by baptism. That stands unless they are refuted either by some clear and evident reason that does not conflict with the holy scriptures, or by the authority of those scriptures themselves.

Now then, so far as the needs of this undertaking allow, let us also look at the passage we put off a little earlier. It is written in the book of Wisdom: "I was a gifted child, and a good soul fell to my lot; and being better still, I came to an undefiled body." This testimony seems to support those who say that souls are not created from parents but come or descend into the body when God sends them. Yet it also stands in the way of their view when it says, "a good soul fell to my lot." For they surely believe that the souls God sends into bodies either flow from a single source, like streams, or are made with an equal nature. They do not believe that some are good or better and others not good or less good. For how could souls be good or better, or not good or less good, except either by their conduct, through the free choice of the will, or through differences in the temperament of bodies, as some souls are weighed down more and others less by the body, which is corruptible and weighs down the soul? But individual souls did no actions before they came into bodies by which their conduct could be told apart. Nor could this man have called his soul good because of a less burdensome body, since he says: "A good soul fell to my lot; and being better still, I came to an undefiled body." For he said that coming to an undefiled body was added to the goodness by which he was already good, having received a good soul by lot. So he was good from some other source before he came to the body. But that was surely not through any difference in conduct, since there was no merit from a life lived beforehand. Nor was it through any difference of body, since he was good before he came to the body. From where, then?

Now take those who assert that souls are created by propagation from the soul of that first transgressor. The words "I came to a body" do not seem to speak in their favor, yet the rest fits their view well enough. Having said, "I was a gifted child," the writer explains why he was gifted and at once adds: "and a good soul fell to my lot," that is, from his father's talent or bodily temperament. Then he says: "and being better still, I came to an undefiled body." If this is understood as the mother's body, then not even the words "I came to a body" will contradict this opinion. They are taken to mean that from his father's soul and body he came to his mother's body, which was undefiled, either by menstrual blood (for this is said to dull the mind) or by the stain of adultery. Thus these words of this book either favor those who speak of the propagation of souls more, or, if the others can also interpret them in their own favor, they hang evenly between the two sides.

Suppose we wish to take these words as spoken by the Lord, in the human nature the Word assumed. There are certainly things in the same context of the reading that do not befit his excellence. Above all, the same speaker in that book, a little before saying the words we are now discussing, confessed that he was curdled in blood from the seed of a man. The virgin birth is wholly foreign to this way of being born, for no Christian doubts that she conceived the flesh of Christ without a man's seed. But consider the Psalms. There he says: "They pierced my hands and my feet; they numbered all my bones; they looked and stared at me. They divided my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots." These things belong properly to him alone. Yet in the same place he also said: "O God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me? Far from my salvation are the words of my sins." These words in turn do not befit him, except insofar as he transfigures in himself the body of our lowliness, since we are members of his body. And in the Gospel itself, "the boy advanced in age and wisdom." So perhaps the words surrounding this sentence in the book of Wisdom can also be applied to the Lord himself, because of his lowly form as a servant and the unity of the body of the Church with its head. If so, who was more gifted than that boy, whose wisdom at twelve years old the elders marveled at? And what soul was better than his? Even if those who affirm the propagation of souls should win, not by arguing but by proving, it will not follow that his soul too must be believed to have come by propagation from that transgressor. Otherwise he too would have been made a sinner through that man's disobedience, though it is through his obedience alone that many are freed from that guilt and made righteous. And what was more undefiled than the virgin's womb? Her flesh came from the propagation of sin, yet she did not conceive by the propagation of sin. So not even Christ's body was sown in Mary's womb by that law which is placed in the members of the body of death and fights against the law of the mind. The holy patriarchs who were married kept this law in check. They gave it free rein for intercourse only as far as was permitted, and yet they did not feel its impulse only as far as was permitted. Accordingly, the body of Christ was taken from the flesh of a woman who had been conceived from that stock of sinful flesh. But because it was not conceived in her in the way she had been conceived, it was not itself sinful flesh but the likeness of sinful flesh. For he did not receive from it the liability to death that shows itself in the involuntary movement of the flesh, which is overcome by the will and against which the spirit lusts. What he received from it was not enough to bring the contagion of the transgression. It was enough to pay a death he did not owe and to show the promised resurrection. The first of these helps us not to fear, the second helps us to hope.

Finally, if I am asked where Jesus Christ received his soul from, I would rather hear better and more learned men on this question. Still, as far as I can grasp it, I would more readily answer "from where Adam received his" than "from Adam." For dust taken from the earth, on which no man had yet worked, was found worthy to be given a soul by God. How much more, then, did a body taken from flesh on which likewise no man had worked receive a good soul by lot! In the one case the man who would fall was being raised up; in the other the one who would lift him up was coming down. And perhaps he says, "a good soul fell to my lot" (if indeed this is to be understood of him), because what is given by lot is usually given by God. Or, as may be said with confidence, the word "lot" was added to remove any suspicion of earlier merits. Otherwise someone might think that even that soul had been raised by some earlier works to such a height that with it "the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us."

In the epistle entitled To the Hebrews there is a passage that well deserves careful consideration. Melchizedek had gone before as a figure of this future reality, and through him the author distinguishes the priesthood of Christ from the priesthood of Levi. He says: "See then how great this man is, to whom even Abraham the patriarch gave a tenth of the firstfruits. And those of the sons of Levi who receive the priesthood have a command under the law to take tithes from the people, that is, from their brothers, although these too came from the loins of Abraham. But he who is not of their lineage took tithes from Abraham and blessed the one who had the promise. Beyond all dispute, the lesser is blessed by the greater. Here, tithes are received by men who die; there, by one of whom it is testified that he lives. And one might even say that Levi, who receives tithes, paid tithes through Abraham, for he was still in his father's loins." This, then, is offered as evidence of how far the priesthood of Christ surpasses the Levitical priesthood: Christ the priest was prefigured by the one who took tithes from Abraham, in whom Levi too paid tithes. If this point carries weight, then surely Christ did not pay tithes to him. And if Levi paid tithes because he was in Abraham's loins, then Christ did not pay tithes because he was not in Abraham's loins. But suppose we take it that Levi was in Abraham only according to the flesh and not according to the soul. Then Christ was there too, since according to the flesh Christ is also of Abraham's seed, and so he too paid tithes. What then are we to make of it? The great difference between Christ's priesthood and Levi's is said to be that Levi paid tithes to Melchizedek while he was in Abraham's loins. But Christ was there too, so both would have paid tithes alike, unless we must understand that in some way Christ was not there. Yet who would deny that he was there according to the flesh? Therefore he was not there according to the soul. So the soul of Christ does not come by propagation from Adam's transgression; otherwise it too would have been there.

Here those who defend the propagation of souls step forward and say that their view is confirmed. They argue that Levi was in the loins of Abraham according to the soul as well, and that when Melchizedek took tithes from Abraham he took them from Levi too, so that Christ can be set apart from Levi in this tithing. Christ did not pay tithes, yet he was in Abraham's loins according to the flesh. It remains, then, that he was not there according to the soul, and so it follows that Levi was there according to the soul. This does not much concern me, since I am still more ready to hear both sides debate than to confirm the view of either. Meanwhile, I wanted to use this testimony to set Christ's soul apart from the origin of this propagation. Perhaps others will find how to answer them on the rest. They may say something that moves me not a little as well: no man's soul is in his father's loins, yet Levi, present in Abraham's loins according to the flesh, paid tithes, while Christ, present there according to the flesh, did not. For Levi was there according to that seminal reason by which he was to come into his mother through intercourse. Christ's flesh was not there according to that reason, although Mary's flesh was there according to it. So neither Levi nor Christ was in Abraham's loins according to the soul. Both were there according to the flesh, but Levi according to carnal concupiscence, and Christ according to bodily substance alone. For in the seed there is both visible bodily matter and an invisible reason, and both ran from Abraham, or even from Adam himself, down to the body of Mary, since her body too was conceived and born in that way. But Christ took the visible substance of his flesh from the virgin's flesh, while the reason of his conception came not from a man's seed but in a very different way, from above. Accordingly, with respect to what he received from his mother, he too was in Abraham's loins.

So the one who paid tithes in Abraham was the one who was in his loins, only according to the flesh, but in the same way that Abraham himself was in his own father's loins. That is, he was born of his father Abraham in the same way that Abraham was born of his father: through the law in the members that fights against the law of the mind, and through invisible concupiscence. The chaste and good laws of marriage do not let it prevail except so far as they can use it to provide for the continuation of the race. But the one whose flesh drew from there not the fever of the wound but the material of the medicine did not pay tithes there. For since the tithing served to prefigure the medicine, what paid tithes in Abraham's flesh was what was being healed, not that by which it was healed. For the same flesh, not only of Abraham but of the first, earthly man himself, held at once both the wound of the transgression and the remedy for the wound. The wound of the transgression lies in the law of the members that fights against the law of the mind; through seminal reason it is, as it were, copied into all the flesh propagated from him. The remedy for the wound lies in what was taken from there, from the virgin, without any act of concupiscence, in bodily matter alone, through the divine reason of conception and formation. This was done so that he might share in death without iniquity and give an example of resurrection without falsehood. Therefore I think that even those who defend the propagation of souls agree that the soul of Christ does not come by propagation from the soul of that first transgressor. For they hold that the seed of the soul is also passed on through the seed of the father in intercourse, and Christ's conception was wholly foreign to that kind of conception. They also agree that if he had been in Abraham according to the soul, he too would have paid tithes. But scripture testifies that he did not pay tithes, and on this ground too it distinguishes his priesthood from the Levitical priesthood.

Perhaps they will say: if he could be there according to the flesh without being tithed, why could he not also be there according to the soul without being tithed? The answer here is this. Not even those who think the soul is a body have supposed that the simple substance of the soul is increased by bodily growth, and among them are chiefly those who believe it is created from the parents. In the seed of the body, then, there can be an invisible power that works out the numbers of the body incorporeally. This power is to be distinguished, not by the eyes but by the understanding, from the bodily mass that is perceived by sight and touch. And the very size of the human body, which incomparably exceeds the small measure of the seed, shows clearly enough that something can be taken from it which does not have that seminal power, but only bodily substance. This is what was divinely taken up and formed into the flesh of Christ, not through the propagation of those who lie together. But who could affirm this of the soul, that it has both, the visible matter of seed and the hidden principle of seed? But why should I labour over a matter that perhaps cannot be made convincing to anyone by words, unless his mind is so great and of such a kind that it can fly ahead of the speaker's effort and not wait for everything to be put into speech? I will sum up briefly, then. If it could happen in the case of the soul too, as perhaps was understood when we spoke of the flesh, then the soul of Christ comes by transmission, but in such a way that it did not draw the stain of transgression along with it. But if it could not come from that source without that guilt, then it does not come from it. As for the origin of the other souls, whether they come from the parents or from above, let those prevail who can. I still waver between the two views and am moved now one way, now the other. I hold to this much only: I do not believe that the soul is a body, or some bodily quality or adjustment (if that is the word for it), which the Greeks call harmonia. With God helping my mind, I am confident that I never will believe it, whoever chatters about such things.

There is another testimony, not to be overlooked, which those who believe that souls come from above can bring forward in their favour. The Lord himself says: "What is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit." "What could settle more decisively than this saying," they say, "that the soul cannot be born of the flesh? For what else is the soul but a spirit of life, created of course, not a creator?"
