The others reply: "What else do we hold, when we say that flesh comes from flesh and soul from soul? For a human being consists of both, and we hold that both come from the parent: the flesh from the flesh of the one who acts, the spirit from the spirit of the one who desires." And this leaves aside for the moment that the Lord was speaking not of carnal generation but of spiritual regeneration.

I have treated these matters as far as time allowed. I would declare that the weight of reasons and testimonies on both sides is equal or nearly equal, were it not that the view of those who think souls are created from the parents gains the advantage from the baptism of infants. What answer could be given to them on this point has not yet occurred to me. If God should perhaps grant me something later, and also grant me the opportunity of writing it for those eager for such things, I shall not be reluctant to do so. For now, however, I give notice beforehand that the testimony of infants must not be so slighted that, if the truth is against it, no one troubles to refute it. Either we should not inquire into this matter at all, and it should suffice for our faith to know where we are going if we live devoutly, even if we do not know where we came from; or else, if it is not shameless for the rational soul to burn with desire to know this too about itself, let there be no stubbornness in disputing, but diligence in seeking, humility in asking, and perseverance in knocking. Then, if he who surely knows better than we do what is good for us knows that this is good for us, he who gives good gifts to his children will give this as well. Nevertheless, the custom of Mother Church in baptizing infants is by no means to be despised, nor in any way to be thought superfluous, and it would not be believed at all were it not an apostolic tradition. For that tender age carries great weight as testimony, the age that was the first to be found worthy of shedding its blood for Christ.

I do urge, as strongly as I can, those who have been taken up by the opinion that souls are propagated from the parents to examine themselves as far as they are able, and meanwhile to understand that their souls are not bodies. For no nature is closer than the one made in God's own image, and none, when carefully examined, better enables us to think incorporeally even of God, who remains unchangeable above all his creation. Nothing lies nearer, or perhaps nothing follows so naturally, than that once the soul is believed to be a body, God too will be believed to be a body. Those who are accustomed to the bodily senses and attached to them refuse to believe that the soul is anything other than a body, for fear that if it were not a body it would be nothing. And so they are all the more afraid to believe that God is not a body, the more they fear to believe that God is nothing. They are so carried away by the fancies or phantoms of images that thought about bodies turns over that, if these are taken away, they dread perishing as though in a void. So they are bound to paint even justice and wisdom in their hearts, in a manner of speaking, with shapes and colours, since they cannot think of them as incorporeal. Yet when they are moved by justice or wisdom, to praise them or to act in accordance with them, they do not say what colour, what stature, what features [or what shapes] they have seen. But we have said a great deal about these things elsewhere, and, God willing, we shall say more where the matter seems to require it. To return to what we had begun to say: whether some people do not doubt that souls are transmitted from the parents, or doubt whether it is so, they should still not dare to believe or say that the soul is a body. This is chiefly for the reason I gave: so that they may not suppose that God himself is nothing other than a body, even if a most excellent one, even if of a special nature surpassing all the rest, but a body all the same.

Tertullian, in fact, believed that the soul is a body for no other reason than that he could not conceive of it as incorporeal, and so he feared that it would be nothing if it were not a body; nor was he able to think otherwise about God. Yet because he is certainly sharp-witted, he is now and then overcome by the truth when he sees it, against his own opinion. What truer thing could he have said than what he says in one place: "Everything bodily is capable of suffering"? He ought therefore to have changed the view he had expressed a little earlier, that even God is a body. For I do not think he was so foolish as to believe that the nature of God is capable of suffering, so that Christ would be believed to be capable of suffering and change not only in the flesh, nor only in flesh and soul, but in the very Word through whom all things were made. Far be that from a Christian heart! Likewise, after he had even given the soul an airy and luminous colour, he came to the senses, with which he tried to equip it limb by limb as though it were a body. He says: "This will be the inner man, the other the outer, one man in two ways. The inner man too has his own eyes and ears, with which the people ought to have heard and seen the Lord; and he has his other limbs as well, which he uses in his thoughts and with which he acts in dreams."

See with what ears and what eyes the people ought to have heard and seen God: those that the soul uses in dreams! Yet if someone saw Tertullian himself in a dream, he would never say that Tertullian had seen him and spoken with him, since Tertullian for his part would not have seen him. Lastly, if the soul sees itself in dreams, when the limbs of its body lie in one place while the soul itself wanders through the various images it sees, who has ever seen it in a dream with an airy and luminous colour, except perhaps in the way that it sees other things that are equally false? For it can see this too. But God forbid that it should believe itself to be like that once it wakes up. Otherwise, when it sees itself differently, which happens more often, either its soul will have changed, or else even then it is not the substance of the soul that is seen but an incorporeal image of a body, formed in a wonderful way, as in thought. What Ethiopian has not almost always seen himself black in his dreams? Or if he saw himself in another colour, was he not all the more surprised, if he remembered it? But I do not know whether he would ever have seen himself with an airy and luminous colour, if he had never read or heard this man.

And what of the fact that people are led on by such visions and want to lay down for us from the Scriptures that it is not the soul but God himself who is something of this kind, as he was shown figuratively to the spirits of the saints, and as he is also presented in allegorical language? Such visions are indeed like such sayings. And so they go astray, setting up in their hearts the idols of an empty opinion. They do not understand that the saints judged their own visions of this kind just as they would have judged such things if they had read or heard them spoken figuratively by God: as the seven ears of grain and the seven cows are seven years, as the sheet tied by four cords, like a dish full of various animals, is the world with all the nations. So it is with everything else, and all the more with what is signified about incorporeal things in bodily terms, not by things but by images.

Tertullian, however, would not have the soul grow in substance as the body does, and he gives the reason for his fear: "So that it may not be said to decrease in substance as well, and so be believed to be liable to perish." And yet, because he stretches the soul spatially through the body, he can find no way out regarding its growth, since he wants it to come from a tiny seed and become equal to the size of the body. He says: "But its power, in which its natural endowments are implanted and preserved, is drawn out gradually along with the flesh, while the measure of the substance with which it was breathed in from the beginning remains intact." Perhaps we would not understand this, had he not made his meaning plain by adding a comparison. "Take," he says, "a certain weight of gold or silver, still an unworked lump. It has a compact form, smaller for the moment than it will be, yet containing within the bounds of its measure everything that is the nature of gold or silver. Then, when the lump is beaten out into a sheet, it becomes larger than it was at the start through the spreading of a fixed weight, not through any addition, by being extended, not by being increased. And yet in this way too it is increased while it is extended, for it can increase in form when it cannot in substance. Then the very lustre of the gold or silver is brought out, which was already there in the lump but dimmer, though not absent. Then one form after another is added, according to the pliancy of the material, in whatever way the craftsman shapes it, contributing nothing to its measure but its appearance. In the same way the growth of the soul is to be considered not substantial but a drawing out."

Who would believe that a man with such a mind could have been so eloquent? But these things are to be trembled at, not laughed at. Would he have been driven to this if he could have conceived of something that exists and yet is not a body? What is more absurd than to think that a lump of some metal can grow in one direction while it is being beaten, unless it shrinks in another, or increase in breadth unless it is reduced in thickness? Or that there is any body which, while the quantity of its nature stays the same, grows in every direction without becoming thinner? How then will the soul, starting from that drop of seed, fill the size of the body it animates, if it too is a body whose substance grows by no addition? How, I say, will it fill the flesh it gives life to, unless it becomes thinner in proportion as what it animates becomes larger? Evidently he feared that it would perish by diminishing if it grew, and did not fear that it would perish by thinning out as it grew. But why should I linger any longer, when my discourse is running on at greater length than the need to finish requires, and my view is already well enough known: what I hold as certain, and where I still have doubts, and why I doubt? So let this book now be brought to a close, so that we may go on to consider what follows.
BOOK ELEVEN

"And they were both naked, Adam and his wife, and they were not ashamed. Now the serpent was the most cunning of all the beasts on the earth that the Lord God had made. And the serpent said to the woman: 'Why is it that God has said, You shall not eat from every tree of paradise?' And the woman said to the serpent: 'We shall eat of the fruit of the trees that are in paradise; but of the fruit of the tree that is in the middle of paradise God has said: You shall not eat of it, nor shall you touch it, lest you die.' And the serpent said to the woman: 'You shall not die the death. For God knew that on the day you eat of it your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil.' And the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was pleasing to the eyes to look at, and that it was fair to know. And she took some of its fruit and ate, and she gave some also to her husband with her, and they ate. And the eyes of both of them were opened, and they knew that they were naked; and they sewed fig leaves together and made themselves aprons. And they heard the voice of the Lord God walking in paradise in the evening, and Adam and his wife hid themselves from the face of the Lord God among the trees of paradise. And the Lord God called Adam and said to him: 'Adam, where are you?' And he said to him: 'I heard your voice as you walked in paradise, and I was afraid, because I am naked, and I hid myself.' And he said to him: 'Who told you that you were naked, unless you have eaten of the tree of which I commanded you that you alone should not eat?' And Adam said: 'The woman you gave to be with me, she gave me some from the tree, and I ate.' And the Lord God said to the woman: 'Why have you done this?' And the woman said: 'The serpent led me astray, and I ate.' And the Lord God said to the serpent: 'Because you have done this, cursed are you above all the cattle and above all the beasts that are on the earth. On your breast and your belly you shall go, and you shall eat earth all the days of your life. And I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed. She shall watch for your head, and you shall watch for her heel.' And to the woman he said: 'I will greatly multiply your sorrows and your groaning. In sorrows you shall bear children, and your turning shall be to your husband, and he shall rule over you.' And to Adam he said: 'Because you listened to the voice of your wife and ate of the tree of which alone I had commanded you not to eat, cursed is the ground in your works; in sorrows you shall eat of it all the days of your life. Thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you, and you shall eat the grass of the field. In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for earth you are, and to earth you shall go.' And Adam called his wife's name 'Life,' because she is the mother of all the living. And the Lord God made for Adam and his wife garments of skin and clothed them. And the Lord God said: 'Behold, Adam has become like one of us in knowing good and evil. And now, lest he at some time stretch out his hand and take from the tree of life and eat, and live for ever.' And the Lord God sent him out of the paradise of delight to till the earth from which he was taken. And he cast Adam out and placed him opposite the paradise of delight; and he stationed the Cherubim and the flaming sword that turns, to guard the way to the tree of life."

Before we treat the text of this passage of Scripture in order, I think I should repeat a warning I recall having given already elsewhere in this work. What we must insist on is that whatever the writer himself narrates as having happened should be defended in its proper literal sense. But if, in the words of God or of any person taken up into the prophetic office, something is said that cannot be understood literally without absurdity, it must without doubt be taken as spoken figuratively for the sake of some meaning; yet we may not doubt that it was actually said. This is required by the trustworthiness of the narrator and the promise of the interpreter.

They were both naked. This is true: the bodies of the two human beings living in paradise were entirely naked. And they were not ashamed. Why would they be ashamed, when they had not yet felt in their members any law at war with the law of their mind? That penalty for sin came upon them after they had committed the transgression, when disobedience seized what was forbidden and justice punished what had been done. Before this happened, they were naked, as Scripture says, and were not abashed. There was no movement in the body that called for modesty; they thought nothing needed covering, because they had felt nothing that needed restraining. How they would have propagated children has already been discussed earlier. But it must not be believed that it would have been in the way they did propagate after the foretold punishment followed upon the crime they committed. Then, even before they died, death had already been conceived in the bodies of the disobedient pair, and by a most just retribution it stirred up the riot of disobedient members. Adam and Eve were not yet like this when they were both naked and were not abashed.

Now the serpent there was the most prudent, but of all the beasts on the earth which the Lord God had made. The word "most prudent", or as many Latin manuscripts have it, "wisest", is used here in a transferred sense. It is not used in its proper sense, in which wisdom is normally taken as something good, whether of God, of the angels or of the rational soul. It is as if we were to call bees or even ants wise, because their works seem to imitate wisdom. Yet this serpent could be called the wisest of all the beasts, not because of its own irrational soul, but because of a spirit not its own, that is, the devil's. However far the angels who transgressed were cast down from their heavenly seats, as their perversity and pride deserved, they are still by nature superior to all the beasts, because of the eminence of reason. So what wonder is it if the devil, already filling the serpent with his own influence and mingling his spirit with it, in the way that the soothsayers of demons are usually filled, had made it the wisest of all the beasts, that is, of all creatures that live by a living but irrational soul? For it is by a misuse of the word that wisdom is spoken of in a bad sense, just as cunning is spoken of in a good one. In its proper and more usual sense, at least in Latin, people are called wise as a term of praise, while the cunning are understood to be ill-minded. This is why some translators, as we find in a good many manuscripts, have rendered the sense rather than the word, to suit Latin usage, and preferred to call this serpent more cunning than all the beasts, rather than wiser. As for the proper usage of Hebrew, and whether in that language people can be called and understood to be wise in a bad sense, not by misuse but properly, let those who know it well judge. We, however, plainly read in another passage of the holy Scriptures of people who are wise for evil, not for good; and the Lord says that the children of this age are wiser than the children of light in providing for their own future, though by fraud and not by right.

Nor indeed should we suppose that the devil chose the serpent as the means through which to tempt and persuade to sin. Rather, since there was in him a desire to deceive, arising from his perverse and envious will, he could do it only through the animal through which he was permitted to be able to do it. For the will to do harm can be wicked and come from one's own mind; but the power comes only from God, and this by a hidden and deep justice, since there is no injustice with God.

If, then, it is asked why God permitted man to be tempted when he foreknew that he would consent to the tempter, I cannot penetrate the depth of his counsel, and I confess that this is far beyond my powers. There may, then, be some more hidden reason, reserved for better and holier people, by his grace rather than by their merits. Yet as far as he either grants me to understand or allows me to say, it does not seem to me that man would have deserved great praise if he were able to live well simply because no one urged him to live badly. For it lay both in his nature to be able, and in his power to will, not to consent to the one urging him, though with the help of him who resists the proud but gives grace to the humble. Why, then, should God not allow him to be tempted, though he foreknew that he would consent? For man was going to do this by his own will, through guilt, and was to be set in order by God's justice, through punishment. In this way God would also show the proud soul, for the instruction of the saints to come, how rightly he himself makes use even of the evil wills of souls, when they make perverse use of good natures.

Nor should we think that this tempter would have brought man down unless there had first been in man's soul a certain exaltation that needed to be checked, so that through the humiliation of sin he might learn how falsely he had presumed upon himself. For it is most truly said: "Before a fall the heart is exalted, and before glory it is humbled." And perhaps it is this man's voice in the psalm: "I said in my abundance, I shall never be moved." Then, having learned by experience what evil there is in proud presumption on one's own power, and what good in the help of God's grace, he says: "Lord, by your will you gave strength to my beauty; but you turned away your face, and I was troubled." But whether this was said of this man or of another, the soul that exalted itself and trusted too much in what it took to be its own strength had to be shown, even by the experience of punishment, how ill it goes with a created nature if it withdraws from the one who made it. For it is especially this that makes plain what a good God is, since it goes well with no one who withdraws from him. Those who delight in deadly pleasures cannot be free from the fear of pain; and those who, in the deeper stupor of pride, do not feel the evil of their desertion at all, appear utterly more wretched to others who know how to discern these things. So if they will not accept the remedy by which such things are avoided, they may at least serve as an example by which others can avoid them. For as the apostle James says: "Each one is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire. Then desire, when it has conceived, gives birth to sin; and sin, when it is full-grown, brings forth death." So when the swelling of pride has been healed, one rises again, if the will that was lacking before the experience, the will to remain with God, is present at least after the experience, the will to return to God.

Some people, however, are so troubled about this temptation of the first man, because God permitted it to happen, as if they did not see now that the whole human race is ceaselessly tempted by the snares of the devil. Why does God permit this as well? Is it not because virtue is tested and exercised, and the palm is more glorious for having been tempted and not consenting than for having been unable to be tempted? Indeed, those who have deserted the Creator and go after the tempter tempt more and more those who remain in the word of God. They provide them with an example to avoid, against desire, and strike into them a holy fear, against pride. Hence the apostle says: "Looking to yourself, lest you too be tempted." It is remarkable how constantly, throughout all the divine Scriptures, care is taken to commend this humility by which we are made subject to the Creator, so that we do not presume on our own strength as if we had no need of his help. Since, then, the righteous make progress even through the unrighteous, and the godly through the ungodly, it is idle to say, "God should not have created those he foreknew would be evil." Why should he not create those he foreknew would benefit the good? So they are born to be useful in exercising and admonishing the good wills of others, and are justly punished for their own evil will.

"He should have made man such," they say, "that he would not wish to sin at all." Very well: we grant that a nature that does not wish to sin at all is better. Let them grant, in turn, that a nature made in such a way that it could avoid sinning if it chose is not an evil nature, and that the sentence by which it was punished was just, since it sinned by will and not by necessity. True reason teaches that a creature that takes no delight at all in anything unlawful is better. Yet true reason teaches no less that a creature is also good which has it in its power to restrain unlawful delight, should it arise, so that it rejoices not only in its other lawful and rightly done acts but also in the very restraint of that wicked delight. Since, then, this nature is good and that one better, why should God have made only that one, and not rather both? Consequently those who were ready to praise God for that one alone ought to praise him more abundantly for both. For the one is found in the holy angels, the other in holy men. But as for those who have chosen the side of iniquity and corrupted a praiseworthy nature by a blameworthy will, it does not follow that they ought not to have been created because they were foreknown. For they too have their place, which they fill in the scheme of things for the benefit of the saints. God has no need even of the righteousness of any upright man; how much less of the iniquity of the perverse!

Who, on sober reflection, would say: "It would have been better for God not to create one whom he foreknew could be corrected by another's iniquity, than to create also one whom he foreknew would have to be condemned for his own iniquity"? That is to say: "It would be better that there should not exist one who, by making good use of another's evil, would be mercifully crowned, than that there should also exist an evil one who would be justly punished according to his deserts." For when sure reason shows two goods that are not equal, one higher and the other lower, the slow of heart do not understand that when they say, "Let both be like the higher," they are saying nothing other than, "Let only the higher exist." So in wanting to make the kinds of good equal, they reduce their number, and by boundlessly increasing one kind they abolish the other. Who would listen to them if they said, "Since the sense of sight is more excellent than hearing, let there be four eyes and no ears"? So too, there is a more excellent rational creature which is subject to God without any comparison with punishment and without any pride. But another, among men, has been so created that it cannot recognize God's kindness to itself except by seeing another's punishment, so that it may not be high-minded but fear, that is, not trust in itself but trust in God. Who with right understanding would say, "Let this one be like that one," and not see that he is saying nothing other than, "Let this one not exist, but let only that one exist"? If that is an ignorant and foolish thing to say, why then should God not create even those he foreknew would be evil, wishing to show his wrath and make known his power, and for this reason enduring with much patience the vessels of wrath made for destruction, in order to make known the riches of his glory toward the vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory? For so he who glories should glory only in the Lord, when he recognizes that it is not his own doing but God's, not only that he exists, but also that it goes well with him only from the one from whom he has his existence.

So it is quite unreasonable to say: "Those to whom God was to grant such great kindness of his mercy should not have existed, if they could not exist without the existence also of those in whom he would display the justice of his vengeance."
For why should both not exist instead, since in both God's goodness and his justice are rightly proclaimed?

"But," they say, "if God had willed it, these too would have been good." How much better was it that God willed this: that they should be what they willed to be, but that the good should not be so without fruit nor the evil without punishment, and that in this very fact they should be useful to others! "But he foreknew that their will would be evil." He foreknew it, certainly; and since his foreknowledge cannot be deceived, the evil will is therefore not his but theirs. Why then did he create those he foreknew would be such? Because just as he foresaw what evil they would do, so he also foresaw what good he himself would do from their evil deeds. For he made them in such a way as to leave them something by which they themselves could act, so that whatever they chose, even blameworthily, they would find him acting praiseworthily in their regard. They have the evil will from themselves; but from him they have both a good nature and a just punishment, a place due to them, and, for others, an aid to their exercise and an example to inspire fear.

"But," someone says, "he could have turned their will to good too, since he is almighty." Of course he could. Why then did he not do so? Because he did not will to. Why he did not will to is his own concern. For we ought not to be wiser than we ought. I think, however, that we have shown sufficiently a little earlier that a rational creature is no small good, even one that guards against evil by comparison with the evil. This kind of good creature would certainly not exist if almighty God had turned the evil wills of all to good and inflicted on no iniquity its due punishment. Then there would exist only that kind which makes progress without any comparison with the sin or the punishment of the wicked. And so, while the more excellent kind would seem to be multiplied, the number of the kinds of good would be reduced.

"So," they say, "there is something among God's works that needs another's evil in order to make progress toward good?" Have people become so deaf and blind, through some zeal for contention, that they do not hear or see how very many are corrected when certain people are punished? What pagan, what Jew, what heretic does not prove this daily in his own household? Yet when it comes to discussion and the search for truth, people will not turn their minds to consider from what work of divine providence the impulse to impose discipline comes to them: so that even if those who are punished are not corrected, others may still fear their example, and the just ruin of some may serve the salvation of others. Is God, then, the author of the malice or wickedness of those by whose just punishment he provides for those whom he has decided should be provided for in this way? Certainly not. But although he foreknew that they would be evil by their own vices, he did not refrain from creating them, assigning them to the benefit of those whom he created in such a kind that they could make progress toward good only by comparison with the wicked. If the wicked did not exist, they would of course benefit nothing. Is it a small good that has been accomplished, that there should exist those who are certainly useful to that kind? Whoever does not want that kind to exist is doing nothing other than ensuring that he himself is not in it.

Great are the works of the Lord, sought out in all his wills! He foresees that some will be good, and he creates them; he foresees that some will be evil, and he creates them. He offers himself to the good to be enjoyed, and bestows many of his gifts even on the wicked. He pardons in mercy and punishes in justice; and likewise he punishes in mercy and pardons in justice. He fears nothing from anyone's malice and needs nothing from anyone's righteousness. He looks to no advantage for himself, and he looks to the advantage of the good not only by the works of the good but even by the punishments of the wicked. Why then should he not permit man to be tempted by that temptation, through which he would be exposed, convicted and punished? For through it his proud desire for his own power would give birth to what it had conceived and be put to shame by its own offspring, and by a just punishment he would deter from the evil of pride and disobedience his descendants, for whom these things were being prepared to be written down and proclaimed.

If it is asked why the devil was permitted to tempt by means of a serpent in particular, who is not reminded that this was done in order to signify something, by a Scripture of such great authority, which in its prophesying works with as many proofs of divinity as there are fulfilments with which the world is now filled? It is not that the devil wished to signify anything for our instruction. But since he could not approach to tempt unless he was permitted, could he do so through anything other than that through which he was permitted to approach? Whatever, therefore, that serpent signified must be attributed to that providence under which the devil himself has his own desire to do harm, but only the ability that is granted him, whether to overthrow and destroy the vessels of wrath or to humble or test the vessels of mercy. We know, then, where the nature of the serpent comes from: for at the word of God the earth brought forth all the cattle, the serpents and the beasts. This whole creation, which has in it a living but irrational soul, is subject by the law of the divine order to the whole of rational creation, whether its will is good or evil. What wonder, then, if the devil was permitted to do something through a serpent, when Christ himself permitted demons to enter into swine?

A more anxious question is usually raised about the nature of the devil itself. Certain heretics, offended by the trouble his evil will causes, try to remove it entirely from the creation of the supreme and true God and to give it another principle, set against God. They cannot understand that everything that exists, insofar as it is some substance, is both good and cannot exist except from the true God, from whom all good comes; and that an evil will is set in disordered motion by preferring lower goods to higher ones. So it came about that the spirit of a rational creature, delighted with its own power because of its excellence, swelled with pride, through which it fell from the blessedness of the spiritual paradise, and wasted away with envy. Yet there is good in it even so, namely that it lives and gives life to a body, whether an airy body, like the spirit of the devil himself or of the demons, or an earthly one, like the soul of any man, even a malicious and perverse one. So, while they refuse to admit that anything God made could sin by its own will, they say that the very substance of God was corrupted and perverted, first by necessity and afterwards irredeemably by will. But I have already said a great deal elsewhere about the utterly insane error of these people.

In this work, however, we must inquire, according to holy Scripture, what should be said about the devil. First, whether from the very beginning of the world, delighted with his own power, he held aloof from that fellowship and charity by which the angels who enjoy God are blessed; or whether for some time he too was in the holy company of the angels, equally righteous and equally blessed. For some say that his fall from the heavenly seats came about because he envied man, who had been made in the image of God. But envy follows pride; it does not precede it. Envy is not the cause of pride; pride is the cause of envy. Since pride is the love of one's own excellence, and envy is hatred of another's happiness, it is plain enough which springs from which. For anyone who loves his own excellence envies either his equals, because they are on a level with him, or his inferiors, lest they become his equals, or his superiors, because he is not their equal. So it is by being proud that a person becomes envious, not by being envious that he becomes proud.

Rightly, then, Scripture has defined pride as the beginning of all sin, saying: "The beginning of all sin is pride." With this testimony the apostle's saying also fits quite well, "The root of all evils is avarice," if we understand avarice in a general sense, by which a person seeks something more than he ought, for the sake of his own excellence and out of a certain love of what is his own. To this the Latin language has wisely given a name, calling it "private", a word which clearly derives from loss rather than from gain, for every privation diminishes. So the very means by which pride seeks to stand out is what thrusts it into narrowness and want, when by a ruinous self-love it is reduced from the common to the private. There is also a particular kind of avarice, more usually called the love of money. By this name the apostle, signifying the genus by the species, meant universal avarice to be understood when he said, "The root of all evils is avarice." For it was by this that the devil fell, who certainly did not love money, but his own power. Accordingly, a perverse love of self deprives the swollen spirit of holy fellowship and confines it in misery, though it longs to be sated through iniquity. Hence in another place, having said, "For men will be lovers of themselves," he immediately added, "lovers of money," descending from that general avarice, of which pride is the head, to this particular kind, which belongs to human beings. For people would not be lovers of money either, unless they thought themselves the more excellent the richer they were. The opposite of this disease is charity, which does not seek its own, that is, does not rejoice in private excellence; and so, rightly, it is also not puffed up.

These two loves arose first among the angels, one in the good, the other in the wicked. The one is holy, the other unclean; the one social, the other private; the one looks to the common good for the sake of the heavenly fellowship, the other brings even what is common under its own power for the sake of arrogant domination; the one is subject to God, the other a rival to God; the one is calm, the other turbulent; the one peaceable, the other seditious; the one puts truth before the praises of those who err, the other is greedy for praise by any means; the one is friendly, the other envious; the one wills for its neighbour what it wills for itself, the other wills to subject its neighbour to itself; the one rules its neighbour for the neighbour's benefit, the other for its own. These two loves have also marked out two cities founded within the human race, under the wonderful and ineffable providence of God, who governs and orders all that he creates: the one city of the righteous, the other of the wicked. Through a certain temporal mingling of these two, the age runs its course until they are separated at the last judgement. Then the one, joined to the good angels, will attain eternal life in its King; the other, joined to the wicked angels, will be sent with its king into eternal fire. Of these two cities we shall perhaps speak at greater length in another place, if the Lord wills.

Scripture does not say when pride cast the devil down, so that he perverted his good nature by a depraved will. Yet reason plainly declares that this happened earlier, and that it was out of pride that he envied man. For it is obvious to anyone who considers the matter that pride is not born of envy; rather, envy is born of pride. It is not unreasonable, however, to think that the devil fell through pride from the beginning of time, and that there was no earlier time in which he lived at peace and in blessedness with the holy angels, but that from the very outset of creation he apostatized from his creator. Then we may take the Lord's words, "He was a murderer from the beginning and did not stand in the truth," so that "from the beginning" applies to both: not only to his being a murderer, but also to his not standing in the truth. He was a murderer, indeed, from that beginning from which man could be killed; but man could not be killed before there was someone to be killed. The devil, then, was a murderer from the beginning, because he killed the first man, before whom there was no human being. But he did not stand in the truth, and this too was from the beginning, from the moment he himself was created, he who would have stood had he willed to stand.

For how can he be believed to have led a blessed life among the blessed angels if he did not foreknow his future sin and punishment, that is, his desertion and the eternal fire? If he did not foreknow them, it is fair to ask why not. For the holy angels are not uncertain of their eternal life and blessedness; how could they be blessed if they were uncertain? Or shall we say that God was unwilling to reveal to the devil, while he was still a good angel, either what he would do or what he would suffer, but revealed to the rest that they would remain in his truth for ever? If so, he was not equally blessed even then; indeed, he was not fully blessed at all, since those who are fully blessed are certain of their blessedness, so that no fear disturbs it. And by what evil desert was he so set apart from the rest that God would not reveal to him the future even in matters that concerned himself? Was God an avenger before the devil was a sinner? Far from it. For God does not condemn the innocent. Or was he perhaps of another kind of angels, to whom God did not grant foreknowledge of the future even about themselves? How such angels could be blessed, when their very blessedness is uncertain to them, I do not see. For some have held this too: that the devil was not of that sublime nature of the angels which is above the heavens, but of those who were made somewhat lower, in the world, and assigned to their various offices. Such beings, perhaps, might even find delight in something forbidden; yet if they did not wish to sin, they could restrain that delight by free choice, just as man could, above all the first man, who did not yet have the penalty of sin in his members. Indeed, even that penalty is overcome by devotion in holy men who are subject to God, through his grace.

Moreover, this question about the blessed life, whether anyone should be said already to have it who is uncertain whether it will remain with him or whether misery will at some time succeed it, can also be raised about the first man himself. For if he was aware of his future sin and of God's punishment, how could he be blessed? In that case he was in paradise without being blessed. But he did not foreknow his future sin. Then because of this ignorance he was either uncertain of that blessedness, and how was he truly blessed? Or he was certain of it through false hope, not through knowledge, and how was he not a fool?

Nevertheless, in the case of a man still set in an animal body, who, if he lived obediently, was yet to be given the fellowship of the angels and a change of body from animal to spiritual, we can understand a blessed life in a certain sense, even if he did not foreknow his future sin. For neither did they foreknow theirs to whom the apostle says, "You who are spiritual, instruct such a one in a spirit of gentleness, looking to yourself, lest you too be tempted." Yet it is neither absurd nor improper to say that they were already blessed by this very fact, that they were spiritual, not in body, but by the righteousness of faith, rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation. How much more, then, and in how much fuller a way, was man blessed in paradise before sin, even though uncertain of his future fall! He so rejoiced in hope because of the reward of the change to come that there was no tribulation for patience to struggle to endure. For he was not certain of what was uncertain through vain presumption, like a fool, but through a hope that was not faithless; and before he laid hold of that life in which he would be entirely certain of his eternal life, he could exult, as it is written, "with trembling." By this exultation he could be blessed in paradise far more abundantly than the saints on this earth: in a certain way lower than in that eternal life of the saints and of the angels above the heavens, but not in no way at all.

But to say of certain angels that they can be blessed in some way of their own while uncertain of their future wickedness and damnation, or indeed of their everlasting salvation, without even the hope that they themselves would one day, through some change for the better, become certain of the matter, is a presumption hardly to be tolerated. Unless perhaps it is also said that these angels were created and assigned to ministries in the world under other, higher and more blessed angels, so that in return for duly carrying out their charges they might receive that blessed and higher life of which they could be entirely certain; and rejoicing in the hope of it, they could not unfittingly be called blessed already. If the devil fell from their number together with his partners in wickedness, this is like the way men too fall from the righteousness of faith, transgressing through a similar pride, either deceiving themselves or consenting to that deceiver.

But let those who can assert these two kinds of good angels: one above the heavens, among whom the one who by falling became the devil never was, and the other in the world, among whom he was. As for me, I confess that for the present nothing occurs to me from the Scriptures by which I could assert this. But pressed by the question whether he foreknew his fall before he fell, and so as not to say that angels are, or ever were, uncertain of their blessedness, I said that it may not unreasonably be thought that the devil fell from the very beginning of creation, that is, from the very beginning either of time or of his own making, and never stood in the truth.

Hence some think that he was not turned aside into this malice by the free choice of his will, but was created in it altogether, albeit by the Lord God, the supreme and true creator of all natures. They cite as evidence the book of Job, since it is written there, when he is being spoken of: "This is the beginning of the Lord's handiwork, which he made to be mocked by his angels." With this view agrees what is written in the psalm: "This dragon, which you formed to mock him," except that

here it says "which you formed," and not, as there, "this is the beginning of the Lord's handiwork," as though God had formed him in the beginning so that he was evil, envious, a seducer, altogether the devil, not depraved by his will but created so.

How is this opinion not contrary to what is written, "God made all things, and behold, they were very good," when on this view the devil is found to be not depraved by his own will but made very bad by the Lord God himself? They try to show this, and it is argued neither foolishly nor ignorantly, by saying that not only in the first making but even now, with so many wills depraved, all things that were created, that is, the whole of creation without exception, are taken as a whole very good. Not that the bad in it are good, but that by their badness they do not cause the beauty and order of the universe, under the rule, power and wisdom of God who governs it, to be disfigured or disturbed in any part; for to each of their wills, even the evil ones, are assigned definite and fitting limits of power and weights of merit, so that even with them fittingly and justly ordered the universe is beautiful. Yet it occurs to anyone, and it is true and plain, that it is contrary to justice itself for God, with no preceding merit, to condemn in anyone the very thing he himself created in him; and the certain and evident condemnation of the devil and his angels is read out from the Gospel, where the Lord foretold that he would say to those on the left, "Go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels." We must therefore by no means believe that it is the nature which God created in him, but his own evil will, that is to be punished with the penalty of eternal fire.

Nor must we believe that his nature is meant by the words, "This is the beginning of the Lord's handiwork, which he made to be mocked by his angels." What is meant is either the airy body which God fitted suitably to such a will; or the very ordering in which he made him useful to the good even against his will; or the fact that, foreknowing he would become evil by his own will, God nonetheless made him, not withholding his goodness in granting life and substance to a will that was going to be harmful, and at the same time foreseeing how much good he would bring about from him by his own marvellous goodness and power. He is called the beginning of the Lord's handiwork, which he made to be mocked by his angels, not because God made him first or made him evil in the beginning, but because, knowing that he would become evil by his own will in order to harm the good, God created him so that through him he himself might benefit the good. For this is what "to be mocked by his angels" means: he is mocked in this way when his temptations, by which he tries to corrupt the saints, profit them, so that the malice in which he chose to exist becomes, against his will, useful to the servants of God, who foresaw this when he formed him. He is called the beginning of what is to be mocked because evil men too, vessels of that same devil and, as it were, the body of which he is the head, whom God likewise created though foreseeing they would be evil, yet for the benefit of the saints, are mocked in the same way: while they wish to harm the saints, the saints gain from the comparison with them caution, devout humility under God, an understanding of grace, practice in bearing with the wicked, and proof of their love for enemies. But he is the beginning of the handiwork that is mocked in this way because he precedes them both in antiquity of time and in primacy of malice. God does this to him through the holy angels by that work of providence by which he governs the natures he has created, subjecting evil angels to good angels, so that the wickedness of the evil can do not as much as it strives to do but as much as it is allowed. And this applies not only to evil angels but also to evil men, until even this righteousness by which we live from faith, which is now exercised patiently in men, is turned into judgment, so that they too may judge not only the twelve tribes of Israel but even angels.

So when it is thought that the devil never stood in the truth, never led a blessed life with the angels, but fell from the very beginning of his making, this must not be taken to mean that he was not depraved by his own will but was created evil by the good God; otherwise he would not be said to have fallen from the beginning, for he did not fall if he was made such. Rather, as soon as he was made, he turned away from the light of truth, swollen with pride and corrupted by delight in his own power. Hence he never tasted the sweetness of the blessed and angelic life. He did not receive it and then disdain it; he forsook it and lost it by refusing to receive it. Accordingly he could not foreknow his fall either, since wisdom is the fruit of piety. But he, impious from the first and consequently blind in mind, fell not from what he had received but from what he would have received had he been willing to be subject to God. And because he was unwilling, he both fell from what he was going to receive and did not escape the power of him under whom he refused to be; and by the weight of his deserts it came about in him that he can neither delight in the light of righteousness nor be freed from its sentence.

Then there is what is said against him through the prophet Isaiah: "How has Lucifer, rising in the morning, fallen from heaven? He who sent to all nations has been crushed to the earth. But you said in your heart, 'I will ascend into heaven, I will set my throne above the stars of heaven, I will sit on a lofty mountain above the lofty mountains that are to the north, I will ascend above the clouds, I will be like the Most High.' But now you will go down to the underworld," and the rest. These words, understood as spoken against the devil under the figure of the king of Babylon, mostly fit his body, which he gathers even from the human race, and especially those who cleave to him through pride, apostatizing from the commandments of God. For just as one who was the devil was called a man, as in the Gospel, "An enemy, a man, has done this," so one who was a man was called the devil, again as in the Gospel: "Did I not choose you twelve? And one of you is a devil." And just as the body of Christ, which is the Church, is called Christ, as in the words, "You are the seed of Abraham," when shortly before he had said, "The promises were made to Abraham and to his seed. It does not say 'and to seeds,' as of many, but as of one, 'and to your seed,' which is Christ"; and again, "For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so also is Christ"; in the same way the body of the devil, whose head is the devil, that is, the whole multitude of the ungodly, and above all those who fall away from Christ or from the Church as if from heaven, is called the devil, and many things are said figuratively of that body which fit not so much the head as the body and its members. So Lucifer, who rose in the morning and fell, can be understood as the race of apostates, whether from Christ or from the Church. Having lost the light it bore, it turns to darkness, just as those who turn to God pass from darkness to light; that is, those who were darkness become light.

Likewise, words spoken through the prophet Ezekiel under the figure of the prince of Tyre are understood as spoken against the devil: "You are the seal of likeness and the crown of beauty; you were in the delights of the paradise of God; you were adorned with every precious stone," and the rest. These fit not so much the prince himself, the spirit of wickedness, as his body. For the Church is called a paradise, as we read in the Song of Songs: "A garden enclosed, a fountain sealed, a well of living water, a paradise with fruit of apples." From it have fallen all heretics, by an open and bodily separation, and, by a hidden and spiritual separation, even though they seem to be in it bodily, all who have returned to their vomit after walking a little while in the way of righteousness following the forgiveness of all their sins. For them the last state has become worse than the first, and it would have been better for them not to know the way of righteousness than, having known it, to turn back from the holy commandment handed down to them. The Lord describes this most wicked generation when he says that an unclean spirit goes out of a man and returns with seven others and enters the house it had found already swept, so that the last state of that man is worse than the first. To such a kind of men, which has now become the body of the devil, these words can fit: "From the day on which you were created with the cherub" — that is, with the seat of God, which is interpreted "multiplied knowledge" — "and I set you on the holy mountain of God" — that is, in the Church, whence the verse, "and he heard me from his holy mountain" — "you were in the midst of fiery stones" — that is, of the saints fervent in spirit, living stones — "you walked without fault in your days, from the day on which you were created, until your offenses were found in you." These things could be treated more carefully, so as perhaps to show not only that this meaning can be in these words, but that no other meaning at all is possible.

But since that would take long and requires another discourse devoted solely to that question, let this summary suffice for now. Either the devil fell through impious pride, from the beginning of his making, from the blessedness which he would have received had he willed it. Or there are other angels of a lower ministry in this world, among whom he lived in a kind of blessedness that lacked foreknowledge, and from whose fellowship he fell through proud impiety, together with the angels subject to him, as their archangel, if this can be asserted in any way, and it would be surprising if it could. Or, at any rate, an explanation must be sought of how all the holy angels, if the devil once lived among them, equally blessed with his angels, did not yet themselves have certain foreknowledge of their everlasting happiness but received it after his fall; or by what desert the devil and his companions were set apart, before his sin, from the other angels, so that he was ignorant of his future fall while they were certain of their perseverance. Meanwhile, let us not doubt at all that, according to the apostolic faith, the sinning angels have been thrust down as into a prison of this murky air around the earth and are being kept to be punished at the judgment; that in that supreme blessedness of the holy angels eternal life is not uncertain; and that, by God's mercy and grace and his most faithful promise, it will not be uncertain for us either, when after the resurrection and the change of these bodies we are joined to them. For it is in this hope that we live, and by the grace of this promise that we are refreshed. But whatever may also be said about the devil, why God created him when he foreknew he would be such, and why the Almighty does not turn his will to good, let it be understood, or believed, in accordance with what we discussed when we asked the same about evil men; or, if anything better can be found, let it be found.

So by him who holds supreme power over all that he has created, acting through the holy angels by whom the devil is mocked even while his malevolence is turned to the good of God's Church, the devil was not permitted to tempt the woman except through the serpent, nor the man except through the woman. In the serpent he himself spoke, using it as an instrument and moving its nature in the way that he was able to move it and it was able to be moved, so as to produce the sounds of words and bodily signs by which the woman might understand the will of the one persuading her. In the woman herself, however, since she was a rational creature able to use her own movement to form words, it was not he who spoke, but his working and persuasion, although by a hidden prompting he assisted inwardly what he had done outwardly through the serpent. Had he acted only by such a more hidden prompting, as he did in Judas so that he betrayed Christ, he could have succeeded in a soul clothed in proud love of its own power. But, as I have already said, the devil has the will to tempt, but it is not in his power either to do it or to choose how to do it. So because he was permitted, he tempted; and as he was permitted, so he tempted. But which kind of men his doing would benefit he neither knew nor wished, and in that very fact he was mocked by the angels.

So the serpent did not understand the sounds of the words that came from it to the woman. For we must not believe that its soul was changed into a rational nature, since not even men, whose nature is rational, know what they are saying when a demon speaks in them in that affliction for which an exorcist is required. How much less would the serpent understand the sounds of words which the devil produced in that way through it and from it, when it would not understand a man speaking even if it heard him while free of diabolical affliction! As for the belief that serpents hear and understand the words of the Marsi, so that at their incantations they often leap out of their hiding places, there too a diabolical force is at work. Thus providence may be recognized everywhere, which subjects one thing to another in the natural order and also, by its most wise power, determines what it permits even to evil wills; so that custom has it that serpents, more than any other kind of animal, are moved by the chants of men. For this too is no small testimony that human nature was first seduced by the serpent's conversation. The demons rejoice that this power is granted them, that they may move serpents at the incantation of men, so as to deceive whomever they can in whatever way. But they are permitted this so as to keep alive the memory of that first deed, whereby they have a certain familiarity with this kind of creature. Moreover, that first deed itself was permitted so that, through the nature of the serpent, there might be shown to the human race, for whose instruction these events had to be written down, a likeness of all diabolical temptation. This will become clear when the divine sentence begins to be pronounced against the serpent.

Accordingly, the serpent was called the most prudent, that is, the most cunning, of all the beasts on account of the devil's cunning, which worked deceit in it and through it. In the same way a tongue is called prudent or cunning when a prudent or cunning person moves it to persuade someone of something prudently and cunningly. For this force or power belongs not to the bodily member called the tongue, but surely to the mind that uses it. So too Scripture speaks of "the lying pen of the scribes"; for being a liar belongs only to what lives and perceives. But the pen is called lying because a liar works lyingly through it, just as this serpent might also be called lying because the devil used it lyingly, like a pen.

I have thought it worth stressing this point so that no one will suppose that animals without reason have human understanding, or are suddenly changed into rational animals, and so be led astray into that ridiculous and harmful opinion about the transmigration of souls, whether of humans into beasts or of beasts into humans. So the serpent spoke to a human being just as the ass on which Balaam sat spoke to a human being, except that the one was the devil's work and the other an angel's. Good and bad angels do some works that look alike, as Moses and Pharaoh's magicians did. But even in these the good angels are more powerful, and the bad angels can do nothing even of such works except what God has permitted through the good angels. In this way each person is repaid according to his heart, or according to the grace of God, and both are done justly and kindly through the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God.

Then the serpent said to the woman: "Why has God said, 'You shall not eat from every tree of paradise'?" And the woman said to the serpent: "We shall eat from the fruit of the trees that are in paradise; but of the fruit of the tree that is in the middle of paradise God said, 'You shall not eat of it, nor shall you touch it, lest you die.'" The serpent asked first and the woman gave this answer so that the transgression would be inexcusable, and it could in no way be said that the woman had forgotten what God had commanded. Even forgetting a command, especially when there was only one and it was so necessary, would have been gravely culpable, a damnable negligence. But the transgression is more evident when the command is kept in memory and God, who is as it were present and standing by in it, is held in contempt. That is why, when the psalm said, "and to those who keep his commandments in memory," it was necessary to add, "to do them." For many keep them in memory only to despise them, and so commit the greater sin of transgression, where forgetfulness is no excuse.

Then the serpent said to the woman: "You shall not die the death. For God knew that on the day you eat of it your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil." How could the woman have believed these words, that God had forbidden them something good and useful, unless her mind already held that love of her own power and a certain proud presumption about herself, which was to be exposed and humbled through that temptation? Finally, not content with the serpent's words, she looked at the tree and saw that it was good for food and beautiful to look at. Not believing that she could die from it, she supposed, I think, that God had said "If you eat, you shall die the death" for the sake of some symbolic meaning. And so she took of its fruit and ate, and she also gave some to her husband with her, perhaps with some persuasive words as well, which Scripture passes over in silence and leaves us to understand. Or perhaps there was no longer any need to persuade the man, since he saw that she had not died from that food?

So they ate. And the eyes of both were opened. Opened to what, if not to desiring each other? This was a penalty for sin, conceived from the very death of the flesh. Their body was now no longer merely animal, a body which, had they kept obedience, could have been changed without death into a better and spiritual condition. It was now the body of death, in which a law in the members fights against the law of the mind. They had not been created with their eyes closed, nor were they wandering blind and groping about in the paradise of delights, so that they touched the forbidden tree without knowing it and fumbled for the forbidden fruit in ignorance. How were the animals and birds brought to Adam for him to see what he would call them, if he could not see? And how was the woman herself brought to the man when she was made, so that he could say of someone he did not see, "This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh," and the rest? And finally, how did the woman see that the tree was good for food, pleasing to the eyes to look at, and beautiful to know, if their eyes were closed?

Still, the whole account is not to be taken figuratively just because one word is used metaphorically. Let the serpent answer for the sense in which he said, "Your eyes will be opened." The writer of the book reported that he said it; in what meaning or with what intent he said it, he left the reader to consider. But the words "And their eyes were opened, and they knew that they were naked" are written in the same way as everything else reported as having happened, and they ought not on that account to lead us into an allegorical reading. The evangelist, as narrator, was not inserting someone else's figurative saying under that person's name, but was narrating in his own person what had happened, when he said of those two disciples, one of whom was Cleopas, that when the Lord broke bread for them their eyes were opened and they recognized him. They had not recognized him on the road. They were not walking with their eyes shut; they were simply unable to recognize him. So just as the narrative is not figurative there, neither is it here, although Scripture used a metaphor in saying that eyes were opened which had been open before. They were opened, that is, to look at and think about something they had never noticed before. A bold curiosity had been stirred to transgress the command, eager to explore hidden things and to find out what would follow from touching what was forbidden. It took delight in breaking the reins of the prohibition with a harmful freedom, and judged it more likely that the death they had feared would not follow. (We must believe that the fruit on that tree was of a kind they had already found harmless on other trees.) They found it easier to believe that God could readily forgive sinners than to bear patiently not knowing what the tree was, or why he had forbidden them to take food from it. So as soon as they had transgressed the command, grace abandoned them within and they were stripped entirely bare, for they had offended that grace by a kind of conceit and a proud love of their own power. Then they cast their eyes on their own members and desired them with a motion they had not known before. Their eyes, then, were opened to this, to which they had not been open before, though they were open to other things.

This death came on the day when what God had forbidden was done. They lost that wonderful condition which was supplied to the body itself by the tree of life through a mystical power. Through it they could neither be attacked by disease nor changed by age. By eating from the tree of life, their flesh, though still animal and destined to be changed for the better later, already showed a sign of what happens in the angels. The angels are fed on the spiritual food of wisdom itself, of which that tree was the sacrament, and by sharing in eternity they are kept from changing for the worse. Once this condition was lost, then, their body took on the diseased and deadly quality that is also found in the flesh of animals. With it came the same motion that produces in animals the appetite for mating, so that the newborn may take the place of the dying. Yet even in this very penalty the rational soul gave proof of its noble birth: it blushed at the bestial motion in the members of its flesh and struck shame into it. It did so not only because it felt this where it had never felt anything of the kind before, but also because that shameful motion came from the transgression of the command. There it came to feel what grace had clothed it before, when it suffered nothing indecent in its nakedness. There these words were fulfilled: "Lord, by your will you gave strength to my beauty; but you turned away your face, and I was troubled." And so in that trouble they ran to fig leaves and sewed themselves aprons, and since they had abandoned what was glorious, they covered what was shameful. I do not think they had any idea that there was something in those leaves which made them fitting for covering members that were now itching with desire. Rather, in that trouble they were driven to it by a hidden instinct, so that they unknowingly produced a sign of their punishment. As an act, it would convict the sinner; as a written record, it would teach the reader.

"And they heard the voice of the Lord God walking in paradise toward evening." It was fitting that people who had fallen away from the light of truth should be visited at that hour. Before this, perhaps, God had spoken with them in other, inward ways, whether these can be put into words or not. He speaks in this way with the angels, enlightening their minds by unchangeable truth itself, where they have the understanding to know all at once things that do not happen all at once in time. Perhaps, I say, he spoke with them in this way. They did not share in divine wisdom as fully as the angels do; it was according to human measure, however much less. But it was still the same kind of visitation and speech. Perhaps he also spoke in the way that happens through a creature: either in an ecstasy of the spirit, through bodily images, or to the bodily senses themselves, through some form presented to be seen or heard, as God is often seen in his angels or speaks from a cloud. But this time, when they heard the voice of God walking in paradise toward evening, it can only have been done visibly through a creature. Otherwise we might believe that the invisible substance of Father, Son and Holy Spirit, which is wholly present everywhere, appeared to their bodily senses moving through place and time.

"And Adam and his wife hid themselves from the face of the Lord in the midst of the tree that is in paradise." When God turns his face away inwardly and a human being is troubled, we should not be surprised that such things happen. They resemble madness, and they come from excessive shame and fear. That hidden instinct was also at work, so that without knowing it they did things that would signify something to the posterity who would one day understand, for whose sake these things were written.

"And the Lord God called Adam and said to him: Adam, where are you?" This is the voice of someone rebuking, not of someone who does not know. And this surely has some significance: the command was given to the man, so that it would reach the woman through him, and so the man is questioned first. The command came from the Lord through the man to the woman, but the sin came from the devil through the woman to the man. These events are full of mystical meanings. The people in whom they took place did not intend them; the most powerful wisdom of God was at work in them. But here we are not unlocking what they signify. We are defending the fact that they happened.

Adam then answered: "I heard your voice in paradise and I was afraid, because I am naked, and I hid myself." It is quite likely that God used to appear to those first humans in human form, through a creature suited to such an action. Yet he never let them notice their nakedness, for he lifted their attention to higher things, until after sin they had felt the shameful motion in their members by the penal law of the members. So they reacted as people usually do under the eyes of other people. This reaction came from the penalty of sin: they wanted to hide from him from whom nothing can be hidden, and to conceal their flesh from him who sees into the heart. But what wonder is it if, proudly wishing to be like gods, they became futile in their thinking and their foolish heart was darkened? They called themselves wise in their abundance, and when he turned his face away they became fools. They were already ashamed before themselves, and that was why they had made themselves aprons. They were far more afraid, even with the aprons on, to be seen by him who, in a familiar and gentle way, brought what were as it were human eyes to see them through a visible creature. If he appeared in this way so that human beings could speak with him as with a human being, as Abraham did at the oak of Mamre, then the very closeness of that friendship, which had given them confidence before sin, weighed them down with shame after sin. They no longer dared to show to such eyes a nakedness that displeased even their own.

So the Lord wished now to punish the sinners, after questioning them as justice requires, with more than the penalty at which they were already forced to blush. "Who told you that you were naked," he said, "unless you have eaten from the tree from which alone I had commanded you not to eat?" For it was from this that death was conceived, by the sentence of God, who had threatened it. This death made them notice their members with desire, which is where their eyes are said to have been opened, and shame followed. "And Adam said: The woman whom you gave with me, she gave me from the tree, and I ate." What pride! Did he say, "I have sinned"? He has the ugliness of confusion but not the humility of confession. These things were written down for a reason, and the questions themselves were surely asked so that they could be written down truthfully and usefully (if falsely, then certainly not usefully). They were written so that we might notice the disease of pride that afflicts people today. Whatever evil they do, they try to lay it on no one but the Creator, while they want the credit for whatever good they do. "The woman whom you gave with me," he says, that is, whom you gave to be with me, "she gave me from the tree, and I ate." As if she had been given to him for this purpose, and not rather so that she would obey her husband and both of them would obey God.

"And the Lord God said to the woman: Why have you done this? And the woman said: The serpent deceived me, and I ate." She does not confess her sin either, but shifts it onto another. Her sex was different, her arrogance the same. Yet from these two was descended one who did not imitate them, a man tried by many evils, who said, and will go on saying until the end of the world: "I said: Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against you." How much better it would have been if they had spoken like this too! But the Lord had not yet cut through the necks of sinners. Still to come were toils, sorrows, deaths, all the crushing hardships of this world, and the grace of God, by which at the right time he comes to the help of human beings whom affliction has taught not to rely on themselves. "The serpent," she says, "deceived me, and I ate": as if anyone's persuasion ought to be put before the command of God.

"And the Lord God said to the serpent: Because you have done this, cursed are you above all the cattle and above all the beasts that are on the earth. On your breast and your belly you shall go, and you shall eat earth all the days of your life. And I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed. She will watch for your head, and you will watch for her heel." This whole sentence is figurative. The writer's faithfulness and the truth of the narrative require only that we not doubt it was spoken. The words "And the Lord God said to the serpent" are the writer's words, and these must be taken in their literal sense. So it is true that this was said to the serpent. The rest are God's words, and the reader is left free to judge whether they should be taken literally or figuratively, as I explained at the beginning of this work. Note too that the serpent was not asked why it had done this. This may suggest that it had not done it by its own nature and will. Rather, the devil had worked from it, through it and in it, and the devil was already destined for eternal fire because of the sin of his impiety and pride. So what is said to the serpent certainly refers to the one who worked through the serpent, and it is undoubtedly figurative. These words describe what that tempter would be to the human race, which began to be propagated when this sentence was pronounced against the devil as though against the serpent. How these words should be understood once their figures are explained, I discussed as best I could in those two books on Genesis that I published against the Manichees. If I can do it more carefully and more fittingly elsewhere, God will help me to do so. For now, though, nothing requires me to turn aside from the task I have undertaken.

"And to the woman he said: I will greatly multiply your sorrows and your groaning; in sorrows you shall bear children, and your turning shall be to your husband, and he shall rule over you." These words of God to the woman are also much better understood figuratively and prophetically. The woman had not yet given birth, however, and the pain and groaning of childbirth come only from the body of death, which was conceived through that transgression of the command. Even then their members were animal, but if man had not sinned they would certainly not have died. They would have lived in another, happier state, until after a life well lived they deserved to be changed for the better, as I have already pointed out in several places above. So this penalty is also referred to the literal sense. But we must consider how the words "your turning shall be to your husband, and he shall rule over you" can be taken literally. For we should not believe that even before sin the woman was made otherwise than to be ruled by the man and to turn to him in service. But we may rightly understand this to mean the kind of servitude that belongs to a legal condition rather than to love. Then even the servitude by which human beings later began to be slaves of other human beings will be found to have arisen from the penalty of sin. The apostle did say, "Through love serve one another"; but he would never say, "Rule over one another." So husband and wife can serve one another through love, but the apostle does not allow a woman to rule over a man. God's sentence gave this rather to the man, and it was not by nature but by her fault that the woman came to have her husband as her master. Yet unless this order is kept, nature will be corrupted still further and the fault will grow.

"And he said also to her husband: Because you listened to the voice of your wife and ate from the tree from which alone I had commanded you not to eat, cursed is the earth in your works; in sorrows you shall eat of it all the days of your life. Thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you, and you shall eat the grass of the field. In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for you are earth, and to earth you shall go." Who does not know that these are the toils of the human race on earth? Nor can there be any doubt that they would not exist if the happiness that had been in paradise had been kept. So let us not hesitate to take these words first in their literal sense. Yet we must keep in view and look for the prophetic meaning, which is above all what God intends as he speaks here. It was not for nothing that Adam himself, by some wonderful instinct, at that time gave his wife the name "Life," adding, "because she is the mother of all the living." These words too must be understood as spoken not by the writer, narrating or asserting, but by the first man himself.
