When he said "because she is the mother of all the living," he was giving the reason for the name he had given her, explaining why he called her "Life."

"And the Lord God made garments of skin for Adam and his wife and clothed them." This too was done for the sake of what it signified, but it was still done, just as those other things were said for the sake of what they signified, but were still said. I have said this often, and I do not mind saying it yet again: we must require of a narrator of things that actually happened that he report as done what was done and as said what was said. With deeds we ask both what was done and what it signifies, and in the same way with words we ask both what was said and what it signifies. Whether what is reported as said was said figuratively or literally, the fact that it was said must not be thought figurative.

"And God said: Behold, Adam has become like one of us in knowing good and evil." Whatever the agent and whatever the means by which this was spoken, it was God who said it. So the words "one of us" can only be understood as a plural used because of the Trinity, as when it was said, "Let us make man," and as when the Lord said of himself and the Father, "We will come to him and make our home with him." So the serpent's suggestion, "and you will be like gods," was thrown back on the proud man's own head, to show the outcome of what he had desired: "Behold," God says, "Adam has become like one of us." These are the words of God, not so much mocking Adam as warning others not to be proud like him, the others for whose sake these things were written. "He has become," he says, "like one of us in knowing good and evil." What else are we to understand but that this was set before us as an example to strike fear into us? For not only did he not become what he wanted to become; he did not even keep what he had been made.

"And now," God says, "lest he ever stretch out his hand and take from the tree of life and eat and live forever." "And the Lord God sent him out of the paradise of delight to till the earth from which he was taken." The first words are God's words; the deed that followed came about because of them. For he was now cut off not only from the life he would have received with the angels if he had kept the command, but also from the life he had been living in paradise in a happy condition of the body, and so he had to be separated from the tree of life. That happy condition of his body may have been sustained for him by that tree [?], a visible thing with an invisible power; or there may have been in it a visible sacrament of invisible wisdom. Either way, he had to be cut off from it, whether because he was now going to die or because he was, so to speak, excommunicated. In the same way in this paradise, that is, the Church, people are commonly barred from the visible sacraments of the altar by church discipline.

"And he cast Adam out and settled him opposite the paradise of delight." This too was done for the sake of what it signified, but it was still done: the sinner was to live in misery opposite the paradise that also signified, spiritually, the life of blessedness. "And he stationed the Cherubim and the flaming sword that turns, to guard the way to the tree of life." We must believe that this was actually done by heavenly powers in the visible paradise, so that through the ministry of angels there was a kind of fiery guard there. Yet there can be no doubt that it was not done without purpose, and that it also signifies something about the spiritual paradise.

I am well aware that some have thought those first humans hastily anticipated their desire for the knowledge of good and evil, and wanted to receive at an unripe time what was being kept for them and deferred to a more fitting moment. On this view the tempter brought it about so that, by plucking too early what did not yet suit people in their condition, they would offend God, and would be shut out, condemned and cut off from the benefit of that thing. If they had approached it in its proper time, as God willed, they could have enjoyed it to their good. If such people choose to take that tree as a figure, and not literally as a real tree with real fruit, this interpretation may reach a conclusion that is acceptable to right faith and to the truth.

Some have also thought that those two first humans stole their marriage. On this view they came together in intercourse before the one who had created them joined them, and this was signified by the name of the tree from which they had been forbidden until they were joined at the fitting time. As if we should believe they were made at an age when they had to wait until they were old enough! Or as if that act would not have been lawful as soon as it could first take place, and would certainly not have taken place while it could not! Perhaps the bride had to be given away by her father, and they had to wait for the solemn vows, the festivities of the wedding banquet, the valuing of the dowry and the drawing up of the marriage contract! That is ridiculous. Besides, it departs from the literal account of events, which we undertook to uphold and have upheld, as far as God was pleased to grant.

What troubles me more is this. If Adam was already spiritual, in mind though not in body, how could he have believed what was said through the serpent? The serpent claimed that God had forbidden them to eat the fruit of that tree because he knew that if they did, they would become like gods by discerning good and evil, as though the creator begrudged his creature so great a good. It would be astonishing if a man endowed with a spiritual mind could have believed that. Or was it because he himself could not believe it that the woman was added? Perhaps she was of small understanding and still lived by the sense of the flesh rather than by the spirit of the mind. Is this why the apostle does not ascribe to her the image of God? For he says: "A man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God; but the woman is the glory of the man." This does not mean that a woman's mind cannot receive that same image, since he says that in that grace we are neither male nor female. Perhaps rather she had not yet attained what comes about in the knowledge of God, and was to attain it gradually under her husband's guidance and direction. For it is not without reason that the apostle also says: "For Adam was formed first, then Eve; and Adam was not led astray, but the woman was led astray and fell into transgression", that is, so that through her the man too transgressed. For he calls Adam too a transgressor where he says, "in the likeness of the transgression of Adam, who is a type of the one who was to come", yet he denies that Adam was led astray. Indeed, when Adam was questioned, he did not say, "The woman you gave to be with me led me astray, and I ate." Rather he said, "She gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate." But she said, "The serpent led me astray."

Take Solomon, a man of such great wisdom. Are we really to believe that he thought there was some benefit in the worship of idols? No, he could not resist his love for women, which dragged him into this evil. He did what he knew should not be done, so as not to grieve those deadly delights for whom he was pining and wasting away. So it was with Adam too. The woman, led astray, had eaten from the forbidden tree and given him some so that they might eat together. He did not want to grieve her, for he believed that she might waste away without his comfort if she were estranged from his affection, and might even perish altogether from that discord. He was not overcome by the desire of the flesh, which he had not yet felt in a law of the members resisting the law of his mind. He was overcome by a kind of friendly goodwill, which very often leads people to offend God rather than have a friend become an enemy. The just outcome of the divine sentence showed that he ought not to have done this.

So he too was deceived, but in some other way. I think he could in no way have been led astray by the serpent's guile, which led the woman astray. The apostle properly called it "being led astray" when something false that is urged on a person is thought true. Here the false claim was that God had forbidden them to touch that tree because he knew that if they touched it they would be like gods, as though the one who had made them human begrudged them divinity. Some pride of mind may have been in the man, which could not be hidden from God, the searcher of inner things. Because of it, a desire to try the fruit may have tempted him when he saw that the woman had not died after eating, as we discussed above. Even so, if he was already endowed with a spiritual mind, I do not think he could in any way have believed that God had forbidden them that tree's fruit out of envy. But why say more? People such as they were could be persuaded into that sin, and so they were persuaded. And it was written down in a way that all ought to read, though few would understand these things as they ought.
BOOK TWELVE

In eleven books we have discussed and written down what we could, and as we could, about the part of holy Scripture entitled Genesis, from its beginning up to where the first man was sent out of paradise. We have sometimes asserted and defended what is certain to us, and sometimes inquired, offered our judgement and raised doubts about what is uncertain. We have not so much prescribed what each person should think about obscure matters. Rather, we have shown that we need to be taught where we have been in doubt, and we have kept the reader from rash assertion where we could not offer firm knowledge. This twelfth book, however, is now free of the task that occupied us in working through the text of the sacred writings. It will therefore deal more freely and at greater length with the question of paradise, so that we will not be thought to have evaded it. For the apostle seems to suggest that paradise is in the third heaven, where he says: "I know a man in Christ who fourteen years ago, whether in the body I do not know, or out of the body I do not know, God knows, was caught up to the third heaven. And I know that this man, whether in the body or out of the body I do not know, God knows, was caught up into paradise and heard ineffable words which no human being may speak."

The first question usually asked about these words is what he means by the third heaven. The next is whether he meant paradise to be understood there. Or perhaps, after being caught up to the third heaven, he was also caught up into paradise, wherever paradise may be. In that case being caught up to the third heaven was not the same as being caught up into paradise; he was caught up first to the third heaven and then from there into paradise. This is so ambiguous that I do not think it can be resolved from the apostle's present words. Someone would have to find something elsewhere, perhaps in other passages of Scripture or by clear reasoning, to show whether or not paradise is in the third heaven. Moreover, it is not plain what the third heaven itself is, and whether it is to be understood as something corporeal or perhaps as something spiritual. It might indeed be said that a man could be caught up with his body only to some corporeal place. But he put it in such a way as to say that he did not know whether he was caught up in the body or out of the body. Who then would dare to say that he knows what the apostle said he did not know? Yet a spirit without a body cannot be caught up to corporeal places, nor a body to spiritual ones. If that is so, his doubt as it were forces us to a conclusion, since no one doubts that he wrote these things about himself. The place to which he was caught up must have been such that he could not tell or discern whether it was corporeal or spiritual.

When images of bodies are formed in sleep or in ecstasy, they are not distinguished from bodies at all. Only when a person is restored to the senses of the body does he recognize that he was among images which he was not taking in through those senses. For who, on waking from sleep, does not at once realize that what he saw was imaginary? Yet while he saw it asleep, he could not distinguish it from the bodily things that waking people see. Still, I know this has happened to me, and so I do not doubt that it could have happened or can happen to others: while seeing things in sleep, I realized that I was seeing them in sleep. Even while asleep I held and perceived most firmly that those images, which usually make a fool of our very assent, were not real bodies but were being presented to me in sleep. Yet in this I was sometimes mistaken. I would try to persuade a friend of mine, whom I was likewise seeing in my sleep, that what we were seeing were not bodies but the images of people dreaming. And yet he too, of course, appeared to me among them in the same way they did. I would also tell him that it was not true that we were talking together, but that he too was at that moment asleep and seeing something else, and had no idea whether I was seeing these things. But while I was striving to persuade him that he himself was not real, I was partly led to think that he was real. I would surely not have been speaking to him if I had been wholly convinced that he was not. So the soul of the sleeper, though wonderfully awake, could not help being led by images of bodies as if they were bodies themselves.

As for ecstasy, I have been able to hear only one person describe it. He was a countryman, barely able to express what he perceived. He knew that he was awake, and also that he was seeing something, but not with the eyes of the body. To use his words as far as I can recall them, he said: "My soul saw him, not my eyes; yet I did not know whether it was a body or the image of a body." He was not the sort of man to make such distinctions, but he was so plainly trustworthy that I listened to him as if I had seen myself what he said he had seen.

Perhaps, then, Paul saw paradise as Peter saw the sheet let down from heaven, or as John saw whatever he wrote that he saw in the Apocalypse. Perhaps he saw it as Ezekiel saw the plain with the bones of the dead and their resurrection, or as Isaiah saw God seated, the Seraphim before him and the altar from which a coal was taken to cleanse the prophet's lips. If so, it is clear that he could have been ignorant whether he saw these things in the body or out of the body.

But suppose they were seen out of the body and were not bodies. We can still ask whether they were images of bodies, or that kind of substance which bears no likeness to a body. Such are God, the human mind itself, understanding and reason, and the virtues: prudence, justice, chastity, charity, piety and whatever others there are. We list, distinguish and define these by understanding and thinking. We certainly do not do so by looking at their outlines or colours, or by noting how they sound, smell or taste, or what they tell those who touch them about heat or cold, softness or hardness, smoothness or roughness. We do it by another kind of vision, another light, another kind of evidence, one far more excellent and certain than the rest.

Let us therefore return once more to these same words of the apostle and examine them more carefully. First let us establish beyond doubt that the apostle knew far better, and incomparably more fully, what we are somehow trying to know about incorporeal and corporeal nature. If, then, he knew that spiritual things cannot be seen through the body at all, nor corporeal things outside the body, why did he not work out from the very things he saw how he could have seen them? If he was certain that they were spiritual, why was he not equally certain that he must have seen them out of the body? And if he knew that they were corporeal, why did he not also know that they could have been seen only through the body? Why then does he doubt whether he saw them in the body or out of the body? Perhaps he also doubts, in the same way, whether they were bodies or likenesses of bodies. So let us first see what there is in this passage that he does not doubt. Then, when what he does doubt is left over, perhaps the things he does not doubt will show how he doubts the rest.

"I know," he says, "a man in Christ who fourteen years ago, whether in the body I do not know, or out of the body I do not know, God knows, was caught up to the third heaven." So he knows that fourteen years ago a man in Christ was caught up to the third heaven. This he does not doubt at all, and so neither should we. But he doubts whether it was in the body or out of the body, and since he doubts it, which of us would dare to be certain? Does it perhaps follow that we should also doubt whether it was the third heaven to which, he said, the man was caught up? If the thing itself was shown, then the third heaven was shown. But if some image resembling corporeal things was produced, that was not the third heaven. The vision would then have been so arranged that he seemed to himself to rise to the first heaven and see another above it. Rising to that one, he would see yet another higher still, and when he reached it he could say that he had been caught up to the third heaven. But he neither doubted nor wanted us to doubt that it was the third heaven to which he was caught up. That is why he put "I know" first and began from there. What the apostle says he knows, only someone who does not believe the apostle will fail to believe is true.

He knows, then, that the man was caught up to the third heaven. So the place to which he was caught up is truly the third heaven, not some corporeal sign. A sign of that kind was shown to Moses, and he understood very well that the very substance of God was one thing, and the visible creature in which God presented himself to human, bodily senses was another. That is why he said, "Show me yourself." Nor was it an image of a corporeal thing, like those John saw in the spirit. When he saw a beast or a woman or waters or something of the kind, he asked what it was, and was told "It is a city", or "They are peoples", or something else. But Paul says: "I know a man caught up to the third heaven."

Suppose he had meant to call a spiritual image resembling a corporeal one "heaven". Then the body in which he was caught up and rose there would likewise have been an image of his body. In that case he would have called it his body, though it was only an image of a body, just as he called that heaven "heaven", though it was only an image of heaven. Nor would he have taken care to distinguish what he knew from what he did not know, that is, that he knew a man was caught up to the third heaven but did not know whether in the body or out of it. He would simply have narrated the vision, calling the things he saw by the names of the things they resembled. We do the same when we tell our dreams or some revelation given in them. We say: "I saw a mountain, I saw a river, I saw three men", and so on, giving those images the names of the very things they resembled. The apostle, however, says: "This I know, that I do not know."
If both appeared as images, then both are equally known or equally unknown. But if the heaven appeared as it really is, and is therefore known, how could that man's body have appeared as an image?

If a corporeal heaven was seen, why was it hidden from him whether he saw it with bodily eyes? But if it was uncertain whether it was seen with the eyes of the body or by the spirit, which is why he said, "whether in the body or out of the body I do not know", how could it not also be uncertain whether a corporeal heaven was truly seen or was shown as an image? Again, suppose an incorporeal substance was seen, not in any image of a body but in the way justice, wisdom and the like are seen, and that this was the heaven. Then it is also clear that such a thing cannot be seen by the eyes of this body. And so, if he knew that he had seen something of that kind, he could not doubt that he had not seen it through the body. "I know," he says, "a man in Christ fourteen years ago." This I know, and let no one who believes me doubt it; "but whether in the body or out of the body I do not know, God knows."

What, then, do you know, which you distinguish from what you do not know, so that believers may not be misled? "That this same man," he says, "was caught up to the third heaven." But that heaven was either body or spirit. If it was body and was seen with bodily eyes, why is it known to be heaven, yet not known to have been seen in the body? If it was spirit, there are two possibilities. It may have presented an image of a body, and then it is as uncertain whether it was a body as whether it was seen in the body. Or it may have been seen as wisdom is seen by the mind, without any images of bodies, and then it is just as certain that it could not have been seen through the body. So either both are certain or both are uncertain. Otherwise, how can what was seen be certain, while the means by which it was seen is uncertain? It is clear that he could not have seen incorporeal nature through the body. Bodies, on the other hand, even if they could be seen without the body, would certainly not be seen in the same way as they are through the body. That way of seeing, if it exists, is very different. It would be strange, then, if it could deceive the apostle by seeming very similar, or force him into doubt. He would then be saying, though he had seen a corporeal heaven without bodily eyes, that he was uncertain whether he had seen it in the body or out of the body.

Perhaps, then, one possibility remains. The apostle could not lie, and he took such care to distinguish what he knew from what he did not know. So we should understand that what he did not know was this: when he was caught up to the third heaven, was he in the body? He might have been in the body in the way the soul is in the body when the body is said to be alive, whether it is awake, asleep, or cut off from the bodily senses in ecstasy. Or he might have gone out of the body altogether, so that the body lay dead until the showing was over. Then the soul would have been restored to the dead limbs. He would not have woken as if from sleep, or come back to his senses as one does after ecstasy; he would have been completely dead and come back to life. Accordingly, what he saw when caught up to the third heaven, which he affirms he knows, he saw as it really is, not as an image. But it was uncertain what that departure from the body involved. It may have left the body completely dead. Or the soul may have remained there as it does in a living body, while his mind was snatched away to see and hear the ineffable things of that vision. That is perhaps why he said: "whether in the body or out of the body I do not know, God knows."

What is seen as it really is, not as an image, and not through the body, is seen by the kind of vision that surpasses all the others. I will try to explain the kinds of vision and the differences between them, as far as the Lord helps me. Take this one commandment: "You shall love your neighbour as yourself." When it is read, three kinds of vision come into play. The first is through the eyes, by which the letters themselves are seen. The second is through the human spirit, by which we think of our neighbour even when he is absent. The third is through the gaze of the mind, by which love itself is understood and seen. Of these three kinds the first is plain to everyone, for by it we see heaven and earth and everything in them that is visible to our eyes. Nor is it hard to explain the second, by which we think of absent bodies in bodily form. We can think of heaven and earth and the things we can see in them even when we are in darkness. There we see nothing with the eyes of the body, yet we behold bodily images in the soul. Some are true images, of bodies we have seen and keep in memory; others are invented, as thought has been able to shape them. For we think in one way of Carthage, which we know, and in another of Alexandria, which we do not know. The third, by which love is understood and seen, contains those things that have no images resembling them which are something other than themselves. A man, a tree, the sun or any other bodies, whether heavenly or earthly, are seen in their own forms when present. When absent, they are thought of in images impressed on the soul. So they give rise to two kinds of things seen: one through the bodily senses, the other through the spirit, which holds those images. But is love seen in one way when present, in the form in which it actually exists, and in another way when absent, in some image resembling it? Certainly not. To the extent that the mind can discern it, one person discerns it more, another less. But if anything of a bodily image is thought of, it is not love itself that is being discerned.

These are the three kinds of vision. We said something about them in the earlier books too, as the subject seemed to require, though we did not mention how many there were. Now that we have briefly introduced them, the question we have taken up demands that we discuss them somewhat more fully. So we ought to mark them with definite and fitting names, so as not to slow ourselves down with constant roundabout phrases. Let us call the first corporeal, because it is perceived through the body and presented to the body's senses. Let us call the second spiritual. Whatever is not a body and yet is something is rightly called spirit. The image of an absent body is certainly not a body, even though it resembles one, and neither is the gaze by which it is discerned. Let us call the third intellectual, from "intellect", because to call it "mental", from "mind", would be a new word and far too absurd.

If I were to give a more detailed account of these terms, the discussion would become both longer and more tangled, and there is no need for it, or at least no great need. It is enough, then, to know that something is called "corporeal" either in the proper sense, when bodies are the subject, or else by a transferred use of the word, as when it is said: "For in him the whole fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily." The Godhead is not a body. But because the apostle calls the sacraments of the Old Testament shadows of things to come, he said, by comparison with those shadows, that the fullness of the Godhead dwells "bodily" in Christ. He meant that in Christ everything foreshadowed by those shadows is fulfilled, so that in a certain sense he is himself the body of those shadows; that is, he is himself the truth of those figures and signs. So just as the figures themselves are called shadows figuratively, by a transferred and not a proper use of the word, so too when he says that the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily, he is using a word in a transferred sense.

"Spiritual," however, is used in several ways. The apostle calls even the body that we shall have at the resurrection of the saints spiritual, where he says: "It is sown an animal body, it will rise a spiritual body." He calls it this because in wonderful ways it will be subject to the spirit, so as to be wholly agile and incorruptible, and will be given life by the spirit alone, without any need of bodily food. He does not mean that it will have an incorporeal substance. After all, the body we now have is called "animal" [from anima, "soul"], yet it does not have the substance of the soul, nor is it what the soul is. Again, "spirit" is the name given to the air or to its blowing, that is, its movement, as it is said: "Fire, hail, snow, ice, the spirit of the storm." The soul too, whether of a beast or of a human being, is called spirit, as it is written: "And who knows whether the spirit of the sons of men goes upward, and whether the spirit of the beast goes downward into the earth?" The rational mind itself is also called spirit; it is a kind of eye of the soul, and to it belong the image and the knowledge of God. So the apostle says: "Be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who has been created according to God," while elsewhere he says of the inner man: "who is renewed in the knowledge of God, according to the image of him who created him." Again, after he had said, "So then, I myself with the mind serve the law of God, but with the flesh the law of sin," he recalls the same thought in another place and says: "The flesh lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, so that you do not do the things you wish." What he had called mind, he here also called spirit. God too is called spirit, as the Lord says in the Gospel: "God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and in truth."

From none of these uses of the word "spirit" that we have listed did we take the term by which we have called this kind of vision, which we are now discussing, "spiritual." We took it instead from one particular use, found in the Epistle to the Corinthians, where spirit is distinguished from mind by the clearest testimony: "For if I pray in a tongue," he says, "my spirit prays, but my mind is unfruitful." Here "tongue" is to be understood as uttering obscure and mystical signs; if you take away the understanding of the mind from them, no one is built up by hearing what he does not understand. That is why he also says: "For one who speaks in a tongue speaks not to men but to God; for no one hears, but the spirit speaks mysteries." He makes it clear enough, then, that in this passage he calls "tongue" that in which there are signs, like images and likenesses of things, which need the gaze of the mind if they are to be understood. When they are not understood, he says they are in the spirit, not in the mind. So he says more plainly: "If you bless with the spirit, how will the one who fills the place of the uninstructed say 'Amen' to your blessing, since he does not know what you are saying?" Now with the tongue, that is, the bodily member we move in our mouth when we speak, it is signs of things that are given; the things themselves are not brought forth. For this reason he used the word "tongue" in a transferred sense for any utterance of signs before they are understood. When understanding, which belongs properly to the mind, is added to it, there comes about revelation, or knowledge, or prophecy, or teaching. Hence he says: "If I come to you speaking in tongues, what good will I do you, unless I speak to you in revelation, or in knowledge, or in prophecy, or in teaching?" That is: when understanding is added to the signs, that is, to the tongue, so that what is done is done not by the spirit alone but also by the mind.

Accordingly, when signs were shown to people in the spirit through likenesses of bodily things, there was as yet no prophecy unless the work of the mind was added so that they were also understood. The one who interpreted what another had seen was more truly a prophet than the one who had seen it. From this it appears that prophecy belongs more to the mind than to this spirit, which is called spirit in a particular sense of its own: a power of the soul lower than the mind, where likenesses of bodily things are formed. So Joseph, who understood what the seven ears of grain and the seven cows signified, was more a prophet than Pharaoh, who saw them in his dreams. Pharaoh's spirit was given a form so that he might see; Joseph's mind was enlightened so that he might understand. In the one, therefore, there was tongue; in the other, prophecy; for in the one there was the imagining of things, in the other the interpretation of the images. Less a prophet, then, is the one who sees in the spirit, by means of images of bodily things, only the signs of the things signified; more a prophet is the one who is gifted only with the understanding of them; but most a prophet is the one who excels in both, so that he both sees in the spirit the likenesses of bodily things that carry meaning and understands them by the liveliness of his mind. Such was the excellence of Daniel, tested and proved when he told the king both the dream he had seen and what it meant. The bodily images themselves were formed in his spirit, and their meaning was revealed in his mind. It is from this use of the word "spirit" in this distinction, the one the apostle followed when he said, "I will pray with the spirit, but I will also pray with the mind," meaning that the signs of things are formed in the spirit and their meaning shines out in the mind, it is according to this distinction, I say, that we have now called "spiritual" the kind of seeing by which we also think of the images of absent bodies.

The intellectual kind is higher; it belongs properly to the mind. It does not occur to me at all that "intellect" can be used in as many different ways as we have found "spirit" to be. Whether we say "intellectual" or "intelligible," we mean the same thing. Some, it is true, have wanted to make a distinction here: the intelligible is the thing itself that can be perceived by the intellect alone, while the intellectual is the mind that understands. But whether there is any thing that can be discerned by the intellect alone and does not itself understand is a great and difficult question. On the other hand, I do not think anyone either supposes or says that there is a thing which perceives by the intellect and cannot itself be perceived by the intellect; for the mind is seen only by the mind. Since, then, the mind can be seen, it is intelligible; and since it can also see, it is intellectual, according to that distinction. So, setting aside that very difficult question, whether there is anything that is only understood and does not understand, we now use "intellectual" and "intelligible" with the same meaning.

These three kinds of vision, then, the corporeal, the spiritual, and the intellectual, must be considered one at a time, so that reason may climb from the lower to the higher. Earlier we gave an example in which all three kinds could be seen in one sentence. When we read, "You shall love your neighbor as yourself," the letters are seen corporeally, the neighbor is thought of spiritually, and love is beheld intellectually. Yet the letters can also be thought of spiritually when they are absent, and the neighbor can be seen corporeally when he is present; but love can neither be seen with the eyes of the body in its own substance nor be thought of in the spirit through an image like a body. It can be known and perceived only by the mind, that is, by the intellect. Corporeal vision, of course, presides over neither of the others; rather, what is perceived through it is reported to spiritual vision as to the one presiding over it. For when anything is seen with the eyes, an image of it is at once formed in the spirit. But we do not recognize that it has been formed until, having turned our eyes away from what we were seeing through them, we find its image in our soul. If the spirit is irrational, like a beast's, the eyes' report goes no further than this. But if the soul is rational, it is reported also to the intellect, which presides over the spirit as well. Then, if what the eyes have taken in and reported to the spirit, so that its image might be formed there, is a sign of something, either its meaning is understood at once, or it is inquired into; for nothing can be either understood or inquired into except by the work of the mind.

King Belshazzar saw the fingers of a hand writing on the wall, and at once, through the bodily sense, the image of this thing that was done in bodily form was impressed on his spirit. When the sight itself had happened and passed, the image remained in his thought. It was seen in the spirit, but it was not understood. Nor had this sign been understood when it was done in bodily form and appeared to his bodily eyes. Yet even then he understood that it was a sign, and this he had from the work of the mind. And since he was asking what it meant, it was certainly the mind that carried out this inquiry as well. When nothing was found, Daniel came forward, and with his mind enlightened by the prophetic spirit, he revealed to the troubled king what was portended by that sign. Through this kind of vision, which belongs properly to the mind, he was more truly a prophet than the king, who had seen in bodily form the sign that was done in bodily form, and who, when it was over, beheld its image in his spirit by thinking of it, yet could do nothing with his intellect except know that it was a sign and ask what it meant.

Peter, in a state where his mind was carried out of itself, saw a vessel tied by four cords let down from heaven, full of all sorts of animals, and he also heard a voice: "Kill and eat." When he had come back to his senses and was pondering the vision, the Spirit told him about the men Cornelius had sent, saying: "Look, men are seeking you. Get up, go down, and go with them, for I have sent them." When he came to Cornelius, he himself made known what he had understood from that vision, in which he had heard, "What God has cleansed, do not call common." He said: "And God has shown me that I should call no man common or unclean." So when he saw that dish, carried out of his bodily senses, he heard those words, "Kill and eat" and "What God has cleansed, do not call common," in the spirit. And when he had come back to his bodily senses, he beheld in that same spirit, by thinking of it, the very thing he had seen and heard and kept in his memory. None of these were bodily things; they were images of bodily things, both when they were first seen in that ecstasy and when they were afterward remembered and thought about. But when he was pondering and seeking to understand those signs, that was the activity of the mind making the attempt; yet success was lacking until the men who came from Cornelius were announced. Then, when this bodily vision was added, and the Holy Spirit spoke to him again in the spirit, "Go with them" (the same spirit in which he had shown him that sign and impressed those words on him), his mind, helped by God, understood what was meant by all those signs. When these and similar cases are carefully considered, it is clear enough that corporeal vision is referred to spiritual vision, and spiritual vision in turn to intellectual.

When we are awake, and our mind is not carried away from the bodily senses but is engaged in corporeal vision, we distinguish from that vision the spiritual vision by which we think of absent bodies through images. We may do this by recalling from memory things we know; or by forming, in some way, in the very thinking of the spirit, things that we do not know but which nonetheless exist; or by inventing, at will or by conjecture, things that exist nowhere at all. From all these we distinguish the bodily things that we see and to which our bodily senses are present, so clearly that we have no doubt that these are bodies and those are images of bodies. But sometimes, whether through too intense a concentration of thought, or through the force of some illness, as often happens to the delirious in a fever, or through the mingling of some other spirit, whether evil or good, images of bodily things are formed in the spirit just as if bodies were presented to the bodily senses themselves, while the attention also remains on the bodily senses. Then the images of bodies formed in the spirit are seen just as bodies themselves are seen through the body, so that a person present is seen with the eyes and at the same time another who is absent is seen in the spirit as if with the eyes. We have known people in this state, and they spoke both with those who were really there and with others who were not there, as if they were. When they come to themselves, some report what they saw and some cannot, just as some people forget their dreams and others remember them. But when the soul's attention is completely turned away and snatched from the bodily senses, then the term usually used is "ecstasy." Then whatever bodies are present are not seen at all, even with the eyes open, and no voices whatever are heard. The soul's whole gaze is either on images of bodies, through spiritual vision, or on incorporeal things not represented by any bodily image, through intellectual vision.

When spiritual vision, with the soul wholly carried away from the bodily senses, is held fast by images of bodily things, whether in sleep or in ecstasy, then if the things seen signify nothing, they are the soul's own imaginings. In the same way people who are awake and healthy, and not affected by any alienation of mind, turn over in their thoughts the images of many bodies that are not present to the bodily senses. The difference is that they distinguish those images from real bodies that are present, by a steady awareness. But if the things seen do signify something, whether they are shown to people asleep, or to people awake who see present bodies with their eyes and at the same time behold the images of absent ones in the spirit as if they were before their eyes, or in the state called ecstasy, when the soul is completely carried away from the bodily senses, it is a wonderful thing if this can happen through the mingling of another spirit, so that it shows what it knows by images of this kind to the one with whom it is mingled, whether that one understands them or they are disclosed so as to be understood by someone else. For if these things are shown, and they certainly cannot be shown by a body, what remains but that they are shown by some spirit?

Some, indeed, hold that the human soul has in itself a certain power of divination. But if so, why can it not always use it, since it always wants to? Is it because it is not always helped to be able to? Then when it is helped, can it be helped by nothing, or by a body? It remains, then, that it is helped by a spirit. Next, how is it helped? Does something happen in the body by which the soul's attention is, as it were, released and flashes out, so that it comes to a point where it sees in itself the meaningful likenesses that were already there but were not seen, just as we have many things in our memory that we do not always look at? Or are things produced there that were not there before? Or are they in some other spirit, into which the soul breaks out and emerges and sees them there? But if they were already in the soul as its own, so to speak, why does it not also understand them as a consequence? For sometimes, indeed most often, it does not understand them. Is it that just as its spirit was helped to see them in itself, so also the mind cannot understand what the spirit holds unless it is helped? Or perhaps it is not that bodily obstacles are removed or, as it were, loosened, so that the soul by its own impulse thrusts out toward what is to be seen, but that it is wholly taken up into these things, whether they are only to be beheld spiritually or also to be known intellectually? Or does it sometimes see these things in itself and sometimes through the mingling of another spirit? Whichever of these is the case, it must not be rashly asserted. This, however, should not be in doubt: bodily images beheld in the spirit are not always signs of other things, whether in those who are awake, or asleep, or sick. But it would be surprising if ecstasy could ever occur without those likenesses of bodily things signifying something.

It is certainly no wonder that even those who have a demon sometimes tell true things that are beyond the senses of those present. This surely happens through some hidden mingling of that same spirit, so that the spirit of the sufferer and of the tormentor are, as it were, one. But when a good spirit takes up or snatches the human spirit into these visions, there is no doubt at all that those images are signs of other things, and of things it is useful to know; for this is a gift of God. Discernment is indeed most difficult when the evil spirit acts in a seemingly calmer way and, having taken possession of the human spirit without any torment of the body, says what it can. Sometimes it even tells true things and foretells useful ones, transforming itself, as it is written, "into an angel of light," so that once it has been trusted in things that are plainly good, it may lead people astray into its own. I do not think it can be detected except by that gift of which the apostle speaks when discussing the various gifts of God: "to another, the discernment of spirits."

For it is no great thing to recognize it once it has arrived at, or led someone to, things contrary to good morals or the rule of faith; at that point many can detect it. But by that gift it is judged at once, at the very outset, when it still appears good to many, whether it is evil.

Nevertheless, both through corporeal vision and through the images of bodily things shown in the spirit, the good instruct and the evil deceive. But intellectual vision is not deceived. Either a person who thinks something other than what is does not understand, or, if he understands, what he understands is at once true. For what can the eyes do when they see a body that resembles another and cannot tell it from the other? Or what can the soul's attention do when a likeness of a body has been formed in the spirit that it cannot distinguish from a body? But the intellect is brought in, asking what these things signify or what useful thing they teach. Either it finds the answer and reaches its reward, or, not finding it, it holds itself in suspense, so as not to slip through some harmful rashness into deadly error.

A sober intellect, helped by God, judges which things, and how important, are such that thinking something other than what is in them does no harm to the soul. When the good think a man good though he is secretly evil, this is not to the peril of those who think so, but rather to his own ruin, provided there is no error about the realities themselves, that is, about the very good by which anyone becomes good. Or does it harm anyone at all that, while asleep, people take the likenesses they see in dreams to be real bodies? Or did it harm Peter at all that when he was freed from his chains and led out by an angel, by a sudden miracle, he thought he was seeing a vision? Or when in that ecstasy he answered, "By no means, Lord, for I have never eaten anything common or unclean," thinking that the things shown in the dish were real animals? When such things are found to be otherwise than they were thought to be when they were seen, we do not regret that they appeared to us that way, since this does not convict us of stubborn unbelief or of vain or sacrilegious opinion. So too when the devil deceives by bodily sights, it does no harm that the eyes are tricked, so long as there is no error in the truth of the faith and in soundness of understanding, which God teaches to those who submit to him. Or if he tricks the soul in spiritual vision with images of bodies, so that it thinks to be a body what is not one, does that harm the soul at all, if it does not consent to his deadly persuasion?

This is why a question sometimes arises about the consent of dreamers, when they seem to themselves to lie with someone, whether against their own resolve or even against lawful morals. This happens only when things that we think about even while awake, not with any approving consent but simply as we also speak of such things for some reason, are called up in sleep and represented so vividly that the flesh is naturally moved by them and emits through the genital passages what it naturally collects. In the same way I certainly could not say this very thing unless I were also thinking of it. Moreover, if the images of bodily things that I necessarily thought of in order to say these things were presented in sleep as vividly as bodies are presented to people who are awake, there would follow what could not happen to someone awake without sin. For who, when he is speaking and the needs of his discourse require him to say something about his own intercourse, could avoid thinking of what he says? And when the very image that forms in the thought of the speaker is represented so vividly in the vision of a dreamer that it cannot be distinguished from a real union of bodies, the flesh is at once moved, and what usually follows that motion follows. Yet this happens as much without sin as a waking person speaks without sin of something which he has undoubtedly had to think of in order to speak of it. Still, because of the good disposition of the soul, which, cleansed by a better desire, slays many desires that have nothing to do with the natural motion of the flesh (a motion which the chaste curb and restrain when awake but cannot when asleep, because they have no control over what vivid bodily image is brought before them, an image that cannot be distinguished from a body), because of that good disposition of the soul, then, some of its merits shine out even in sleep. For even while asleep Solomon preferred wisdom to all things and, disregarding everything else, asked the Lord for it; and, as Scripture testifies, this was pleasing in the sight of the Lord, and he did not put off a good reward for a good desire.

This being so, bodily sense pertains to bodily things that are seen. It is distributed through five channels, so to speak, of differing power. That which is subtlest in the body, and therefore closer to the soul than the rest, namely light, is first diffused on its own through the eyes and flashes out in the rays of the eyes to behold visible things. Then, by a kind of mixture, first with pure air, second with misty and cloudy air, third with a more corporeal moisture, and fourth with earthy density, it produces the five senses, together with the sense of the eyes itself, where it is supreme on its own, as I recall having discussed in the fourth book and again in the seventh. Now this heaven that is visible to the eyes, from which the luminaries and the stars shine, is certainly more excellent than all the bodily elements, just as the sense of sight excels in the body. But since every spirit is beyond doubt superior to every body, it follows that spiritual nature, even that in which images of bodily things are represented, is superior to this bodily heaven, not by its position in space but by the dignity of its nature.

Here something wonderful appears. Although spirit is prior to body, and the image of a body is posterior to the body, nevertheless, because what is later in time comes about in what is prior by nature, the image of a body in the spirit is superior to the body itself in its own substance. Nor indeed should we suppose that the body produces anything in the spirit, as though the spirit were subject to the body as its maker, in the role of material. For whoever makes something is in every way superior to the thing from which he makes it, and the body is in no way superior to the spirit; on the contrary, the spirit is plainly superior to the body. So although we first see some body that we had not seen before, and from then on its image begins to exist in our spirit, by which we remember it when it is absent, it is not the body that makes this image of it in the spirit but the spirit itself that makes it in itself, with a wonderful swiftness that is indescribably far removed from the slowness of the body. As soon as the body has been seen by the eyes, its image is formed in the spirit of the one seeing it without the interval of a single moment of time. Likewise with hearing: unless the spirit at once formed in itself an image of the sound perceived by the ears and retained it in memory, one would not know whether the second syllable was the second, since the first would certainly no longer exist, having struck the ear and passed away. And so all use of speech, all the sweetness of song, and finally every bodily movement in our actions would fall apart and perish and make no progress, if the spirit did not hold in memory the movements of the body already performed, so as to connect the following ones to them in acting; and it certainly holds them only as images that it has made in itself. Even the images of movements still to come go ahead of the completion of our actions. For what do we do through the body that the spirit has not first anticipated by thinking, first seeing in itself the likenesses of all visible works and in some way arranging them?

How these spiritual likenesses of bodily things in our mind become known even to unclean spirits, or what hindrance our soul suffers from this earthly body so that we cannot see them in one another's spirits, is difficult to discover and explain. Yet it has been established among us by the surest evidence that people's thoughts have been revealed by demons. If, however, the demons could perceive the inner beauty of the virtues in human beings, they would not tempt them; just as, had the devil been able to perceive that noble and wonderful patience in Job, he would surely not have chosen to be defeated by the man he tempted. As for their announcing things that have happened somewhere far away, which are confirmed as true some days later, that is not surprising. For they can do this not only through a keenness in perceiving even bodily things that is incomparably greater than ours, but also through the wonderful speed of their own bodies, which are far subtler.

We have also learned of a man suffering from an unclean spirit, who was staying at home, and who used to tell when a priest had set out to come to him from twelve miles away, and at every point of the journey where he was and how near he was coming, and when he was entering the estate, then the house, then the bedroom, until he stood before him. Although the sufferer did not see all this with his eyes, he could not have reported it so accurately unless he had seen it in some way. He had a fever and said these things as if in delirium. Perhaps he really was delirious, but because of these things he was thought to be suffering from a demon. He would take no food for nourishment from his own family, but only from that priest. He even resisted his family violently, as far as he was able; only when that priest came did he become calm. He was submissive to him alone and answered him submissively. Yet even for that priest the derangement of mind, or the demon, did not depart until he recovered from the fever, as delirious people usually recover, and he never suffered anything of the kind afterwards.

We also know beyond doubt of a delirious man who foretold the coming death of a certain woman, not in the manner of someone prophesying, but as though recalling something done and past. When she was mentioned in his presence, he said, "She is dead; I saw her carried out; they went past this way with her body," although she was alive and well. A few days later she suddenly died and was carried out along the very route he had foretold.

There was also a boy among us who, at the onset of puberty, suffered a very sharp pain in his genitals. The doctors were quite unable to determine what it was, except that the member itself was drawn inward and hidden, so that even when the foreskin, which hung down to an excessive length, was cut away, it could not be seen, and afterwards it was found only with difficulty. A sticky, acrid fluid oozed out and burned his testicles and groin. The sharp pain was not continuous, but when he suffered it he would wail loudly and toss his limbs about, while fully in his right mind, as usually happens in the torment of bodily pain. Then, in the midst of his cries, he would be carried away from all his senses and lie with his eyes open, seeing none of those standing around him and not moving at any pinch. After a while, as if waking up and no longer in pain, he would tell what he had seen. Then, after a few days, he would suffer the same thing again. In all or nearly all of his visions he said that he saw two persons, one older and the other a boy, by whom the things he reported having heard and seen were either told or shown to him.

One day he saw the joy of the faithful singing psalms in a wonderful light, and the various and most dreadful punishments of the wicked in darkness, with those two guiding him and showing him, and explaining what had earned the happiness of the one group and the misery of the other. He saw this on Easter Sunday, after he had felt no pain at all through the whole of Lent, though before that he had scarcely been spared for an interval of three days. At the very beginning of Lent he had seen them promising him that for forty days he would feel no pain. Afterwards they themselves gave him what amounted to medical advice: that the excessive length of his foreskin should be cut off; and when this was done he was free of pain for a long time. But when he again suffered pain in the same way and began to see similar things, he again received advice from them: that he should go into the sea up to his groin and come out after staying there for a while. They promised that from then on he would not suffer that violent pain, but only the discomfort of the sticky fluid; and that is how it turned out. Never afterwards did he suffer any such withdrawal of the mind from the senses, nor did he see anything of the kind, except when previously, in the midst of his pains and terrible cries, he would suddenly fall silent and be carried away. Later, however, when the doctors had treated and cured the rest of his condition, he did not persevere in his resolve to lead a holy life.

If anyone can track down the causes and workings of these visions and divinations and grasp them with certainty, I would rather listen to him than be expected to discuss them myself. Yet I will not conceal what I think, in such a way that the learned may not laugh at me as if I were asserting it, nor the unlearned accept it from me as if I were teaching it, but both may take me as one who discusses and inquires rather than one who knows. I compare all these visions to the visions of dreamers. For just as these are sometimes false and sometimes true, sometimes disturbed and sometimes calm, and the true ones are sometimes entirely like the future events or plainly stated, and sometimes foretold in obscure signs and, as it were, figurative expressions, so it is with all those others. But people love to marvel at what they have not experienced and to seek the causes of unusual things, while for the most part they do not care to know the everyday things of the same kind, which often have an even more hidden origin. With words, that is, the signs we use in speaking, when people hear an unusual word they first ask what it is, that is, what it means; and once they know that, they then ask why it is called so, although they are unconcernedly ignorant of why so many words that they use in ordinary speech are called as they are. In the same way, when something unusual happens in things, whether bodily or spiritual, they anxiously inquire into its causes and explanation and demand that teachers give it to them.

When someone asks me, for example, what catus means, and I answer "wise" or "sharp," and that does not satisfy him, but he goes on to ask why it is called catus, I usually ask in turn why acutus is called acutus. He was just as ignorant of that, of course, but because it was a familiar word, he was content not to know its origin; whereas when something new sounds in his ears, he thinks he knows too little about it if he knows only what it means, unless he also finds out why it is so called. So whoever asks me where visions resembling bodily things come from when they appear in ecstasy, which rarely happens to the soul, I in turn ask where they come from when they appear to sleepers, which the soul experiences every day, and which no one cares, or cares much, to inquire into. As if the nature of such visions were any less wonderful because it is an everyday matter, or deserved less attention because it is common to all! Or, if those who do not inquire into these are right, they would be more right not to be curious about the others either. For my part, I marvel far more, and am utterly astonished, at the speed and ease with which the soul fashions in itself images of the bodies it has seen through the eyes of the body, than at the visions of dreamers or even of those in ecstasy. Whatever the nature of these visions may be, it is beyond doubt not a body. Whoever is not satisfied to know this may ask others where they come from as well; I confess that I do not know.

This much, plainly, can be gathered from the evidence of examples. Pallor, flushing, trembling, or even illness in the body sometimes have their cause in the body and sometimes in the soul: in the body, when some humor spreads through it, or food, or something else is introduced into the body from outside; in the soul, when it is disturbed by fear, or confounded by shame, or is angry, or loves, or anything of that sort. And not without reason: if what animates and rules the body is moved more violently, it also agitates the body more violently. In the same way, when the soul itself turns to visions that are conveyed to it not through the senses of the body but through an incorporeal substance, and turns to them in such a way that it cannot tell whether they are bodies or likenesses of bodies, this sometimes comes about from the body and sometimes from the spirit. From the body, either through its natural cycle, as with the visions of dreamers, since sleep comes to a person from the body; or through some illness that disturbs the senses, as when the delirious see both bodies and visions resembling bodies, as if these too were present before their eyes; or when the senses are completely shut off, as often happens with people seriously ill, when some disease grows worse and, though their body is present, they are absent for a long time, and afterwards, when restored to those around them, they say that they have seen many things. From the spirit, on the other hand, when people whose bodies are entirely sound and whole are snatched away into a state of alienation, either in such a way that they see bodies through the bodily senses and at the same time in the spirit certain likenesses which they cannot distinguish from bodies, or in such a way that they are entirely turned away from the senses of the flesh and, perceiving nothing at all through them, dwell by that spiritual vision among likenesses of bodies. But when an evil spirit seizes people into these states, it makes them demoniacs, or possessed, or false prophets; when a good spirit does so, it makes them faithful people speaking mysteries, or, if understanding is added as well, true prophets, or else people who see and tell, for the time being, what must be shown through them.

But when the cause of seeing such visions lies in the body, it is not the body that produces them; for it does not have the power to form anything spiritual. Rather, when the passage of attention from the brain, by which the manner of perceiving is directed, has been put to sleep, or disturbed, or even blocked, the soul itself, which by its own motion cannot cease from this activity, because it is not allowed by the body, or not fully allowed, to perceive bodily things or to direct the force of its attention toward bodily things, produces likenesses of bodily things in the spirit or beholds them presented to it. If it produces them itself, they are only fantasies; if it beholds them presented to it, they are revelations. Thus when the eyes are sore or have lost their sight, visions of this kind do not occur, because the cause is not in the seat of the brain from which the attention of sensing is directed, although the body does present an obstacle to seeing bodily things. Indeed, the blind see more when asleep than when awake. For in sleepers the path of sensation in the brain, which leads attention to the eyes, is lulled to sleep, and so the attention itself, turned elsewhere, sees the visions of dreams as though bodily forms were present, so that the sleeper seems to himself to be awake and thinks he is looking not at likenesses of bodies but at bodies themselves. But when the blind are awake, the attention of seeing is led along those paths, and when it reaches the place of the eyes it does not go out but stays there, so that they feel that they are awake and are in darkness rather when awake, even by day, than when asleep, whether by day or by night. For many who are not blind also sleep with their eyes open, seeing nothing through them, yet not for that reason seeing nothing, since they see the visions of dreams with the spirit. But if they are awake with their eyes closed, they have available neither the visions of sleepers nor those of the waking. Still, it makes this much difference that the path of sensation reaches from the brain all the way to their eyes, neither lulled asleep, nor disturbed, nor blocked, and leads the soul's attention right up to the doors of the body, even though they are closed: images of bodies are indeed thought of, but they are in no way taken for the bodies that are perceived through the eyes.

So great is the difference made by where the impediment to perceiving bodily things occurs, when it occurs in the body. If it occurs only in the entrances and, as it were, the doors of the senses, as in the eyes, the ears, and the other senses of the body, only the perception of bodily things is impeded; the attention of the soul is not turned elsewhere in such a way that it takes images of bodies for bodies. But if the cause is within, in the brain, from which the paths for perceiving external things are directed, then the very channels of attention, on which the soul relies for looking at or perceiving external things, are put to sleep, or disturbed, or blocked. Since the soul does not lose this effort, it forms likenesses so vividly that, unable to distinguish images of bodily things from bodily things, it does not know whether it is among the former or the latter; and when it does know, it knows in a very different way from when likenesses of bodies are dwelt on or come to mind in thinking. This way can scarcely be grasped at all except by those who have experienced it. That is why, while asleep, I knew that I was seeing in dreams, and yet I did not distinguish the likenesses of bodily things that I was seeing from the bodily things themselves in the way we usually distinguish them when we think of them with our eyes closed or when we are in the dark. So great is the difference whether the attention of the mind is carried all the way to the senses, even though they are closed, or is turned elsewhere in the brain itself, from which it strains toward them, because some cause is present there. In the latter case, even though the soul sometimes knows that it is seeing not bodies but likenesses of bodies, or, being less instructed, thinks they are actual bodies yet feels that it sees them not with the body but with the spirit, it is nonetheless far removed from the condition in which it is present to its own body. This is how even the blind know that they are awake: they distinguish with sure awareness the likenesses of bodies that they think of from the bodies that they cannot see.

But when the body is sound and the senses are not lulled by sleep, and the soul is carried off by some hidden spiritual working into those visions that resemble bodily things, it does not follow, just because the manner is different, that the nature of what is seen is also different. For even among the causes that arise from the body there is certainly a difference, sometimes even an opposite one. The delirious, not by sleeping, have the paths of sensation in the head disturbed, so that they see the kinds of things dreamers see, whose attention, by sleeping, is turned away from the waking sense and turned toward seeing such things. So although the one happens without sleep and the other in sleep, what is seen is still of no other kind than of the nature of spirit, from which or in which the likenesses of bodies are made. Likewise, although the cause of the alienated attention is different when, in someone awake and sound of body, the soul is carried off by some hidden spiritual power so as to see in the spirit vivid likenesses of bodily things in place of bodies, the nature of what is seen is still the same. Nor can it be said that when the cause is in the body, the soul then turns over images of bodies on its own, without any foreknowledge of the future, as it usually does in thinking, but that when it is taken up into seeing them by the spirit, these things are shown to it by God. For Scripture plainly says, "I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh, and your young men shall see visions and your old men shall dream dreams," attributing both to divine working; and again, "An angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying, 'Do not be afraid to take Mary as your wife,'" and again, "Take the child and go into Egypt."

So I do not think that the human spirit is taken up by a good spirit to see these images unless they signify something. But when the cause that makes the human spirit intent on beholding them more vividly lies in the body, we should not believe that they always signify something; they do signify, however, when they are inspired by a spirit that reveals them, whether to someone asleep or to someone suffering something else in the body that has cut him off from the senses of the flesh. We also know that thoughts have been put into the minds of people who were awake, neither afflicted by any illness nor driven by frenzy, by some hidden prompting, so that in uttering them they prophesied. This has happened not only to people intent on something else, as the high priest Caiaphas prophesied although his intention included no wish to prophesy, but also to people who had undertaken to say something by way of divination.

Some young men, for instance, while travelling and staying at an inn, pretended for a joke to be astrologers so as to fool people, though they did not even know whether there were said to be twelve signs. When they saw that their host marvelled at what they said and declared it to be perfectly true, they grew bolder and went further. And he declared everything true and marvelled at it all. Finally he asked them about the safety of his son. He had long missed him while he was away, and because the son was unexpectedly late, he was anxious that something might have happened to him. They did not care what truth might come to light after they left, so long as they made the man happy for the moment. Since they were about to leave, they answered that his son was safe, was on his way, and would arrive that very day on which they were speaking. They had no fear that, once the whole day had passed, he would follow them the next day to accuse them of lying. In short, while they were already preparing to leave, suddenly, before they had gone, the son arrived.

Again, during a certain pagan festival, another man was dancing in front of a musician in a place where there were many idols. He was not seized by any spirit. He was playfully imitating those who are possessed, and the bystanders and spectators knew it. For it was the custom that, before the meal, once the sacrifices had been performed and the frenzied devotees had worked themselves up, any young men who wished to play in that manner after the meal were not prevented. So this man, in the middle of his dancing, had silence made for him. Joking, with a laughing crowd around him, he foretold that on the coming night a man would be killed by a lion in the nearby wood, and that at daybreak the crowd would flock to see the corpse and desert the place of the festival. And so it happened. Yet it had been perfectly clear to everyone present, from all his movements, that he had said this in play and in jest, with his mind in no way disturbed or deranged. And he himself marvelled at what happened all the more, since he knew better than anyone in what spirit and in what manner he had said it.

How do these visions come into the human spirit? Are they first formed there, or are they brought in already formed and seen through some kind of union? If the latter, then angels show human beings their own thoughts and the likenesses of bodily things which they form in advance in their own spirit through their knowledge of the future. In the same way they also see our thoughts, not with eyes, since they see not with a body but with the spirit. Yet there is this difference: they know our thoughts even against our will, whereas we cannot know theirs unless they are shown to us. For they have the power, I think, to hide their thoughts by spiritual means, just as we hide our bodies from other people's eyes by putting obstacles in the way. And what happens in our spirit, so that sometimes images that signify something are merely seen, but it is not known whether they signify anything; sometimes they are perceived to signify something, but what they signify is not known; and sometimes, as though by a fuller revelation, the human soul sees both the images themselves with the spirit and what they signify with the mind? All this is very difficult to know, and even if we did know it, it would be most laborious to discuss and explain.

But what I think it enough to suggest now is this: it is certain that there is in us a kind of spiritual nature in which likenesses of bodily things are formed. This happens when we touch some body with a bodily sense, and its likeness is at once formed in the spirit and stored in the memory; or when we think of absent bodies that we already know, so that a kind of spiritual sight is formed from things that were already in the spirit even before we thought of them; or when we look upon likenesses of bodies that we have not known but do not doubt exist, picturing them not as they really are but as they occur to us; or when we think, at will or by conjecture, of other things that either do not exist or are not known to exist; or when, from wherever it may be, without our doing it or willing it, various forms of bodily likenesses move about in our mind; or when, about to do something with the body, we arrange the very things that will be involved in that action and go over them all beforehand in thought; or when, already in the act itself, whether we are speaking or doing something, all our bodily movements are preceded inwardly in the spirit by their likenesses so that they can be carried out — for not even the shortest syllable would have sounded in its proper order unless it had been foreseen; or when sleepers see dreams that signify either nothing or something; or when, the inner pathways of sensation being disturbed by bodily illness, the spirit so mixes the images of bodies with real bodies that they can scarcely be told apart, or not at all, and either they signify something or they arise without any meaning; or when some disease or bodily pain grows severe and blocks within the paths by which the soul's attention used to go out and strive in order to perceive through the flesh, and the spirit is withdrawn more deeply than in sleep, and images of bodily things arise or are shown, either signifying something or appearing without any meaning; or when, with no bodily cause at all, but through some spirit taking hold of it and carrying it away, the soul is lifted up to see likenesses of bodies of this kind, mixing bodily sights with them, since it is also using the senses of the body at the same time; or when, through a spirit taking hold of it, the soul is so withdrawn and turned away from every bodily sense that it is wholly occupied with the likenesses of bodies alone in spiritual vision — and in that case I do not know whether anything that signifies nothing can be seen.

This spiritual nature, then, in which not bodies but the likenesses of bodies are expressed, has visions of a lower kind than that light of the mind and understanding by which these lower things are judged, and by which those things are seen that are neither bodies nor bear any forms resembling bodies: for example, the mind itself and every good disposition of the soul, to which are opposed its vices, which are rightly blamed and condemned in human beings. For in what other way is understanding itself seen except by understanding? So too love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, self-control, and the other things of this kind by which we draw near to God; and God himself, from whom are all things, through whom are all things, in whom are all things.

So although these visions all take place in the same soul — whether those perceived through the body, such as this bodily heaven and earth and whatever in them can be known, insofar as they can; or those seen by the spirit as likenesses of bodies, about which we have already said a great deal; or when things are understood by the mind which are neither bodies nor likenesses of bodies — they certainly have their own order, and one is more excellent than another. Spiritual vision is superior to bodily vision, and intellectual vision in turn is superior to spiritual vision. For bodily vision cannot exist without spiritual vision, since at the very moment a body is touched by a bodily sense, something of the same kind also arises in the soul — not the thing itself, but something like it. If this did not happen, there would not even be the sense by which things lying outside us are perceived. For it is not the body that perceives, but the soul through the body, which it uses as a kind of messenger in order to form within itself what is announced from outside. So bodily vision cannot take place unless spiritual vision also takes place at the same time; but the difference is not noticed until the sense has been withdrawn from the body, so that what was seen through the body is found in the spirit. Spiritual vision, on the other hand, can take place even without bodily vision, when likenesses of absent bodies appear in the spirit, and many are fashioned at will or are shown apart from our will. Again, spiritual vision needs intellectual vision in order to be judged, but intellectual vision does not need this lower spiritual vision. Accordingly, bodily vision is subject to spiritual vision, and both are subject to intellectual vision. So when we read, 'The spiritual person judges all things, but is himself judged by no one,' we must not take this according to the sense of 'spirit' in which it is distinguished from the mind, as in the saying, 'I will pray with the spirit, I will pray with the mind also,' but according to the sense in which it was said, 'Be renewed in the spirit of your mind.' For we have already shown above that in another sense the mind itself is also called spirit, and it is according to this that the spiritual person judges all things. For this reason I think it neither absurd nor inappropriate to hold that spiritual vision occupies a kind of middle position between intellectual and bodily vision. For I think it not unfitting to call 'middle' that which is not a body but is like a body, lying between that which truly is a body and that which is neither a body nor like a body.

The soul is deceived by the likenesses of things, not through any fault in them, but through a fault in its own judgment, when, falling short of understanding, it accepts things that are like others in place of the things they resemble.
