It is deceived in bodily vision, then, when it thinks that what happens in the bodily senses happens in the bodies themselves. Thus to people sailing, things on land that stand still seem to move; to those gazing at the sky, the stars, which move, seem to stand still; when the eyes' rays diverge, two images of a lamp appear; an oar looks broken in water; and there are many things of this sort. Or it is deceived when it thinks that something is what is similar in color, or similar in sound, smell, taste or touch. Hence a waxy medicine cooking in a pot is taken for vegetables; the noise of a passing cart is taken for thunder; if it is not examined by any other sense and is left to smell alone, citron is taken for the herb called balm; food flavored with some sweet juice is taken to be seasoned with honey; and an unfamiliar ring handled in the dark is taken to be gold, though it is bronze or silver. Or again it is deceived when, disturbed by sudden and unexpected bodily sights, the soul thinks it is seeing in a dream or is affected by some spiritual vision of that kind. For this reason, in all bodily sights the testimony of the other senses is called upon, and above all that of the mind and reason itself, so that whatever is true in this class of things may be found, so far as it can be found. In spiritual vision, that is, in the likenesses of bodies seen by the spirit, the soul is deceived when it supposes that what it sees in this way are bodies themselves, or when it thinks that what it has invented for itself by suspicion and false conjecture also exists in bodies that it has not seen but only guesses at. But in intellectual visions it is not deceived. For either it understands, and then what it understands is true; or, if it is not true, it does not understand. Hence it is one thing to err about what one sees, and another to err because one does not see.

Therefore, when the soul is carried away into those visions which are seen by the spirit and resemble bodily things, so that it is turned away from the bodily senses altogether, more than usually happens in sleep but less than in death, it is a matter of divine prompting and help that it should know that what it sees spiritually are not bodies but visions resembling bodies, just as some people know that they are seeing in a dream even before they wake up. And if future things are also seen there, so that the future events whose images are seen as present are fully known — whether because the person's own mind is helped by God, or because someone within the visions themselves explains what they signify, as was explained to John in the Apocalypse — then it is a great revelation, even if the one to whom these things are shown perhaps does not know whether he has left the body or is still in the body, but is seeing these things with his spirit withdrawn from the bodily senses. For someone carried away in this way can be unaware of this, if this too is not shown to him.

Furthermore, suppose that just as he was carried away from the bodily senses so as to be among these likenesses of bodies which are seen by the spirit, he is also carried away from these, so as to be lifted up into that region, as it were, of intellectual or intelligible things, where clear truth is seen without any likeness of a body and is not darkened by any clouds of false opinions. There the virtues of the soul are not toilsome and laborious. For there desire is not curbed by the work of temperance, nor adversities endured by the work of fortitude, nor wrongs punished by the work of justice, nor evils avoided by the work of prudence. There the one and entire virtue is to love what you see, and the highest happiness is to possess what you love. For there the blessed life is drunk at its source, from which something is sprinkled upon this human life, so that amid the temptations of this world we may live temperately, bravely, justly and prudently. It is indeed for the sake of attaining that place, where there will be untroubled rest and an ineffable vision of the truth, that we undertake the labor of restraining ourselves from pleasure, of bearing adversities, of helping the needy, and of resisting deceivers. There the glory of the Lord is seen, not through a signifying vision, whether bodily, as it was seen on Mount Sinai, or spiritual, as Isaiah saw it, or John in the Apocalypse, but in its true form and not in riddles, so far as the human mind can grasp it, according to the grace of God who takes it up, so that God may speak mouth to mouth with the one whom he has made worthy of such converse — not the mouth of the body but of the mind. This, I think, is how we should understand what is written about Moses.

For, as we read in Exodus, he had longed to see God — not, of course, as he had seen him on the mountain, nor as he saw him in the tabernacle, but in that substance by which he is God, without taking on any bodily creature to be presented to the senses of mortal flesh, nor through likenesses of bodies pictured in the spirit, but in his own form, so far as a rational and intellectual creature can grasp it when it is withdrawn from every bodily sense and from every signifying riddle of the spirit. For it is written: 'If, then, I have found favor in your sight, show me yourself; let me see you plainly'; and yet a little earlier we read: 'And the Lord spoke to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend.' So he perceived what he saw, and he longed for what he did not see. For a little later, when God had said to him, 'For you have found favor in my sight, and I know you above all,' he answered him, 'Show me your glory.' And then indeed he received from the Lord a figurative answer, which it would take too long to discuss now, when he said to him: 'You cannot see my face and live; for no one shall see my face and live.' Then he went on and said to him: 'See, there is a place beside me, and you shall stand upon the rock. As soon as my majesty passes by, I will put you in a cleft of the rock, and I will cover you with my hand until I pass by. Then I will take away my hand, and you shall see my back; but my face shall not appear to you.' Yet Scripture, in what follows, does not relate that this was also done bodily, and this shows clearly enough that it was spoken figuratively, signifying the Church. For she is the place beside the Lord, since the Church is his temple, and she is built upon the rock; and the other things said there fit the same interpretation. Nevertheless, if Moses had not been granted to see the glory of God that he longed and yearned for, God would not have said to Aaron and Miriam, his brother and sister, in the book of Numbers: 'Hear my words. If there is a prophet among you, I will make myself known to him in a vision and speak to him in a dream. Not so with my servant Moses, who is faithful in all my house. I will speak to him mouth to mouth, in clear form and not in riddles; and he saw the glory of the Lord.' Nor is this to be understood according to a bodily substance presented to the senses of the flesh; for certainly that was how he spoke to

Moses face to face, opposite one another, even at the time when Moses said to him, 'Show me yourself'; and that was how he was speaking even now to those whom he was rebuking and to whom he was preferring Moses' merit in this way: through a bodily creature presented to the senses of the flesh. In that other way, then, in the form by which he is God, he speaks far more secretly and more intimately, with an ineffable speech, where no one sees him while living this life, the mortal life lived in these bodily senses, unless a person in some way dies to this life — whether by leaving the body altogether, or by being so turned away and withdrawn from the senses of the flesh that, as the Apostle says, he rightly does not know whether he is in the body or out of the body, when he is carried away and lifted up into that vision.

Suppose, then, that the apostle called this third kind of vision "the third heaven": the kind that is higher not only than every bodily vision, by which bodies are perceived through the bodily senses, but also than all spiritual vision, by which likenesses of bodies are seen by the spirit and not by the mind. In that case, it is in this vision that the brightness of God is seen, and hearts are cleansed so that they may see it. Hence it was said: "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God." They will see him not through some sign shaped in bodily or spiritual form, as through a mirror in an enigma, but face to face, or "mouth to mouth," as was said of Moses. That is, they will see him by direct sight, by which God is seen as whatever he is, to whatever small degree the mind can grasp him. The mind is not what he is, but it can grasp him once it has been cleansed of every earthly stain, separated and snatched away from every body and every likeness of a body. We are pilgrims away from him, weighed down by a mortal and corruptible burden, as long as we walk by faith and not by sight, even when we live justly here. Why, then, should we not believe that God wished to show so great an apostle, the teacher of the Gentiles, when he was caught up to this most excellent vision, the life in which we are to live for ever after this life? And why should this not be called paradise, besides the paradise where Adam lived in the body among trees that were leafy and bore fruit? After all, the church too, which gathers us into the bosom of charity, has been called a paradise with fruit trees. But this was said figuratively, as if the paradise where Adam actually lived signified the church as a type of what was to come. Yet those who consider the matter more carefully may perhaps find that the bodily paradise, where Adam lived in the body, signified both this life of the saints which is now lived in the church and the life that will follow it for ever. In the same way Jerusalem, whose name means "vision of peace," is shown to be an earthly city, and yet it signifies Jerusalem our eternal mother in heaven. This heavenly Jerusalem is found either in those who have been saved in hope and, hoping for what they do not see, wait for it with patience, in whose sense "the children of the desolate woman are more than those of her who has a husband"; or in the holy angels themselves, to whom the manifold wisdom of God is made known through the church. With them, after this pilgrimage, we are to live without toil and without end.

But we might take the third heaven, to which the apostle was caught up, to mean that there is a fourth heaven too, and several more heavens above, with this third heaven below them. Some say there are seven heavens, some eight, others nine or even ten, and they maintain that within the one heaven called the firmament there are many heavens set in stages. On this basis they either argue or suppose that these heavens are bodily. It would take too long to discuss their reasoning or their opinion now. It is also possible that someone might claim, or even show if he can, that among spiritual or intellectual visions too there are many degrees, distinguished by a greater or lesser advance in the clarity of revelations. However that may be, and however anyone wishes to take it, one this way and another that way, I myself have so far been unable to know or to teach any kinds of things seen, or of visions, besides these three: by the body, by the spirit, and by the mind. But I confess that I do not know how many differences there are within each kind, or how great they are, so that in each kind one vision rises above another by degrees.

In the realm of bodily light there is the sky which we look up to above the earth, where the lights and stars shine, and these bodies are far better than earthly ones. In the same way, in that spiritual kind of vision, where likenesses of bodies are seen in a light that is incorporeal and its own, there are certain things that are excellent and rightly called divine. Angels show these things in wonderful ways. Do they make their own visions ours as well by some easy and very powerful joining or mingling? Or do they know some way of shaping our vision within our own spirit? This is hard to perceive and harder still to put into words. There are also other visions, ordinary and human, which either arise in many ways from our own spirit or are somehow suggested to the spirit by the body, depending on how we are affected in the flesh or in the mind. For people not only turn their cares over in their thoughts while awake, using likenesses of bodies, but often also dream when asleep of what they need. They carry on their business out of the mind's desire, and if they have gone to sleep hungry and thirsty, they greedily fall upon food and drink. I think all these, compared with those angelic showings, should be regarded in the same way as earthly things compared with heavenly ones in the realm of bodies.

So too, in the kind of things seen by the intellect, some are seen within the soul itself, such as the virtues, to which the vices are opposed. Some virtues will last, such as piety. Others are useful for this life and will not exist afterward, such as faith, by which we believe what we do not yet see; hope, by which we wait with patience for what is to come; and patience itself, by which we bear all adversity until we arrive where we wish to be. These and similar virtues are very necessary now for completing this pilgrimage, but they will not exist in the life they are needed to attain. Yet they too are seen by the intellect, since they are not bodies and have no forms resembling bodies. But the light by which the soul is enlightened is something else, the light that lets it see truly everything it understands, whether in itself or in that light. For that light is God himself, while the soul is a creature, though a rational and intellectual one made in his image. When it tries to gaze at that light it trembles in its weakness and lacks the strength. Yet from that light comes whatever it understands, as far as it is able. So when the soul is caught up there and, withdrawn from the senses of the flesh, is brought more clearly before that vision, not across distances in space but in a manner of its own, it sees even above itself the light by whose help it sees whatever it sees by understanding within itself as well.

Someone may ask whether the soul, when it leaves the body, is carried to some bodily places, or to incorporeal places resembling bodily ones, or to neither but to what is higher than both bodies and the likenesses of bodies. I would readily answer that it is either not carried to bodily places at all unless it has some body, or else is not carried to them in a spatial way. Whether it has some body when it leaves this body, let anyone who can show it do so; I do not think it has. But according to its merits it is carried to spiritual places. These may be places of punishment resembling bodily ones, such as have often been shown to people who were caught away from the senses of the body and lay like the dead and saw the punishments of the underworld. For they too bore within themselves a certain likeness of their own body, through which they could be carried to those places and experience such things by means of likenesses. I do not see why the soul should have a likeness of its own body when the body lies without sense, though not yet completely dead, and the soul sees such things as many have described after being restored to the living from that withdrawal, and yet not have it when it has left the body completely in actual death. So the soul is carried either to those places of punishment or to places likewise resembling bodily ones, but places of rest and joy rather than of punishment.

It cannot rightly be said that those punishments are false, or that that rest and gladness are false. Things are false only when, through an error of judgment, one thing is taken for another. Peter was certainly mistaken when he saw the sheet and thought that what was in it were bodies and not likenesses of bodies. But he was no less mistaken on another occasion, when he had been freed from his chains by the angel and was walking in the body, surrounded by bodily forms, yet thought he was seeing a vision. For the forms in the sheet were spiritual forms resembling bodily ones, and the bodily reality of his release from his chains resembled a spiritual one because of the miracle. In both cases the soul was mistaken only because it took one thing for the other. So the things by which souls stripped of their bodies are affected, whether for good or ill, are not bodily but resemble bodily things, since the souls themselves appear to themselves in the likeness of their bodies. Yet these things are real, and the gladness and the distress, made of spiritual substance, are real. Even in sleep it makes a great difference whether we are in happy or sad circumstances. Some people, set in the midst of things they had longed for, have been sorry to wake up; others, tormented and harassed by terrible fears and torments, have been afraid to fall asleep again once they woke, in case they were brought back into the same evils. And there is no doubt that what are called the infernal places are more vivid, and are therefore felt more intensely. For people who have been withdrawn from the senses of the body, less completely than if they had died outright but more fully than if they were asleep, have said that what they saw was more vivid than anything they could have told of their dreams. So the underworld is certainly real, but I think its substance is spiritual, not bodily.

We should not listen to those who claim that the underworld is worked out in this life and does not exist after death. Let them see how they interpret the inventions of the poets. We must not depart from the authority of the divine Scriptures, which alone are to be believed on this subject. Even so, we could show that the wise men among those people too had no doubt that the underworld is real and receives the souls of the dead after this life. But it is reasonable to ask why the underworld is said to be beneath the earth if it is not a bodily place, or why it is called the underworld, the lower world, if it is not beneath the earth. I dare to declare that the soul is not bodily, and I do not merely think so but plainly know it. Yet anyone who denies that it can have a likeness of a body and of all the bodily limbs can deny that it is the soul which in dreams sees itself walking or sitting, or carried here and there on foot or even in flight. That does not happen without some likeness of a body. So if the soul bears this likeness in the underworld too, a likeness not bodily but resembling a body, then it also seems to be in places that are not bodily but resemble bodily ones, whether in rest or in pain.

I confess, however, that I have not yet found the place where the souls of the just are at rest called the underworld. It is not without reason that people believe Christ's soul went as far as the places where sinners are tormented, to free from their torments those whom, by his justice hidden from us, he judged were to be freed. Scripture says: "whom God raised from the dead, having loosed the pains of the underworld, because he could not be held by them." I do not see how else this is to be understood, unless we take it that he loosed the pains of certain people in the underworld by the power by which he is Lord, to whom every knee bends, in heaven, on earth and under the earth. By that same power he could not be held by those pains which he loosed. Abraham, and the poor man in his bosom, that is, in the secret place of his rest, were not in pain; we read that a great chasm was fixed between their rest and those torments of the underworld. Nor were they said to be in the underworld. For Scripture says: "It came to pass that the poor man died and was carried by the angels into Abraham's bosom; and the rich man also died and was buried. And being in torments in the underworld," and so on. So we see that the underworld is mentioned not in connection with the poor man's rest but with the rich man's punishment.

Then there is what Jacob says to his sons: "You will bring down my old age with sorrow to the underworld." He seems rather to have feared that he would be so disturbed by excessive sorrow that he would go, not to the rest of the blessed, but to the underworld of sinners. Sorrow is no small evil for the soul: the apostle too was anxiously afraid that a certain man might be swallowed up by excessive sorrow. So, as I said, I have not yet found, and I am still looking, any place where Scripture, at least canonical Scripture, uses the word "underworld" in a good sense. But I do not know whether anyone could bear to hear that Abraham's bosom and the rest to which the angels carried the devout poor man are not to be taken in a good sense. And so I do not see how we can believe that this rest is in the underworld.

But while we are looking into this and either finding the answer or not, the length of this book presses us to bring it at last to a close. We began this discussion of paradise because the apostle says that he knows a man who was caught up to the third heaven, though he does not know whether in the body or out of the body, and that he was caught up into paradise and heard unspeakable words which it is not lawful for a man to utter. We do not rashly assert whether paradise is in the third heaven, or whether he was caught up to the third heaven and then caught up again from there into paradise. Strictly speaking, a paradise is a wooded place; but if the word is used figuratively, then any region, even a spiritual one, where the soul is at peace may rightly be called a paradise. Then not only the third heaven, whatever it is, which is certainly something great and sublimely glorious, but also a certain gladness of good conscience within a person is a paradise. Hence the church too is rightly called a paradise for the saints who live soberly, justly and devoutly, rich as it is in an abundance of graces and in chaste delights. For even in tribulations it glories, rejoicing greatly in patience itself, because according to the multitude of sorrows in its heart God's consolations gladden its soul. How much more, then, may Abraham's bosom after this life also be called a paradise, where there is no more temptation, where there is such rest after all the sorrows of this life? For there is light there too, a light proper to it and of its own kind, and certainly a great one. The rich man saw it from the torments and darkness of the underworld, from so far away and with a great chasm between, yet clearly enough to recognize there the poor man he had once despised.

If this is so, the underworld is said or believed to be beneath the earth because it is fittingly shown in the spirit through those likenesses of bodily things. Since the souls of the dead who deserve the underworld have sinned through love of the flesh, what usually happens to the dead flesh itself, namely burial beneath the earth, is presented to them through those likenesses of bodies. In Latin, after all, the underworld is called inferi because it lies below (infra). In bodies, if they keep the order of their weight, all the heavier things are lower; in the same way, in the spirit, all the sadder things are lower. Hence in the Greek language too, the word for the underworld is said to echo, in its origin, the fact that it has nothing sweet in it. Yet our Savior, who died for us, did not disdain to visit even this part of the world, in order to free from it those whom, according to divine and secret justice, he could not fail to know were to be freed. Therefore, to the soul of the thief to whom he said, "Today you will be with me in paradise," he did not give the underworld, where sinners are punished. He gave either the rest of Abraham's bosom, since there is nowhere Christ is not, for he is the wisdom of God reaching everywhere because of his purity, or else that paradise, whether in the third heaven or wherever else it is, to which the apostle was caught up after the third heaven, unless these are one and the same thing called by different names, where the souls of the blessed are.

Suppose, then, that we rightly understand the first heaven to be, in a general sense, this whole bodily realm, whatever lies above the waters and the earth. The second would be what is seen by the spirit in bodily likeness, like the heaven from which the sheet full of animals was let down to Peter in ecstasy. The third would be what is seen by the mind when it is so set apart, removed and wholly snatched away and cleansed from the senses of the flesh that it can, through the charity of the Holy Spirit, see and hear in an unspeakable way what is in that heaven, and the very substance of God, and God the Word, through whom all things were made. Then we think it not unfitting that the apostle was caught up there, and that perhaps paradise is there too, better than all others and, if one may say so, the paradise of paradises. For if a good soul takes gladness in the good things found in every creature, what gladness is more excellent than the gladness that is in the Word of God, through whom all things were made?

But someone may be troubled by the question why the spirits of the dead need to receive their bodies back at the resurrection, if that supreme happiness can be given them even without bodies. This question is too difficult to be fully settled in this discussion. Still, there should be no doubt that a person's mind, when caught up from the senses of the flesh, and after death when the flesh itself has been laid aside and even the likenesses of bodily things have been passed beyond, cannot see the unchangeable substance as the holy angels see it. This may be for some other, more hidden reason, or because the mind has a certain natural desire to govern a body. By this desire it is somehow held back from pressing on with its whole attention toward that highest heaven, as long as there is no body under it in whose governance that desire can be satisfied. Moreover, if the body is such that governing it is difficult and burdensome, like this flesh which is corruptible and weighs down the soul, springing as it does from the stock of the transgression, then the mind is turned away from that vision of the highest heaven much more. That is why it had to be snatched away from the senses of this flesh, so that the vision might be shown to it in the way it could grasp it. But when the soul, made equal to the angels, has received this body back, no longer as an animal body but, through the change to come, as a spiritual one, it will possess the full measure of its nature, obeying and commanding, given life and giving life, with such unspeakable ease that what was once its burden will be its glory.

These three kinds of vision will certainly exist then too, but no falsehood will lead anyone to take one thing for another, whether in bodily or in spiritual visions, and much less in intellectual ones. The soul will enjoy these so clearly present and so plainly seen that, by comparison, the bodily forms we now reach through the senses of the flesh are far less evident to us. Yet many people are so devoted to these forms that they think they alone exist, and believe that whatever is not of this sort does not exist at all. The wise, however, though they live among these bodily things they see, and though these seem more present to them, are nevertheless more certain of the things they somehow glimpse by understanding, apart from any bodily form or likeness of a body, even though they cannot see them with the mind as clearly as they see bodily things with the bodily senses. The holy angels, on the other hand, preside over these bodily things, judging and governing them, and yet are not drawn to them as though they were more present and familiar. They discern in the spirit the likenesses that signify these things, and somehow handle them with such power that they can even mingle them with human spirits by way of revelation. And they behold the unchangeable substance of the Creator in such a way that, in vision and in love, they set it above all things, judge all things according to it, are directed toward it so as to be moved by it, and from it direct whatever they do. Finally, although the apostle was caught away from the senses of the flesh into the third heaven and paradise, one thing at least was lacking to him for that full and perfect knowledge of things that the angels have: he did not know whether he was in the body or out of the body. This will certainly not be lacking when bodies have been received back at the resurrection of the dead, and this corruptible body puts on incorruption and this mortal body puts on immortality. For all things will be evident, without any falsehood and without any ignorance, each set in its proper order, bodily, spiritual and intellectual, in a nature made whole and in perfect happiness.

I know, indeed, that some of those who are praised for having expounded the holy Scriptures in the catholic faith before us have explained the apostle's words about the third heaven in another way. They wanted them to be understood here as the differences between the bodily, the animal and the spiritual man, and held that the apostle was caught up to contemplate with surpassing clarity that kind of incorporeal reality which spiritual people love above all else even in this life and long to enjoy. Why I have preferred to say "spiritual" and "intellectual" where they perhaps said "animal" and "spiritual," so that I would merely be giving other names to the same things, I have explained sufficiently in the first parts of this book. If we have discussed these matters properly, as far as our small ability allows, then either the spiritual reader will approve them, or else, with the help of the Holy Spirit, he will gain something from this reading toward becoming spiritual. But now at last we bring this whole work, contained in twelve books, to its end.
